docs.title: Probabilities, Evidence, and Execution
docs.text:
An original, practical textbook for readers who can write Python and know basic probability.

Prediction-market trading is not just classification with a dollar sign attached. The target is a contractual payout; information arrives at particular times; prices reflect incentives and market structure; an order may never fill; and cash can remain committed after an event becomes obvious. A model that predicts outcomes accurately can still lose money. A trader who makes money can still have a bad model and an unrepeatable result.

This book connects those distinctions rather than treating them as footnotes. It begins with what the contract promises, develops probability and data discipline, introduces machine learning only after baselines and evaluation, and then studies execution, evidence, portfolios, and paper operations. Its last five chapters offer practical workflows, not a promise to earn a dollar.

docs.title: How to read this book
docs.text:
Read Chapters 01-10 in order. They supply the definitions on which the rest depends. Chapters 11-16 develop modeling choices; their purpose is to help you choose the simplest defensible model, not to make every problem a neural-network problem. Chapters 17-24 ask whether forecasts can survive actual trading constraints. Chapter 25 proposes research directions with explicit falsification criteria. Chapters 26-30 turn the preceding ideas into reproducible exercises and a conditional manual decision checklist.

The reader-facing support files are notation, glossary, references, and exercise navigation. The companion README contains installation instructions. The research ledger explains what was inspected and which claims remain limited by their evidence.

docs.title: Book and companion working directories
docs.text:
This self-contained book directory is documentation and educational material within the trading-system repository. The repository README states the trading-system project's purpose; the book's paper-only operating boundary applies to its educational companion, not to every future system component at the Git root.

Run chapter examples, companion tests, the offline NOAA study, and optional public-snapshot commands from the companion project root. Starting at the trading repository root:

Set-Location book\companion

Create and use .venv in that directory as described in the companion setup. Relative paths such as examples\payoffs.py, experiments\noaa_study.py, and data\fixtures\recurring_events.csv in runnable chapter instructions are relative to book\companion. Change directory once, not before every subsequent example in the same shell.

Manuscript maintenance is separate and uses standard-library Python from the trading repository root, not from book\companion:

python book\scripts\assemble_claims.py --check
python book\scripts\manuscript_inventory.py
python -m unittest discover -s book\tests -q

docs.title: The book's evidence contract
docs.text:
Four kinds of statements appear in this book, and they do different jobs.

A derivation establishes what follows from specified assumptions. It can be completely correct while its assumptions are a poor description of a real market. A no-arbitrage result for compatible contracts does not establish compatibility for two headlines that happen to sound similar.

An empirical finding describes a particular population, sample, measurement procedure, and historical period. Its relevance to another venue must be argued, not presumed. Results about forecasting accuracy are not automatically results about executable profit.

A synthetic illustration deliberately invents data to isolate a mechanism. It can demonstrate accounting, a model failure, or a statistical trap. It cannot demonstrate that a real exchange offers an economic opportunity. The companion's default offline examples are labeled teaching fixtures for this reason.

A hypothesis is a question worth investigating. It earns its place through a plausible mechanism, a relationship to existing work, and a test that could reject it. It is not made true by a sophisticated architecture or a persuasive narrative.

Citation links identify the sources that support claims. They are not decoration or a guarantee that every assumption has been satisfied. The source ledger distinguishes publication status, access depth, and limitations. Official documentation describes a product at the time it was inspected, not a permanent contract with future API users.

docs.title: The practical boundary
docs.text:
The executable learning path is paper-only. No program in the book should submit a funded order, sign a wallet transaction, transfer collateral, or silently fall back to production trading. A paper result can be useful even when the final decision is to abstain.

The final chapter addresses readers who may independently consider a small manual live trade. They must be eligible, understand the exact rules, recheck current fees and execution conditions, and be able to afford the loss. The book supplies an analytical checklist, not personal financial or legal advice.

The phrase "first dollar" is a motivating goal, not a statistical guarantee. A strategy can have positive expected value and lose its next trade; a negative-value strategy can win. What matters is whether a predeclared process produces credible evidence under honest assumptions and remains within a risk budget.

docs.title: Why the order matters
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Contract and rules] --> B[Information available at decision]
    B --> C[Probability forecast]
    C --> D[Evaluation and uncertainty]
    D --> E[Executable costs and constraints]
    E --> F[Paper decisions and accounting]
    F --> G[Evidence review or abstention]

There is deliberately no automatic arrow from a favorable backtest to a live order. The missing arrow is a human decision under uncertainty, not a feature that the software forgot to implement.

docs.title: Editorial and implementation contract
docs.text: This file defines the shared conventions for this original book and its companion. It is contributor documentation, not a chapter in the reading sequence.

docs.title: Scope and voice
docs.text:
Write for a Python-capable reader who knows basic probability but not quantitative finance. Explain the economic or statistical question before introducing notation or an algorithm. Teach from first principles. The complete book targets 60,000-90,000 words; substantive chapters should generally contain 2,000-2,800 useful words rather than compressed outlines.

Do not consult, reproduce, paraphrase chapter-by-chapter, or reuse code from the linked Packt textbook. Use primary research and original worked examples. Do not imply that prediction markets themselves lack a long research history.

Each chapter needs a descriptive title, prerequisites, learning objectives, a motivating case, developed explanations, assumptions and failure modes, worked reasoning, a companion-example link where appropriate, exercises, and solution sketches. Put exercise solutions in the chapter for reliable local context; solutions.md will provide navigation rather than duplicate them.

Use ordinary, direct prose, not marketing copy. Label empirical evidence, mathematical derivations, synthetic illustrations, and hypotheses accurately. Never fabricate data, measured performance, a source, or a verification claim. A negative or inconclusive experiment is a legitimate result.

docs.title: Stable shared conventions
docs.text:
contents.json fixes chapter filenames, order, and companion script names. Do not change it from an author workstream. Use the notation in notation.md.

Illustrative contracts pay USD 1 per unit if YES and zero if NO, unless an example explicitly introduces a different payout. Actual venues may have different collateral or exceptional settlement; identify those separately.

Use a canonical accounting example across the book: buy 10 YES units at USD 0.40, with a hypothetical flat USD 0.01 fee per unit, and hold to binary settlement. Initial cost is USD 4.10, profit is USD 5.90 on YES or minus USD 4.10 on NO. At a model probability of 0.55, modeled expected net profit is USD 1.40. This is a cost illustration, not an actual venue fee or empirical edge. A sale at USD 0.46 with a further USD 0.01-per-unit exit fee produces USD 0.40 realized profit.

Report Brier score for a binary outcome as the mean of one squared YES-probability error per event, not twice that value. Use natural logarithms for log loss. State exact zero/one handling rather than silently clipping probabilities.

Keep event time, source publication time, local observation time, decision time, fill time, label availability time, and settlement time distinct. Use timezone-aware UTC timestamps. Repeated snapshots or contracts sharing a realized event are not independent labels. A time gap alone does not cure an event-group leak.

Use executable asks for buying and bids for selling; a midpoint is a forecasting benchmark, not a fill. Treat fees, collateral, depth, partial fills, latency, cancellation, adverse selection, and settlement consistently. Never infer resting-order fills from quote touches alone. Do not assume all complementary questions share the same resolution rules.

docs.title: Sources and claims
docs.text:
The shared book\research\sources.json (from the trading repository root) is a JSON array of source objects. Each object has id, title, authors (array), year, kind, status, url, doi (nullable), accessed, verification, supports (array), and limitations (array). Additional useful fields such as locator are permitted. Verification must honestly distinguish full-text inspection, abstract/metadata inspection, and official documentation.

From chapter files, use bibliography links such as [WZ2006](../references.md#wz2006) for source-backed statements. Bibliographic sections use ## WZ2006 so the lowercase key is a stable anchor. Never add a citation key that does not exist in the ledger without coordinating the addition.

Authors own their chapter files and one CSV fragment at book\research\claim-fragments\<group>.csv; do not edit the shared ledger, aggregate claim map, reference list, contents, notation, or another author's files. CSV columns are claim_id,chapter,claim,source_ids,locator,evidence_type,limitations. Separate multiple source keys with semicolons. Map material nontrivial sourced claims to a section/table/theorem/page when supported. A derived classroom identity does not need to masquerade as an empirical citation.

Primary research is not automatically true or transferable to prediction markets. Label stock-market microstructure results as analogies with assumptions. Working papers are not peer-reviewed journal articles. "Source exists" is not the same as "source supports this sentence." If only an abstract was inspected, keep the claim within that abstract or flag the full-text requirement.

docs.title: Runnable companion boundary
docs.text:
Examples import shared implementations from prediction_market_lab; avoid duplicating accounting or statistical helpers in chapter snippets. Their project root and virtual environment live in book\companion. Starting from the trading repository root, canonical commands use:

Set-Location book\companion
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe examples\payoffs.py

Follow the companion README for installation; create .venv and run package installation from book\companion, not the Git root. All default examples are offline, deterministic, labeled teaching demonstrations. Do not invent API methods, flags, filenames, result values, or measured accuracy. Read the completed example before documenting its actual output.

The educational companion has no funded-order submission, signing, deposit, or live-mode flag. Optional external acquisition is explicit and read-only. This boundary does not describe unrelated trading-system code at the repository root. The final live-trade chapter is a manual checklist, not an automation recipe.

Chapter authors may explain a future experiment, but must distinguish a proposed procedure from an implemented capability. A historical price series or synthetic book does not support a claim of historically executable profit.

docs.title: Review standard
docs.text:
Technical review covers calculations, claims, inference, data provenance, and executable behavior. A separate editor reads all 30 complete chapters in order, including transitions and supporting reference material. Reports must identify actual coverage, material findings, fixes, and limitations; no unsupported claim of academic peer review or certified profitability.

Use GitHub Markdown math ($...$ and $$...$$). Use URI separators in Markdown links and Windows backslashes in shell/file-access paths. Keep new source files ASCII unless a particular existing format requires otherwise.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
These definitions establish the book's usage. Venue-specific legal or API terminology can differ; the contract rules and relevant documentation govern actual behavior.

Abstention. Choosing not to issue a forecast or not to trade because the evidence, information, rules, or execution conditions fail a specified requirement. It is a valid output, not a software error to be disguised.

Adverse selection. The tendency for counterparties who trade against a quote to be better informed about value than the quote setter. A resting bid's chance of filling can increase precisely when the outcome has become less favorable to its buyer.

Ask. A price at which a specified quantity is offered for sale. Buying requires executable offers; a displayed best ask does not promise unlimited quantity or a fill after latency.

Available cash. Cash that is actually free to support another action after accounting for settled balances and reservations. It is not necessarily the same as account equity or the face value of collateral.

Backtest. An explicitly specified simulation using historical observations. Its usefulness depends on which information, order states, costs, and settlement facts could genuinely have been known and acted on at each point.

Bankroll. Capital assigned to a defined strategy or account, with its valuation convention stated. Total equity, available cash, outstanding reservations, and maximum affordable loss are different quantities; a sizing formula must specify which one its wealth variable represents.

Base rate. The prevalence of an outcome in a specified reference population. There is no meaningful base rate without a definition of that population and the information conditioning it.

Basis risk. Risk that an alleged hedge differs in its payoff from the position it is meant to offset. Two event contracts can differ through wording, observation times, resolution sources, cancellation policies, or collateral even if their short titles match.

Bid. A price at which a specified quantity is sought for purchase. An immediate liquidity-taking sale crosses executable bids; a resting maker ask can instead sell if a buyer later matches it.

Binary contract. A contract with two ordinary mutually exclusive outcomes. A simplified USD 1 YES contract pays one dollar on YES and zero on NO. Actual exceptional settlements must be handled according to the rules, not forced into this simplification.

Brier score. The mean squared difference between a probability forecast and a binary outcome. This book uses one YES-probability error per observation, rather than a two-class sum that would double the result.

Calibration. Agreement, in a specified population and conditioning scheme, between forecast probabilities and outcome frequencies. Finite-sample calibration estimates carry uncertainty. A constant base-rate forecast can be calibrated while providing little useful discrimination.

Capital lockup. The period in which funds are committed to a position or settlement process and cannot be deployed elsewhere. An annualized return calculated from an optimistic holding period can misrepresent this constraint.

Categorical event. An event with a specified set of outcomes. Sum-to-one relationships require the outcomes to be mutually exclusive and exhaustive under compatible rules; a user-interface grouping alone does not establish that property.

Collateral. Assets securing a position's obligations. Their availability, conversion, custody, and release rules affect practical value independently of the forecast about the event.

Confidence interval. An interval constructed by a procedure with a stated repeated-sampling coverage property under its assumptions. A computed interval is not automatically valid after strategy selection or repeated unadjusted inspection.

Credible interval. A posterior probability interval under a specified Bayesian model and prior. It quantifies uncertainty within that model; it does not immunize the decision against misspecification.

Decision cutoff. The latest information time admitted to a particular forecast or action. A point-in-time pipeline must enforce it for features, revised records, labels used in training, and ancillary information.

Dependence group. A set of observations that share relevant uncertainty, such as contracts resolving on the same event or snapshots of one market. Grouping decisions should match the estimand and dependence mechanism, not merely convenient database identifiers.

Depth. Quantities available at different order-book prices. A strategy's expected execution price depends on depth, order size, and how the book evolves before matching.

Discrimination. The ability of a forecasting system to distinguish cases with different outcome frequencies. Ranking performance and calibration answer different questions.

Drawdown. A decline from a prior peak in a specified wealth series. A paper equity curve marked at midpoints can understate the drawdown realizable by liquidating through available bids.

Edge. A positive expected advantage relative to a specified feasible action and its costs, under an explicitly stated probability model. Calling an estimate an edge requires evidence beyond a favorable difference between two numbers.

Effective sample size. A summary of how much information a dependent sample contains relative to a reference independent sample. It is model- and estimand-dependent, not automatically the number of rows or trades.

Embargo. A withheld region around evaluation boundaries intended to reduce certain forms of temporal contamination. It does not by itself prevent shared-event or unavailable-label leakage.

Event family. A documented group of related events, often a recurring question template or shared underlying process. It may be useful for pooling or dependency handling, but should not be treated as an arbitrary label that guarantees independence across families.

Executable price. A price at which the chosen quantity and side could actually transact under the specified order policy. Last trades, midpoints, and a retrospective candle low are not interchangeable executable prices.

Expected value. A probability-weighted average of possible payoffs or net outcomes. In a model-driven trade it is conditional on estimated probabilities and execution assumptions; it is not a promise about the next outcome.

Fill. An actual or explicitly simulated match of an order quantity against a counterparty. A paper simulator must state what evidence or invented process produces its fills.

Fill-conditioned forecast. A forecast about the outcome conditional on the order actually filling and on the information associated with that event. It can differ materially from a forecast made when the quote was posted.

Forecast horizon. The interval between a specified forecast time and a specified outcome-related time. An event's occurrence, its public confirmation, and final settlement can have different horizons.

Hypothesis. A proposed relationship or mechanism that has not been established by the evidence at hand. A useful research hypothesis includes a plausible alternative explanation and a procedure that could show it fails.

Information set. The observations admitted to a probability assessment or decision. Stating an information set is central to interpreting whether a claimed improvement is new information or a restatement of what the market already knows.

Inventory. Positions owned or owed by a trader. Inventory risk depends on event dependence and contractual payoffs, not simply on the count of tickets in an account.

Kelly criterion. A framework for maximizing expected log wealth under specified opportunities and probabilities. Its recommended exposure is sensitive to estimation error, dependence, feasible positions, and whether its repeated-decision assumptions describe the situation.

Label availability. The time at which an outcome label could legitimately enter training. A historical database containing the final outcome does not make that label available to a model trained before resolution.

Leakage. Use of information in model design, fitting, evaluation, or simulated decisions that would not legitimately have been available for the stated exercise. It includes shared outcomes, revised data, tuning on the test period, and future-trained text models.

Limit order. An instruction to trade subject to a specified limit price and other conditions. It controls acceptable price, not whether a fill will occur.

Liquidity. The practical ability to transact a size within acceptable price and time constraints. It is not synonymous with historical trading volume or the presence of a displayed quote.

LMSR. Logarithmic market scoring rule, a particular automated market-maker construction. Its cost function and bounded-loss properties rely on its defined mechanism; they are not universal attributes of order-book venues.

Log loss. A proper scoring loss based on the negative logarithm of the probability assigned to the realized outcome. This book uses natural logs. Assigning zero probability to an outcome that occurs incurs infinite loss.

Market maker. A participant or mechanism providing trading opportunities to others. A human or algorithm posting limit orders can lose to informed flow, inventory changes, fees, and operational failures even when it earns a quoted spread.

Mark-to-market. Valuing an open position using a specified current reference price. The mark must be distinguished from cash and from what a particular position could actually be sold for.

Multiple testing. Evaluating several hypotheses or strategy variants in a way that increases the chance of selecting an impressive result by luck. The relevant search includes informal feature, period, threshold, and reporting choices, not just a final model list.

No-arbitrage constraint. A relationship required to exclude a specified riskless payoff opportunity under explicit trading, settlement, and financing assumptions. An observed apparent violation is only a candidate until those assumptions are checked.

Order-book replay. A simulation driven by recorded order-book information. Its fidelity is limited by the observed message types, timestamps, missing states, participant identifiers, and effects of the simulated orders themselves.

Paper trading. Applying a decision process to simulated balances and fills rather than funded orders. It is useful for learning and operational rehearsal, but cannot reproduce all effects of actual participation.

Point-in-time data. Data representing what could have been known at a specified historical cutoff. Retrieval time, publication time, revisions, and label availability all matter.

Proper scoring rule. A scoring system for which reporting one's probability distribution optimizes expected score under stated conditions. Strict propriety makes that optimum unique. This is a statement about the scoring objective, not a claim about trading profits.

Queue priority. The ordering rules used to determine which resting orders execute. Without adequate queue information, a simulator must not assume its own order always stood at the front.

Realized profit. Net profit recognized through a specified completed sale or settlement, after relevant costs. In the companion it is explicitly simulated unless the context says otherwise.

Reference class. The set of cases used to estimate or interpret an outcome frequency. Changing it after seeing results can be a form of strategy selection.

Resolution. The process that determines the contractual outcome or payout. It may include proposals, disputes, official sources, clarifications, and exceptional states, depending on the product.

Selection bias. Distortion caused by how observations, markets, time periods, or reported results were chosen. A dataset of conveniently resolved markets can exclude important unresolved or disputed cases.

Settlement. The process by which contractual obligations are discharged and collateral or payouts become available. A market can be economically decided before settlement is complete.

Sharpness. Concentration of predictive distributions. Sharpness is useful in conjunction with calibration; confident wrong forecasts are not improved forecasts.

Slippage. The difference between a stated execution reference and the eventual fill price under a defined convention. Do not count the bid/ask spread twice by subtracting it again after using executable prices.

Survivorship bias. Analysis based only on entities or records that remain observable under a selection mechanism. Markets disappearing from a live endpoint may require an historical endpoint rather than an inference that they never existed.

Synthetic fixture. Intentionally generated data used to illustrate a mechanism or exercise code. It must be labeled, reproducible, and kept distinct from evidence of historical performance.

Untouched evaluation. Data withheld from all decisions that define a reported model or strategy until a predeclared final assessment. Repeatedly inspecting it and adjusting the process destroys the intended separation.

Vintage. A version of a data release as it existed at a particular publication time. Using a latest revised series in place of the contemporary vintage can introduce information unavailable to historical decision-makers.

Walk-forward evaluation. A sequence of model-fitting and evaluation steps ordered through time, with explicit information cutoffs. It does not automatically solve dependence, tuning, or repeated-testing problems.

docs.title: Notation and accounting conventions
docs.text:
The same symbol should mean the same thing across a forecast, a simulation, and a trade log. This registry is part of the book's contract with the reader.

Symbol Meaning \(E\) An explicitly defined event, with its contractual resolution rules. \(Y\) A binary contractual outcome, zero or one. It is not necessarily identical to an informal description of the real-world event. \(R\) Actual terminal payout per unit, in the specified collateral currency. In the ordinary USD 1 binary example, \(R=Y\); exceptional settlement can differ. \(p\) A conditional probability under a stated model or information set; not an observable oracle for the true event chance. \(\hat p\) An estimated forecast of the contractual YES probability. \(p_L\) A deliberately conservative probability bound or scenario, with its inference method stated. It is not automatically a valid confidence bound. \(a\), \(b\) Executable ask and bid per unit, respectively, for a particular outcome and size. \(m\) A specified market forecasting benchmark, often the midpoint when fresh and meaningful. It is not an executable price. \(Q\) Number of contract units. Classroom examples use whole units unless otherwise stated; venues can impose different quantity grids. \(f\) Hypothetical per-unit transaction cost in the simplest classroom calculations. Real fee functions can depend on price, size, side, time, and rounding. \(F(Q,a)\) An explicitly specified total fee function for an order or fill. \(\Pi\) Net profit or loss, with currency, time horizon, and realized/unrealized status stated. \(W\) Bankroll or equity, with a clear distinction between available cash and collateral reserved for positions or orders. \(x\) Feature vector known by the relevant decision cutoff. \(t\) A timestamp or time index whose meaning is explicitly specified. \(n\) Number of evaluation observations; report the number of independent or dependence-grouped events separately. \(\lambda\) A regularization or penalty parameter, defined locally. \(\beta\) Statistical-model coefficients. \(B\) LMSR liquidity parameter, to avoid confusing it with the executable bid \(b\). \(\phi\) Fraction of bankroll spent on a position in Chapter 22; distinct from per-unit fee \(f\). \(\kappa\) Fraction of the full log-growth-optimal spend used in a fractional-Kelly illustration.

Modeling chapters explicitly introduce additional local symbols. In LMSR, \(q_i\) counts cumulative shares sold, not probabilities; \(\pi_i\) denotes its marginal price. Superscripted neural-network \(b^{(1)}_j\) denotes a bias, not a quoted bid. Chapter 23's bandit \(b(a\mid s)\) is a behavior-policy probability and its local \(R\) is net reward, not this registry's terminal payout. Keep these qualified local uses distinct from unqualified trading symbols.

A convex average of valid probabilities remains a valid probability, but need not preserve calibration. Under Brier or log loss on the same cases, convexity bounds the blend's loss by the weighted average component loss; it does not guarantee beating the best component.

docs.title: A common worked example
docs.text:
Buy 10 YES units at USD 0.40 with an illustrative flat fee of USD 0.01 per unit. These are invented teaching costs, not a Kalshi or Polymarket fee schedule.

\[ \text{initial cost}=10(0.40+0.01)=4.10. \]

Under ordinary binary settlement, the terminal payout is USD 10 if YES and USD 0 if NO. Net profit is therefore USD 5.90 or minus USD 4.10. There is no exit fee in this hold-to-settlement example unless a separately stated rule introduces one.

If the model assigns \(\hat p=0.55\), its modeled expected net profit is

\[ \mathbb{E}_{\hat p}[\Pi]=10(0.55-0.40-0.01)=1.40. \]

The subscript matters: this is an expectation under a forecast that might be wrong, not evidence that the trader possesses an edge. It says nothing about the next realized outcome by itself.

If instead all units can actually be sold at a bid of USD 0.46 with an additional USD 0.01-per-unit exit fee, realized round-trip profit is

\[ 10(0.46-0.40-0.01-0.01)=0.40. \]

Do not count the spread a second time after already using the ask to buy and bid to sell. Slippage is an additional difference between a specified reference executable quote and the realized price, not an invitation to subtract the same cost twice.

docs.title: Forecast scores
docs.text:
For one YES forecast per binary evaluation observation, the Brier score is

\[ \operatorname{BS}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\hat p_i-y_i)^2. \]

Some multiclass conventions sum both YES and NO errors and give twice this value. This book uses the single-YES convention. Log loss uses natural logarithms:

\[ \operatorname{LL}=-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[y_i\log\hat p_i+(1-y_i)\log(1-\hat p_i)\right]. \]

A probability of zero on an outcome that occurs incurs infinite loss. Numerical stabilization, when used in fitting, must be disclosed rather than retrospectively altering an evaluated forecast. A perfectly confident correct forecast contributes zero, using the limiting convention for the otherwise undefined zero-times-log-zero expression.

An average over observations is not automatically an average over independent events. Specify whether scoring is per event, horizon, contract, or timestamp and why the weighting answers the research question.

docs.title: Time and availability
docs.text:
Use timezone-aware UTC. Keep at least these concepts distinct: event time, source publication time, local observation time, decision time, fill time, outcome-label availability time, and final settlement time. Historical revisions must not be treated as information available before their publication.

A forecast model fitted at a past cutoff may use only labels available at that cutoff. A chronological split of rows can still leak a shared outcome across training and evaluation. Event grouping and time order are joint constraints, not alternatives.

docs.title: Costs, currencies, and statistical language
docs.text:
Price and payout units must match. A token redeemable for a collateral asset is not a promise that the collateral has no custody, conversion, or exchange-rate risk. Clearly identify any USD, stablecoin, token, or other collateral example.

"Expected profit" means a model-conditional expectation. "Realized profit" requires an actual or explicitly simulated fill and recognized payout or sale. "Marked profit" depends on a disclosed valuation convention. "Statistically supported edge" requires a specified estimand, data, dependence model, uncertainty procedure, and protection against selection; it is not established by an attractive point estimate.

For a trade that can be lost in full, affordable loss is a prerequisite, not a mathematical guarantee of safety. No universal confidence level, sample count, Kelly fraction, or paper-trading duration removes model risk.

docs.title: References and evidence boundaries
docs.text:
This bibliography supports Machine Learning for Prediction Markets: Probabilities, Evidence, and Execution. Citation headings are stable link targets. All access dates are 2026-09-10. Years for mutable official documents identify the inspected edition, not an asserted original publication date.

Inspection is not uniform. Each entry says whether an abstract, relevant full-text section, official page, or only bibliographic metadata was inspected. Publisher-deposited Crossref records verify bibliographic identity but are not a reading of the paper. A metadata-only entry is a qualified further-reading pointer, not sole evidence for a detailed claim. The machine-readable source ledger and initial claim map retain these boundaries.

No paper here, by itself, establishes prediction-market profitability. Forecasting, mathematical mechanism design, simulation, and historically executable trading are different evidence categories.

docs.title: WZ2006
docs.text:
Justin Wolfers and Eric Zitzewitz. Interpreting Prediction Market Prices as Probabilities. NBER Working Paper 12200, 2006. DOI: 10.3386/w12200. NBER record.

Use: The inspected NBER abstract describes sufficient conditions relating market prices to average beliefs, and useful but sometimes biased approximations beyond those conditions. Risk preferences and belief distributions matter. Boundary: This working-paper version is not a peer-reviewed journal article; average belief is not an oracle for event probability. Full text was not inspected.

docs.title: MANSKI2004
docs.text:
Charles F. Manski. Interpreting the Predictions of Prediction Markets. NBER Working Paper 10359, 2004. DOI: 10.3386/w10359. NBER record.

Use: The inspected abstract presents partial identification of beliefs under heterogeneous beliefs, risk neutrality, and price taking. Boundary: It does not say all prediction-market prices are useless. Cite this working paper as this version, not with an unverified later journal DOI.

docs.title: WZ2004
docs.text:
Justin Wolfers and Eric Zitzewitz. Prediction Markets. Journal of Economic Perspectives 18(2), 107-126, 2004. DOI: 10.1257/0895330041371321. AEA publisher page.

Use: The inspected publisher abstract synthesizes empirical forecasting comparisons and information-aggregation mechanisms. It also distinguishes conditional-market information from causal interpretation. Boundary: Selected historical comparisons are not a universal contemporary benchmark or a trader's net return.

docs.title: BERG2008
docs.text:
Joyce E. Berg, Forrest D. Nelson, and Thomas A. Rietz. Prediction market accuracy in the long run. International Journal of Forecasting 24(2), 2008. DOI: 10.1016/j.ijforecast.2008.03.007. Iowa Electronic Markets institutional page.

Use: The inspected institutional abstract reports comparisons with 964 national polls across five U.S. presidential elections, 1988-2004; contemporaneous IEM vote-share forecasts were closer to the eventual two-major-party vote split in 74% of those comparisons. Boundary: Five elections are not 964 independent outcomes. This is vote-share accuracy, not necessarily winner-probability calibration or executable profit. Metadata discrepancy: The IEM page gives pages 283-298; publisher-deposited DOI metadata gives 285-300. The direct publisher text was inaccessible, so the discrepancy remains disclosed.

docs.title: HANSON2007
docs.text:
Robin Hanson. Logarithmic Market Scoring Rules for Modular Combinatorial Information Aggregation. The Journal of Prediction Markets 1(1), 3-15, 2007. DOI: 10.5750/jpm.v1i1.417. Publisher record.

Use: The inspected publisher abstract explains market scoring rules and special probability-preservation properties of their logarithmic versions. Boundary: The full theorem/cost-function derivation was not audited; independently derived classroom LMSR examples are not live-exchange descriptions. The publisher's issue and citation metadata say 2007 despite later web-deposit metadata. Its indexed title contains a spacing typo, normalized here.

docs.title: GNEITING2007
docs.text:
Tilmann Gneiting and Adrian E. Raftery. Strictly Proper Scoring Rules, Prediction, and Estimation. Journal of the American Statistical Association 102(477), 359-378, 2007. DOI and primary publisher locator: 10.1198/016214506000001437.

Use: The author-hosted article was inspected at the abstract, Section 1, Section 2.1 definitions, Section 2.3, and Sections 3.1-3.2 (pp. 359-360 and 362-364). These sections define proper and strictly proper scores, present the categorical representation and quadratic/logarithmic examples, and require score comparisons on the same forecast cases. Boundary: The article uses higher-is-better rewards; this book uses losses. Its categorical squared-error sum gives twice the single-YES binary loss after reversing sign. Infinite log loss is possible. Strict propriety is an expectation-level incentive property, not guaranteed finite-sample calibration or profit; outcome-dependent normalized skill scores need not retain propriety. Not all article proofs or case studies were inspected.

docs.title: BRIER1950
docs.text:
Glenn W. Brier. Verification of Forecasts Expressed in Terms of Probability. Monthly Weather Review 78(1), 1-3, 1950. DOI and publisher locator: 10.1175/1520-0493(1950)078<0001:VOFEIT>2.0.CO;2.

Use: Historical probability-verification reading. Verification boundary: The original remains metadata-only after AMS abstract/PDF requests returned 403 and the legacy NOAA archive hostname failed to resolve. Do not claim original-text inspection or an exact original normalization. The independently inspected GNEITING2007 Section 3.1, Example 1, now supplies substantive support for the categorical Brier score; the book explicitly reduces this to one squared YES-probability error per binary event.

docs.title: MURPHY1973
docs.text:
Allan H. Murphy. A New Vector Partition of the Probability Score. Journal of Applied Meteorology 12(4), 595-600, 1973. DOI and publisher locator: 10.1175/1520-0450(1973)012<0595:ANVPOT>2.0.CO;2.

Use: Reading pointer for score decomposition. Verification boundary: Publisher-deposited metadata only; follow-up AMS abstract and public PDF endpoints remained inaccessible. A population decomposition, an exact finite-table identity, and an arbitrary binned estimate must not be conflated. Keep detailed Murphy attribution qualified until the original is inspected; independently derived classroom identities should be labeled as such.

docs.title: GUO2017
docs.text:
Chuan Guo, Geoff Pleiss, Yu Sun, and Kilian Q. Weinberger. On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks. ICML 2017, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 70, 1321-1330. Primary proceedings.

Use: The inspected proceedings abstract reports miscalibration in studied modern neural classifiers and effective temperature scaling on most examined datasets. Boundary: These image/document experiments do not ensure calibration on small, shifting event-market samples. The paper is peer-reviewed conference research, not a venue performance study.

docs.title: NICULESCU2005
docs.text:
Alexandru Niculescu-Mizil and Rich Caruana. Predicting good probabilities with supervised learning. ICML 2005, 625-632. DOI and publisher locator: 10.1145/1102351.1102430.

Use: The Cornell author manuscript was inspected at PDF pp. 1-3 and 8: abstract, calibration methods, dataset/qualitative setup, Figure 8 discussion and conclusions. It explains why calibration should use data independent of base-model fitting, contrasts sigmoid and isotonic maps, and reports both benefits and harms depending on model and sample size. Boundary: The eight binary-classification datasets use random samples, not event-grouped chronological validation. Calibration data are reused for model selection in the paper, with a distinct final test set; this is not permission to tune on the final evaluation set. The 2005 neural-network results and GUO2017's modern architectures are not contradictory universal laws.

docs.title: KULL2017
docs.text:
Meelis Kull, Telmo Silva Filho, and Peter Flach. Beta calibration: a well-founded and easily implemented improvement on logistic calibration for binary classifiers. AISTATS 2017, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 54, 623-631. Primary proceedings.

Use: The inspected abstract discusses isotonic overfitting in small samples and circumstances in which logistic calibration can make probabilities worse; it proposes beta calibration. Boundary: Its classifier-specific comparisons do not establish a universally best calibration method.

docs.title: FRIEDMAN2010
docs.text:
Jerome H. Friedman, Trevor Hastie, and Rob Tibshirani. Regularization Paths for Generalized Linear Models via Coordinate Descent. Journal of Statistical Software 33(1), 1-22, 2010. DOI: 10.18637/jss.v033.i01. Publisher page.

Use: The inspected publisher abstract covers coordinate-descent paths for linear, logistic, and multinomial models with lasso, ridge, and elastic-net penalties, including sparse features. Boundary: Efficient fitting does not settle penalty selection, calibration, causal interpretation, or market usefulness.

docs.title: TIBSHIRANI1996
docs.text:
Robert Tibshirani. Regression Shrinkage and Selection Via the Lasso. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B 58(1), 267-288, 1996. DOI and publisher locator: 10.1111/j.2517-6161.1996.tb02080.x.

Use: The inspected publisher-deposited abstract describes constraining the sum of absolute coefficients in least squares and obtaining exact zero coefficients. Boundary: This is not evidence that selected predictors are causal or stable. Direct full text was not inspected; generalized-model computation is separately covered by FRIEDMAN2010.

docs.title: GELMAN2008
docs.text:
Andrew Gelman, Aleks Jakulin, Maria Grazia Pittau, and Yu-Sung Su. A weakly informative default prior distribution for logistic and other regression models. The Annals of Applied Statistics 2(4), 2008. DOI: 10.1214/08-AOAS191. Author-deposited manuscript.

Use: The inspected author abstract proposes weakly informative Student-t priors with explicit predictor scaling and discusses complete separation. Boundary: A proposed default is not a universally optimal prior. The journal year is 2008; 2009 is the repository-deposit year. Full text was not audited.

docs.title: BREIMAN2001
docs.text:
Leo Breiman. Random Forests. Machine Learning 45(1), 5-32, 2001. DOI: 10.1023/A:1010933404324. Breiman/Cutler explanatory website.

Use: Relevant author-site text explains bootstrap tree samples, randomized feature subsets at splits, and aggregation of tree votes. Boundary: Journal identity was checked against publisher-deposited metadata, but journal proofs were not inspected. Votes are not automatically calibrated probabilities, and out-of-bag machinery does not automatically respect time or event grouping.

docs.title: FRIEDMAN2001
docs.text:
Jerome H. Friedman. Greedy function approximation: A gradient boosting machine. The Annals of Statistics 29(5), 2001. DOI and publisher locator: 10.1214/aos/1013203451.

Use: A reading pointer for gradient boosting. Verification boundary: The original remains metadata-only: follow-up Project Euclid requests failed, the historical Stanford hostname did not resolve, and the current author manuscript endpoint had an expired TLS certificate. Certificate validation was not disabled. The metadata does not certify a particular pseudocode implementation, convergence claim, or event-market result. CHEN2016 and FRIEDMAN2010 remain separately inspected related sources, not substitutes falsely labeled as this article.

docs.title: CHEN2016
docs.text:
Tianqi Chen and Carlos Guestrin. XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System. KDD 2016. DOI: 10.1145/2939672.2939785. Author manuscript.

Use: The inspected abstract describes sparse-data processing, weighted quantile sketches, and systems techniques for scalable boosting. Boundary: Its benchmark scalability does not prove forecasting skill in small event samples. This citation does not imply that the companion reimplements XGBoost or requires its package.

docs.title: COX1972
docs.text:
D. R. Cox. Regression Models and Life-Tables. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B 34(2), 187-202, 1972. DOI: 10.1111/j.2517-6161.1972.tb00899.x. Publisher locator.

Use: The inspected publisher-deposited abstract describes censored failure times and a covariate-modulated hazard with an unspecified baseline. Boundary: Hazard assumptions must be justified. Event occurrence, contract close, and settlement are different clocks. Direct article text was not inspected.

docs.title: KALMAN1960
docs.text:
R. E. Kalman. A New Approach to Linear Filtering and Prediction Problems. Journal of Basic Engineering 82(1), 35-45, 1960. DOI and publisher locator: 10.1115/1.3662552.

Use: The inspected publisher-deposited abstract describes state-transition linear filtering and recursive error covariance. Boundary: This is a filtering foundation, not an assertion that binary prices have Gaussian observation noise or a diffusion law. Original full text was not inspected.

docs.title: ADAMS2007
docs.text:
Ryan Prescott Adams and David J. C. MacKay. Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection. arXiv:0710.3742, 2007. DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.0710.3742. Author preprint.

Use: The inspected abstract describes an online posterior over current run length under a changepoint model. Boundary: This entry is a preprint; a later peer-reviewed version was not established here. Independence of segment parameters is an explicit model assumption. A detected change is not proof of an exploitable economic regime.

docs.title: MANNING2008
docs.text:
Christopher D. Manning, Prabhakar Raghavan, and Hinrich Schuetze. Introduction to Information Retrieval. Cambridge University Press, 2008. Author-hosted book website.

Use: Inspected HTML sections on term frequency, inverse document frequency, and the initial multinomial Naive Bayes derivation support bag-of-words representations, document-frequency weighting, and log-space probability calculations. Boundary: Only the named relevant sections, not the whole textbook, were read. Text representation is not evidence of market prediction skill; publication-time provenance and training-corpus contamination remain separate questions.

docs.title: RUMELHART1986
docs.text:
David E. Rumelhart, Geoffrey E. Hinton, and Ronald J. Williams. Learning representations by back-propagating errors. Nature 323(6088), 533-536, 1986. DOI: 10.1038/323533a0. Publisher locator.

Use: The Hinton author copy was visually inspected on pp. 533-535, including the abstract, differentiable feed-forward setup, squared-error objective, chain-rule equations 1-9, gradient/momentum updates, and local-minimum discussion. Boundary: The paper explicitly does not guarantee reaching a global minimum. Its illustrative representations are not market-forecasting or calibration evidence. Do not claim exclusive historical priority; it acknowledges independently discovered variants. The final page was not inspected.

docs.title: HOCHREITER1997
docs.text:
Sepp Hochreiter and Juergen Schmidhuber. Long Short-Term Memory. Neural Computation 9(8), 1735-1780, 1997. DOI and publisher locator: 10.1162/neco.1997.9.8.1735.

Use: The inspected publisher-deposited abstract introduces LSTM to address decaying error flow when learning long dependencies. Boundary: Artificial long-delay sequence experiments are not evidence of market forecasting advantage. Full article text was not inspected, and quote frequency does not increase the number of independent event outcomes.

docs.title: ATTENTION2017
docs.text:
Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion Jones, Aidan N. Gomez, Lukasz Kaiser, and Illia Polosukhin. Attention Is All You Need. NeurIPS 2017. Author repository; inspected later HTML version.

Use: The abstract and Section 4 were inspected. They introduce attention-based sequence transduction and compare computational complexity, parallelism, and dependency path length with recurrence and convolution. Boundary: Translation/parsing results are not calibrated event probabilities. Attention is not automatically an explanation. The inspected version is v7, dated 2023, not a retrieved historical 2017 snapshot.

docs.title: DEVLIN2019
docs.text:
Jacob Devlin, Ming-Wei Chang, Kenton Lee, and Kristina Toutanova. BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding. Proceedings of NAACL-HLT 2019, Volume 1, 4171-4186. DOI: 10.18653/v1/N19-1423. ACL publisher record.

Use: The inspected publisher abstract describes bidirectional text pretraining and task-specific fine-tuning. Boundary: Language-task performance does not establish financial forecasting skill. A model trained after an evaluation period may encode future information; this source does not certify an as-of model archive.

docs.title: GANIN2016
docs.text:
Yaroslav Ganin, Evgeniya Ustinova, Hana Ajakan, Pascal Germain, Hugo Larochelle, Francois Laviolette, Mario Marchand, and Victor Lempitsky. Domain-Adversarial Training of Neural Networks. Journal of Machine Learning Research 17(59), 1-35, 2016. Primary journal page.

Use: The inspected abstract describes representations that discriminate source-task labels while discouraging discrimination between source and target domains; examples include sentiment and image classification. Boundary: Domain adaptation has assumptions and is not a universal cure for market shift. JMLR's page and BibTeX shorten Marchand to March; author-deposited arXiv metadata confirms the full surname used here.

docs.title: BATES1969
docs.text:
J. M. Bates and C. W. J. Granger. The Combination of Forecasts. Operational Research Quarterly 20(4), 451-468, 1969. DOI and current publisher locator: 10.1057/jors.1969.103.

Use: The complete primary publisher abstract, present in the page's structured data but omitted by simplified fetching, was inspected. It describes combining two airline-passenger forecast sets, possible reduction in mean-square error, and combination weights estimated from past forecast errors. Boundary: The full article was not inspected; no specific optimal-weight formula is certified. Improvement is possible, not universal, and point-forecast results do not establish calibration of averaged probabilities. The modern publisher uses the successor journal title; its later online date must not replace 1969.

docs.title: GNEITING2013
docs.text:
Tilmann Gneiting and Roopesh Ranjan. Combining predictive distributions. Electronic Journal of Statistics 7, 2013. DOI: 10.1214/13-EJS823. Earlier author manuscript.

Use: The inspected author abstract treats linear and nonlinear aggregation through coherence, calibration, and dispersion, with simulations and weather/return case studies. Boundary: Publication identity was cross-checked in publisher-deposited metadata; a complete version comparison was not performed. Averaging alone does not guarantee calibration or trading profit.

docs.title: YAO2018
docs.text:
Yuling Yao, Aki Vehtari, Daniel Simpson, and Andrew Gelman. Using Stacking to Average Bayesian Predictive Distributions (with Discussion). Bayesian Analysis 13(3), 2018. DOI: 10.1214/17-BA1091. Author manuscript.

Use: The inspected author abstract extends stacking to predictive distributions and compares alternatives in an M-open setting. Boundary: Its leave-one-out calculation is not automatically suitable for chronological event data. The discussion and all proofs were not inspected; weights still need leakage-safe fitting.

docs.title: BAILEY2017
docs.text:
David H. Bailey, Jonathan Borwein, Marcos Lopez de Prado, and Qiji Jim Zhu. The Probability of Backtest Overfitting. Journal of Computational Finance, 2017. DOI: 10.21314/JCF.2016.322. Western Michigan University record.

Use: The inspected institutional abstract proposes a probability-of-backtest-overfitting framework and combinatorially symmetric cross-validation implementations. Boundary: The cited journal publication is 2017, not an earlier working-paper year. CSCV is not a universal cure for dependent event labels, and the paper's warning about holdout in investment research is not permission to repeatedly inspect the test set.

docs.title: WHITE2000
docs.text:
Halbert White. A Reality Check for Data Snooping. Econometrica 68(5), 1097-1126, 2000. DOI: 10.1111/1468-0262.00152. Econometric Society record.

Use: The University of Wisconsin article copy was inspected at the abstract/introduction opening (p. 1097) and Section 2a-2b through p. 1104. It tests the best expected candidate performance relative to a benchmark, gives a least-favorable-null construction, and uses common random-length bootstrap blocks for dependent data. Boundary: The setup assumes stationary strong-mixing observations, point-in-time predictors and additional asymptotic regularity. Candidate-family records, treatment of parameter estimation and block-length conditions matter. All Appendix assumptions/proofs were not audited. The method cannot recover undisclosed trials, fix leakage or validate fictitious fills and missing costs.

docs.title: BENJAMINI1995
docs.text:
Yoav Benjamini and Yosef Hochberg. Controlling the False Discovery Rate: A Practical and Powerful Approach to Multiple Testing. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B 57(1), 289-300, 1995. DOI: 10.1111/j.2517-6161.1995.tb02031.x. Publisher locator.

Use: The inspected publisher-deposited abstract defines the false-discovery-rate objective and states a control result for independent test statistics. Boundary: Do not assert arbitrary-dependence validity for the original procedure. Valid p-values and a defined testing family remain necessary; direct full text was not inspected.

docs.title: POLITIS1994
docs.text:
Dimitris N. Politis and Joseph P. Romano. The Stationary Bootstrap. Journal of the American Statistical Association 89(428), 1303-1313, 1994. DOI and publisher locator: 10.1080/01621459.1994.10476870.

Use: The complete primary publisher abstract was inspected. It describes geometrically distributed random block lengths, a conditionally stationary resampled pseudo-series, and asymptotic inference for weakly dependent stationary observations. The author publication list corroborates identity; WHITE2000 supplies a separately inspected construction. Boundary: Neither the original full proofs nor a particular block-length choice was audited. Do not extend the abstract to arbitrary dependence, nonstationarity or an incorrectly chosen event sampling unit.

docs.title: HOWARD2021
docs.text:
Steven R. Howard, Aaditya Ramdas, Jon McAuliffe, and Jasjeet Sekhon. Time-uniform, nonparametric, nonasymptotic confidence sequences. The Annals of Statistics 49(2), 2021. DOI: 10.1214/20-AOS1991. Author repository; inspected HTML v9.

Use: The abstract and relevant Section 2 text were inspected, including the average-conditional-expectation estimand, filtration, and exponential-supermartingale setup. They explain simultaneous-in-time coverage under stated conditions. Boundary: Time-uniform does not mean assumption-free, and sequential machinery does not cure leakage or turn repeated quotes into independent outcomes. The inspected author version is later than the journal publication.

docs.title: KELLY1956
docs.text:
J. L. Kelly, Jr. A New Interpretation of Information Rate. Bell System Technical Journal 35(4), 917-926, 1956. DOI and publisher locator: 10.1002/j.1538-7305.1956.tb03809.x.

Use: All ten pages of the Princeton-hosted reproduction, explicitly marked reproduced with AT&T permission, were inspected. The paper distinguishes expected log-growth from expected capital, shows the ruin problem with repeated all-in stakes, and allows unbet capital when there is a track take. Boundary: The general setup assumes independent symbols/noise; the conclusion identifies reinvestment and stake control as essential and explicitly limits its dominance comparison to fixed allocations for each received symbol. It leaves broader adaptive-policy results open. This is not finite-horizon safety, a theorem for uncertain estimated probabilities, or support for a universally safe fractional-Kelly rule. Its base-two logarithm rescales growth relative to natural logs without changing the optimizer.

docs.title: GLOSTEN1985
docs.text:
Lawrence R. Glosten and Paul R. Milgrom. Bid, ask and transaction prices in a specialist market with heterogeneously informed traders. Journal of Financial Economics 14(1), 71-100, 1985. DOI and publisher locator: 10.1016/0304-405X(85)90044-3.

Use: The Milgrom author-hosted reprint was visually inspected on copy pp. 1-3: abstract and opening Section 1. It explains positive spreads from informational adverse selection even with a risk-neutral specialist and zero expected transaction profits, and values a trade conditional on its direction. Boundary: This stock-market analogy assumes competitive zero-profit pricing without transaction costs or binding inventory/cash constraints. The text explicitly warns that binding inventory constraints require departures. Remaining formal propositions/proofs were not inspected, and no actual event-market spread estimate is established.

docs.title: KYLE1985
docs.text:
Albert S. Kyle. Continuous Auctions and Insider Trading. Econometrica 53(6), 1315-1336, 1985. DOI: 10.2307/1913210. Econometric Society record.

Use: The complete primary publisher abstract was inspected in the raw HTML after simplified fetching omitted it. It identifies one risk-neutral insider, random noise traders and competitive risk-neutral market makers; its continuous-trading equilibrium limit produces Brownian prices, constant depth and eventual information incorporation. Boundary: These are model-dependent equilibrium conclusions, not empirical laws for bounded event contracts or evidence about a particular counterparty. Full article proofs were not inspected and no authenticated access was attempted.

docs.title: AVELLANEDA2008
docs.text:
Marco Avellaneda and Sasha Stoikov. High-frequency trading in a limit order book. Quantitative Finance 8(3), 217-224, 2008. DOI and publisher locator: 10.1080/14697680701381228.

Use: The NYU author-hosted article was inspected through Sections 1-3 (pp. 217-223), including the price/utility/arrival assumptions, reservation valuation, approximate quotes and numerical simulations. The main setup uses driftless arithmetic-Brownian stock prices, constant volatility, exponential terminal-wealth utility and distance-dependent Poisson fills. Boundary: Equations 29-30 are approximate simple quotes under symmetric exponential arrival rates, not the general exact control solution. The paper focuses on inventory risk rather than a full adverse-selection model. Continuous costless quote changes, one-share fills and a terminal midpoint mark omit important real execution frictions. Its results are simulation comparisons, not historical executable profit; bounded event payouts and settlement jumps invalidate automatic stock-model transfer. The Appendix was not fully inspected.

docs.title: ABERNETHY2013
docs.text:
Jacob Abernethy, Yiling Chen, and Jennifer Wortman Vaughan. Efficient Market Making via Convex Optimization, and a Connection to Online Learning. ACM Transactions on Economics and Computation 1(2), article 12, 1-39, 2013. DOI: 10.1145/2465769.2465777. Microsoft Research institutional record.

Use: The inspected institutional abstract describes convex-cost market design, bounded-payoff securities, convex-hull optimization, and connections with online learning. Boundary: This is mechanism-design theory, not a claim that a quoted basket is executable or that separately worded contracts have compatible settlement.

docs.title: DUDIK2011
docs.text:
Miroslav Dudik, John Langford, and Lihong Li. Doubly Robust Policy Evaluation and Learning. ICML 2011. Author-deposited manuscript.

Use: The inspected abstract addresses evaluation from contextual-bandit logs when target and logged action distributions differ, combining reward and past-policy models. Boundary: It does not establish validity without action support or appropriate logging assumptions. Passive historical order books are not automatically action-and-reward logs for a proposed trading policy. This entry identifies the 2011 paper, not a later expanded version.

docs.title: FUJIMOTO2019
docs.text:
Scott Fujimoto, David Meger, and Doina Precup. Off-Policy Deep Reinforcement Learning without Exploration. ICML 2019, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 97, 2052-2062. Primary proceedings.

Use: The inspected abstract reports extrapolation problems in fixed-batch off-policy deep reinforcement learning and proposes batch-constrained behavior. Boundary: Continuous-control results are not evidence of executable trading performance or simulator fidelity. Restricting a policy does not guarantee a safe live strategy.

docs.title: KALSHI_DEMO
docs.text:
Kalshi. Test In The Demo Environment. Official documentation, inspected 2026. Official page; documentation index.

Use: The complete inspected page describes mock funds, separate credentials, and demo endpoints. Boundary: It expressly warns that demo prices and behavior may not reflect real markets. Demo success is a mechanics result, not evidence of live liquidity or profitability.

docs.title: KALSHI_HISTORY
docs.text:
Kalshi. Historical Data. Official documentation, inspected 2026. Official page.

Use: Inspected sections explain moving live/historical cutoffs and object-specific partition times. Boundary: The listed historical endpoints do not establish a full historical order-book or queue archive. Public API documentation is not a redistribution license or a guarantee of complete coverage.

docs.title: KALSHI_BOOK
docs.text:
Kalshi. Orderbook Responses. Official documentation, inspected 2026. Official page.

Use: The inspected schema uses string-valued fixed-point dollar prices and quantities in YES/NO bid arrays; opposite-outcome bids imply asks under ordinary binary mechanics. Boundary: Recheck schema/version and units. Displayed depth is not a guaranteed fill, and a current response is not historical evidence.

docs.title: KALSHI_ROUNDING
docs.text:
Kalshi. Fee Rounding. Official documentation, inspected 2026. Official page.

Use: The complete inspected page distinguishes trade fee, rounding fee, rebate, balance precision, and a per-order accumulator across fills. Boundary: This is not a complete market-specific fee schedule. A hypothetical flat classroom charge must never be labeled the venue's actual fee.

docs.title: POLYMARKET_FEES
docs.text:
Polymarket. Fees. Official predictions-product documentation, inspected 2026. Official page; documentation index.

Use: Inspected fee structure and precision sections describe price/quantity-dependent, market-specific taker fees and distinctions by market category. Boundary: Do not assume universal zero fees or freeze the current category table as timeless. Different regional products and USDC/pUSD units need separate verification; rebates do not establish a profitable market-making strategy.

docs.title: POLYMARKET_RESOLUTION
docs.text:
Polymarket. Resolution. Official documentation, inspected 2026. Official page.

Use: Inspected rules, dispute, UMA Vote, clarification, and redemption text explains why titles alone do not determine payout. An exceptional Unknown/50-50 result pays 0.50 per outcome token. Boundary: Timelines are descriptive, not guarantees; retain actual contract rules and exceptional payouts instead of coercing every observation into a binary label.

docs.title: POLYMARKET_COLLATERAL
docs.text:
Polymarket. Polymarket USD. Official documentation, inspected 2026. Official page.

Use: Inspected descriptive sections identify pUSD as a Polygon ERC-20 collateral wrapper representing a USDC claim and describe onchain wrapping/unwrapping with a pause gate. Boundary: This is the operator's description, not an independent reserve, code, or custody audit. A token claim is not insured cash; this page should not be applied to a different regional product.

docs.title: POLYMARKET_BOOK
docs.text:
Polymarket. Prices and Order Books. Official public-CLOB documentation, inspected 2026. Official page.

Use: Inspected token mapping and response examples include price/size levels, timestamp, state hash, minimum order size, and tick size. Boundary: A response hash does not prove complete history or queue position. Public access is not unrestricted data-reuse permission.

docs.title: POLYMARKET_TERMS
docs.text:
Polymarket. Terms of Use | Polymarket. Partial official page response, inspected 2026. Official locator.

Use: The retrieved geographic notice said trading on polymarket.com was blocked in the United States and directed readers to the separate polymarket.us product. Boundary: Complete operative terms were not exposed in the response. This source does not establish a full eligibility matrix, data redistribution permission, or an individual reader's legal right to trade. Never bypass geographic restrictions.

docs.title: KALSHI_SETTLEMENT
docs.text:
Kalshi. Market Settlement. Official documentation, inspected 2026. Official page.

Use: The complete inspected page describes ordinary payouts, net positions, variable settlement timing, and a distinction between simple YES/NO settlement and sub-cent scalar-settlement fees/rounding. Boundary: Do not assume immediate settlement or identical treatment for every product. Preserve actual rule and payout fields.

docs.title: POLYMARKET_MARKETS
docs.text:
Polymarket. Markets & Events. Official documentation, inspected 2026. Official page.

Use: The inspected page distinguishes market identifiers and outcome tokens from event containers and notes that only some multi-market events are mutually exclusive. It also identifies an order-book eligibility field. Boundary: Shared grouping alone does not prove an exhaustive partition or compatible settlement. Verify rules before treating a set of tokens as an executable basket.

docs.title: NOAA_CO2
docs.text:
NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory, Carbon Cycle and Greenhouse Gases group. Mauna Loa CO2 monthly mean data. Mutable observational dataset, inspected 2026. Primary data text.

Use: Inspected header/schema and real initial observations establish a concrete monthly series with measurement and interpolation flags. The header identifies early Scripps provenance and the 2022-2023 Maunakea substitution. Boundary: This is current-vintage observational data, not an issued-forecast archive or a prediction-market dataset. The book's completed NOAA-period study freezes, hashes, and attributes its extract while retaining the retrospective-data limitations.

docs.title: NOAA_DATA
docs.text:
NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory. Trends in Atmospheric Carbon Dioxide: Data. Official data documentation, inspected 2026. Official page.

Use: Inspected text warns that quality-control checks can revise values and supplies provider citation guidance. Boundary: Small expected revisions are not proof of harmless historical leakage or stable threshold labels. No publication-vintage archive was established.

docs.title: NOAA_POLICY
docs.text:
NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory. Disclaimer. Official use policy, inspected 2026. Official policy.

Use: The inspected policy describes government-server information as public domain unless annotated otherwise, with attribution, no implied endorsement, and clear labeling of modifications. Boundary: Third-party data are separately qualified. Do not silently extend the government-work policy to early Scripps records or imply NOAA endorsement of this book.

docs.title: Exercises and solution sketches
docs.text:
Exercises and their solution sketches live in the chapter that introduces their assumptions. Keeping them together avoids an answer silently using a different fee convention, data cutoff, or contract definition. Try an exercise before reading its solution.

The complete contents links all 30 chapters. Use this guide to choose practice by topic.

Practice Chapters Contract payoff tables, probability updates, costs, and market mechanisms 01, 02, 03, 04, 05, 06 Availability audits, leakage, exploration, and probability scoring 07, 08, 09, 10 Statistical, nonlinear, temporal, text, neural, and combined models 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16 Decisions, simulation, strategy-search evidence, and contract consistency 17, 18, 19, 20 Market making, sizing, learned policies, and paper operations 21, 22, 23, 24 Research design and falsification 25 End-to-end practice and conditional manual decision-making 26, 27, 28, 29, 30

docs.title: How to judge a solution
docs.text:
A numerical answer is incomplete unless its units, assumptions, and information cutoff are clear. For a trading exercise, distinguish quantity, price, total cost, possible payout, expected profit, realized profit, and maximum loss. For a modeling exercise, state the target and sampling unit before choosing a metric.

Some exercises deliberately have no uniquely profitable action. "The data do not identify the requested quantity," "the contracts are not equivalent," and "do not trade" can be correct conclusions. Their value lies in the explanation, not in the refusal to calculate.

For a research-design exercise, a convincing solution identifies an observable target, a baseline, what data would be needed, how observations depend on one another, how selection is controlled, and a result that would falsify the proposal. It does not invent returns to make a research idea sound finished.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: No prior chapters. You should be comfortable with ordinary algebra, basic set notation (union, intersection, complement), and running a Python script from a command line. Quantitative finance background is not assumed anywhere in this book.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this chapter you should be able to: state the difference between an informal real-world event and a contract's payout rule; classify an event contract as categorical, threshold, or complement-based; explain why "the contract paid out" is a statement about rules, not a statement about physical reality; and compute the cash flows of a simple bounded-payout position using the book's canonical accounting example.

docs.title: 1.1 Why "not a stock" matters before any modeling begins
docs.text:
A share of common stock represents fractional ownership of a company with an indefinite holding period, no fixed expiration, a payoff driven by future cash flows and market sentiment together, and (usually) no explicit written rule that converts a real-world happening into a dollar amount. An event contract is a different object entirely. It has an explicit textual description of what will be observed, a specified resolution source, a specified observation window, a specified settlement value or set of settlement values, and — critically — an expiration after which the contract stops existing and is replaced by a cash or token payout.

This distinction is not pedantic. Every later chapter in this book depends on it. A forecasting model that predicts "will candidate X win the election" is predicting an informal proposition. A trading decision executes against a contract whose payout depends on the exact resolution language: which office, which jurisdiction's certified count, which date, and what happens if the race is contested or a candidate withdraws. Treating the informal proposition and the contractual payout as identical is the single most common source of confusion for a reader arriving from general machine learning or from equity markets.

Borrow the notation registry's terms directly. Let \(E\) denote an explicitly defined event, meaning a natural-language description together with its contractual resolution rules — the source, the cutoff, and any exception clauses. Let \(Y\) denote the binary contractual outcome that the rules actually assign, and let \(R\) denote the realized payout per unit in the specified collateral currency. In the ordinary case, \(Y\in\{0,1\}\) and \(R=Y\) dollars per unit. But \(R=Y\) is a simplifying convention this book uses for its default examples, not a law of nature: a contract can specify a payout of USD 0.50 under a documented exceptional condition, in which case \(R=0.5\) while no ordinary binary \(Y\) is well defined at all. Chapter 6 works through documented cases of exactly this kind. For now, the important habit is to keep three things separate in your head: the informal real-world proposition, the contract's resolution rule applied to that proposition, and the realized payout that rule produces.

docs.title: 1.2 Three shapes of event contract
docs.text:
Nearly every event contract you will encounter reduces to one of three logical shapes, sometimes combined.

Categorical contracts partition a question into a fixed, enumerated set of mutually exclusive and — ideally — exhaustive outcomes: which of five candidates wins a primary, which of four teams wins a tournament round, which named storm category is reached first. If the outcomes \(\{o_1,\dots,o_k\}\) are genuinely mutually exclusive and exhaustive under compatible rules, then a complete set of associated YES contracts should have probabilities summing to one, and at most one of them settles YES. The qualifier "under compatible rules" is doing real work here. A venue's user-interface grouping of several markets into one "event" container does not, by itself, establish that the grouped outcomes are exhaustive or mutually exclusive; the documented Polymarket data model explicitly separates an event container from a guaranteed exclusive partition of outcomes, and states that only some multi-market events represent genuinely mutually exclusive alternatives. POLYMARKET_MARKETS Two markets that look categorically related from their titles can have different resolution sources, different observation windows, or an allowed "no winner" state that breaks the exhaustiveness assumption. Verifying exclusivity and exhaustiveness from the actual rules, not from a shared page layout, is a recurring task in this book (it returns with more machinery in Chapter 20).

Threshold contracts ask whether a numeric quantity crosses a specified level by a specified time, using a specified source: will year-over-year CPI exceed 3.0% for a named reporting month as published by a named statistical agency; will a company's quarterly unit sales exceed a stated figure in a stated filing. Threshold contracts hide two design questions that matter enormously for a forecaster. First, what happens exactly at the boundary — does "exceed 3.0%" resolve YES at exactly 3.0%, or only above it, and is the published figure rounded before the comparison is applied? Second, which data vintage counts — the originally published figure, or a later revision? A statistical agency frequently revises a headline number weeks or months after first release. A contract that does not pin down "as originally published" versus "as later revised" has genuine rule ambiguity, and a forecaster building point-in-time features (the subject of Chapter 8) must decide which vintage the contract actually keys off, not which vintage happens to be easiest to download.

Complement contracts are the two-sided special case: a single proposition with a YES side and a NO side. With only ordinary binary outcomes, \(P(\text{YES})+P(\text{NO})=1\). For valuation, however, the decisive condition is that the two payouts sum to the unit payout in every permitted state. A third settlement state can break the two-label probability description without breaking that constant-payout relationship: if both tokens pay USD 0.50 in an exceptional state, their combined payout is still USD 1. A void or refund rule must likewise be checked from its actual cash flows, not inferred from its name. With common settlement timing, no financing or collateral risk, and frictionless feasible trading, a constant USD 1 combined payout has value USD 1; with positive financing costs it has the corresponding present value. Executable asks and bids need not separately sum to that value because of spreads and constraints. Chapter 20 derives the relevant inequalities. Keep the probability of an ordinary YES label distinct from the expected payout of a YES token when exceptional states exist.

docs.title: 1.3 The canonical worked example
docs.text:
This book uses one running numerical scenario for its simplest accounting illustrations, matching the notation registry exactly so that no chapter silently changes the arithmetic underneath a reader.

A trader buys 10 YES units of a complement-style binary event contract at an executable ask of USD 0.40 per unit. A hypothetical, purely illustrative flat fee of USD 0.01 per unit applies to the fill. This fee is invented for teaching; it is not a Kalshi or Polymarket fee schedule, which are described with their actual documented mechanics in Chapter 6. The initial cash outlay is

\[ \text{initial cost}=10\times(0.40+0.01)=4.10. \]

Under ordinary binary settlement, the contract pays USD 1.00 per unit if the contractual outcome is YES and USD 0.00 per unit if it is NO. Net profit is therefore

\[ \Pi_{\text{YES}}=10\times1.00-4.10=5.90,\qquad \Pi_{\text{NO}}=10\times0.00-4.10=-4.10. \]

Notice what this arithmetic does and does not say. It says: if the contract settles YES, this specific position nets USD 5.90; if it settles NO, this specific position loses the full USD 4.10 committed. It says nothing about which outcome is more likely. That requires a probability estimate, which is the subject of Chapter 2, and turning a probability estimate into a comparison against this cost structure is the subject of Chapter 3. Anticipating that step slightly: if a model assigns probability \(\hat p=0.55\) to YES, the model's own expected net profit is

\[ \mathbb{E}_{\hat p}[\Pi]=10\times(0.55-0.40-0.01)=1.40, \]

which is positive only because the model's assessed probability (0.55) exceeds the all-in per-unit cost (0.41) by enough to clear the ten-unit size. The subscript on the expectation is a reminder that this number is conditional on the model being correct about \(\hat p\); it is not an empirical measurement of anything that has actually happened.
