Finally, if the position is instead closed before settlement by selling at an executable bid of USD 0.46 with an additional exit fee of USD 0.01 per unit, realized round-trip profit is

\[ 10\times(0.46-0.40-0.01-0.01)=0.40. \]

Notice that the entry used the ask (0.40) and the exit used the bid (0.46); the bid-ask spread has already been paid once, on each side, by using the correct executable price for each leg. There is no additional "spread cost" to subtract afterward — doing so would count the same friction twice.

docs.title: 1.4 Real event versus contractual payout: three failure modes
docs.text:
The distinction between \(Z\) (an informal real-world proposition), \(Y\) (the contractual binary outcome the rules actually assign), and \(R\) (the realized payout) is not academic hair-splitting. Here are three concrete ways the distinction bites.

Timing mismatch. The informal event "does the central bank raise rates this year" might seem to resolve at the moment a decision is announced. The contract, however, specifies an observation window and a settlement source; if the announcement happens one minute after the contract's stated cutoff, the informally "true" event and the contractually "YES" outcome diverge, sometimes for reasons that have nothing to do with the underlying economic reality.

Boundary and rounding disputes. A threshold contract at "3.0% or higher" resting on a statistic reported to one decimal place behaves very differently from the same threshold resting on a statistic reported to two decimal places, because the effective probability mass sitting exactly on the boundary changes with the source's precision. A forecaster who is careless about whether the boundary is inclusive can build a model that is systematically miscalibrated near the threshold, independent of any market inefficiency.

Exceptional and fractional settlement. Some contracts contemplate more than two payout values. Kalshi's own settlement documentation distinguishes ordinary YES/NO determinations from scalar or partial settlements that can carry different rounding and fee treatment. KALSHI_SETTLEMENT Polymarket's resolution documentation describes a dispute process that can, in a defined exceptional case, resolve a market at an "Unknown" state in which each side's token redeems for USD 0.50 rather than USD 0 or USD 1. POLYMARKET_RESOLUTION In either case, \(R\notin\{0,1\}\), and the tidy binary label \(Y\) used by a machine learning pipeline is simply not defined for that observation. Chapter 6 develops this in full detail, including how the companion code represents a payout that has no valid binary label at all rather than silently forcing one.

docs.title: 1.5 Assumptions, counterexamples, and failure modes
docs.text:
The clean categorical/threshold/complement taxonomy and the canonical accounting example both rely on assumptions worth stating explicitly, because each one can fail in a real contract.

Assumption: the rules are stable once trading opens. Real venues sometimes issue clarifications after a market opens, and a documented additional-context clarification can change what a "yes" answer actually requires. POLYMARKET_RESOLUTION A model trained on an earlier version of the rules is implicitly trained on a slightly different contract than the one it is later scored against.

Assumption: settlement is binary. As shown above, this fails for scalar or exceptional settlements. A pipeline that assumes every historical row has a label in \(\{0,1\}\) will either crash or, worse, silently coerce a fractional payout into an incorrect binary label.

Assumption: a shared event page implies mutual exclusivity. As discussed for categorical contracts, this must be verified against the documented rules rather than assumed from a user interface grouping. POLYMARKET_MARKETS

Assumption: the fee schedule used in the canonical example reflects a real venue. It does not. The USD 0.01 flat per-unit fee is an invented pedagogical constant chosen for arithmetic simplicity. Chapter 6 works through Kalshi's actual documented distinction between a trade fee, a rounding fee, and a rebate, which depends on price, size, and account type rather than being a flat per-unit constant. KALSHI_ROUNDING

A genuine counterexample worth sitting with: two contracts titled almost identically — say, "does the bill pass the chamber this session" on two different platforms — can have different resolution sources (an official government record versus a specified news outlet), different session-end cutoffs, and different treatment of a bill that passes in amended form. They are not the same event contract merely because a human reader would describe them with the same sentence. This is a basis-risk problem (see the glossary entry) that recurs throughout the book, especially in Chapter 20's discussion of cross-market consistency.

docs.title: 1.6 Companion example
docs.text:
The companion script payoffs.py builds the canonical position described above: ten YES units bought at USD 0.40 with the invented USD 0.01 per-unit fee, then walks through three settlement paths (YES, NO, and an exceptional fractional payout of USD 0.50) plus the resale-before-settlement path. It also demonstrates that attempting to score a fractional-payout observation with an ordinary binary proper-scoring function is rejected rather than silently coerced, which is the concrete code-level version of the \(Y\)-versus-\(R\) distinction from Section 1.4. The underlying accounting is an in-memory paper ledger for one Python process, not a durable or production order-management system; nothing about a position survives after the process exits. Run it from the companion project root (book\companion) after installing the package:

Command working directory: run this chapter's Python commands from book\companion. From the trading repository root, run Set-Location book\companion once first. The .venv belongs to that companion project; see companion setup.

.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe examples\payoffs.py

Read its output next to Section 1.3 above rather than re-deriving the arithmetic from scratch; the script's numbers and this chapter's numbers are the same worked example by construction.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1.1. A categorical event contract group lists five outcomes on a venue's event page. You discover from the actual rules that one of the five permits a shared "co-winner" resolution in which two outcomes can both settle YES simultaneously. What does this do to the claim that the five associated YES probabilities must sum to one, and what single piece of documentation would you need to check before treating any two of the five as complements of each other?

Solution sketch. Mutual exclusivity is required for the probabilities to sum to exactly one; if two outcomes can both resolve YES, the five outcomes no longer partition the sample space, and their YES probabilities can sum to more than one without any pricing error existing. You would need to check the specific tie-breaking or co-winner clause in the contract rules (not the event page's grouping) for every pair you intend to treat as mutually exclusive, and confirm whether it applies to the particular pair you care about.

Exercise 1.2. Using the canonical example (10 YES units at USD 0.40 ask, USD 0.01 per-unit fee), compute the net profit if the contract instead settles at an exceptional scalar payout of USD 0.20 per unit. Is this outcome representable as a binary machine-learning label under this book's convention?

Solution sketch. Net profit is \(10\times(0.20-0.40-0.01)=10\times(-0.21)=-2.10\). Because the payout 0.20 is not in \(\{0,1\}\), the binary label is undefined under this book's convention (the notation registry's \(R=Y\) simplification does not apply); an evaluation pipeline should treat this observation as unlabeled for binary scoring purposes rather than rounding it to 0.

Exercise 1.3. A threshold contract resolves YES if a reported inflation figure is "3.0% or higher" for a specified month, using the value "as originally published in the agency's initial release." Two months later, the agency revises that month's figure downward across the 3.0% boundary. Does the contract's settlement change? Justify your answer using only the stated rule text.

Solution sketch. No. The rule text explicitly keys the outcome to the originally published value, so a later revision, even one crossing the threshold, is not the value the contract's rule is defined against. This is exactly the vintage-versus-revision distinction the notation registry insists on; a model or a settlement process that substitutes the revised figure would be using information and a value that the contract's own rule does not reference.

Exercise 1.4. Explain in one or two sentences why "the market price moved because the event became more likely" is a claim about \(Z\) (the informal event), while "the contract settled YES" is a claim about \(Y\) (the contractual outcome), and why conflating them can mislead a modeler who is building point-in-time training labels.

Solution sketch. Price movement reflects participants' evolving beliefs about the informal proposition and about execution conditions, while settlement reflects the rules' mechanical application to whatever the resolution source reports; a modeler who labels historical training rows using informal "what actually happened" judgments rather than the documented contractual outcome can introduce label noise exactly where rule text and reality diverge (timing, rounding, or exceptional settlement), degrading the very evaluation the model is meant to support.

docs.title: Sources and further reading
docs.text: This chapter's claims about documented rule mechanics are limited to Kalshi's and Polymarket's officially inspected pages as retrieved during this book's audit; both operators can and do update their documentation, and neither source establishes a universal rule that all venues share. KALSHI_SETTLEMENT KALSHI_ROUNDING POLYMARKET_RESOLUTION POLYMARKET_MARKETS Chapter 6 revisits all four documents in full, including their stated limitations and the parts of each that remain unresolved by a partial official response.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Chapter 1 (event contracts, categorical/threshold/complement shapes, and the \(Z\)/\(Y\)/\(R\) distinction). Comfort with basic set notation and simple algebra. No prior statistics course is assumed; the chapter derives what it needs.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this chapter you should be able to: state the probability axioms and derive Bayes' rule from the definition of conditional probability; convert between probability and odds; explain what a base rate is and why it requires a stated reference population; distinguish independent from dependent events with a concrete event-contract example; and compute the single-YES Brier score and natural-log loss for a small set of forecasts exactly as this book defines them.

docs.title: 2.1 Probability is a commitment, not a vibe
docs.text:
"I think it's likely" is not a probability. A probability is a number in \([0,1]\) attached to a precisely specified event, under a precisely specified information set, that obeys a small set of consistency rules. The rules matter more than they might seem to at first, because they are what make a probability combinable: they let you take two forecasts and merge them, compare a forecast to a price, or later score a forecast against what actually happened.

The axioms this book relies on are the ordinary Kolmogorov ones, stated for a discrete or countable outcome space (continuous cases replace sums with integrals, but nothing in this book's contract-pricing content requires that generality): every event \(A\) has \(P(A)\geq 0\); the certain event has \(P(\Omega)=1\); and for mutually exclusive events, probabilities add, \(P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)\) when \(A\cap B=\emptyset\). From these three rules, the complement rule \(P(A^c)=1-P(A)\) follows immediately by taking \(B=A^c\) in the additivity axiom. This is exactly why, in Chapter 1's complement contracts, YES and NO probabilities must sum to one when no third exceptional state is contractually possible — the axiom requires exhaustiveness and mutual exclusivity, and a documented "Unknown/50-50" settlement state is precisely a violation of exhaustiveness over the two-outcome frame, not a mathematical paradox.

Conditional probability is defined, not derived, as

\[ P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)},\qquad P(B)>0. \]

Everything else in this chapter is algebra performed on that one definition.

docs.title: 2.2 Bayes' rule, derived, not quoted
docs.text:
Bayes' rule is often presented as a black box. It is worth deriving it once, slowly, because the derivation is what tells you exactly which quantities you need and what happens when one of them is zero.

Start from the definition of conditional probability applied twice, once for \(P(A\mid B)\) and once for \(P(B\mid A)\):

\[ P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)},\qquad P(B\mid A)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(A)}. \]

Both expressions share the same numerator, \(P(A\cap B)\). Solve the second equation for that shared numerator: \(P(A\cap B)=P(B\mid A)P(A)\). Substitute this into the first equation:

\[ P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(B\mid A)\,P(A)}{P(B)}. \]

That is Bayes' rule. Nothing was assumed beyond the definition of conditional probability applied in two directions. The denominator \(P(B)\) is usually not known directly and must be expanded using the law of total probability. If \(A\) has a binary complement \(A^c\),

\[ P(B)=P(B\mid A)P(A)+P(B\mid A^c)P(A^c). \]

Putting the two together gives the working form used throughout this book:

\[ P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(B\mid A)\,P(A)}{P(B\mid A)P(A)+P(B\mid A^c)P(A^c)}. \]

Read this equation as a recipe with three ingredients: a prior \(P(A)\) (what you believed before seeing evidence \(B\)), a likelihood ratio implicit in \(P(B\mid A)\) versus \(P(B\mid A^c)\) (how much more or less likely the evidence is under each hypothesis), and the posterior \(P(A\mid B)\) (what you believe after). If \(P(B\mid A)=P(B\mid A^c)\), the evidence is equally likely regardless of \(A\), and the posterior equals the prior exactly: evidence that does not discriminate between hypotheses cannot move your belief, no matter how dramatic it feels.

Worked case. Take a prior \(P(A)=0.20\) that some event contract's underlying proposition is true. Suppose a piece of evidence \(B\) (say, a leaked internal report) has \(P(B\mid A)=0.80\) — quite likely if the proposition is true — and \(P(B\mid A^c)=0.10\) — fairly unlikely if it is false. The marginal probability of observing this evidence at all is

\[ P(B)=0.20\times0.80+0.80\times0.10=0.16+0.08=0.24. \]

The posterior is

\[ P(A\mid B)=\frac{0.16}{0.24}=0.6\overline{6}\approx0.667. \]

A prior of 0.20 moved to roughly 0.667 after one piece of evidence that was eight times more likely under the true hypothesis than under its complement. This is an invented classroom scenario matching the companion script's demonstration inputs; it is not a claim about any real contract, and the numbers 0.20, 0.80, and 0.10 were chosen for illustration, not estimated from data. Notice also what happens at a boundary: if \(P(B\mid A)=0\) and \(P(B\mid A^c)=0\), the evidence has zero probability under every hypothesis in the model, and the update is undefined (division by zero) rather than silently returning the prior — this is a modeling failure to flag, not a case to paper over with an arbitrary convention.

docs.title: 2.3 Odds, and why traders often think in them
docs.text:
The odds of an event are \(o=p/(1-p)\), with inverse \(p=o/(1+o)\). Odds are algebraically equivalent to probability but multiply nicely under Bayesian updating: dividing the two branches of Bayes' rule by each other, the posterior odds equal the prior odds times the likelihood ratio,

\[ \frac{P(A\mid B)}{P(A^c\mid B)}=\frac{P(A)}{P(A^c)}\times\frac{P(B\mid A)}{P(B\mid A^c)}. \]

For the worked case above, prior odds are \(0.20/0.80=0.25\), the likelihood ratio is \(0.80/0.10=8\), and posterior odds are \(0.25\times8=2.0\), which converts back to \(p=2/(1+2)=0.667\) — matching the direct calculation and providing a useful arithmetic cross-check. A probability of 0.40 has odds in favor of \(0.40/0.60=2/3\), or "2-to-3 in favor"; equivalently, the odds against are \(0.60/0.40=3/2\), or "3-to-2 against." Reading a USD 0.40 contract price as that probability requires the additional price-interpretation assumptions of Chapter 4. Converting a stated probability to odds is algebra; interpreting a price as a probability is not.

docs.title: 2.4 Base rates need a stated population
docs.text:
A base rate is the prevalence of an outcome in an explicitly defined reference population; it is meaningless without saying what that population is. "Incumbents usually win" is not a base rate until you specify: which office, which country, which time period, and which subset of incumbents (all who sought re-election, or only those who survived a primary). Changing any of those changes the number, sometimes substantially, and changing the reference population after looking at a specific race you are trying to forecast is a form of selection that can silently manufacture whatever base rate is convenient.

Base rates interact with Bayes' rule in a way that is easy to state and easy to forget under pressure: a base rate is the prior, and it should be updated by genuinely new, discriminating evidence — not by evidence that merely restates the base rate in different words. A forecaster who reads five news articles that all report the same underlying poll and updates five times because there were "five pieces of evidence" is double-, triple-, and quadruple-counting a single observation. This is the same dependence problem raised again more forcefully in Section 2.5 and in Chapter 4's discussion of aggregating many correlated poll readings into a single forecast.

docs.title: 2.5 Independence and dependence, with an event-contract example
docs.text:
Two events \(A\) and \(B\) are independent exactly when \(P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)\), equivalently \(P(A\mid B)=P(A)\): learning \(B\) tells you nothing new about \(A\). This is a strong, specific, checkable condition, not a default assumption to reach for out of convenience.

Event contracts frequently violate independence in ways that are easy to miss because the contracts look unrelated on the surface. Consider two contracts: "does the incumbent party win the presidency" and "does the incumbent party retain control of the legislature," observed in the same election cycle. Both outcomes are driven substantially by shared factors — the state of the economy, the incumbent's approval rating, national mood — so learning that one resolved YES makes the other's YES resolution more likely than its unconditional probability alone would suggest. Treating these two contracts as independent when sizing a combined position understates the true joint risk: both can go wrong, or right, together far more often than the product of their individual probabilities implies. The glossary's "dependence group" concept flags sets of observations or contracts that share this kind of common exposure, so a downstream calculation does not treat them as independent draws.

A related and even more common failure is treating repeated snapshots of the same contract, taken minutes or hours apart, as independent observations. They share the same eventual settlement; a sequence of ten price quotes leading up to one binary outcome is not ten independent bets on that outcome, no matter how many rows it occupies in a spreadsheet. This exact issue, applied to poll readings rather than price quotes, is the central empirical caution in Chapter 4's discussion of comparing prediction-market forecasts against many correlated polls from a small number of elections.

docs.title: 2.6 Quantifying probability uncertainty: proper scores
docs.text:
A probability forecast is only useful if there is a disciplined way to say whether it was good. This book uses two scoring rules for a binary outcome, both defined precisely so every chapter uses the same convention.

The general concept behind both is a proper scoring rule: a rule for scoring a probability forecast against a realized outcome such that, in expectation, a forecaster who reports their true believed distribution cannot do better by reporting anything else. Gneiting and Raftery's inspected treatment states this as a theorem — reporting the generating distribution optimizes the expected score, with strict propriety making that optimum unique relative to the stated class of forecasts — and confirms that both the categorical quadratic (Brier) score and the logarithmic score are strictly proper. GNEITING2007 This is a statement about the scoring objective's incentive properties, not a claim about trading profit; a strictly proper score rewards honesty about probability, it does not reward a correct guess about a single coin flip.

For one YES-probability forecast \(\hat p_i\) per binary observation \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\), the Brier score is the mean squared error of the YES probability against the realized binary label:

\[ \operatorname{BS}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n(\hat p_i-y_i)^2. \]

This is the single-YES convention. Gneiting and Raftery's inspected categorical treatment sums the squared error over both outcomes, which is exactly twice this book's single-YES value once the reward-versus-loss sign convention is reversed; a Brier score quoted elsewhere is not automatically comparable to this book's numbers without checking which convention was used. GNEITING2007

Log loss uses the natural logarithm of the probability the forecast assigned to whatever actually happened:

\[ \operatorname{LL}=-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\Big[y_i\log\hat p_i+(1-y_i)\log(1-\hat p_i)\Big]. \]

A forecast of exactly zero on an outcome that occurs contributes an infinite loss; this is an intended property of the scoring rule, not a numerical bug to be quietly clipped away. A forecast that is exactly correct with full confidence contributes zero, using the limiting convention that \(0\log 0=0\).

Worked case. Take four invented binary observations with labels \(y=(0,1,0,1)\) and forecasts \(\hat p=(0.1,0.7,0.4,0.8)\) — the same small example used by the companion script, so its printed output can be checked directly against this arithmetic. The squared errors are \((0.1-0)^2=0.01\), \((0.7-1)^2=0.09\), \((0.4-0)^2=0.16\), and \((0.8-1)^2=0.04\); their mean is

\[ \operatorname{BS}=\frac{0.01+0.09+0.16+0.04}{4}=\frac{0.30}{4}=0.075. \]

For log loss, the probability assigned to the realized outcome in each row is \(0.9,\,0.7,\,0.6,\,0.8\) respectively (using \(1-\hat p\) where \(y=0\)). Their natural logs are approximately \(-0.1054,\,-0.3567,\,-0.5108,\,-0.2231\), summing to about \(-1.1960\); dividing by \(n=4\) and negating gives

\[ \operatorname{LL}\approx0.2990. \]

Two comparison cases sharpen the infinite-loss boundary: a forecaster who is correctly certain, with \(y=(0,1)\) and \(\hat p=(0,1)\), incurs log loss exactly \(0\); a forecaster who is confidently wrong, with \(y=(1)\) and \(\hat p=(0)\), incurs log loss of \(+\infty\). Log loss is far harsher on confident wrongness than the Brier score, whose worst case for a single observation is bounded at \(1\). Choosing between the two, or reporting both, is developed further in Chapter 10.

docs.title: 2.7 Assumptions, counterexamples, and failure modes
docs.text:
Assumption: the information set is stated. Every probability in this book is conditional on some stated information set \(\mathcal I\); "the true probability" without reference to an information set is not a meaningful object. Two honest forecasters with different information can correctly hold different probabilities for the same event.

Assumption: likelihoods are known or estimable. Bayes' rule is only as good as \(P(B\mid A)\) and \(P(B\mid A^c)\). In practice these are themselves estimates with their own uncertainty; treating a posterior as exact when its inputs were rough guesses overstates how much you actually know. The registry's \(p_L\) symbol — a deliberately conservative probability bound, whose inference method must be stated — keeps this humility explicit.

Counterexample to naive independence. Two contracts on the same underlying race, phrased with different wording ("candidate wins the popular vote" and "candidate wins the electoral college"), are correlated through shared information, not independent just because they are formally different contracts with different titles.

Failure mode: treating price movement as new evidence when it reflects old evidence being repeated. If ten outlets all cover the same single poll release, a Bayesian updater that treats each article as independent confirming evidence will overshoot its posterior. The base-rate discipline of Section 2.4 and the dependence discussion of Section 2.5 are the guardrails against exactly this.

Failure mode: silently clipping probabilities to avoid infinite log loss. If a fitting procedure needs numerical stabilization (for example, nudging a predicted 0 to \(10^{-6}\) to avoid a crash), that stabilization must be disclosed as part of the model, not retroactively applied to change how an already-issued forecast is scored.

docs.title: 2.8 Companion example
docs.text:
The companion script bayes_scoring.py runs the Bayes update and the scoring computations worked through above, using the same numbers (prior 0.2, likelihood-if-yes 0.8, likelihood-if-no 0.1; labels \((0,1,0,1)\) against forecasts \((0.1,0.7,0.4,0.8)\)), and demonstrates the rejected-update case when the observed evidence has zero probability under the stated model. It also reports calibration bins, grouping forecasts into equal-width probability ranges and comparing each bin's mean forecast to its observed outcome rate — a first step toward the fuller calibration treatment in Chapter 10. Run it after installing the package:

Command working directory: run this chapter's Python commands from book\companion. From the trading repository root, run Set-Location book\companion once first. The .venv belongs to that companion project; see companion setup.

.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe examples\bayes_scoring.py

Compare its printed posterior, Brier score, and log loss against Sections 2.2 and 2.6 above; they are the same worked numbers by construction, which is a useful way to build trust in both the hand derivation and the code.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 2.1. Derive the posterior odds form of Bayes' rule directly from the two conditional-probability definitions used in Section 2.2, without going through the total-probability expansion. Then use it to recompute the worked case's posterior from prior odds and a likelihood ratio, and convert the result back to a probability.

Solution sketch. Divide \(P(A\mid B)=P(B\mid A)P(A)/P(B)\) by the analogous expression for \(P(A^c\mid B)=P(B\mid A^c)P(A^c)/P(B)\); the shared denominator \(P(B)\) cancels, giving posterior odds equal to prior odds times the likelihood ratio. With prior odds \(0.20/0.80=0.25\) and likelihood ratio \(0.80/0.10=8\), posterior odds are \(2.0\), giving \(p=2/(1+2)\approx0.667\), matching Section 2.2's direct computation.

Exercise 2.2. A base rate is quoted as "70% of contracts of this type resolve YES," drawn from a reference population of 40 historical contracts. You are told, after the fact, that 15 of those 40 came from a single recurring weekly series sharing one underlying process. Explain why this base rate may overstate the effective evidence behind it, using the dependence-group concept from Section 2.5.

Solution sketch. If 15 of the 40 observations are draws from one recurring, correlated process rather than 15 independent trials, the true number of effectively independent data points is smaller than 40; a base rate computed by simple counting treats all 40 as equally informative, overstating precision and potentially anchoring on whatever idiosyncratic run of outcomes that one series happened to produce. A defensible estimate would either model the within-series correlation explicitly or report the base rate separately by series alongside an honest, smaller effective sample size.

Exercise 2.3. Using the four-observation example from Section 2.6, suppose a fifth forecast is added: \(\hat p_5=0.0\) for an observation where \(y_5=1\). Recompute the Brier score and explain what happens to the log loss, without performing a numerical clipping workaround.

Solution sketch. The Brier score becomes \(\frac{0.01+0.09+0.16+0.04+1.00}{5}=\frac{1.30}{5}=0.26\): a finite, if much larger, number, because the squared error contribution from a maximally wrong confident forecast is bounded at 1. Log loss, by contrast, becomes \(+\infty\), because the fifth term is \(-\log(0)\), which diverges; the correct response is to report and investigate this infinite loss (it flags a forecaster who was certain and wrong), not to substitute a small nonzero probability after the fact to make the number finite.

Exercise 2.4. Explain, using the odds form of Bayes' rule, why evidence that is equally likely under a hypothesis and its complement cannot move a Bayesian forecaster's probability, however emotionally compelling that evidence feels.

Solution sketch. If \(P(B\mid A)=P(B\mid A^c)\), the likelihood ratio is exactly 1, so posterior odds equal prior odds, and therefore posterior probability equals prior probability; the evidence carries zero Bayesian information regardless of how vivid or persuasive it seems, because "informativeness" here is defined strictly by how differently the evidence's probability depends on the hypothesis, not by its emotional salience.

docs.text: The Brier score and log loss conventions in this chapter are the book's own explicit definitions, chosen for consistency with the notation registry. Gneiting and Raftery's proper-scoring-rules paper has been directly inspected for this book (its abstract, Section 1, the Section 2.1 definitions, Section 2.3, and Sections 3.1-3.2 including Theorem 2 and the categorical Brier/log-score examples), and is the source substantively supporting Section 2.6's propriety claims and the single-YES-versus-doubled-categorical-sum comparison above; its remaining unread pages and proofs were not inspected, so treat any claim beyond the cited sections as unverified. GNEITING2007 Brier's original verification paper and Murphy's score-decomposition paper remain qualified bibliographic pointers in the source ledger — their original text was not accessible during this book's research audit — so they are recorded here as further reading rather than as verification of any specific historical formula or decomposition. BRIER1950 MURPHY1973 Chapter 10 returns to proper scoring in more depth, including calibration and discrimination, once forecast-evaluation infrastructure has been introduced in Part II.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Chapters 1 and 2 (event contract shapes, the \(Z\)/\(Y\)/\(R\) distinction, probability, Bayes' rule, and proper scoring). Comfort with basic algebra and the notion of an expected value as a probability-weighted average.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this chapter you should be able to: distinguish a model probability from an executable price; compute expected value using executable costs rather than a naive midpoint; explain why capital commitment and abstention are legitimate parts of a decision, not afterthoughts; and reproduce the book's canonical cost, expected-value, and exit-profit arithmetic from first principles.

docs.title: 3.1 A probability is not a decision
docs.text:
Chapter 2 built the machinery to hold a disciplined belief, \(\hat p\), about a contract's YES outcome. That belief is not, by itself, a decision to buy, sell, or do nothing. A decision additionally requires: an executable price at which the position can actually be entered; the costs of entering and, eventually, exiting or holding to settlement; a bound on how much capital the decision commits and for how long; and a comparison against whatever the trader would otherwise do with that capital and attention. Skipping any of these steps and comparing a forecast probability directly to a market's last-traded price or midpoint is one of the most common and most consequential shortcuts a newcomer takes.

The registry is explicit about this distinction: \(m\), a market forecasting benchmark such as a fresh, meaningful midpoint, is not an executable price. For an immediate liquidity-taking action, a buyer sweeps executable asks \(a\) and a seller sweeps executable bids \(b\), at the specified size. A resting maker order can instead buy at its own bid or sell at its own ask if a counterparty later matches it; that requires a separate fill assumption, not a midpoint fill. A forecast that beats the midpoint by a wide margin can still fail to beat the ask by any margin at all, particularly when the bid-ask spread is wide relative to the apparent edge.

docs.title: 3.2 Expected value with executable costs
docs.text:
Expected value, in this book's model-conditional sense, is a probability-weighted average of the net outcomes of a specified action, computed under a stated model and a stated set of executable prices and costs. For a simple buy-\(Q\)-units-of-YES decision at ask \(a\) with a per-unit fee \(f\), held to ordinary binary settlement, the total executable cost is

\[ \text{cost}=Q(a+f), \]

and the model-conditional expected net profit at model probability \(\hat p\) is

\[ \mathbb E_{\hat p}[\Pi]=Q\hat p - \text{cost} = Q(\hat p-a-f). \]

This is the same arithmetic introduced in Chapter 1, now stated as a general rule rather than a single number. Applying the book's canonical values, \(Q=10\), \(a=0.40\), \(f=0.01\), \(\hat p=0.55\):

\[ \text{cost}=10(0.40+0.01)=4.10,\qquad \mathbb E_{0.55}[\Pi]=10(0.55-0.40-0.01)=10(0.14)=1.40. \]

The expression \(Q(\hat p-a-f)\) makes the decision's sensitivity explicit: profitability under the model requires \(\hat p\) to exceed the all-in per-unit cost \(a+f\), not merely to exceed the raw ask \(a\). A forecaster who checks only "is my probability above the ask" while ignoring fees is systematically overstating how many opportunities clear a genuine bar. Two immediate consequences of the linear form are worth internalizing. First, size \(Q\) scales expected profit linearly but does not change whether the sign of the per-unit edge is positive; a bad per-unit edge does not become good by trading more units, it just becomes a bigger version of the same bad decision. Second, the expression is a conditional expectation under \(\hat p\): it says nothing about the variance of the outcome (a single YES/NO settlement is about as high-variance as a bet can be, since the entire quantity resolves to one of two values), and it says nothing about whether \(\hat p\) itself is well-calibrated. Chapter 22 develops sizing and portfolio-level risk in depth; this chapter deliberately isolates the single-position expected-value calculation from that larger question.

docs.title: 3.3 Costs are not always a flat per-unit constant
docs.text:
The canonical example's flat USD 0.01 per-unit fee is chosen for arithmetic clarity, not realism. Two complications matter in practice, and both are represented faithfully in the companion code rather than glossed over.

Depth-limited execution. A displayed best ask is only good for a limited quantity. If a trader wants to buy 15 units but only 10 are available at the best ask of USD 0.40, with the next 20 units available at USD 0.42, the realized cost of a full-size buy sweeps both levels:

\[ \text{gross}=10(0.40)+5(0.42)=4.00+2.10=6.10, \]

for an average fill price of \(6.10/15\approx0.4067\), worse than the best-ask price alone. Adding the same flat fee of USD 0.01 per unit across all 15 units gives a total fee of USD 0.15, for an all-in executable cost of USD 6.25. This is not slippage in the sense of an unexpected price move; it is the mechanical consequence of finite displayed depth, known in advance from the order book itself. A decision process that assumes unlimited quantity at the best-displayed price will misprice any order whose size approaches or exceeds the top-of-book quantity.

Reserved cash for resting orders. A resting limit order that has not yet filled still requires cash to be set aside for its worst-case fill price, not merely its expected fill price, because the order could fill at any price up to its limit. The companion's screen uses the worst displayed price needed for the requested size as its proposed limit. Its reservation then allows for separate one-unit fills, rounding each unit's price upward to cents and adding the independently rounded one-unit fee before multiplying by quantity. The broker uses the order's submitted limit for the same calculation. This reserved amount can exceed an aggregate sweep cost because of better actual prices or less fragmented rounding. That is why "available cash" and "cash committed to open orders" must be tracked separately.

docs.title: 3.4 Capital commitment and the cost of being tied up
docs.text:
Buying a contract and holding it to settlement commits capital for the entire holding period, during which that capital cannot fund another opportunity. This is the glossary's "capital lockup" concept, and it matters even when the expected-value arithmetic above is positive. A contract with a modeled expected profit of USD 1.40 held for one day is a very different proposition from an otherwise identical contract held for six months, even though the per-unit expected-value calculation in Section 3.2 does not, by itself, contain a time dimension.

Two practical consequences follow. First, comparing two candidate positions purely on expected profit without regard to their expected holding periods can favor a position that ties up capital for far longer to earn a similar or even smaller total return; an implicit "return per unit of time committed" framing is often more useful for ranking candidates than raw expected profit, though this book does not endorse any single universal annualization convention, since holding periods for event contracts are frequently uncertain rather than fixed. Second, a risk budget must account for reserved cash from all open positions and orders simultaneously, not just the incremental order under consideration; a decision that looks safe in isolation can violate a portfolio-level cash constraint once existing commitments are included.

docs.title: 3.5 Abstention is a legitimate output
docs.text:
A recurring theme of this book, stated plainly in the glossary, is that abstention — choosing not to trade — is a valid decision, not a failure of the analysis. Two distinct reasons justify abstention, and it is worth keeping them separate because they call for different remedies.

The modeled edge does not clear costs. If \(\hat p\leq a+f\) (or more generally, if the expected net profit does not exceed some minimum required buffer, which might be strictly positive to account for model uncertainty), the arithmetic of Section 3.2 says the expected value of buying is non-positive under the stated model, and abstaining is simply the decision that arithmetic. Suppose the model instead assigns \(\hat p=0.40\), exactly equal to the ask: \(\mathbb E_{0.40}[\Pi]=10(0.40-0.40-0.01)=10(-0.01)=-0.10\), which is negative, so the decision is to abstain even though the model's assessed probability equals the market's headline price — the fee alone is enough to flip the sign.

The risk budget does not permit the size. Even a positive expected-value trade can and should be rejected if it would exceed a stated maximum order cost or push total committed cash past a stated ceiling. This is a deliberate, separate check from the expected-value sign; a small, clearly profitable-looking trade should still be refused if the account cannot actually afford its worst-case cash requirement, or if it would leave too little cash available for other, unrelated obligations.

Both reasons are visible directly in the companion's screening function, which returns a structured decision rather than a bare yes/no: a status of "NO_TRADE" together with a stated reason (either that the modeled edge does not exceed the stated cost buffer, or that the cash and loss budget does not permit the size), or a status the companion labels "PAPER_CANDIDATE_ONLY" — a label chosen deliberately to avoid implying that clearing both checks constitutes live trading evidence. Passing both checks means the arithmetic and the budget are consistent with a candidate paper position; it is explicitly not a claim of a validated live edge.

docs.title: 3.6 Exit before settlement, and not double-counting the spread
docs.text:
A position need not be held to settlement. Selling ten units at an executable bid of USD 0.46, with an additional exit fee of USD 0.01 per unit, realizes

\[ 10(0.46-0.40-0.01-0.01)=10(0.04)=0.40 \]

in round-trip profit — between the binary settlement outcomes of minus USD 4.10 and plus USD 5.90. Once the stated sale actually fills, that profit is realized rather than conditional on the eventual settlement; before the fill, the bid is still only a quote. The entry used the ask (0.40); the exit used the bid (0.46); each leg already reflects its own side of the spread. Subtracting an additional "spread cost" would double-count a friction already included. Slippage is a further difference between a stated reference executable quote and the actual fill — for instance, if the bid moved to 0.44 before execution — not a second subtraction of the same spread.

docs.title: 3.7 Assumptions, counterexamples, and failure modes
docs.text:
Assumption: the displayed book is stale-free. Every calculation above assumes the order book snapshot used to compute cost is fresh relative to the decision. A stale quote can display a price and depth that are no longer available by the time an order actually reaches the venue; a decision process should check quote age against a stated maximum before trusting the sweep-cost calculation.

Assumption: the model probability is well-calibrated. Section 3.2's arithmetic is entirely conditional on \(\hat p\) being a reasonable assessment. A systematically overconfident model can make many trades look individually profitable in expectation while losing money in aggregate; expected-value screening is not a substitute for the calibration checks introduced in Chapter 2 and developed further in Chapter 10.

Counterexample: a positive expected value that should still be refused. A trade with \(\mathbb E_{\hat p}[\Pi]=+0.50\) but a worst-case cash reservation that would push committed cash from 80% to 140% of a stated ceiling should be refused on budget grounds regardless of its positive sign; a single attractive number should never override an explicit risk constraint.

Failure mode: comparing \(\hat p\) to the midpoint instead of the ask. If the book shows a bid of 0.38 and an ask of 0.40, comparing a model probability of 0.39 to the midpoint of 0.39 makes the trade look exactly break-even; comparing correctly to the ask of 0.40 (plus fees) shows the trade is actually unprofitable in expectation. The midpoint is a forecasting benchmark, useful for evaluating a model against a market's implied belief, not an executable price for sizing a trade.

Failure mode: ignoring depth when sizing. As Section 3.3 showed, assuming the best-displayed price applies to an entire order size understates cost whenever the order size approaches or exceeds the top-of-book quantity; this failure grows more severe exactly when the trader most wants to act at scale.

docs.title: 3.8 Companion example
docs.text:
The companion script payoffs.py, already introduced in Chapter 1 for its settlement paths, also runs the expected-value screening decision described in Section 3.5: given a model probability of 0.55, a size of ten units, the canonical fee schedule, a stated risk budget, and stated available and committed cash, it reports the executable cost, the modeled expected profit, and the resulting decision status. It also runs the resale calculation from Section 3.6 using the same position. The screening decision and the cash it tracks live only in that Python process's in-memory paper ledger; there is no durable order-management system, and reconciliation inside the companion is an internal consistency check, not exchange-grade bookkeeping. Run it from the companion project root (book\companion):

Command working directory: run this chapter's Python commands from book\companion. From the trading repository root, run Set-Location book\companion once first. The .venv belongs to that companion project; see companion setup.

.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe examples\payoffs.py

Compare its reported initial_cost and modeled_expected_profit_at_p_0_55 fields against Section 3.2's USD 4.10 and USD 1.40, and its resale_realized_profit field against Section 3.6's USD 0.40; all three are the same worked arithmetic performed by independent code rather than by hand.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 3.1. A trader wants to buy 25 units of YES. The book shows an ask of USD 0.55 for 10 units and USD 0.58 for the next 30 units. A flat fee of USD 0.02 per unit applies. Compute the total executable cost and the average fill price.

Solution sketch. Gross cost is \(10(0.55)+15(0.58)=5.50+8.70=14.20\). Fees are \(25(0.02)=0.50\). Total executable cost is \(14.70\), and the average fill price (excluding fees) is \(14.20/25=0.568\), worse than the best-displayed ask of 0.55 because the order exhausted the first level.

Exercise 3.2. Using the cost from Exercise 3.1, at what model probability \(\hat p\) does the expected value of this 25-unit trade become exactly zero, ignoring any minimum required buffer?

Solution sketch. Expected value is \(25\hat p - 14.70 = 0\), so \(\hat p = 14.70/25 = 0.588\). Any model probability at or below 0.588 makes this specific trade non-positive in expectation; note this breakeven probability is above the best-displayed ask of 0.55 precisely because of depth-limited execution and fees.

Exercise 3.3. A risk budget sets a maximum order cost of USD 10.00 and a maximum committed cash of USD 12.00. The trader already has USD 9.00 committed to other open positions. A new candidate order costs USD 3.50 and has positive expected value. Should it be permitted?

Solution sketch. The order cost (3.50) is below the maximum order cost (10.00), but total committed cash after the trade would be \(9.00+3.50=12.50\), which exceeds the maximum committed cash of 12.00. The order should be refused on portfolio-level cash grounds even though its individual cost and its expected value are both favorable in isolation.

Exercise 3.4. Explain why "the model says 0.55 and the market's last trade was at 0.40" is not, by itself, sufficient justification to buy, and list the two additional pieces of information required before a decision can be made.

Solution sketch. A last-traded price is neither an executable ask nor a guarantee that the same price remains available; the decision additionally requires (1) the current executable ask (and its available depth) at the size intended, together with any applicable fees, to compute an actual cost, and (2) a check against a stated risk budget covering both the individual order's worst-case cost and its effect on total committed cash, since a favorable-looking expected value can still be refused on capital grounds.

docs.title: Sources and further reading
docs.text: This chapter's expected-value, cost, and abstention framework is developed independently from the notation registry's stated conventions and from the companion code's implemented risk-screening logic; no external source is claimed as its origin. The distinction between executable prices and a forecasting-benchmark midpoint, and the requirement to treat abstention as a legitimate decision, recur throughout the empirical price-interpretation literature discussed in Chapter 4, particularly the caution that a market price approximates a belief under specific conditions rather than serving as a free, frictionless executable quote. WZ2006

docs.title: 4. What a market price can tell you
Prerequisites
docs.text: Chapters 1-3 (contracts versus payouts, probability and Bayes' rule, expected value with executable costs). Comfort with the idea that an average combines information from multiple sources, and with basic sampling intuition (that repeated correlated observations are not the same as repeated independent observations).

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this chapter you should be able to: explain the economic mechanism by which a market price can aggregate dispersed information; state precisely what conditions are required for a price to approximate a mean belief, and why "price equals objective probability" is a stronger and generally unsupported claim; describe one real empirical comparison between a prediction market and an alternative forecasting method, together with its stated sample limitations; and avoid three specific inferential mistakes that this literature warns against.

docs.title: 4.1 The economic intuition: why aggregation can work at all
docs.text:
Before any citation or formula, it is worth building the mechanism in plain terms. Suppose one hundred people each hold a noisy, independent piece of information relevant to whether some proposition is true, and each person is willing to trade an event contract up to the price at which their own private assessment says the trade stops being profitable for them. A person who believes the true probability is 0.70 is willing to buy YES up to a price near 0.70 and would sell if the price rose above roughly 0.70; a person who believes it is 0.30 behaves the mirror image. As these hundred people trade against each other, the price tends to settle somewhere that reflects a weighted blend of their individual assessments, because anyone who thinks the current price is wrong relative to their own belief has a direct financial incentive to trade it toward their belief, and that trading pressure only stops (in a stylized, frictionless picture) when the marginal participant is indifferent.

This is the essential mechanism behind calling a price an aggregator of dispersed information: it is not that the price "knows" the truth, but that it reflects the net effect of many participants each acting on their own partial information, weighted (in general) by how much they are each willing to risk. That weighting-by-willingness-to-trade is precisely where the mechanism gets complicated, and where the careful theoretical literature earns its keep, because willingness to trade depends on more than just belief — it depends on risk tolerance, available capital, and the cost of being wrong, none of which are the same thing as "how correct someone is."

docs.title: 4.2 Price as an approximation to a mean belief, not an oracle
docs.text:
Wolfers and Zitzewitz's analysis of interpreting prediction-market prices as probabilities gives sufficient conditions under which a price is closely related to the mean belief of market participants, while also showing that this relationship is an approximation whose quality depends on assumptions such as participants' risk attitudes and the shape of the distribution of their beliefs; outside those conditions the approximation can be biased in a specific, analyzable direction, not merely "less accurate" in a vague sense. WZ2006 The precise, load-bearing phrase here is mean belief, not objective truth. A price can faithfully reflect what a group of participants collectively believes while that collective belief is still wrong, if the group shares a common blind spot, is working from stale information, or is dominated by a small number of large, risk-tolerant participants whose private views happen not to represent the wider available evidence.

Manski's identification analysis sharpens this further and, in some ways, makes it more restrictive. Under a specified model with risk-neutral, price-taking traders holding heterogeneous beliefs, the equilibrium price only partially identifies the central tendency of those beliefs, and does not identify their dispersion at all. MANSKI2004 In plain terms: even granting a fairly favorable set of modeling assumptions, a single scalar price cannot, by construction, tell you both "what most people think" and "how much people disagree" — two pieces of information that a raw price necessarily collapses into one number. This is not a claim that markets fail to aggregate information; it is a precise statement about what a single equilibrium price can and cannot identify even in a model built to be friendly to the aggregation story. A reader who wants a dispersion estimate needs additional structure — for example, several related contracts, a full distribution of prices across different thresholds of the same underlying quantity, or an entirely different data source — not just one price.

Taken together, these two results support a specific, carefully bounded claim used throughout this book: a price approximately reflects a mean belief under stated conditions; it is not, without further argument, the true objective probability of the underlying event. The gap between "approximates a mean belief" and "equals the truth" is exactly where naive interpretations of prediction markets go wrong, and it is why this book consistently writes \(p\) as a probability under a stated model or information set rather than as a mysterious ground truth that a price reveals.

docs.title: 4.3 An actual empirical comparison, and what its numbers do and do not support
docs.text:
Theoretical identification results tell you what is possible in principle; empirical work tells you what has actually been observed in a specific historical setting. Berg, Nelson, and Rietz compared the Iowa Electronic Markets' contemporaneous vote-share forecasts against 964 national polls spanning five United States presidential elections from 1988 through 2004, and reported that the market's forecast was closer to the eventual two-major-party vote split than the polls in 74 percent of those comparisons. BERG2008

This is a genuine, specific, real result, and it deserves to be stated precisely rather than either dismissed or oversold. Four qualifications, all directly tied to the source's own stated scope, must accompany it.

First, 964 polls are not 964 independent elections. The underlying reference-class problem is exactly the one raised in Chapter 2: if a large share of those 964 polls are drawn from a small number of election cycles — here, five — then many of the individual poll comparisons share a common outcome and common macro-level drivers (the state of the economy, the incumbent's approval, the specific candidates running that year). Treating 964 as if it represented 964 separately drawn, independent tests of "market versus polls" substantially overstates the statistical weight of this evidence.

To make the shrinkage concrete without pretending to reproduce the source's own internal statistics: suppose, purely as an illustrative assumption and not a measured figure, that polls within a single election cycle are equicorrelated with correlation \(\rho\), and there are on average \(n\approx964/5\approx193\) polls per cycle. The variance of the mean of \(n\) equicorrelated observations, each with variance \(\sigma^2\), is \(\sigma^2(1+(n-1)\rho)/n\), so the effective sample size — the number of independent observations that would produce the same variance — is

\[ n_{\text{eff}}=\frac{n}{1+(n-1)\rho}. \]

At a hypothetical \(\rho=0.5\) (chosen only to illustrate the mechanism, not measured from the source), \(n_{\text{eff}}=193/(1+192\times0.5)=193/97\approx1.99\): under this variance model, the 193 within-cycle measurements have the same mean variance as roughly two independent measurements. Five independent, equally sized cycles would give roughly ten such effective measurements, not 964. This is not an effective-sample-size estimate for Berg and colleagues' analysis: actual cycle sizes, correlations, and the quantity being averaged matter. The directly established count is five election outcomes behind the 964 comparisons.

Second, the estimand is vote share, not winner-take-all probability. The comparison is about how close each forecasting method came to the actual percentage of the two-party vote, not about how well either method predicted the probability that a given candidate would win. These are different targets: a vote-share forecast of 52% for the incumbent is a point prediction on a continuous scale, while a winner-probability forecast of 0.90 is a probabilistic statement about a binary outcome, and the same underlying data can produce a good vote-share forecast alongside a poorly calibrated win-probability forecast or vice versa. A reader should not silently substitute "the market predicts winners better than polls" for what the source actually measured.

Third, five elections is a small and selected setting. All five cycles come from one country's presidential elections, using one specific market (the Iowa Electronic Markets), over a bounded historical period. Whether the same relationship holds for legislative races, other countries, other time periods, or markets with different participant compositions, liquidity, and rules is a separate empirical question that this comparison does not answer.

Fourth, forecast accuracy does not establish post-cost trading profit. The comparison concerns which forecasting method landed closer to the eventual vote share; it says nothing about whether a trading strategy built on that market's prices would have cleared executable costs, capital lockup, and risk constraints of the kind developed in Chapter 3. A closer forecast is not the same claim as a profitable trade, and this source should not be cited as evidence for the latter.

It is also worth noting, as a small point about intellectual honesty in sourcing, that the institutional page hosting this abstract lists a different page range than the publisher-deposited bibliographic record for the same article; the source ledger discloses that discrepancy rather than silently picking one number, the same standard of care this chapter asks you to apply to the 964-versus-five-elections distinction.

docs.title: 4.4 A broader empirical synthesis, with the same caution
docs.text: Wolfers and Zitzewitz's separate 2004 survey assembles evidence on information aggregation and predictive accuracy across several prediction-market contexts, beyond the single election-focused comparison above. WZ2004 It is valuable as a synthesis spanning multiple settings, but it inherits the limitations of the underlying studies it draws on, and it does not, by itself, distinguish correlation from causation in every surveyed context: a market being associated with accurate outcomes in a historical episode does not establish that the market's structure caused the accuracy, as opposed to both being driven by the same information environment. Read this source, like the comparison above, as specific historical findings bounded by their own settings, not a general law that transfers automatically to a different venue, contract type, or era.

docs.title: 4.5 Assumptions, counterexamples, and failure modes
docs.text:
Assumption: the relevant trader-behavior model applies. Manski's cited model assumes risk-neutral, price-taking traders; Wolfers and Zitzewitz instead discuss how risk preferences and the belief distribution affect price interpretation. Risk neutrality is not a shared prerequisite of both results. A market dominated by a few large or strategically motivated participants can depart from a proposed aggregation model; identify which assumptions fail rather than treating any risk aversion as disqualifying.

Assumption: the market is liquid and current. A thin, stale, or recently reopened market's price reflects whatever small amount of trading has occurred, which may not represent a meaningful aggregate of anything. Applying the "price approximates mean belief" reasoning to an illiquid market with a handful of trades is exactly the kind of context the underlying theory does not cover.

Counterexample: a well-aggregated price that is still wrong. If every participant in a market shares access to the same incomplete public information set and no one holds superior private information, the price can faithfully aggregate that shared, incomplete view — and still be wrong once withheld or not-yet-public information is later revealed. Good aggregation of available information is not the same as omniscience about future information.

Failure mode: treating market accuracy in one historical episode as a permanent property. The empirical results in Sections 4.3 and 4.4 describe specific historical settings. A prediction market operating today, on a different platform, with different participants, contract designs, and liquidity, is not automatically covered by a result observed in 1988-2004 U.S. presidential politics.

Failure mode: inferring a trading strategy from a forecasting-accuracy result. As stated in Section 4.3, "the market's price was closer to the truth than the polls" is not the same claim as "buying at the market's price and holding to settlement would have been profitable after costs," and the two should never be conflated when writing up research.

docs.title: 4.6 A worked illustration of aggregation and its limits
docs.text:
Consider three hypothetical forecasters (not real market participants) who separately assess a proposition's probability at 0.30, 0.50, and 0.70. If we explicitly choose an equal-weight linear opinion pool, the result is \((0.30+0.50+0.70)/3=0.50\). This illustrates combining assessments, not a theorem about market clearing: equal capital and distinct information alone do not imply that an actual equilibrium price equals the arithmetic average.

Now suppose a fourth participant enters holding the same information as the second (0.50) but expresses it as two separately sized trades rather than one, effectively appearing twice in the record of "who traded at what price." If a market microstructure analysis naively treats each trade as an independent unit of evidence, it will overweight this duplicated view relative to the two forecasters holding genuinely distinct information — precisely the dependence problem from Section 4.3's discussion of correlated poll readings, now recast as a market-microstructure version of the same mistake. The remedy in both cases is the same: identify the actual number of independent information sources behind an aggregate figure before treating that figure's apparent precision at face value.

docs.title: 4.7 Companion example
docs.text:
The companion script bayes_scoring.py, introduced in Chapter 2 for Bayesian updating and proper scoring, also reports calibration bins that group a set of forecasts by predicted probability and compare each bin's mean forecast to its observed outcome rate. That mechanism is the same statistical tool this chapter uses conceptually to ask whether a market's implied probabilities, taken as forecasts, are well-calibrated against realized outcomes over many markets — a question that requires a genuinely large, non-duplicated, and appropriately time-ordered sample to answer credibly, for exactly the dependence reasons discussed above. Run it from the companion project root (book\companion):

Command working directory: run this chapter's Python commands from book\companion. From the trading repository root, run Set-Location book\companion once first. The .venv belongs to that companion project; see companion setup.

.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe examples\bayes_scoring.py

The script's calibration-bin output is a mechanical demonstration on invented forecasts, not a measurement of any real market's calibration; treat it as a way to see the bin construction concretely before applying the same idea to real, appropriately deduplicated market data in later chapters.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 4.1. A dataset contains 500 rows of market-price snapshots for a single event contract, taken every ten minutes over the final two days before settlement. A colleague proposes treating these 500 rows as 500 independent tests of "does the market price predict the outcome." Explain what is wrong with this proposal, connecting it explicitly to Section 4.3's discussion of the 964-poll comparison.

Solution sketch. All 500 snapshots share exactly one eventual settlement outcome; they are highly autocorrelated repeated observations of a single underlying belief process converging toward one binary resolution, not 500 independent draws. This mirrors the caution that 964 polls drawn from five elections are not 964 independent elections: the correct unit of independent evidence here is closer to "one event," and a rigorous evaluation would need many distinct events, not many snapshots of one.

Exercise 4.2. Explain, in your own words, why Manski's identification result implies that a single market price cannot simultaneously tell you "what most participants believe" and "how much they disagree," and why this matters for a researcher trying to build a confidence interval around a market-implied probability.

Solution sketch. A price is one number, produced by aggregate trading behavior; under the stated risk-neutral, price-taking, heterogeneous-belief model, that one number is shown to only partially reveal the central tendency of participants' beliefs and not to reveal their dispersion at all, since dispersion is a separate feature of the belief distribution that does not have to leave a distinguishable mark on the single equilibrium price. A researcher wanting an uncertainty band around a market-implied probability therefore cannot construct one from the price alone; they need an explicit model of belief dispersion or additional data (such as multiple related contracts) that the raw price does not supply by itself.

Exercise 4.3. A vote-share forecast of 51.5% for a candidate is reported alongside a separate binary win-probability forecast of 0.62 for the same candidate in the same race. Explain why these two numbers are not contradictory even though 51.5% sounds like "barely over half" while 0.62 sounds like "clearly favored."

Solution sketch. The two forecasts answer different questions: the vote-share forecast is a point estimate on a continuous scale describing the expected proportion of votes, while the win-probability forecast describes the probability of crossing whatever threshold determines victory (which may not simply be 50%, depending on the electoral mechanism), incorporating the uncertainty around that point estimate. A close point estimate on the vote share can still correspond to a substantially favored win probability if the estimated uncertainty around that point estimate is small relative to the margin, since even a modest lead becomes a strong favorite once its estimated variability is tight enough.

Exercise 4.4. A research report claims: "because our market-derived forecasts were closer to actual outcomes than a competing poll-based method in a historical backtest, a trading strategy based on buying whichever side the market forecast favored would have been profitable." Identify the specific inferential gap in this claim using Section 4.3's fourth qualification.

Solution sketch. Forecast accuracy (closeness to the eventual outcome) and trading profitability are different estimands; the claim silently substitutes evidence about the former for a conclusion about the latter without ever introducing executable prices, fees, capital lockup, or a risk budget, any of which could turn an accurate-looking forecast into an unprofitable trade once real costs and constraints from Chapter 3 are applied.

WZ2006 MANSKI2004 The synthesis of empirical prediction-market accuracy draws on Wolfers and Zitzewitz's 2004 published survey.
