docs.title: 5. Order books and automated market makers
Prerequisites
docs.text: Chapters 1-4, especially the executable-price discipline of Chapter 3 and the price-interpretation cautions of Chapter 4. Comfort with exponentials, logarithms, and basic algebra. One optional differentiation step connects a cost function to its marginal prices; the loss bound itself uses only elementary inequalities.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this chapter you should be able to: describe how a real central limit order book (CLOB) represents depth, queue priority, and order types, and why that representation differs from a textbook single "price"; derive the logarithmic market scoring rule's (LMSR) cost function behavior and its bounded-loss property from first principles, given the liquidity parameter \(B\); compute LMSR prices and trade costs for a small worked example and explain what the parameter \(B\) controls economically; and state clearly why LMSR is a mechanism-design construction, not a description of how either Kalshi or Polymarket's live order books work.

docs.title: 5.1 Two different objects called "a market"
docs.text:
This book has so far treated "the market" as a source of an executable ask and bid. That is a black-box view, sufficient for the decision arithmetic in Chapter 3, but it hides two structurally different mechanisms that produce those prices in real venues, and understanding both matters once you start reasoning about depth, price impact, and what a "thin" market really means.

A central limit order book (CLOB) is a list of resting orders on each side of the market, sorted by price and, within a price level, typically by arrival time. Kalshi's documented orderbook response schema returns arrays of bid levels for each side, with a stated dollar price and a fixed-point quantity at each level, and explains that opposite-outcome bids imply the corresponding asks under ordinary binary mechanics. KALSHI_BOOK Polymarket's documented public book interface similarly identifies a specific outcome token and returns price and size levels alongside market constraints and book-state metadata. POLYMARKET_BOOK In a CLOB, prices and depth emerge from whatever independent participants have chosen to post; there is no single formula generating them, and a large buy order sweeps through however much resting liquidity happens to be posted, exactly as Chapter 3's depth-limited sweep-cost example showed.

An automated market maker (AMM), by contrast, is a specified mathematical mechanism that always quotes a price as a function of its own current inventory or state, without requiring an opposing human order to be resting at that moment. The logarithmic market scoring rule, the subject of the rest of this chapter, is one influential AMM design among others, and it is not how either venue examined in this book's documentation operates its central markets — worth stating plainly before working through the mechanism, so the mathematics below is never mistaken for a description of Kalshi's or Polymarket's live books.

docs.title: 5.2 Real CLOB mechanics: depth, queues, and order types
docs.text:
A CLOB's practical behavior depends on several features a single "current price" number does not capture.

Depth is the quantity available at each price level away from the best bid and ask. As Chapter 3 demonstrated, an order whose size exceeds the best level's quantity sweeps into worse prices, and the realized average price depends on the entire depth profile, not just the touch price. A market can have a tight bid-ask spread and still be effectively illiquid for any order beyond a small size if the depth behind the touch is thin.

Queue priority determines which resting order at a given price level executes first when an opposing order arrives. Common conventions prioritize orders by arrival time within a price level, meaning two resting orders at the identical price can have very different chances of filling depending purely on when they were placed. A backtest that does not model queue position, and simply assumes its own hypothetical resting order fills whenever the touch price crosses it, can substantially overstate historical fill rates; the glossary's "queue priority" and "order-book replay" entries flag exactly this risk.

Order types commonly include market orders (execute immediately against the best available opposing depth, accepting whatever price results), limit orders (execute only at a specified price or better, controlling acceptable price but not whether or when a fill occurs), and various conditional or time-in-force variants. A limit order sitting unfilled is not "no position"; it can represent reserved cash (Chapter 3's worst-case reservation logic) with no guarantee of ever executing, and a canceled limit order that never filled produced no cash flow at all despite having been live in the book for some period.

Fixed-point and rounding conventions matter more than they might seem. Kalshi's documented order-book schema represents prices and fixed-point quantities as decimal strings; quantities must not be assumed to be whole integers. Its separate fee-rounding documentation describes rounding behavior accumulated across the fills of a single order rather than applied independently per unit. KALSHI_BOOK KALSHI_ROUNDING A classroom flat per-unit fee, as used in Chapters 1 and 3, is a simplification precisely because it ignores this kind of rounding-accumulator behavior; Chapter 6 returns to the fee-rounding documentation in more depth.

docs.title: 5.3 The LMSR cost function, derived
docs.text:
The logarithmic market scoring rule is a mechanism for a specified automated market maker to always quote a price for each of \(n\) mutually exclusive, exhaustive outcomes, parameterized by a single liquidity parameter \(B\) (written with a capital letter throughout this book specifically to avoid confusion with the executable bid \(b\)). Hanson's foundational treatment develops market scoring rules as a way to combine individual elicitation with group information aggregation, with the logarithmic form carrying particular conditional-probability preservation properties; this book did not independently inspect the full proof of those properties and presents the derivation below as an original, self-contained classroom construction rather than a reproduction of the source's proof. HANSON2007

Let \(q=(q_1,\dots,q_n)\) denote the market maker's current cumulative position in each outcome (how many shares of each outcome have net been sold by the mechanism so far). Assume \(B>0\) and normalize each winning share's payout to one unit of account, so \(C\) is a cost in that unit. Define the cost function

\[ C(q)=B\,\log\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n e^{q_i/B}\right). \]

The price of outcome \(i\) at state \(q\) is the partial derivative of \(C\) with respect to \(q_i\), which works out (by direct differentiation of the log-sum-exp expression) to the softmax function

\[ \pi_i(q)=\frac{e^{q_i/B}}{\sum_{j=1}^n e^{q_j/B}}. \]

These marginal prices are positive and sum to one by construction. That normalization is consistent with the mutually exclusive, exhaustive payout structure assumed here, but it cannot establish that the actual contracts have that structure. The designer still has to verify the outcome space; a softmax over incompatible contracts would normalize prices for the wrong payoff model.

The cost of a trade moving the position from \(q\) to \(q+\delta\) is simply \(C(q+\delta)-C(q)\): the mechanism charges exactly the change in its own cost function, which is why \(C\) is called a cost function rather than merely a pricing function.

docs.title: 5.4 Why the cost function is numerically stable, and why that matters
docs.text:
A direct computation of \(\sum_i e^{q_i/B}\) can overflow for large \(q_i/B\), since exponentials grow extremely fast. The standard remedy, used in the companion implementation, is to factor out the largest term before summing: writing \(q_{\max}=\max_i q_i\),

\[ C(q)=q_{\max}+B\log\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n e^{(q_i-q_{\max})/B}\right), \]

which follows by factoring out \(e^{q_{\max}/B}\) and using \(B\log(e^{q_{\max}/B}S)=q_{\max}+B\log S\). Each remaining exponent is nonpositive; at least one exponential is exactly one, and the sum lies between one and \(n\). This avoids overflow in the exponentials. It does not remove every floating-point limitation: extremely large inputs or subtracting two nearly equal large costs can still lose precision. The companion's large-position example checks a particular finite calculation, not arbitrary numerical magnitudes.

docs.title: 5.5 A worked numerical case: buying into an LMSR market
docs.text:
Take a two-outcome LMSR market (YES/NO) with liquidity parameter \(B=10\), starting from the neutral state \(q=(0,0)\). Initial prices are \(\pi=(0.5,0.5)\) by symmetry, matching the softmax of two equal values.

A trader buys 10 YES shares, moving the position from \((0,0)\) to \((10,0)\). Applying the cost function directly:

\[ C(0,0)=10\log(e^0+e^0)=10\log 2\approx6.9315, \] \[ C(10,0)=10\log(e^{1}+e^{0})\approx10\log(2.71828+1)=10\log(3.71828)\approx13.1326. \]

The trade cost is the difference, \(13.1326-6.9315\approx6.2011\) dollars for 10 shares — noticeably more than the naive \(10\times0.5=5.00\) that the initial price alone would suggest, because the mechanism's price rises continuously as the position moves toward YES. The post-trade price is \(\pi_{\text{YES}}=e^{1}/(e^{1}+e^{0})\approx0.7311\): after this single trade, buying the next marginal share of YES would cost roughly 73 cents, not 50.

Now repeat the identical trade with a larger liquidity parameter, \(B=100\). The same computation gives \(C(0,0)=100\log2\approx69.3147\) and \(C(10,0)=100\log(e^{0.1}+1)\approx74.4397\), so the cost of the same 10-share trade is only about \(5.1249\) — much closer to the naive \(5.00\) — and the post-trade price moves only to about \(0.5250\). This is the precise economic meaning of \(B\): it controls how much the mechanism's price moves in response to a given trade size, in exactly the same conceptual role that order-book depth plays in a CLOB. A larger \(B\) means a "deeper," less price-sensitive market that can absorb larger trades with smaller price impact, at the cost of the operator being willing to accept a larger worst-case loss, which is exactly the quantity derived next.

docs.title: 5.6 The bounded-loss property, derived
docs.text:
A classic and useful property of this cost function is that the market maker's worst-case loss, over all possible sequences of trades and all possible eventual winning outcomes, is bounded by \(B\log n\), independent of how much volume actually trades. Deriving this cleanly requires one elementary inequality about the log-sum-exp function: for any real vector \(x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)\),

\[ \max_i x_i \;\leq\; \log\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n e^{x_i}\right) \;\leq\; \max_i x_i + \log n. \]

The left inequality holds because the sum of exponentials includes the single term \(e^{\max_i x_i}\) plus other nonnegative terms, so the sum is at least \(e^{\max_i x_i}\), and taking logs preserves the inequality. The right inequality holds because every term in the sum satisfies \(e^{x_i}\leq e^{\max_i x_i}\), so the sum is at most \(n\,e^{\max_i x_i}\), and taking logs gives \(\log(\text{sum})\leq \max_i x_i+\log n\).

Apply this with \(x_i=q_i/B\), and multiply through by \(B\):

\[ \max_i q_i \;\leq\; C(q) \;\leq\; \max_i q_i + B\log n. \]

Now consider the mechanism's loss if outcome \(k\) is the one that eventually settles YES: every share of outcome \(k\) that was sold by the mechanism must be paid one dollar, so the mechanism's total payout obligation is \(q_k\) (the final cumulative position in the winning outcome), while the total cash the mechanism collected over all trades is \(C(q)-C(0)\), by repeated application of the cost-difference rule from Section 5.3 summed over every trade. The mechanism's loss is therefore

\[ \text{loss}_k = q_k - \big(C(q)-C(0)\big). \]

Because \(q_k\leq\max_i q_i\leq C(q)\) (the left half of the bound above, applied to the final state), we have \(q_k - C(q)\leq0\), so \(\text{loss}_k\leq C(0)\). And \(C(0)=B\log(\sum_i e^0)=B\log n\) exactly, since every \(q_i\) starts at zero. Therefore

\[ \text{loss}_k \;\leq\; B\log n \quad\text{for every possible winning outcome } k, \]

with the bound approached as the winning outcome's position exceeds every losing position by an arbitrarily large amount. Increasing all positions equally does not approach the bound because only relative positions affect prices. For two outcomes and \(B=10\), the bound is \(10\log2\approx6.93\) units of account. It bounds this cost-function mechanism's payout loss under its stated assumptions, not operational failures, changing payout rules, or an operator's unrelated liabilities. A larger \(B\) buys deeper quoted liquidity at the cost of a larger possible subsidy; the bound is not a profit guarantee.

docs.title: 5.7 Assumptions, counterexamples, and failure modes
docs.text:
Assumption: outcomes are genuinely mutually exclusive and exhaustive. The softmax-sums-to-one structure in Section 5.3 depends on this being true by construction of the outcome space fed into the mechanism. If the underlying real-world outcomes are not actually exclusive (recall Chapter 1's categorical-contract caution), an LMSR built over a mis-specified outcome set produces prices summing to one over the wrong partition — a modeling error, not a mechanism failure.

Assumption: the operator can absorb the bounded loss. The \(B\log n\) bound is an upper limit, not a guarantee the loss is small or affordable; larger \(B\) directly increases the maximum possible loss, so choosing \(B\) trades depth against worst-case subsidy cost rather than being a free parameter to maximize.

Counterexample: splitting an order does not remove its LMSR impact. With no intervening trades, splitting the same net purchase into pieces costs exactly the same as one purchase: \([C(q+\delta_1)-C(q)]+[C(q+\delta_1+\delta_2)-C(q+\delta_1)]=C(q+\delta_1+\delta_2)-C(q)\). The intermediate costs cancel. Waiting can change the result only if other trading changes the state (or additional fees or rules intervene); it does not mechanically make a path-independent cost function cheaper.

Failure mode: treating LMSR as a universal description of live venues. Neither Kalshi's documented order-book schema nor Polymarket's documented public book interface describes an LMSR cost function; both describe conventional order-book structures with independently posted bid and ask levels. KALSHI_BOOK POLYMARKET_BOOK Do not import LMSR's bounded-loss or truthful-elicitation properties into either venue's actual order book without separately verifying that the venue uses this mechanism.

Failure mode: assuming LMSR generalizes beyond two outcomes without checking exclusivity. The multi-outcome case requires the same exclusivity verification Chapter 1 demanded of any categorical contract; convex market-design work extends bounded-payoff mechanism ideas to combinatorial outcome spaces, but design feasibility is a different claim from a guarantee that any two real markets can be costlessly combined into one such structure. ABERNETHY2013

It explicitly labels its own output as illustrating a stable, finite LMSR calculation rather than any real order book's bid. Run it from the companion project root (book\companion):

Compare its reported initial and final marginal prices against Section 5.5's \((0.5,0.5)\) and \(\approx(0.7311,0.2689)\), and its reported trade cost against the derived \(\approx6.2011\); these are the same worked example computed independently by code.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 5.1. Using \(B=100\) (Section 5.5's second case), compute the LMSR price after a much larger trade that moves the position to \(q=(50,0)\), and compare the price impact to the \(q=(10,0)\) case.

Solution sketch. \(\pi_{\text{YES}}=e^{0.5}/(e^{0.5}+e^{0})\approx1.6487/2.6487\approx0.6225\). Compared to the price of about 0.525 after a 10-share trade at the same \(B\), a 50-share trade moves the price noticeably further, illustrating that price impact grows with trade size even at a fixed liquidity parameter, not just as \(B\) shrinks.

Exercise 5.2. For a three-outcome LMSR market with \(B=5\), compute the worst-case bound on the operator's loss, and explain in one sentence why adding a fourth genuinely exclusive outcome to the same market, at the same \(B\), increases that bound.

Solution sketch. The bound is \(B\log n=5\log3\approx5.4931\). Adding a fourth outcome increases \(n\) to 4, giving \(5\log4\approx6.9315\); the bound grows with \(\log n\) because the initial cost \(C(0)=B\log n\) (the cost of committing to quote prices for a wider exclusive partition before any trading occurs) itself grows with the number of outcomes being simultaneously covered.

Exercise 5.3. A backtest replays a historical order book by assuming a hypothetical resting limit order at the touch price always executes whenever a later trade crosses that price level. Explain, using the queue-priority concept from Section 5.2, why this assumption can overstate historical performance, and propose one concrete way to make the assumption more conservative.

Solution sketch. Without knowing the hypothetical order's actual arrival time relative to other resting orders at the same price, the backtest cannot know its true queue position; if many other orders were already resting ahead of it, the touch price could be crossed several times over by other participants' orders before the hypothetical order would actually reach the front of the queue and fill, so assuming an immediate fill overstates the number and speed of fills the strategy would have realized. A more conservative approach would require the touch price to be crossed by some minimum multiple of the hypothetical order's own size, or require a specified time delay past the first crossing, before assuming a fill, and would report both assumptions explicitly as replay simplifications rather than as measured executions.

Exercise 5.4. Explain why the statement "LMSR guarantees the market maker will lose at most \(B\log n\)" is a statement about mechanism design, not a statement that any real prediction-market venue examined in this book is bounded-loss, and identify the specific documentation gap that prevents extending the claim to Kalshi or Polymarket.

Solution sketch. The \(B\log n\) bound is a mathematical property of the specific cost function \(C(q)=B\log\sum e^{q_i/B}\) derived in Section 5.6; it applies only to a mechanism that actually implements this cost function as its pricing rule. Neither Kalshi's inspected order-book documentation nor Polymarket's inspected order-book documentation describes such a cost function; both describe independently posted bid/ask levels from a central limit order book, so there is no basis in the inspected documentation for attributing an LMSR-style bounded-loss guarantee to either venue's actual market structure.

Hanson's foundational paper and Abernethy, Chen, and Vaughan's convex-optimization extension are recorded as further reading for the general market-scoring and convex-mechanism-design literature that motivates this construction, and their full theorem statements were not independently inspected for this book. docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Chapters 1-5, especially Chapter 1's \(Z\)/\(Y\)/\(R\) distinction (informal event, contractual outcome, realized payout) and Chapter 5's order-book mechanics. No new mathematics is introduced; this chapter is about reading and reasoning carefully about documented rules.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this chapter you should be able to: enumerate the specific documented settlement, void, and exceptional-payout mechanics of Kalshi and Polymarket as inspected in this book's research audit; compute the accounting consequences of a void, fractional, or delayed settlement using the book's canonical position; distinguish collateral, custody, and currency-unit risk from event-probability risk; and identify, rather than paper over, the current unknowns in each venue's documentation, including geographic eligibility.

docs.title: 6.1 Why this chapter is deliberately narrow and citation-heavy
docs.text:
Every other chapter in this book builds general concepts that should remain true regardless of which specific venue a reader eventually uses. This chapter is different by design: it works through two specific, real venues' documented rules, because settlement risk is not a generic mathematical object you can derive from first principles the way Bayes' rule or the LMSR cost function can be derived. It is a matter of what a specific operator's specific documentation, retrieved on a specific date, actually says. Every claim in this chapter about Kalshi or Polymarket is tied to a named, dated source in the research ledger, and every claim carries the same warning the ledger itself carries: official documentation describes the retrieved page at the time it was inspected, not a permanent contract with future readers, and it can change.

This chapter's treatment is also explicitly incomplete in scope. It is not marketing material, a comparison ranking, an endorsement, or a complete legal or fee summary for either operator. It is a worked demonstration of the specific documented mechanics that bear on the \(Y\)/\(R\) distinction from Chapter 1, on the accounting conventions used throughout this book, and on the unresolved questions a careful reader should keep asking rather than assume away.

docs.title: 6.2 Kalshi: settlement, rounding, and the live/historical boundary
docs.text:
Kalshi's documented settlement guide describes ordinary YES/NO contracts paying out according to net-position settlement, with settlement timing that varies by contract rather than being instantaneous or uniform across all markets. KALSHI_SETTLEMENT The same documentation distinguishes zero fees for a simple, ordinary YES/NO determination from the possibility of sub-cent scalar-settlement fees and rounding effects on other contract types, meaning "settlement" is not a single uniform mechanical event across every contract Kalshi lists; a scalar or otherwise non-binary contract can carry settlement mechanics that a purely binary mental model misses entirely. KALSHI_SETTLEMENT

The separate fee-rounding guide distinguishes trade fee, rounding fee, and rebate, with balance precision depending on membership or clearing type and an accumulator across fills of one order. KALSHI_ROUNDING That differs from both the canonical flat classroom fee and the companion's independent cent rounding per fill. An accumulator may offset rounding that would otherwise accumulate across fragmented fills; its existence alone does not prove that splitting an order raises the final fee. Trace the actual applicable schedule, accumulator, and rebates before drawing that conclusion for a real account.

Kalshi's historical-data documentation describes a live/historical partition governed by moving cutoff timestamps, retrievable through a documented endpoint, with different object types (for example, individual markets versus broader event or series containers) subject to different partition times; events and series remain available through their original endpoints even as individual market data moves across the cutoff. KALSHI_HISTORY The important limitation, stated plainly in the ledger, is that this endpoint list does not establish that a complete historical order-book archive exists or is retrievable; a researcher should verify what depth of historical order-book state, if any, is actually available for a specific historical window before assuming a full historical order-book replay (Chapter 5's order-book mechanics, applied retrospectively) is possible.

Finally, Kalshi's own demo environment documentation is worth citing precisely because of what it explicitly disclaims: it provides a mock-funds environment with credentials separate from production, and it explicitly warns that demo prices and behavior may not reflect real markets. KALSHI_DEMO A mechanics test conducted in a demo environment is a legitimate way to learn an API's request and response shapes; it is not evidence about real liquidity, real price behavior, or real profitability, and this book does not treat it as such anywhere.

docs.title: 6.3 Polymarket: resolution, disputes, and the Unknown outcome
docs.text:
Polymarket's documented resolution process states directly that a contract's specific rules, not its market title, determine settlement, and describes a proposal-and-challenge flow (a proposed outcome, a challenge period during which the proposal can be disputed, and — for disputed cases — a documented vote table) rather than an instantaneous automatic determination. POLYMARKET_RESOLUTION The documentation further describes an "Unknown" exceptional outcome, reached through this dispute process, under which each side's token redeems for USD 0.50 rather than USD 0 or USD 1 — a genuine, documented third state that a purely binary \(Y\in\{0,1\}\) model cannot represent. POLYMARKET_RESOLUTION

This is directly the fractional-payout case introduced abstractly in Chapter 1 and demonstrated concretely in the companion code, now grounded in an actual documented mechanism at a specific real venue. Consider the canonical classroom position: ten YES units bought at USD 0.40 with the invented USD 0.01 per-unit fee, for an initial cost of USD 4.10. Applying a half-unit payout to that USD example gives total receipts of USD 5.00 and net profit

\[ 10\times0.50-4.10=5.00-4.10=0.90, \]

a positive but structurally different result from either ordinary binary outcome (+5.90 or -4.10). It does not establish which side of the original question was correct. Nor does it make the two tokens cease to have a constant combined payout: 0.50 plus 0.50 is still one unit of collateral. Contrast this with a hypothetical full-refund void convention: if an operator returned the entire USD 4.10, including the invented entry fee, net profit would be zero. If only the USD 4.00 purchase notional were refunded, profit would instead be minus USD 0.10. Neither refund convention is established for either venue by the inspected resolution page; "void" alone does not specify the cash flows. A training pipeline must predeclare how ordinary binary outcomes, exceptional fractional payouts, and any actual refund rules are represented rather than rounding them all into binary labels. Section 6.4 separately explains why a venue's collateral payout is not automatically risk-free cash USD.

Polymarket's documentation additionally describes "additional context" clarifications that can be issued for a market after trading has already begun. POLYMARKET_RESOLUTION This is the concrete, documented instance of the Chapter 1 assumption that "the rules are stable once trading opens" can fail: a clarification issued mid-market changes what a correct forecast needed to account for, and a model trained purely on the earliest version of a market's rules text may be implicitly trained on a slightly different contract than the one that eventually settles.

The Polymarket markets-and-events documentation, already introduced in Chapters 1 and 5 for its caution about event groupings not automatically being exclusive partitions, adds one further operational detail relevant here: order-book trading additionally requires a specific enableOrderBook property on the market, meaning not every listed market necessarily supports the central-limit-order-book trading model described in Chapter 5 at all. POLYMARKET_MARKETS A researcher assuming uniform order-book access across an entire dataset of listed markets should verify this property rather than assume it.

docs.title: 6.4 Collateral and custody: pUSD, USDC, and what "USD" means
docs.text:
This book's canonical accounting examples are written in plain USD for pedagogical simplicity. Real collateral mechanics can differ substantially from an implicit assumption of simple, riskless cash. Polymarket's documentation describes its own collateral instrument, referred to as pUSD, as a Polygon-network ERC-20 token representing a claim on underlying USDC, with documented wrapping and unwrapping operations and an operator-controlled pause gate. POLYMARKET_COLLATERAL Separately, Polymarket's fee documentation describes market-specific taker fees that depend on share price and quantity, together with a distinction between fee-free categories and maker-side treatment, rather than a single flat schedule. POLYMARKET_FEES

Three distinct units appear across this cluster of documentation, and they are not interchangeable: USD, the plain currency unit this book's classroom examples use; USDC, a specific stablecoin that Polymarket's own materials describe pUSD as representing a claim on; and pUSD, the wrapped token that actually moves through the platform's own trading and settlement flows. A trader holding pUSD holds a token whose value is designed to track USDC, which is in turn designed to track the US dollar, but each link in that chain is a distinct claim with its own operational mechanics — wrapping, unwrapping, a pause gate, smart-contract risk, and reliance on the issuing entities behind the stablecoin — rather than a single riskless unit. The operator's own description of these mechanics is exactly that: an operator description, not an independent audit of reserves, contract security, or redemption guarantees, and this book does not treat it as one. A model's probability estimate about an event's outcome says nothing whatsoever about the separate question of whether the collateral backing a position can actually be redeemed at face value when needed.

Kalshi's documented settlement and fee-rounding materials, by contrast, describe cash balances directly rather than an intermediate wrapped token, but they too specify balance precision that depends on membership or clearing type, meaning "how much cash you actually have, to what precision" is itself governed by documented account-level rules rather than being a universal constant. KALSHI_ROUNDING

docs.title: 6.5 Changes, latency, and eligibility: what remains genuinely unknown
docs.text:
Two categories of documented limitation deserve to be named directly rather than smoothed over.

Documentation changes and latency. Every official-documentation source cited in this chapter was retrieved on a single audit date; each source's own status explicitly notes that it describes mutable documentation. KALSHI_SETTLEMENT KALSHI_ROUNDING KALSHI_HISTORY POLYMARKET_RESOLUTION POLYMARKET_COLLATERAL POLYMARKET_FEES A fee schedule, a rounding accumulator, a historical-data cutoff, or a dispute-resolution timeline read today may differ from the same page next month; any implementation relying on these mechanics must be rechecked against current documentation before being trusted, and this book's own citations should be understood as a snapshot, not a permanent specification.

Eligibility is a genuinely open question, not a resolved one. This book's research audit attempted to inspect Polymarket's terms of use and received only a partial official response: the retrieved page displayed a geographic and product notice stating that trading on the main polymarket.com product was blocked for the United States, pointing instead to a separate polymarket.us product, without the audit successfully retrieving the complete operative terms for either product. POLYMARKET_TERMS This is explicitly recorded in the ledger as a partial official response, not a verified statement of full eligibility rules, current account requirements, or data-reuse permissions for any reader in any jurisdiction. Do not treat this chapter, or any other part of this book, as resolving whether a particular reader in a particular location is currently eligible to use a particular product; that determination requires independently and currently checking the specific operator's specific current terms for the specific product in question, at the time of the reader's own inquiry, not this book's audit-date snapshot.

docs.title: 6.6 Assumptions, counterexamples, and failure modes
docs.text:
Assumption: settlement is a single instantaneous event. Both Kalshi's variable settlement timing and Polymarket's proposal-challenge-vote flow show that "settled" can be a process with a duration and, in disputed cases, a nontrivial timeline, not an instant. A capital-lockup calculation (Chapter 3) that assumes zero settlement delay can understate how long capital is actually tied up.

Assumption: a binary label always exists. Section 6.3's Unknown/50-50 case and the void-with-refund case both produce payouts, or absence of payout, that do not correspond to \(Y\in\{0,1\}\). A machine learning pipeline that blindly assigns 0 or 1 to every historical row destroys real information and can introduce systematic label noise concentrated exactly in the contracts that were, by nature, the most contested or ambiguous ones.

Counterexample: two "identical-sounding" contracts with different rule mechanics. A binary contract on one venue and a superficially similar contract on another venue can have different dispute processes, different exceptional-state payouts, and different collateral instruments; treating them as fungible for a cross-venue arbitrage argument (a topic developed further in Chapter 20) requires verifying all of these, not just comparing headline prices.

Failure mode: assuming a demo environment measures real liquidity. Kalshi's own documentation disclaims this directly; a strategy validated only against demo-environment behavior has not been validated against real order-book depth, real counterparty behavior, or real fee application.

Failure mode: treating a wrapped collateral token as risk-free cash. pUSD's documented wrapping and pause-gate mechanics introduce operational and smart-contract risk layers that a plain-USD accounting model, like this book's canonical examples, does not represent; a real position denominated in pUSD carries risk beyond the modeled event probability.

Failure mode: assuming current eligibility from an old reading of terms. Given the partial and time-stamped nature of the terms-of-use inspection recorded here, any claim of eligibility more than momentarily should be independently rechecked at the time of actual use, not inferred from this chapter's audit-date snapshot.

docs.title: 6.7 Companion example
docs.text:
The companion script payoffs.py, already used in Chapters 1 and 3, includes exactly the exceptional-fractional settlement path discussed in Section 6.3: it settles the canonical ten-unit position at a payout of USD 0.50 per unit, reports the resulting realized profit and cash balance, and confirms that the resulting binary label is undefined (not 0, not 1) under this book's settlement representation. It also demonstrates that attempting to compute an ordinary binary proper score against that fractional-payout observation is explicitly rejected rather than silently coerced into a binary label. As throughout this book, the settlement is applied to an in-memory paper ledger for illustration; it is not a durable record and it is not a substitute for a venue's own settlement process described in Sections 6.2 and 6.3. Run it from the companion project root (book\companion):

Command working directory: run this chapter's Python commands from book\companion. From the trading repository root, run Set-Location book\companion once first. The .venv belongs to that companion project; see companion setup.

.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe examples\payoffs.py

Compare its reported profit for the exceptional_fractional settlement path against Section 6.3's computed USD 0.90, and note that its binary_ML_label field for that same path is reported as undefined rather than as a rounded 0 or 1 — the direct code-level expression of this chapter's central caution about settlement risk and machine learning labels.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 6.1. Using the canonical position (10 YES units, USD 0.40 ask, USD 0.01 per-unit fee, USD 4.10 initial cost), compute net profit under: (a) ordinary YES settlement, (b) ordinary NO settlement, (c) the documented Unknown/50-50 exceptional outcome, and (d) a full-refund void. State which, if any, produce a well-defined binary machine-learning label.

Solution sketch. (a) \(10(1.00)-4.10=5.90\); (b) \(10(0)-4.10=-4.10\); (c) \(10(0.50)-4.10=0.90\); (d) refund of the full USD 4.10 cost basis gives net profit of exactly \(0.00\). Only (a) and (b) produce payouts in \(\{0,1\}\) per unit and therefore a well-defined binary label; (c) and (d) require an explicit non-binary or missing-label representation, not a rounded substitute.

Exercise 6.2. A researcher builds a training dataset by pulling every historical Kalshi market's final settlement value from a database, without checking each row's source vintage against the documented live/historical cutoff mechanism. Identify one concrete way this could introduce an error, referencing Section 6.2.

Solution sketch. Because different object types (individual markets versus event or series containers) are documented to move across the live/historical boundary at different times, a naive bulk pull risks mixing records retrieved through different endpoints with different completeness or update guarantees, and does not by itself establish that historical order-book depth (as opposed to final settlement values) is available for the same historical window; a researcher should verify, per object type, which endpoint and cutoff actually governs the specific fields being used, rather than assuming uniform coverage.

Exercise 6.3. Explain why "pUSD tracks USDC, and USDC tracks the US dollar" is not the same claim as "a position denominated in pUSD carries no risk beyond the underlying event's probability," using the specific documented mechanics from Section 6.4.

Solution sketch. Each link in that chain (pUSD-to-USDC, USDC-to-USD) is itself a distinct claim resting on separate operational mechanics — Polymarket's own documented wrapping, unwrapping, and pause-gate controls for pUSD, and separately, the reserve and redemption mechanics of the underlying stablecoin issuer for USDC — none of which have been independently audited by this book; a probability estimate about the underlying event says nothing about whether any of these additional mechanical or counterparty links function as intended when a trader actually attempts to redeem value.

Exercise 6.4. A reader outside the United States asks whether they are eligible to trade on a specific Polymarket product today. What does this chapter's research actually establish about that question, and what should the reader do before concluding they are eligible?

Solution sketch. This chapter's research establishes only that a retrieved page displayed a notice blocking the main polymarket.com product for United States users and pointing to a separate polymarket.us product, without the audit successfully retrieving either product's complete current operative terms; it establishes nothing about a non-U.S. reader's eligibility for either product. The reader should independently retrieve and read the specific product's current terms of use at the time of their own inquiry, since eligibility rules are exactly the kind of mutable, product- and jurisdiction-specific detail this book's audit-date documentation snapshot cannot settle on their behalf.

docs.title: Sources and further reading
docs.text: Every substantive factual claim in this chapter about Kalshi or Polymarket mechanics is tied to a specific official-documentation source inspected during this book's research audit on a stated date, and each source's own recorded limitations apply in full: mutable documentation describes the retrieved page, not a permanent specification, and a partial official response (as for Polymarket's terms of use) must not be silently upgraded into a verified eligibility or permission claim. KALSHI_DEMO KALSHI_HISTORY KALSHI_BOOK KALSHI_ROUNDING KALSHI_SETTLEMENT POLYMARKET_FEES POLYMARKET_RESOLUTION POLYMARKET_COLLATERAL POLYMARKET_BOOK POLYMARKET_MARKETS POLYMARKET_TERMS None of these sources, individually or together, establishes a guarantee of profitability, a permanent fee schedule, or unrestricted geographic eligibility for any reader.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Read Part 1, especially the distinction between an informal event and a contractual instrument (Chapter 1), probability as a modeled quantity rather than an oracle (Chapter 2), and rules, venues, and settlement risk (Chapter 6). This chapter assumes you can read a schema table, reason about set membership, and compute a weighted average by hand. It does not assume prior experience with data engineering.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this chapter you should be able to: separate an event family, an event instance, a venue contract, an outcome token, and a rule version into distinct identifiers; explain why a non-binary or exceptional payout must be represented before it is coerced into a YES/NO label; design a predeclared selection rule that keeps unresolved and excluded records visible instead of silently dropped; and state, for a candidate dataset, which of five provenance categories it belongs to: an invented synthetic fixture, a real retrospective extract, a live market snapshot, a genuinely prospective collection, or an authorized exchange archive. You should also be able to explain why a licensing gap is a research-design constraint, not an afterthought to resolve once collection is finished.

docs.title: 7.1 Four things a headline conflates
docs.text:
A market's short title is a compressed description of something the book already warned against treating as self-explanatory. Before any statistical work can begin, a research dataset needs to separate at least four distinct concepts that a headline collapses into one sentence.

An event family is a recurring question template: the same kind of proposition, asked repeatedly with a similar structure, such as "will the recorded monthly value exceed the previous month's recorded value." A family is a design convenience for pooling related observations. It is not evidence that every instance behaves identically, and treating family membership as automatic independence is a mistake this book returns to repeatedly.

An event instance is one concrete realization of that family tied to a specific calendar period or occurion, for example the specific comparison between one named month and its predecessor. A contract is a particular venue's tradable object that references an event instance: it has its own rules text, its own resolution source, its own token identifiers, and potentially its own effective dates, even when two contracts on two venues appear to ask the same informal question. An outcome token is the specific tradable side of a contract, such as its YES leg or one option within a categorical event; a binary contract ordinarily has two complementary tokens, while a categorical event can have several, and the token identifier is what actually trades, not the informal outcome description.

Finally, a rule version is a specific, dated statement of the resolution procedure. Rules can be clarified or amended after a contract begins trading. The inspected Polymarket resolution documentation describes an additional-context clarification process and an exceptional Unknown/50-50 outcome in which each token redeems at 0.50 rather than a binary 0/1 payout. POLYMARKET_RESOLUTION That single documented fact already tells you two design requirements: the payout space for a contract is not always {0, 1}, and the resolution text that governs a particular historical decision must be the version that was in force at that time, not whatever version happens to be currently displayed.

docs.title: 7.2 Why the separation is not academic
docs.text:
Consider a concrete, if invented, scenario to see why conflating these identifiers damages a study rather than merely complicating its paperwork. Suppose a researcher is building a dataset of "will candidate X be certified as the winner in region Y" questions. Two different venues each list a contract for what looks like the same underlying election. If the dataset assigns each venue's contract its own independent event identifier, an evaluation that reports one score per row will implicitly treat the two venues' realized outcomes as two independent pieces of evidence about the world. They are not: both contracts typically resolve from the same underlying authoritative announcement. A single certification event produces two correlated contractual labels, not two independent draws.

The fix is not to discard one of the two contracts. It is to record a dependence-group identifier that both contracts share, distinct from either contract's own identifier, so that any later evaluation or resampling procedure can treat them as one cluster of dependent observations rather than as two independent rows. The companion's EventRow schema, examined in the next chapter, keeps event_id, group_id, and family_id as three separate fields for exactly this reason: its synthetic fixture happens to set group_id equal to event_id because each invented event has only one realized outcome represented by two feature snapshots of the same event, but a real cross-venue dataset would need group_id to span multiple contract identifiers whenever they share an underlying settlement source. Recording this distinction at schema-design time is cheap. Reconstructing it after the fact, once two years of rows have already been logged with only a flat contract identifier, is often impossible, because the information linking the two venues' contracts to a shared settlement event may not have been retained anywhere in the collected data.

A parallel conflation happens with rule versions. If a dataset stores only "the current rules text" alongside a historical row, and that text is later edited after a clarification, the dataset silently rewrites history: a contract that traded for six months under one resolution definition now appears, in the stored data, to have always operated under the amended definition. The remedy is to store a rule-version identifier and its effective timestamp alongside every contract row, and to change that identifier only when the underlying text changes, never retroactively.

docs.title: 7.3 The non-binary payout, worked from first principles
docs.text:
Say a category-style contract can resolve to one of three payouts: one dollar, forty cents, or zero, depending on which of three documented resolution branches applies. Write \(R\) for the realized per-unit payout and \(\mathcal R=\{0,\,0.40,\,1\}\) for its possible values. A model assigns probabilities \(P(R=1)=0.52\), \(P(R=0.40)=0.18\), and \(P(R=0)=0.30\); these three numbers must sum to one, and they do here: \(0.52+0.18+0.30=1.00\).

The expected payout is the probability-weighted sum over the payout set:

\[ \mathbb E[R]=\sum_{r\in\mathcal R} r\,P(R=r)=1(0.52)+0.40(0.18)+0(0.30)=0.52+0.072=0.592. \]

Now compare two ways of building a "binary classification target" from this same contract. The careless approach collapses \(R\) into \(Y=\mathbf 1\{R>0\}\), treating the forty-cent branch as an ordinary YES. Under that coding, \(P(Y=1)=0.52+0.18=0.70\), and a classifier trained on \(Y\) would be predicting a quantity that no longer corresponds to any tradable payout: a position bought at an ask of USD 0.65 would look attractive against a 0.70 YES probability, yet the actual expected payout is USD 0.592, and the arithmetic edge the naive framing suggested (0.70 - 0.65 = 0.05) has nothing to do with the true expected settlement value (0.592 - 0.65 = -0.058, before any fee). The disciplined approach keeps \(R\) as the labeled quantity, models its full distribution over \(\mathcal R\), and only forms a binary label when a specific research question genuinely calls for one, documenting the coding rule explicitly rather than assuming it away.

This is not a claim that categorical contracts are common or that this specific 0.52/0.18/0.30 split describes any actual market; the numbers are invented to make the arithmetic concrete. The lesson transfers directly to the documented Polymarket exception: if a dataset simply assigns \(Y=1\) to every settled-YES row and \(Y=0\) to every settled-NO row, an Unknown/50-50 resolution has no honest binary code. Recording it as either 0 or 1 manufactures a label that never existed; the schema needs a place to keep the actual payout value, a way to flag it as exceptional, and a decision, made in advance of any analysis, about whether such rows are excluded, retained as a separate multiclass target, or converted into an appropriately weighted training instance.

docs.title: 7.4 Selection: who gets to be a row
docs.text:
A dataset does not assemble itself. A researcher chooses an eligibility rule, and that choice is itself part of the empirical claim. Suppose the intended population is "all contracts within event family \(F\) that began trading between two fixed dates." A naive collection strategy queries a live listing endpoint at the end of that window and keeps whatever contracts still appear. This strategy silently excludes any contract that was already delisted, cancelled, or moved to a historical-only endpoint before the query ran; the documented Kalshi historical-data guide explicitly warns that live and historical partitions are governed by moving cutoffs and object-specific fields, so a query against only the live surface at one point in time is not equivalent to a complete historical listing. KALSHI_HISTORY The glossary calls this failure mode survivorship bias, and it applies as much to a dataset-construction script as it does to a trading backtest.

A workable predeclared rule instead fixes the population by a stable identifying property, not by what a single query happens to return. For example: "every contract of family \(F\) whose rule text was published between the two dates, collected from both the live and historical endpoints, with an explicit record of which endpoint supplied each row." A concrete accounting example makes the bookkeeping habit explicit. Suppose 500 candidate contract identifiers are found across both endpoints. Of these, 40 are excluded because no rule text could be retrieved for any version, and a further 15 remain unresolved (no final payout recorded) as of the freeze date chosen for the study. The dataset should report all three numbers: 500 candidates, 40 excluded for missing rules, 15 retained as censored unresolved rows, and 445 retained with a realized payout. Reporting only "445 labeled contracts" without the other three numbers hides exactly the information a reader needs to judge whether the missingness could be related to the outcome being studied, for example if markets that resolve unfavorably to a popular narrative are disproportionately represented among the unresolved set at freeze time.

Selection also interacts with licensing. A predeclared eligibility rule cannot include data a researcher is not permitted to redistribute or, in some cases, even to retain past a specified period. That constraint has to be decided before collection, not discovered afterward when a contributor tries to publish the resulting extract.

docs.title: 7.5 A conceptual minimum schema
docs.text:
The table below states a conceptual minimum for a multi-source research dataset. It is a design target, not a claim that the companion already implements every column. Its EventRow is a small recurring-event schema with distinct event, publication, observation, decision, and label-availability timestamps, but only one shared publication/observation pair for all features in a row. It does not represent every feature's separate source clock or the cross-venue, categorical-payout generality shown here. Those require additional provenance and validation.

Field Conceptual role event_family_id Recurring question template; a pooling convenience, not proof of independence. event_instance_id One concrete calendar realization within a family. contract_id A specific venue's tradable object referencing the instance. venue The operator and product, since two venues' rules can differ even for a shared instance. outcome_token_id The specific tradable side actually quoted and filled. dependence_group_id Shared identifier across contracts/instances tied to one underlying settlement source. rule_version_id and rule_effective_at The dated resolution text actually in force for this row. resolution_source The stated authority or procedure that determines the payout. payout_space The full set of contractually possible payout values, not assumed to be {0, 1}. realized_payout The actual settled value, kept distinct from any derived binary label. censored_flag Whether an outcome remained undetermined as of the dataset's freeze time. license_basis The specific permission or public-domain basis for retaining and sharing this row.

Building every column in this table for a live venue is a substantial undertaking, and this book does not claim to have done so. What it commits to is smaller and more honest: keeping these concepts distinct in any schema you do build, and refusing to compress them prematurely for convenience.

docs.title: 7.6 Provenance categories, and why this book keeps five separate ones
docs.text:
The feasibility review behind this book's real-data chapters reached a specific, narrow conclusion: no established, small, redistributable, complete point-in-time prediction-market order-book dataset was identified. Official venue documentation is a useful interface for future prospective collection, but an accessible API is not a redistribution license, and a historical price series is not a historical order book. This book therefore keeps five provenance categories strictly apart, and every dataset or example you encounter later should be identifiable as exactly one of them.

A synthetic fixture is intentionally invented data, generated by a documented deterministic process, used to exercise a mechanism or an algorithm. The companion's recurring-event fixture is exactly this: 180 invented events with a stated random seed, an invented logistic latent process, and an explicitly labeled synthetic=True flag on every row. It teaches point-in-time discipline and model plumbing; it says nothing about any real market.

A real retrospective extract is genuine historical observational data, collected and frozen for a specific study, with its provenance, exclusions, and vintage limitations documented. This book's chosen example is the NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory's Mauna Loa monthly carbon-dioxide series, restricted to January 1975 through December 2025 to avoid the earlier Scripps-attributed period, with interpolation-flagged months excluded and the December 2022-July 2023 Maunakea substitution recorded as a location discontinuity. NOAA_CO2 This is real data about a real physical process. It is not prediction-market data, not an issued forecast archive, and not evidence about market prices.

That design has since been carried through to a completed, hash-verified frozen comparison, documented in experiments/README.md: a target-calendar-month Beta(1,1) forecaster scores a single-YES Brier of about 0.032 against an expanding-overall-rate baseline's roughly 0.230 on 132 primary evaluation events (85 YES outcomes, an observed rate near 0.644), with a closely similar paired difference on a 123-event sensitivity cohort that removes the Maunakea-affected months and refits both models on the reduced admitted labels. Reporting this real, checkable number does not loosen any of this section's provenance boundaries. The underlying series remains current-vintage, not a reconstructed historical-vintage archive; its forecast-availability clock is stated plainly, in the study's own protocol, as an explicitly hypothetical retrospective convention, not a verified historical publication record; and the comparison contains no market price, no executable contract, and no claim about trading profitability. A strong, honestly reported seasonal effect in a real physical series is a genuine empirical result about that series and a fair illustration of everything this book asks a frozen confirmatory design to look like; it is not, by itself, evidence about prediction markets, and this book does not claim otherwise anywhere.

A current market snapshot is a live read of a venue's present state, such as a single order-book query. It is useful for understanding today's mechanics and for building a prospective collector, but a single snapshot is not a time series and must never be presented as if it had been recorded historically.

A genuinely prospective record is one collected going forward from the moment of collection, with its own observation timestamps, so that its point-in-time properties are actually true by construction rather than reconstructed after the fact. The companion now ships exactly this kind of collector as an explicitly optional module, prediction_market_lab.market_data, documented in data/README.md and in the examples' own README. It is opt-in in every sense that matters for this chapter's licensing discussion: constructing its client without an explicit acknowledge_terms=True acknowledgement fails outright, its command-line form requires the same --acknowledge-terms flag before any network call, no default example or test ever invokes it, and it acquires and commits no actual venue payload as part of this book. Its acknowledgement flag is a recorded user acknowledgement, not a legal eligibility determination, and this book still has not established an unrestricted venue-data redistribution license for either inspected venue. KALSHI_HISTORY POLYMARKET_TERMS Chapter 8 discusses, and this module's saved snapshot schema concretely implements, what such a collector needs to record; it is not a live broker, not a historical archive, and its native fields are kept entirely separate from anything PaperBroker accepts.

An authorized exchange archive is a dataset obtained under an explicit, checked permission from a venue or data provider, covering historical activity the requester did not personally observe as it happened. This book has not obtained such an archive, and no example claims to use one. If you pursue this path yourself, the licensing question must be resolved and documented before a single row is retained, exactly as the terms-of-use gaps identified for both inspected venues make clear. KALSHI_HISTORY POLYMARKET_TERMS

docs.title: 7.7 Assumptions and failure modes
docs.text:
Every schema choice above rests on assumptions that can fail quietly.

Assumption: a family's instances are behaviorally homogeneous. Failure mode: template drift. A recurring question's exact wording, threshold, or resolution source can shift slightly across instances even while a human reader would call them "the same kind of question." A model or evaluation that pools across a family without checking wording stability can be blindsided by a change that looks cosmetic but alters the actual payout rule.

Assumption: an outcome token maps one-to-one onto a contract. Failure mode: shared liquidity or shared settlement across a set of tokens within one categorical event. The inspected Polymarket documentation on markets and events explicitly separates market and outcome-token identifiers from an event container, and notes that only some multi-market events are mutually exclusive; grouping by container is not proof of an exhaustive, non-overlapping partition. POLYMARKET_MARKETS

Assumption: rule text is stable between collection and analysis. Failure mode: a documented clarification or dispute resolution changes the applicable rule after trading has already occurred under an earlier reading. Recording only "current rules" erases this history.

Assumption: licensing can be resolved after collection. Failure mode: a dataset is built, analyzed, and prepared for release before anyone checks whether redistribution is permitted, at which point the only honest options are to discard the collection effort or restrict the release to derived, non-redistributable summaries.

Assumption: unresolved rows can simply be dropped for convenience. Failure mode: if unresolved status correlates with the outcome under study, for example because contentious or slow-to-resolve markets are also the ones most likely to move against a popular expectation, dropping them silently biases every downstream estimate.

docs.title: Exercise 1: four identifiers, one headline
docs.text:
A news aggregator lists "Will the index close above its prior close on Friday" as a single question. Two venues each offer a contract on this question, with different resolution sources (one uses a real-time feed, one uses an end-of-day settlement print). Name the four identifiers this book asks you to keep distinct here, and state which of them the two venues' contracts do and do not share.

Solution sketch. The event family is the recurring "close above prior close" template. The event instance is this specific Friday's realization. The venues create distinct contracts and outcome tokens because their rules and sources differ. Nevertheless, both contracts depend on the same underlying Friday index movement and should be grouped for that shared exposure, or handled by an explicitly justified dependence model. Their labels need not be identical to be dependent. A dependence group is not a certificate of contractual equivalence: the different source definitions still prevent assuming a riskless hedge.

docs.title: Exercise 2: coercing a non-binary payout
docs.text:
A contract's payout space is \(\{0, 0.30, 1\}\) with modeled probabilities 0.55, 0.10, and 0.35. Compute the expected payout. Then compute what a careless YES/NO coding with \(Y=\mathbf 1\{R>0\}\) would report as \(P(Y=1)\), and explain why the two numbers should not be compared to the same ask price.

Solution sketch. Expected payout is \(1(0.35)+0.30(0.10)+0(0.55)=0.35+0.03=0.38\). The careless binary coding gives \(P(Y=1)=0.35+0.10=0.45\). Comparing an ask price to 0.45 answers a question about a manufactured label that does not correspond to any single tradable payout; comparing it to the true expected payout of 0.38 is the only calculation with a defensible economic interpretation, and even that comparison still needs the executable ask, applicable fees, and the model's own uncertainty before it says anything about a favorable action.

docs.title: Exercise 3: reporting selection honestly
docs.text:
A collection effort finds 240 candidate contracts. Eighteen have no retrievable rule text at any version and are excluded. Twelve remain unresolved at the freeze date. Report the full accounting a reader would need, and explain one plausible way the unresolved group could bias a naive "resolved-only" analysis.

Solution sketch. Report 240 candidates, 18 excluded for missing rule text, 12 retained as censored/unresolved, and 210 with a realized payout. If, for instance, the unresolved 12 are disproportionately contracts nearing a disputed or delayed resolution because the underlying event turned out to be genuinely ambiguous, dropping them could remove exactly the harder cases that a model most needs to be evaluated against, inflating apparent performance on the easier, already-resolved remainder.

docs.title: Exercise 4: naming the provenance category
docs.text:
A student downloads a single current order-book snapshot from a venue's public API, saves it to a file, and later builds a chart from ten such snapshots taken every hour over one afternoon. Which of the five provenance categories in this chapter applies, and what must the student avoid claiming about it?

Solution sketch. This is a genuinely prospective record: each snapshot is collected going forward from its own observation time, with real timestamps. The student must avoid presenting it as historical evidence beyond that single afternoon, avoid treating the ten snapshots as a complete order-book history (gaps exist between polls), and avoid assuming any redistribution permission beyond what the venue's terms actually grant.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: Chapter 8 takes the identifiers and provenance categories introduced here and builds the actual pipeline machinery that keeps every relevant clock, publication, receipt, decision, fill, label availability, and settlement, honestly separated as data moves from a source through to a model.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Read Chapter 7 first: this chapter assumes you already accept that an event family, an instance, a contract, and a rule version must be tracked separately, and that a dataset's provenance category must be stated honestly. You should be comfortable with UTC timestamps and simple set/interval reasoning. No new probability theory is required yet; this chapter is about what a decision is allowed to see, not about how to model it.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this chapter you should be able to: name and distinguish seven clocks relevant to one forecasting decision; explain, with a worked timeline, why "download the latest data" silently violates a point-in-time constraint; describe why a paginated, cutoff-partitioned API requires deliberate query design rather than a single bulk request; explain what a snapshot-based order-book feed can and cannot establish about history; and specify the minimum provenance record a disciplined collector must keep. You should also be able to trace, in the companion's actual validation code, how an availability check and a grouped chronological split enforce these constraints mechanically rather than by convention alone.

docs.title: 8.1 Seven clocks for one decision
docs.text:
A single forecasting decision touches more moments in time than casual description usually admits. This book keeps seven of them separate, because collapsing any two of them into one silently changes what a study claims to have shown.

The event time is when the real-world matter the contract is about actually occurs or is realized, for example the moment a measurement is taken or a vote is certified. The source publication time is when some outside publisher first releases information relevant to the event, which can be before the event (an announced schedule), at the event, or well after it (a delayed release of a measurement). The local observation time is when your own system actually receives and records that publication; a fast publisher and a slow ingestion pipeline can create meaningful separation here that a naive schema ignores. The decision time is the instant your process commits to a forecast or an action, and it is the single most important cutoff: everything used to produce that decision must have been available, in the sense defined below, no later than this moment. The fill time is when an actual order is matched, which can be simultaneous with the decision (aggressive marketable order) or arbitrarily later, or never (a resting order that never executes). The label availability time is when the outcome needed to score or train on this decision becomes knowable, which need not coincide with either the event time or any settlement action. The settlement time is when contractual funds or payouts are actually and finally transferred, which can trail label availability by a dispute or processing window.

None of these seven moments needs to equal any other, and a pipeline that assumes two of them coincide by default is choosing a shortcut, not a law of nature.

docs.title: A concrete worked timeline
docs.text:
The companion's synthetic recurring-event fixture makes a specific, disclosed choice among these clocks, and walking through its actual numbers is a useful way to see the distinctions operate rather than merely list them. For one invented event, the event time is set at 18:00 UTC on a given day. The fixture's decision time is set either twelve or three hours before that event time, representing two snapshots of the same underlying event. For the twelve-hour snapshot, the invented bulletin's publication time is ten minutes before that decision time, and the local observation time is two minutes before the decision. The invented outcome's label availability time is set twelve hours after the event time. All of this is drawn from the same generator used by examples\point_in_time.py, and every one of these fields is an explicit column in the stored fixture, not an inferred convention.

Two lessons follow immediately from writing the numbers down this way. First, publication (ten minutes before decision) and observation (two minutes before decision) are both comfortably before the decision cutoff in this invented design, so both clocks pass an availability check; the fixture also includes, in its own example script, a deliberately constructed "late" row whose observation time is moved to one second after the decision time, and that row is correctly rejected by the availability check. Second, the twelve-hour and three-hour rows for the same event share one outcome and one label availability time, twelve hours after the shared event, even though their decision times differ by nine hours; they must be scored, split, and reported as two dependent glimpses of one event, never as two independent trials.

docs.title: 8.2 Why "download the latest" breaks the clock
docs.text:
A tempting shortcut is to query a provider's current endpoint and treat its value as though it had always been available. NOAA's documentation warns that later quality-control checks can revise monthly values. NOAA_DATA No particular revision magnitude was measured here. For an invented example, suppose a month's mean was first released as 421.30 parts per million and later revised to 421.34. Using 421.34 as an input to a decision that could only have seen 421.30 leaks future information. Even a small revision can also flip a threshold label, but that raises a separate target-definition question: a contract tied to the initial release must be scored against the initial release, whereas a predeclared final-vintage target can legitimately be scored later against its final outcome. Evaluation labels are normally unknown at prediction time; leakage occurs when those future labels or revisions influence an earlier feature, fit, calibration, or selection decision, not merely because the eventual target was uncertain.

The general principle is that a data field has a vintage: a version of a record as it existed at a specific publication time. A complete point-in-time archive would store, for every reported value, every vintage and the timestamp at which each vintage became public, so that a historical query can ask "what did this field say as of this specific past date" rather than "what does this field say now." This book's data-feasibility review is explicit that no such vintage archive was established for the NOAA series used in its real-data study; the chosen extract is therefore explicitly a current-vintage retrospective series, and a date-ordered split of it cannot recover the historical vintages a contemporary decision-maker would actually have seen. The honest response is not to pretend the limitation away, but to state it plainly in every place the dataset is used, exactly as the data-feasibility document does, and to avoid any claim that a chronological ordering of a current-vintage series reconstructs historical information availability.

docs.title: 8.3 Paginated, cutoff-partitioned APIs
docs.text:
A live trading venue's historical interface is rarely a single flat file. It is typically a paginated API: each request returns a bounded page of records plus a cursor or continuation marker, and a complete retrieval for a given window requires repeatedly requesting subsequent pages until the provider signals there are no more. A pipeline that requests only the first page, or that stops as soon as it has "enough" rows for a quick look, has silently applied an undocumented, request-order-dependent selection rule to its own dataset.

Cutoffs compound this. The inspected Kalshi historical-data documentation describes live and historical partitions governed by moving cutoffs, with different object types, such as market settlement records and trade creation records, governed by different cutoff fields. KALSHI_HISTORY A pipeline that queries only the "live" surface for a window that has since aged past the live cutoff will silently miss records that moved to the historical surface, and a pipeline that assumes every object type shares one cutoff will misdate some of what it retrieves. The general design requirement, independent of any single provider's exact field names, is threefold: identify which surface (live or historical) is authoritative for the requested window before querying; paginate exhaustively rather than opportunistically; and record, for every retrieved record, which surface and which page it came from, so a later audit can distinguish "this record was never observed" from "this record was skipped by an incomplete pagination loop."

docs.title: 8.4 Order-book gaps and provenance
docs.text:
An order book is not a static object; it is a live, continuously updated structure, and any archived view of it is a snapshot: a picture of the book's state at one moment. The inspected Kalshi order-book documentation describes string-valued fixed-point dollar prices and quantities in YES/NO bid arrays, with ordinary binary contracts implying an ask from the opposite side's bid. KALSHI_BOOK The inspected Polymarket documentation for its public CLOB similarly returns price and size levels alongside a timestamp, a state hash, a minimum order size, and a tick size. POLYMARKET_BOOK Both are genuinely useful interfaces for observing current depth. Neither establishes a complete historical record of every book state that ever existed, and a state hash identifying one returned snapshot is evidence about that snapshot, not proof that no state was missed between two consecutive polls.

Call the interval between two consecutive recorded snapshots a gap. During a gap, orders can be placed, modified, cancelled, or filled without leaving any trace in a snapshot-based archive; a resting order that appears in one snapshot and is simply absent from the next may have been cancelled, may have been fully filled, or may have been partially filled and then cancelled, and a snapshot-only record generally cannot distinguish these possibilities without an additional trade or fill feed. A disciplined collector therefore has to record, alongside every snapshot, the elapsed time since the previous successfully recorded snapshot for that same book, flag any interval exceeding an expected polling cadence as a gap, and refuse to silently treat a large gap as if it were a normal short interval. This matters directly for anything built on top of the archive: a simulated fill inferred from "the quote was touched at some point between two snapshots" is an assumption about what happened inside a gap, not an observed fact, and the book's glossary is explicit that a resting-order fill must never be inferred from a quote touch alone.

The minimum provenance record for any collected snapshot, whether from an order book, a trade feed, or a rules page, should include: the exact endpoint and parameters requested; the request time and the response receipt time, both timezone-aware UTC; the raw response content or a verifiable hash of it; the schema or version identifier the provider reports, if any; and, for paginated retrieval, the sequence of cursors used to reach completeness. None of this is exotic engineering. It is the difference between a dataset whose limitations can be audited and one whose limitations can only be guessed at.

The companion's now-shipped optional prediction_market_lab.market_data module is a concrete, checkable instance of exactly this discipline, not merely an argument for it. Its documented saved-snapshot schema records, for every page, the exact requested URL, the UTC receive time, an explicit historical_point_in_time: false and snapshot_scope: CURRENT_ONLY label, the original response bytes and a hash of them, a separate hash of the parsed payload, and pagination metadata including whether the traversal was truncated and which cursor or offset a continuation would need. It also records what it does not know: the bundle's own publication_history field is explicitly UNKNOWN rather than guessed from the receive time, and eligibility_or_redistribution_rights_verified is recorded as false rather than silently assumed. Every acquisition requires an explicit --acknowledge-terms flag or acknowledge_terms=True construction argument before any network call is made, no default example or test invokes it, and it writes only new, gitignored .snapshot.json files, never an overwrite of an existing one. It is worth being precise about what this module is not: it is not a live broker, it places no orders and accepts no credentials; it is not a historical archive, since snapshot_scope: CURRENT_ONLY is exactly this chapter's warning that a current read is not a historical vintage; and its preserved native fields, Kalshi's string-valued fixed-point dollar/quantity arrays or Polymarket's native bid/ask levels, are kept entirely separate from PaperBroker, which never receives a raw venue payload from this module.

docs.title: 8.5 How the companion actually enforces these cutoffs
docs.text:
It is worth walking through the actual validation logic. available(published_at, observed_at, cutoff) requires both publication and observation to be at or before the cutoff. Early publication does not help a process that has not received the information, and a receipt timestamp alone cannot make a later publication available sooner. This comparison does not itself validate the ordering or authenticity of the two source timestamps. EventRow.features_available(cutoff) uses the row's decision_at by default. Construction validates field shapes and selected invariants, but does not reject a feature-late row: the deliberately late example can therefore be constructed. The grouped splitter and model feature construction subsequently call the availability check and reject such a row.

grouped_chronological_split builds on this by additionally purging dependence groups, not individual rows, that straddle a training, validation, or test cutoff. Concretely: for each group identifier, the function computes the earliest and latest decision times among that group's rows. A group is assigned to a cohort only if its entire span of decision times falls within that cohort's boundary and every row's label was available by that cohort's own cutoff; if a group's earliest decision time falls before one cutoff while its latest decision time falls after it, the whole group, not just the straddling rows, is excluded from every cohort and recorded in excluded_groups. Applied to the fixture's teaching split, with training up to April 1, validation up to May 16, and final test up to July 1, 2025, this means the two decision-time snapshots belonging to one invented event are never allowed to land in two different cohorts on the strength of clock position alone; they travel together or they are dropped together.
