This is the code-level answer to a common mistake: a time gap between two rows, by itself, cannot certify that they are safe to separate, because if they share a label or a dependence group, the gap says nothing about whether that shared information has leaked across the split.

Running the shipped examples\point_in_time.py against this fixture confirms the mechanism with actual numbers rather than only its logic: of 180 realized events (360 rows), the split assigns 89 events to training, 44 to validation, and 45 to the final test cohort, and it purges exactly two event groups, recorded as toy-0089 and toy-0134, because their decision times or label availability straddled a cohort boundary. Note also that for the fixture's very first row, an explicit check of label_available_at <= decision_at is false, confirming numerically what Section 8.1 argued from the schema alone: this invented label, twelve hours after the event, is never available at either of that event's own decision times, which sit before the event itself. Both facts are observed properties of this one synthetic fixture and its fixed cutoffs; they illustrate the mechanism correctly enforcing itself, not a claim about any real dataset's event counts.

docs.title: 8.6 The label-availability and settlement clocks are not the same
docs.text:
It is tempting to assume that once an event's outcome is publicly known, the corresponding contract is effectively over. The fixture's own design resists this shortcut by keeping label_available_at as its own field, distinct from any notion of final settlement. In a real venue, the analogous distinction is sharper still: the inspected Polymarket resolution documentation describes a challenge period and a dispute process that can follow an initial proposed outcome, meaning that the economically informative outcome may become knowable well before funds are actually and finally released. POLYMARKET_RESOLUTION A pipeline that conflates "the label is knowable" with "the position has settled" risks understating the capital lockup a strategy would actually experience, since funds committed to a position cannot be redeployed elsewhere until settlement, whatever the state of public knowledge about the outcome.

The fill clock deserves the same care. A decision to submit an order is not the same event as that order being matched. A marketable order crossing the visible book may fill close to instantaneously; a resting limit order may fill much later, partially, or never. Treating "decision time" and "fill time" as interchangeable silently assumes perfect, immediate execution, which this book's companion explicitly does not assume: its paper-trading fixtures require an explicit user-supplied event to register any fill, precisely so that a fill is never manufactured out of a quote touch or a decision timestamp alone.

docs.title: 8.7 Assumptions and failure modes
docs.text:
Assumption: publication time equals knowledge time. Failure mode: a publisher can re-release older information, or a report can be embargoed and then released as if new; treating a publication timestamp as automatically fresh information can misdate what a market participant actually learned at that moment.

Assumption: a historical API endpoint is a complete archive. Failure mode: as the Kalshi documentation itself makes clear, historical partitions are cutoff-governed and object-specific; a satisfied query is not proof of completeness, and account-level fill records are not a substitute for every trader's order history.

Assumption: a fixed polling interval has no gaps. Failure mode: network failures, rate limiting, and provider outages create irregular gaps even under a nominally fixed schedule; only an explicit gap-detection check, comparing actual elapsed time between successful snapshots to the intended cadence, catches this.

Assumption: a current-vintage series can be sliced by date to imitate a historical vintage. Failure mode: any revision that occurred after the fact is invisibly baked into every date-sliced value, silently granting a simulated historical decision access to information from its own future.

Assumption: label availability implies settlement, or the reverse. Failure mode: either overstating how quickly capital would actually be freed, or understating how early an economically meaningful outcome could have informed a subsequent decision.

docs.title: Exercise 1: ordering five clocks
docs.text:
An event occurs at 12:00 UTC. A wire report about it is published at 12:05 UTC. Your system actually logs receipt of that report at 12:09 UTC. Your process commits to a forecast at 12:10 UTC. The outcome becomes publicly knowable at 12:30 UTC, but the venue does not release funds until 09:00 UTC the next day. Using the available rule from Section 8.5, was this decision's feature usable at decision time, and is the position settled by the time the label is available?

Solution sketch. The later of publication (12:05) and observation (12:09) is 12:09, which is before the 12:10 decision cutoff, so the feature is usable. The label becomes available at 12:30, well before the next day's 09:00 settlement; the outcome is knowable roughly twenty hours before funds are actually released, illustrating that label availability and settlement are genuinely different clocks here.

docs.title: Exercise 2: a revision at the threshold
docs.text:
A monthly series' first-released value for March is 100.02 and for April is 100.00, so the naively coded "did April exceed March" label is initially NO. A later quality-control revision changes April's value to 100.05. Explain the leakage risk of using the revised value in a study whose stated decision cutoff is one day after the initial April release.

Solution sketch. If the target is the first-released April increase, replacing its NO label with the revised YES changes the target and is incorrect. If the predeclared target is instead the eventual revised increase, that later YES can legitimately be used for evaluation once available; predicting an unknown future label is the point of forecasting. In either design, the revised value cannot enter features, fitting, or calibration before its actual availability. Record both the target's vintage definition and the model's fitting cutoff rather than imposing the impossible requirement that every evaluation outcome already be known at prediction time.

docs.title: Exercise 3: pagination and silent selection
docs.text:
A collector requests one page of 100 historical contract records, receives a cursor for further pages, and stops there because 100 records "look like enough." List two concrete ways this could bias a subsequent analysis.

Solution sketch. If the provider returns records in a systematic order, for example by creation time or by identifier, stopping at one page could concentrate the sample in a narrow slice of the intended date range, silently excluding a large share of the true population. It could also correlate with an unintended property of the excluded majority, such as more recently created or more recently modified contracts being pushed to later pages, biasing any temporal or maturity-related feature computed only from the retained page.

docs.title: Exercise 4: a gap in the order book
docs.text:
Two consecutive successfully recorded book snapshots for one contract are 47 minutes apart, though the intended polling cadence is 5 minutes. A resting bid visible in the first snapshot is absent from the second. What must a disciplined pipeline record, and what must it refuse to claim?

Solution sketch. It must flag the 47-minute interval as a gap relative to the 5-minute intended cadence and record that flag alongside both snapshots. It must refuse to claim that the missing bid was filled; cancellation, a partial fill followed by cancellation, and a full fill are all consistent with its disappearance, and only an independent trade or fill feed, not the order book alone, could distinguish them.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: Chapter 9 uses these same clocks to examine exploratory data analysis: how to look at a dataset honestly before modeling it, without letting that very act of looking quietly consume the evidence a later confirmatory test depends on.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Read Chapter 7 and Chapter 8 first. You should already be comfortable with dependence groups, the seven clocks, and the available and grouped_chronological_split mechanics. This chapter assumes basic descriptive statistics: means, variances, and simple correlation, at the level of an introductory course.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this chapter you should be able to: state what exploratory analysis is for and what it must never be used to justify; apply a feature-availability gate before any exploratory plot or summary; recognize when a naive descriptive statistic silently treats dependent observations as independent, and correct for it at the level of the summary itself; distinguish a predeclared inclusion rule from a convenience filter chosen after looking at results; build a catalog of leakage patterns specific to the exploratory phase; and design a frozen confirmatory analysis that is genuinely protected from everything that came before it.

docs.title: 9.1 What exploration is allowed to do
docs.text:
Exploratory data analysis exists to help a researcher understand structure: what a variable's distribution looks like, whether an expected relationship shows up at all, where data quality problems live, and which modeling choices are even plausible given what the data can support. It generates hypotheses and informs design decisions. It is an essential, legitimate stage of research.

What exploration must never do is quietly become the evidence for the claim a later chapter reports as a result. If a researcher tries several candidate features, several thresholds, and several groupings while looking at how each choice affects apparent performance on the same records that will later be called a "test set," the resulting favorable configuration is not evidence that the configuration works; it is evidence that a sufficiently flexible search process, given enough attempts, can find something that looks good on a fixed sample by chance. This is the essence of the glossary's definition of multiple testing, and it applies just as much to informal visual inspection and ad hoc feature engineering as it does to a documented grid search over model hyperparameters.

The discipline this chapter asks for is not "do not explore." It is: decide, in advance, which portion of your data exploration is allowed to touch, and treat any subsequent confirmatory claim as valid only to the extent that the untouched portion was genuinely never inspected, adjusted for, or used to steer a choice before that claim was finalized.

docs.title: 9.2 The first gate: is this feature even legitimately visible?
docs.text:
Before a predictive feature is plotted as something a historical decision could use, check that it was observable by that row's decision cutoff. Labels obey a different clock: they need to be available by the research or model-fitting cutoff at which they are consumed, not by their own earlier forecast times. Retrospective exploration of training outcomes is legitimate; using eventual test outcomes to design the model is not. Keeping these roles separate prevents both leakage and the mistaken requirement that a forecaster already know its target.

Consider a concrete illustrative mistake. A researcher, while poking at a dataset built from the recurring-event fixture, computes a new candidate summary feature: "the variance of the invented signal across both of this event's recorded snapshots." This sounds like an innocuous descriptive statistic. But an event's later, three-hour-horizon snapshot is only available close to the event itself; a decision made at the twelve-hour horizon cannot possibly know the value that will be recorded three hours before the event, because that later value does not exist yet at the earlier decision time. A "variance across both snapshots" feature computed and then attached to the twelve-hour row has silently pulled information from after that row's own decision cutoff. The fix is not clever statistics; it is running exactly the same features_available check on every derived, engineered exploratory feature that the pipeline already runs on raw fields, before that feature is allowed into any plot, correlation table, or model input, confirmatory or otherwise.

The same discipline applies to summaries that never become model inputs. Looking at the future test period can steer later choices even without an explicit numeric feature entering a fit. On the allowed exploratory period, however, an audit may deliberately compare first and later vintages or examine eventual outcomes to diagnose data quality. Label that work retrospective and keep those later values out of earlier predictive features.

docs.title: 9.3 Repeated observations are not repeated independent evidence
docs.text:
The recurring-event fixture stores 180 invented events, each with two snapshot rows, for 360 rows. To isolate how a sample-count error affects uncertainty, consider the familiar standard-error approximation \(1/\sqrt{n-3}\) for Fisher's transformed correlation, \(z=\tfrac12\log((1+r)/(1-r))\), under independent bivariate-normal sampling. This is not the standard error of the raw correlation \(r\), and the fixture's binary labels do not satisfy that bivariate-normal model. Used only as an arithmetic illustration, plugging in \(n=360\) gives

\[ \frac{1}{\sqrt{360-3}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{357}}\approx 0.053. \]

Duplicating each of 180 genuinely independent pairs does not create 360 independent pairs. Under the illustration's sampling assumptions, the standard error would still be

\[ \frac{1}{\sqrt{180-3}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{177}}\approx 0.075. \]

The ratio is about \(0.075/0.053\approx1.42\): the appropriate standard error in this illustration is about 42 percent larger than the duplicated-row calculation. This is not a measured interval for the fixture's signal-label correlation. Dependence does not universally increase variance: the direction depends on covariances of the statistic's contributions, and negative dependence can reduce it. Nor are 180 and 360 universal lower and upper effective-sample-size bounds. For the companion, one predeclared latest snapshot per event makes the weighting and unit explicit; for an actual correlation claim with binary outcomes, use a justified event-level or grouped uncertainty calculation rather than importing this illustrative normal-theory formula.

The shipped examples\forecast_models.py script shows this same dependency concretely, with an actually observed pair of numbers rather than a hypothetical one. It rescoring a single already-fitted logistic model against both of one specific event's decision-time snapshots, event toy-0135, produces 0.258916 at the twelve-hour horizon and 0.258227 at the three-hour horizon. Those two numbers come from one frozen model evaluated twice, not from two independently trained forecasters, and they describe one realized event whose outcome will eventually be a single shared label; an exploratory summary that averaged or compared these two rows as though they were separate pieces of evidence about two different events would repeat exactly the Section 9.3 mistake with real, not invented, output. It is also worth being precise about what this rescoring is not: it is a fixed model's output evaluated at two different input snapshots, not a fitted sequence model that learns how a forecast should evolve as a horizon shortens, and the companion's own reported limitation for this demonstration says as much, that its early-horizon calibration is unvalidated.

docs.title: 9.4 Selection during exploration
docs.text:
A closely related trap is choosing, mid-exploration, to restrict attention to "the interesting cases": markets with enough volume to be liquid, events that actually resolved by the time you looked, or records with no missing fields. Each of these restrictions can be entirely reasonable. The problem is deciding on them only after seeing how they affect a result you already have an opinion about.

The remedy from the previous two chapters carries over directly: write down the inclusion rule, and its justification, before computing the statistic it will be used to filter. If a liquidity threshold is later found to change the qualitative conclusion, report both the filtered and unfiltered pictures rather than quietly keeping only the one that supports the conclusion you started with. Keep a record of every filtering rule considered during exploration, not just the one eventually adopted; this record becomes essential input to the multiple-testing discussion below, because an unreported sequence of "what if we exclude these" attempts is exactly the kind of informal search that invalidates a naive significance claim on whatever filter is finally chosen.

docs.title: 9.5 A leakage catalog specific to exploration
docs.text:
Three exploration-specific leakage patterns deserve their own names, because each one can occur even when a researcher is being careful about the basic availability gate from Section 9.2.

Aggregated future-looking features. A summary statistic computed "over the whole event" rather than "as of the decision cutoff" quietly imports information from after that cutoff, exactly as in the Section 9.2 example. This pattern is common because aggregation feels like a modeling convenience rather than an information-flow decision.

A temporal gap is not a leakage cure. It is tempting to believe that if a training row's decision time is months before a test row's decision time, the two rows cannot possibly share information. That belief is false whenever the two rows belong to the same dependence group, or to two different groups that share an underlying settlement source, as in the cross-venue certification example from Chapter 7. A nine-hour gap between an event's twelve-hour and three-hour snapshots does not make them independent; they share one outcome and one label-availability time regardless of how far apart their decision timestamps sit. grouped_chronological_split's behavior reflects exactly this: it purges an entire dependence group that straddles a cutoff rather than trusting decision-time separation alone to protect the split.

Repeated informal inspection of the confirmatory cohort. Even without adjusting any code, looking at descriptive plots of what will later be called the test set, and letting that look influence any subsequent choice about features, thresholds, or model family, quietly consumes some of that cohort's evidentiary value. The formal literature on this problem is directly relevant here. White's reality check for data snooping addresses inference after a search over many candidate rules; the false discovery rate framework of Benjamini and Hochberg addresses the risk of reporting an impressive result out of many tested hypotheses; and Bailey, Borwein, Lopez de Prado, and Zhu's probability-of-backtest-overfitting work is specifically concerned with the danger of repeatedly consulting a supposedly held-out sample during model or strategy development. WHITE2000 BENJAMINI1995 BAILEY2017 This book's evidence ledger has directly inspected White's original article through its abstract, introduction, and Section 2a-2b, as far as the stationary-bootstrap construction and the start of its Assumption C. The inspected text is precisely on point for this section's warning: it tests whether the best expected performance across an entire specified candidate family exceeds a stated benchmark, rather than testing only whichever single rule was eventually reported, which is exactly the guard this chapter is asking for when it says that repeated informal looks, not merely a final documented parameter search, belong in the accounting. Its construction resamples dependent data in common random-length blocks under stated stationary, strong-mixing conditions and point-in-time predictors; this book has not audited its full proofs or every regularity assumption, and the method itself cannot retroactively recover an undisclosed history of informal looks that were never logged. The false-discovery-rate abstract inspected here describes an independence-based control result, not an unconditional guarantee under arbitrary dependence; and the Bailey et al. institutional abstract, which was actually inspected, proposes a probability-of-overfitting framework and a combinatorially symmetric cross-validation method, while explicitly warning that repeated holdout inspection undermines exactly the kind of confirmatory claim this chapter is trying to protect. None of these three sources is being used here to certify a specific numeric threshold for this book's own synthetic fixture; they are cited as the established literature behind a principle this chapter derives and applies in its own words: an embargo period placed around a cutoff, by itself, reduces certain forms of adjacency contamination but does not, on its own, cure a shared dependence group or an unavailable label, a distinction the glossary makes explicit under "embargo."

docs.title: 9.6 Designing a frozen confirmatory analysis
docs.text:
The practical fix for all of the above is to split the research process itself into two stages with a hard boundary between them, not merely to split the data.

In the exploratory stage, work only with the training and validation cohorts established by a predeclared, availability-respecting split. Use this stage to understand distributions, check for the leakage patterns above, settle on a small number of candidate feature definitions and model families, and write down, before looking at the confirmatory cohort at all, the exact metric, the exact cohort definition, and the exact comparison that will be reported as the confirmatory result.

In the confirmatory stage, apply that exact, predeclared procedure to the test cohort exactly once. If the result invites a follow-up question, that follow-up is a new piece of exploratory work requiring its own, separately protected confirmatory data, not a second look at the same test cohort with a slightly adjusted procedure. This is a demanding standard, and it is routinely violated in casual research precisely because a single additional look feels harmless in isolation. Its cost is cumulative: each additional look at the same nominally held-out data increases the chance that whatever appears favorable is an artifact of that look count rather than a genuine property of the underlying process, which is the shared concern behind the reality-check, false-discovery-rate, and backtest-overfitting literatures cited above.

docs.title: 9.7 A worked exploratory-to-confirmatory walkthrough
docs.text:
Put the pieces together with one concrete, fully disclosed walkthrough using the synthetic fixture's own cutoffs: training through April 1, validation through May 16, and test through July 1, 2025. During exploration, a researcher restricts every computation to the training and validation cohorts only. Following Section 9.3's lesson, the researcher first collapses each event down to its single latest available snapshot using latest_per_event, producing one row per event rather than two. Following Section 9.2's lesson, the researcher checks that every candidate feature passes features_available before it is even plotted. Following Section 9.4's lesson, the researcher writes down, before looking at any performance number, that the planned comparison is a fixed logistic model against the fixed overall training-cohort event rate, scored by the single-YES Brier score defined formally in the next chapter, on the test cohort's own predeclared latest-snapshot rows.

Only after the plan is fixed does the hypothetical researcher compute the final comparison. An unfavorable result is reported, not used to select a replacement feature set on the same test cohort. The companion enforces part of that discipline: evaluate_forecaster rejects overlap with both fitted event IDs and fitted dependence-group IDs, and selects one latest row per event. It cannot determine whether a human already inspected the test outcomes or chose the design after seeing them. The reproducible toy run illustrates the mechanics, not a software certificate of untouched research.

docs.title: 9.8 Assumptions and failure modes
docs.text:
Assumption: an engineered summary feature respects the same cutoff as its raw inputs. Failure mode: aggregating "across the whole event" silently reaches past the decision cutoff that governs one particular row, as in the cross-snapshot variance example.

Assumption: a wide time gap between two rows is sufficient to treat them as independent. Failure mode: shared dependence groups, shared settlement sources, or shared underlying processes can make two temporally distant rows highly dependent; the gap alone proves nothing.

Assumption: informal visual inspection of a test cohort is harmless because no code was changed. Failure mode: a researcher's subsequent choices, made with that inspection in mind even unconsciously, are no longer independent of the outcome being evaluated, undermining the confirmatory claim exactly as a documented parameter search would.

Assumption: a convenience filter chosen after seeing preliminary results is equivalent to a predeclared inclusion rule. Failure mode: the filter becomes an unreported extra degree of freedom in the analysis, inflating the apparent strength of whatever conclusion survives it.

Assumption: one favorable confirmatory result licenses an additional look at the same test cohort to refine it. Failure mode: each additional look degrades the very property, being untouched before finalization, that made the original result meaningful in the first place.

docs.title: Exercise 1: catching a future-looking feature
docs.text:
A researcher proposes a feature: "the number of snapshots eventually recorded for this event." Explain why this fails the Section 9.2 availability gate for an early-horizon row, and propose an available replacement.

Solution sketch. At the twelve-hour decision point, the process cannot yet know whether a later three-hour snapshot will exist; that count is only knowable once the event's full recording history is complete, which is after the decision. An available replacement is "the number of snapshots recorded for this event strictly before the current decision time," which is zero or a count using only what already exists at decision time.

docs.title: Exercise 2: correcting an inflated correlation claim
docs.text:
A colleague reports a highly significant correlation between a feature and an outcome, computed over 500 rows, and states the standard error using \(n=500\). You learn the 500 rows come from only 210 distinct events, each contributing on average roughly 2.4 rows. What should you ask for before accepting the significance claim, and what is the qualitative direction of the correction?

Solution sketch. Ask for the observation weighting, a predeclared event-level summary, and an uncertainty calculation justified for the actual dependence structure. Repeated positively correlated contributions commonly make the naive standard error too small, but the direction is not guaranteed for every statistic or covariance pattern. Collapsing rows can also change the estimand and point estimate, so it is not merely replacing 500 with 210 in an otherwise unchanged formula.

docs.title: Exercise 3: an embargo is not a cure
docs.text:
A pipeline adds a thirty-day embargo between its training cutoff and its test cutoff, discarding any row whose decision time falls in that window. Does this guarantee that no training row and test row share an outcome-relevant dependence? Justify your answer using the definitions in this chapter.

Solution sketch. No. An embargo removes rows adjacent in decision time, but two rows can share a dependence group, or share an underlying settlement source, without their decision times being adjacent at all, as in the cross-venue certification example. The embargo helps with certain short-range contamination patterns but does nothing by itself to prevent a shared-event or shared-label leak that spans a much larger time gap.

docs.title: Exercise 4: one look too many
docs.text:
After a predeclared confirmatory test shows the candidate model underperforming the base rate, a researcher proposes trying two alternative feature sets against the same test cohort "just to see." What should happen instead, and why?

Solution sketch. The predeclared result should be reported as the finding, including the underperformance, since a negative or inconclusive result is a legitimate outcome. Any further feature sets should be evaluated only against a newly designated, previously untouched confirmatory cohort, or clearly labeled as renewed exploratory work whose conclusions require their own future confirmatory test; reusing the same test cohort a second time turns a confirmatory claim into an informally searched one.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: Chapter 10 turns the disciplined cohorts and dependence groups built here into an actual scoring framework: what a proper probability score is, why it rewards honesty, how to decompose it, and how to attach a dependence-aware notion of uncertainty to the result.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Read Chapter 7, Chapter 8, and Chapter 9 first. You should be comfortable with expectation, variance, and a first derivative as a way to find a minimum, at the level of an introductory calculus-and-probability course. No prior exposure to forecast verification is assumed; every scoring identity used here is derived from these tools rather than quoted from an external theorem.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this chapter you should be able to: derive, rather than merely state, why the single-YES Brier score and natural-log loss are minimized in expectation by a truthful forecast; explain the notation registry's single-YES convention and why it differs from a two-class sum; compute log loss's infinite penalty for an exactly wrong, exactly certain forecast and explain why that is a feature, not a bug; distinguish calibration, sharpness, and discrimination as separate properties of a forecasting system; derive a reliability-resolution-uncertainty identity and show, with a worked numerical counterexample, why it holds exactly only under a grouped-forecast convention and only approximately when applied to a post hoc binned summary of individual forecasts; use a base rate and a market price as baselines without assuming either is beaten; and build a simple, self-derived, dependence-aware adjustment to naive uncertainty estimates for repeated event snapshots.

docs.title: 10.1 What a proper scoring rule promises
docs.text:
A scoring rule assigns a numeric penalty to a probability forecast once the outcome is known. This book calls a scoring rule proper for a stated class of forecasts if, when a forecaster's true belief about the outcome distribution is \(p^*\), reporting \(p=p^*\) minimizes the forecaster's own expected penalty under that belief. It is strictly proper if that minimizer is unique. This is a purely mathematical statement about incentives inside the scoring exercise. It says nothing about whether \(p^*\) was itself a good model of the world, and it says nothing about whether a market price already embedded a better estimate than the forecaster's own. Keeping the incentive property and the real-world question separate is the discipline this whole chapter is built around.

Every propriety argument below is derived independently, from an expectation and a derivative, rather than quoted from an external theorem; the two derivations are this chapter's own, so that the argument stands on its own algebra even where a cited source goes further. Gneiting and Raftery's article on strictly proper scoring rules is the standard foundational treatment of the general theory this section specializes to the binary case, and this book's evidence ledger has now directly inspected its abstract, Section 1, Section 2.1's definitions, Section 2.3, and Sections 3.1-3.2, including its Theorem 2, Examples 1 and 3, and its categorical representation, though not every one of the article's twenty pages or proofs. GNEITING2007 Two details from that inspected text matter directly here. First, the article states its propriety results as rewards to be maximized, the opposite orientation from this chapter's losses to be minimized; every citation below silently reverses that sign convention rather than importing it unchanged. Second, and more importantly for Section 10.3, the article's own categorical squared-error representation sums an error term for every outcome category, which for a binary event is exactly twice this book's single-YES convention, a fact this chapter can now attribute to inspected text rather than only to its own derivation. Strict propriety, the inspected text is also careful to note, is an expectation-level incentive property; it does not by itself guarantee finite-sample calibration or a profitable decision once execution costs are introduced, and an outcome-dependent normalized skill score built on top of a proper score need not remain proper itself. Brier's original 1950 paper remains the historical origin of the quadratic probability score used throughout this book, but it remains a metadata-only record in this evidence ledger after repeated retrieval attempts failed; no specific theorem, numbering, or original formula from Brier's own text is attributed here beyond that bibliographic pointer. BRIER1950

docs.title: 10.2 Deriving that the single-YES Brier score rewards honesty
docs.text:
Let \(Y\) be the realized binary outcome, with \(\Pr(Y=1)=p^*\) under the forecaster's own belief, and let \(p\in[0,1]\) be whatever probability the forecaster chooses to report for \(Y=1\). Define the single-observation Brier penalty as \((p-Y)^2\). Its expectation under the forecaster's own belief is

\[ \mathbb E[(p-Y)^2]=p^*(1-p)^2+(1-p^*)(0-p)^2 . \]

Expand both terms: \(p^*(1-p)^2=p^*-2p^*p+p^*p^2\), and \((1-p^*)p^2=p^2-p^*p^2\). Adding them, the \(p^*p^2\) terms cancel, leaving

\[ \mathbb E[(p-Y)^2]=p^*-2p^*p+p^2. \]

Differentiate with respect to the reported \(p\): the derivative is \(-2p^*+2p\). Setting it to zero gives \(p=p^*\), and the second derivative is \(2\), which is strictly positive, confirming a unique minimum, not a maximum or a saddle point. In plain language: whatever the forecaster genuinely believes about \(p^*\), the expected single-YES Brier penalty is smallest exactly when the reported number matches that belief, and it is smallest by a strict margin, not merely tied with some other report. This is a complete, self-contained derivation of strict propriety for this particular scoring rule; it required nothing beyond expanding a square and taking one derivative.

docs.title: 10.3 Why single-YES, not twice that
docs.text: A different, also common convention scores both the YES and NO probabilities and sums their squared errors: \((p-Y)^2+((1-p)-(1-Y))^2\). Since \((1-p)-(1-Y)=Y-p=-(p-Y)\), this second term equals \((p-Y)^2\) as well, so the two-class sum is exactly \(2(p-Y)^2\), twice the single-YES version. Both conventions are proper scoring rules, by the same argument as above up to a positive constant multiplier, which does not change where the expected penalty is minimized. This is not only this chapter's own algebra: the inspected categorical representation in Gneiting and Raftery's Section 3.1 sums an error term over every outcome category, which collapses to exactly this same doubled two-class sum for a binary event, confirming from directly inspected text that the categorical convention and this book's single-YES convention differ by precisely a factor of two, not by some other unstated amount. GNEITING2007 But the two conventions report different numbers for the same forecasts, and mixing them silently in one manuscript would make a stated score meaningless without knowing which convention produced it. This book's registry fixes the single-YES convention: one squared YES-probability error per binary event, not a doubled two-class sum, and every reported Brier score in this book, in the companion's scoring.brier_score, and in every worked exercise below follows that convention consistently.

docs.title: 10.4 Deriving that natural-log loss rewards honesty, and its infinite penalty
docs.text:
Define the single-observation log loss as \(-Y\log p-(1-Y)\log(1-p)\), using the natural logarithm. Its expectation under the forecaster's belief \(p^*\) is

\[ \mathbb E[-Y\log p-(1-Y)\log(1-p)]=-p^*\log p-(1-p^*)\log(1-p). \]

Differentiate with respect to \(p\): \(\dfrac{d}{dp}\left(-p^*\log p-(1-p^*)\log(1-p)\right)=-\dfrac{p^*}{p}+\dfrac{1-p^*}{1-p}\). Setting this to zero and multiplying through by \(p(1-p)\) gives \(-p^*(1-p)+(1-p^*)p=0\), which simplifies to \(-p^*+p^*p+p-p^*p=0\), and then to \(p=p^*\). The second derivative, \(\dfrac{p^*}{p^2}+\dfrac{1-p^*}{(1-p)^2}\), is strictly positive whenever \(p^*\) is strictly between zero and one, confirming a unique minimum at \(p=p^*\). Natural-log loss is therefore also a strictly proper scoring rule for interior beliefs, derived here the same elementary way as the Brier score: expand, differentiate, check the sign of the second derivative.

Now consider what happens at the boundary. If a forecaster reports \(p=0\) and the outcome turns out to be \(Y=1\), the loss is \(-\log(0)\), which is not a large finite number; it is unbounded, and this book follows the natural-log convention of recording it as infinite rather than silently substituting a small clipped probability. The companion's bayes_scoring.py example computes exactly this case and confirms it directly: log_loss([1], [0]) returns inf, verified by running the shipped example in this book's own environment. By contrast, log_loss([0, 1], [0, 1]), a perfectly confident forecast that happens to be exactly correct on both observations, returns 0.0, using the ordinary calculus limit that \(y\log y\to 0\) as \(y\to 0^+\) so that a correct certain forecast contributes nothing to the loss. The asymmetry is deliberate and important: log loss punishes confident wrongness without any upper bound, while confident correctness costs nothing, which is exactly the incentive a disciplined forecaster wants, since it makes issuing an extreme probability a claim that must be backed by genuine certainty rather than a way to game an average score.

docs.title: 10.5 Calibration, sharpness, and discrimination are different questions
docs.text:
A forecasting system can fail, or succeed, along at least three distinct axes, and conflating them is one of the most common mistakes in reading a scoring result.

Calibration asks whether, among all the cases assigned a particular probability, the outcome actually occurs at close to that rate. A system that always reports the same base rate, say 0.30 for every event in a population where 30 percent of events actually occur, is perfectly calibrated in that narrow population sense: 30 percent of its 0.30-labeled cases really do occur. It is also nearly useless for distinguishing individual cases from one another.

Sharpness concerns concentration of each predictive distribution, independently of the realized outcome. For a Bernoulli forecast, \(p(1-p)\) measures dispersion: probabilities near zero or one are sharper than probabilities near one-half. Sharpness is not distance from a base rate. A constant 0.01 forecast is sharp even though it offers no ranking of individual cases.

Discrimination asks whether a system actually separates cases that go on to occur from cases that do not, regardless of whether its stated numbers are calibrated. A system that ranks events correctly by their true likelihood, while being poorly calibrated on the numeric scale it reports, has good discrimination but bad calibration.

The always-base-rate example shows why these axes are not redundant: it can be calibrated without discrimination, and its sharpness depends on how close that base rate is to zero or one. A confidently wrong system can be sharp while miscalibrated and poorly discriminating. A useful forecasting system seeks sharpness subject to calibration and checks discrimination separately; none of the three alone is a complete report card.

docs.title: Post-hoc recalibration in the companion, and where the literature sits
docs.text:
A model's raw output need not be calibrated even when it discriminates well. The companion fits an IsotonicRegression map to boosted-model predictions and labels on the validation cohort, separate from the training cohort used to fit the trees. The resulting boosted_calibrated forecasts are then evaluated on the test cohort. Validation is the calibrator's fitting data, not its independent performance check.

The literature motivates assessment rather than automatic correction. Guo and colleagues' inspected ICML abstract reports miscalibration and useful temperature scaling on studied image/document classifiers, not a guarantee for small event-market samples. GUO2017 Kull and colleagues' inspected abstract warns that isotonic calibration can overfit small samples and logistic calibration can worsen some probabilities; beta calibration is their proposed alternative, not an implemented companion method. KULL2017 The inspected sections of Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana discuss sigmoid and isotonic maps, independent calibration examples, and model- and sample-dependent benefits and harms. Their eight benchmark datasets used random samples, not the event-grouped chronological design needed here. NICULESCU2005

None establishes a universally best method. An isotonic map can emit exact zero or one, incurring infinite log loss if a later outcome contradicts that certainty. In this toy run the observed test losses are finite but worse after calibration. That result is consistent with small-sample overfitting; the score comparison alone does not identify its cause or prove the same method would underperform on another sample.

docs.title: 10.6 An exact grouped-score identity, and why binning changes the score
docs.text:
There is a classical way to decompose an average Brier score into a calibration-related term, a discrimination-related term, and an irreducible term tied only to the base rate. This book derives its own version of that identity from scratch, rather than attributing a specific formula to Murphy's 1973 paper, whose full text this book's evidence ledger has not inspected beyond its bibliographic record. MURPHY1973

Suppose observations are grouped into \(K\) bins, indexed \(k=1,\dots,K\), with \(n_k\) observations in bin \(k\), and suppose, for this derivation only, that every observation in bin \(k\) is assigned the same reported forecast \(\bar p_k\), the bin's representative value. Write \(\bar o_k\) for the empirical outcome rate within bin \(k\), and \(\bar o\) for the overall outcome rate across all \(n=\sum_k n_k\) observations. For any single observation \(i\) in bin \(k\), since its own forecast equals \(\bar p_k\) by assumption, \((\bar p_k-y_i)^2=(\bar p_k-\bar o_k)^2+(y_i-\bar o_k)^2+2(\bar p_k-\bar o_k)(\bar o_k-y_i)\); summing over \(i\) within bin \(k\), the cross term vanishes because \(\sum_i(\bar o_k-y_i)=n_k\bar o_k-n_k\bar o_k=0\). Because \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\), \(\sum_i(y_i-\bar o_k)^2=n_k\bar o_k(1-\bar o_k)\), the usual variance of a Bernoulli sample. Summing over all bins and dividing by \(n\) gives

\[ \mathrm{BS}=\frac1n\sum_k n_k(\bar p_k-\bar o_k)^2+\frac1n\sum_k n_k\,\bar o_k(1-\bar o_k). \]

The first term is the reliability term, zero exactly when every bin's reported forecast equals its own realized rate. The second term can itself be split, using the standard identity that total outcome variance equals within-group variance plus between-group variance: \(\frac1n\sum_k n_k\bar o_k(1-\bar o_k)=\bar o(1-\bar o)-\frac1n\sum_k n_k(\bar o_k-\bar o)^2\). Substituting gives the full decomposition

\[ \mathrm{BS}=\underbrace{\frac1n\sum_k n_k(\bar p_k-\bar o_k)^2}_{\text{reliability}}-\underbrace{\frac1n\sum_k n_k(\bar o_k-\bar o)^2}_{\text{resolution}}+\underbrace{\bar o(1-\bar o)}_{\text{uncertainty}}. \]

Reliability should be small and resolution large, since it is subtracted. The uncertainty term is the score of the constant empirical base-rate forecast, not a lower bound on achievable score. A perfect forecast has zero reliability and resolution equal to uncertainty, giving total score zero. The term itself is fixed by this outcome sample; an informative forecast can improve on it through resolution.

The derivation above depended on one specific assumption: that every observation in a bin is literally assigned the bin's representative forecast \(\bar p_k\). That assumption holds exactly for an old-style categorical forecaster who genuinely issues one of \(K\) discrete probability categories. It does not generally hold when a continuous, individually varying forecast is only summarized into bins after the fact for a calibration diagnostic, which is exactly what the companion's scoring.calibration_bins function does: it reports each bin's mean probability and observed rate for display, without ever claiming that the raw Brier score computed from the original individual forecasts equals the reliability-resolution-uncertainty formula applied to those bin summaries.

A concrete counterexample makes the gap tangible. Take \(p=(0.1,0.7,0.4,0.8)\) and \(y=(0,1,0,1)\), as in bayes_scoring.py. Their raw single-YES Brier is \(0.075\). Define a low bin by \(p<0.5\), containing \((0.1,0)\) and \((0.4,0)\), and a high bin containing \((0.7,1)\) and \((0.8,1)\). Their mean forecasts are 0.25 and 0.75 and observed rates zero and one. The bin-summary identity gives reliability \(0.0625\), resolution \(0.25\), and uncertainty \(0.25\), combining to \(0.0625\), not \(0.075\). If forecasts were actually replaced by the bin means in the original observation order, they would be \((0.25,0.75,0.25,0.75)\) and their raw score would indeed be \(0.0625\).

The missing terms can be derived by writing \(p_i=\bar p_k+d_i\) within bin \(k\), where \(\sum_{i\in k}d_i=0\). Expanding the square gives

\[ \mathrm{BS}_{\mathrm{raw}}-\mathrm{BS}_{\mathrm{bin\ means}} =\frac1n\sum_k\sum_{i\in k} \left[d_i^2-2d_i(y_i-\bar o_k)\right]. \]

Thus within-bin forecast variance and forecast-outcome covariance matter. In this particular example, outcomes are constant within each bin, so the covariance term is zero; the gap is entirely \((0.15^2+0.15^2+0.05^2+0.05^2)/4=0.0125\). Other samples can have a nonzero covariance term and a gap of either sign, as Exercise 3 shows. No approximation is needed for the grouped-score identity itself; the mistake is applying it to a different set of individually varying forecasts.

The lesson is not that binned calibration summaries are useless; they are a legitimate and standard diagnostic. The lesson is that a population-level identity derived under a grouped-forecast assumption is not automatically an exact statement about a raw, continuously varying, individual-level score, and a report that quotes "reliability" and "resolution" numbers computed from bins must say so plainly rather than implying they reconstruct the underlying Brier score exactly.

The same calibration_bins function, run on the logistic model's actual 45-event test-cohort forecasts in examples\forecast_models.py, illustrates the diagnostic at a more realistic scale: four bins contain 3, 23, 16, and 3 observations respectively, with mean forecasts of 0.212908, 0.393523, 0.626452, and 0.809405 against observed rates of 0.333333, 0.391304, 0.6875, and 1.0. Read as a diagnostic, the middle two bins, holding 39 of the 45 events, track their own mean forecast reasonably closely, while the two edge bins, each with only three observations, show larger gaps that a three-observation sample cannot pin down precisely. Reporting this table is useful for judging where a model's stated probabilities are and are not trustworthy; treating its bin-level reliability and resolution as an exact recovery of the model's already-reported raw Brier score of 0.198372 would repeat exactly the conflation this section has just shown, with the hand-checked four-point example, to be unjustified in general.

docs.title: 10.7 Baselines: a base rate and a market price are not automatically beaten
docs.text:
A forecast score is only informative relative to a stated comparison. This book insists on at least two baselines wherever a model score is reported. The first is the overall base rate: the unconditional event frequency in the relevant training population, exactly the reference_rate field the companion's FittedForecaster.predict method reports alongside its model outputs, computed as the mean training-cohort outcome. The second, when available, is the market price itself, treated as a forecasting benchmark rather than an executable quote, exactly the market_probability field the same method reports.

Neither baseline is a strawman to be casually outscored. The inspected NBER working-paper abstract by Wolfers and Zitzewitz gives sufficient conditions under which an equilibrium market price reflects an average belief about an event's probability, while explicitly discussing biased approximations outside those conditions; this book has inspected only that abstract, not the paper's full derivations, so it is cited here as a reading pointer for why a market price deserves to be treated as a serious probabilistic estimate, not as a certified proof that any particular market price equals the true event probability. WZ2006 A model that beats the base rate but not the market price has shown it captures some structure the base rate misses; it has not shown it captures anything the market did not already know. A model that beats neither has provided no evidence of anything beyond its own internal consistency. Reporting a model's score without reporting both of these comparisons, on the same predeclared evaluation cohort, invites exactly the kind of unearned impressiveness this book has repeatedly warned against.

Running examples\forecast_models.py on the fixed 45-event test cohort reports single-YES Briers: base rate 0.249699; invented market benchmark 0.207439; logistic 0.198372; boosted 0.220607; validation-calibrated boosted 0.2672; and fixed equal-weight logistic/calibrated-boosted blend 0.224694. Logistic beats both baselines on this sample; boosted beats the base rate but not the market benchmark; calibration worsens the boosted model's score here. These are observed synthetic results from one seed, not general model rankings or market-beating evidence. Small-sample overfitting is a plausible explanation for the calibration deterioration, consistent with the literature's warning, but not a cause established by this one comparison. KULL2017

docs.title: 10.8 Population versus sample: what should \(n\) mean
docs.text:
The Brier score and log loss defined above as expectations are population quantities: they describe the forecaster's own belief distribution exactly, with no sampling involved. Any number actually computed from data, including every number in Sections 10.6 and 10.7, is a sample estimate of some population quantity, subject to sampling variability that shrinks only as genuinely new, independent information accumulates. Reporting a sample average without acknowledging that it estimates, rather than equals, an underlying population score is a common and avoidable overstatement.

The notation registry is explicit that \(n\) should count evaluation observations, with the number of independent or dependence-grouped events reported separately. This chapter's next two sections show why that separation matters in practice: raw row counts routinely overstate how much independent information a dataset actually contains.

docs.title: 10.9 Repeated quotes on one outcome are not independent evaluation observations
docs.text: A dataset with 360 rows from 180 events contains 180 realized outcomes, not 360 independent outcomes. Scoring all snapshots can nevertheless be legitimate if the estimand is average performance across specified horizons and the uncertainty calculation respects grouping. Reporting \(n=360\) is then a row count, not an independence claim; report 180 event groups alongside it and explain the weights. The companion instead chooses one latest predeclared snapshot per event. evaluate_forecaster applies latest_per_event to the supplied cohort, yielding 45 test events in the default run, not the full fixture's 180 events. This answers a latest-horizon question and deliberately does not validate all-horizon performance.

docs.title: 10.10 A temporal gap does not cure a shared label, restated for evaluation
docs.text:
The same principle from Chapters 8 and 9 applies once more, now specifically to scoring rather than to splitting or exploring: if a training cohort and an evaluation cohort share a dependence group, the fact that their decision timestamps are far apart does not make their scores independent contributions to different questions. grouped_chronological_split's purging of straddling groups exists precisely so that the score computed on a later cohort reflects genuinely unseen dependence groups, not merely temporally later rows drawn from an already-seen event.

A closely related requirement is that training and calibration labels must actually have been available by their own cohort's cutoff before being used to fit or calibrate anything scored afterward. The companion's fit_forecaster and its internal _validate_split check enforce this directly: they raise an error if any cohort's rows have a label available after that cohort's own cutoff, or if any event or dependence group appears in more than one cohort. A reported evaluation score is only as trustworthy as the guarantee that nothing scored on the test cohort quietly informed, through a shared label or a shared group, any earlier fitting or calibration step.

docs.title: 10.11 A worked design-effect derivation for dependence-aware uncertainty
docs.text:
Section 10.9 established that raw row counts can overstate independent information; this section derives, from first principles, one simple way to quantify that overstatement, then points to more rigorous established alternatives for a serious analysis.

Suppose an evaluation sample consists of \(G\) dependence groups (events), each contributing exactly \(m\) observations (snapshots), for a total of \(n=Gm\) rows. Suppose, for this illustrative derivation, that any two observations within the same group share a common correlation \(\rho\) in whatever quantity is being averaged, for example a per-observation score contribution, and that observations in different groups are uncorrelated, each with variance \(\sigma^2\). The variance of the sum of all \(n\) observations is the sum of \(n\) individual variances, \(n\sigma^2\), plus the sum of all within-group covariance pairs. Each group of size \(m\) has \(m(m-1)\) ordered pairs, each contributing covariance \(\rho\sigma^2\), and there are \(G\) such groups, giving total covariance \(Gm(m-1)\rho\sigma^2\). The variance of the grand mean is this total variance divided by \(n^2=(Gm)^2\):

\[ \operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\frac{Gm\sigma^2+Gm(m-1)\rho\sigma^2}{(Gm)^2}=\frac{\sigma^2\left[1+(m-1)\rho\right]}{Gm}. \]

A naive calculation that assumed all \(n=Gm\) observations were independent would instead compute \(\sigma^2/(Gm)\), understating the true variance by the factor \(1+(m-1)\rho\) whenever \(\rho>0\). Equivalently, the effective sample size is \(n_{\text{eff}}=n/[1+(m-1)\rho]\), the number of genuinely independent observations that would produce the same variance as the actual dependent sample.

Apply this to the recurring-event fixture's structure: \(m=2\) snapshots per event, \(G=180\) events, \(n=360\) rows. Take an invented, clearly hypothetical value \(\rho=0.5\), chosen only to illustrate the arithmetic and not measured from any real evaluation: the design-effect factor is \(1+(2-1)(0.5)=1.5\), and the effective sample size is \(n_{\text{eff}}=360/1.5=240\), well below the naive row count of 360 but, reassuringly, also comfortably above the 180 realized events, since two positively correlated but not perfectly identical snapshots still carry more information together than either alone. If \(\rho\) were instead 1, perfect redundancy, the effective sample size would collapse exactly to 180, matching the number of realized events, exactly as the extreme case in Chapter 9 anticipated.

This derivation is a simple, self-contained heuristic, not a substitute for a properly justified dependence model. Two more rigorous tools are worth knowing as further reading. The stationary bootstrap of Politis and Romano is a resampling method designed for dependent time-series data, using randomly chosen block lengths to preserve dependence structure under stated stationarity assumptions. This book's evidence ledger has inspected the complete primary publisher abstract, which describes geometrically distributed random block lengths and a conditionally stationary resampled pseudo-series, developed for asymptotic inference under weak dependence and stationarity; it has not inspected the original article's full proofs or a specific recommended block-length choice, and Chapter 9's inspection of White's related reality-check construction supplies a more detailed, separately verified exposition of a closely related common-random-length block bootstrap. POLITIS1994 Neither source should be read as guaranteeing confidence-interval validity for nonstationary data or for an arbitrarily chosen dependence unit; naming a bootstrap is not a substitute for correctly specifying the sampling unit, exactly as this section's own design-effect derivation had to specify its event-versus-row unit explicitly rather than assume it. Howard, Ramdas, McAuliffe, and Sekhon's work on time-uniform, nonparametric confidence sequences, whose abstract and relevant Section 2 setup this book's evidence ledger did inspect, including its average-conditional-expectation estimand and exponential-supermartingale construction, offers a genuinely different guarantee: simultaneous-in-time coverage that remains valid even if a researcher looks at the running estimate repeatedly, rather than only at one predetermined sample size. HOWARD2021 That property is attractive for the kind of repeated confirmatory temptation Chapter 9 warned against, but it is not a license to ignore dependence; a time-uniform guarantee is not automatically an assumption-free one, and it does not by itself turn a shared-event leak into an independent observation.

docs.title: 10.12 Accuracy is not edge
docs.text: Every derivation and worked example in this chapter concerns forecast quality: how well a probability matches an outcome, evaluated by a rule constructed so that honesty is the best policy. None of it is a statement about trading profitability. A model can achieve an excellent Brier score, beat the base rate convincingly, and even edge out the market price on a predeclared, dependence-aware, properly grouped evaluation, and still offer no positive expected trading value once executable asks and bids, fees, capital lockup, and adverse selection are accounted for, because none of those costs and frictions appear anywhere in a Brier score or a log loss computation. Conversely, a genuinely well-calibrated forecast can be scored favorably while telling a trader nothing new, if the market price already embedded the same information; a favorable score relative to the base rate is not automatically a favorable score relative to the market, and only the latter comparison starts to speak to whether a model contributes information beyond what was already priced. Evaluating a forecast and evaluating a trading decision are related but distinct exercises, and this book keeps them in separate chapters for that reason: this chapter is about the first, and the decision-and-cost machinery of the earlier chapters, revisited with execution realism in Part 4, is about the second.

docs.title: Assumptions and failure modes
docs.text:
Assumption: the reported probability is genuinely the forecaster's belief, not a strategically shaded number. Failure mode: propriety only rewards honesty if nothing external, such as a scoring-based bonus structure with its own distortions, incentivizes misreporting; this chapter's derivations assume the forecaster is simply trying to minimize expected penalty under their own belief.

Assumption: a binned calibration summary is an exact decomposition of the raw score. Failure mode: as Section 10.6 showed by direct computation, it generally is not, unless forecasts are genuinely constant within each bin; treating the two as interchangeable overstates precision.

Assumption: beating a base rate is evidence of a tradable edge. Failure mode: it is evidence only that a model captures some structure a constant forecast misses; it says nothing about whether that structure was already reflected in an executable price.

Assumption: raw row count is the right sample size for uncertainty. Failure mode: repeated snapshots of one event inflate the apparent sample size and understate true uncertainty, as the design-effect derivation in Section 10.11 quantifies.

Assumption: a wide date range in an evaluation cohort guarantees temporal stability. Failure mode: pooling a long evaluation window into one summary score can hide a structural change partway through; grouping evaluation by calendar period, for example by quarter, and inspecting whether scores are stable across those periods, is a useful complement to a single pooled number, though small per-period counts can themselves be noisy and should not be over-interpreted individually.

docs.title: Exercise 1: deriving the minimizer directly
docs.text:
Using the expansion in Section 10.2, verify by direct substitution that reporting \(p=p^*\) gives expected Brier penalty \(p^*(1-p^*)\), and explain in words why this quantity can never be negative and is largest at \(p^*=0.5\).

Solution sketch. Substituting \(p=p^*\) into \(p^*-2p^*p+p^2\) gives \(p^*-2(p^*)^2+(p^*)^2=p^*-(p^*)^2=p^*(1-p^*)\). This is the variance of a single Bernoulli draw, which is never negative, and it is maximized at \(p^*=0.5\) because that is where an outcome is hardest to anticipate; a forecaster facing a coin-flip-like event cannot achieve as low an expected penalty as one facing a near-certain event, no matter how honestly they report.

docs.title: Exercise 2: the cost of an overconfident wrong forecast
docs.text:
A forecaster reports \(p=0.02\) for an event that occurs. Compute the natural-log loss, and contrast it with the loss if the same forecaster had instead reported the base rate for that population, \(p=0.30\).

Solution sketch. The loss for the overconfident wrong report is \(-\log(0.02)\approx 3.91\). The loss for reporting the base rate instead is \(-\log(0.30)\approx 1.20\). Confidently betting against an outcome that occurs costs roughly three times as much as simply reporting the base rate would have, illustrating why unjustified sharpness is penalized heavily under log loss.

docs.title: Exercise 3: reproducing the decomposition gap
docs.text:
Using the bin definitions in Section 10.6, recompute reliability, resolution, and uncertainty if the "low" bin's two observations are \(p=0.2,y=0\) and \(p=0.3,y=1\), keeping the "high" bin unchanged. Compare the decomposition's combined value to the true raw Brier score for these four observations, and state whether they still match.

Solution sketch. The raw Brier score is \(\tfrac14[(0.2-0)^2+(0.3-1)^2+(0.7-1)^2+(0.8-1)^2]=\tfrac14[0.04+0.49+0.09+0.04]=0.165\). The low bin's mean forecast is \(0.25\) and its observed rate is \(0.5\) (one of its two observations occurred), giving reliability contribution \(2(0.25-0.5)^2=0.125\); the high bin is unchanged at \(2(0.75-1)^2=0.125\); total reliability is \(0.25/4=0.0625\). Three of the four observations now occur in total, so the overall rate is \(\bar o=0.75\), giving uncertainty \(0.75(1-0.75)=0.1875\). The low bin's resolution term is \(2(0.5-0.75)^2=0.125\) and the high bin's is \(2(1-0.75)^2=0.125\), giving resolution \(0.25/4=0.0625\). Combined: \(0.0625-0.0625+0.1875=0.1875\), which does not equal the raw score of \(0.165\); the two again differ by \(0.0225\), reinforcing that the match in Section 10.6's grouped case was a property of that specific constant-within-bin construction, not a general guarantee.

docs.title: Exercise 4: computing an effective sample size
docs.text:
An evaluation set has \(G=90\) events with \(m=4\) snapshots each. Assuming a within-event correlation of \(\rho=0.3\), compute the design-effect factor and the effective sample size, and compare it to the naive row count.

Solution sketch. The design-effect factor is \(1+(4-1)(0.3)=1.9\). The naive row count is \(n=360\). The effective sample size is \(360/1.9\approx 189.5\), far closer to the 90 realized events than to the 360 raw rows, illustrating that even a modest within-event correlation sharply reduces the amount of independent evaluation information a larger snapshot count appears to offer.

docs.title: Exercise 5: base rate, market, and model together
docs.text:
A model reports a Brier score of 0.18 on a predeclared test cohort where the base-rate benchmark scores 0.21 and the market-price benchmark scores 0.16. What, if anything, can be concluded about the model's tradable value?

Solution sketch. The model beats the base rate, showing it captures some structure a constant forecast misses, but it does not beat the market price, so there is no evidence here that it adds information beyond what was already reflected in executable prices. Nothing in this comparison addresses fees, executable spreads, capital lockup, or dependence-aware uncertainty around these three numbers; a defensible conclusion is limited to relative forecast quality on this specific cohort, not a claim of tradable edge.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: Chapter 11 begins Part 3 by building transparent statistical baseline models on exactly the disciplined, availability-checked, dependence-grouped data this chapter has shown how to evaluate honestly.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: You should be comfortable with conditional probability and Bayes' rule, the definitions of Brier score and natural-log loss, and the point-in-time discipline built across the data part of this book: decision cutoffs, label-availability cutoffs, and grouped chronological splits that keep an event's repeated snapshots on one side of a split. Chapter 10's forecast-evaluation material is assumed rather than repeated. The notation registry fixes the symbols \(\hat p\), \(x\), \(\beta\), \(\lambda\), and \(n\) used below; keep the registry open while reading.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this chapter you should be able to: derive logistic regression as maximum-likelihood fitting of a log-odds-linear model and show why that likelihood is the same quantity as log loss; explain ridge and lasso penalties as constrained or penalized likelihood and connect them to specific Bayesian priors; explain what partial pooling buys you when many event families each have too few labeled outcomes to fit separately; and state, precisely, why a model's posterior interval or penalty choice is not a guarantee against misspecification, leakage, or an unrepresentative sample.

docs.title: 11.1 Why start with a baseline you can fully explain
docs.text:
A prediction-market forecasting project is tempting to start with the most flexible model available. This book starts somewhere else: with a model whose every coefficient can be inspected, whose likelihood is an explicit function you can write on one line, and whose failure modes are well understood. That choice is not conservatism for its own sake. A transparent baseline gives you a number to beat, a diagnosis tool when a fancier model disagrees with it, and a fallback when data are too thin for anything more elaborate to be trustworthy.

"Too thin" is the ordinary condition in this domain, not an edge case. A recurring weekly question template might generate a few dozen resolved events per year. A one-off contract generates exactly one label, ever. Compare that to a typical supervised-learning benchmark with millions of rows, and the difference in what a model is entitled to claim becomes stark. Chapter 7 already established that dependence groups, not raw rows, are the currency of sample size here; this chapter is about models that respect that currency honestly.

The companion script for this chapter, forecast_models.py, fits a plain logistic-regression baseline (this chapter), a boosted-tree model with held-out calibration (Chapter 12), and inspects the same fitted logistic model at two snapshots of one event (Chapter 13). Run it from the companion project root (book\companion):

Command working directory: run this chapter's Python commands from book\companion. From the trading repository root, run Set-Location book\companion once first. The .venv belongs to that companion project; see companion setup.

.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe examples\forecast_models.py

Its fixture is generate_recurring, an invented threshold-like process with 180 synthetic events, each observed at two decision times before a single resolution. Every EventRow carries exactly three numeric features available at its own decision time: signal, horizon_hours, and market_probability. There is no fourth feature quietly smuggled in. The chapter's arithmetic below is worked by hand and checked with a small script, independent of that fixture, so you can follow the algebra without running anything.

docs.title: 11.2 From odds to a linear model: deriving logistic regression
docs.text:
Start from a question a decision-maker actually asks: given a feature vector \(x\), what probability should I assign to \(Y=1\)? A convenient way to guarantee an output between 0 and 1 without clipping is to model the log-odds as a linear function of \(x\):

\[ \log\frac{\hat p}{1-\hat p} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \cdots + \beta_k x_k . \]

Solving for \(\hat p\) gives the logistic (sigmoid) function of the linear score \(z=\beta_0+\sum_j \beta_j x_j\):

\[ \hat p = \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}. \]

Two sanity checks are worth doing once rather than trusting from memory. As \(z\to -\infty\), \(e^{-z}\to\infty\), so \(\hat p\to 0\); as \(z\to\infty\), \(\hat p\to 1\); at \(z=0\), \(\hat p=0.5\). A concrete point: with \(\beta_0=-0.5\), \(\beta_1=1.4\), and \(x=0.9\), \(z = -0.5+1.4(0.9)=0.76\), and \(\sigma(0.76)=0.681354\) (five out of six decimal places checked with a script; report the number you actually computed, not a memorized constant).

Now ask how to choose \(\beta\). The natural criterion is: pick the coefficients that make the observed outcomes as probable as possible under this model. For \(n\) independent-given-\(x\) observations, the likelihood is

\[ L(\beta) = \prod_{i=1}^n \hat p_i^{\,y_i}(1-\hat p_i)^{1-y_i}. \]

Taking the log (monotone, so it does not change the maximizer) and negating (so we can minimize instead of maximize) gives

\[ -\log L(\beta) = -\sum_{i=1}^n \big[y_i\log \hat p_i + (1-y_i)\log(1-\hat p_i)\big]. \]

Divide by \(n\) and you have exactly the book's log-loss formula from notation.md. This is not a coincidence dressed up as one: fitting a logistic regression by maximum likelihood is the same optimization as minimizing average log loss on the training data. The forecasting evaluation criterion from Chapter 10 and the fitting criterion in this chapter are the same function, evaluated on different samples with different purposes. That identity is worth internalizing, because it explains why a logistic model's training log loss is usually optimistic: the coefficients were chosen specifically to make the training log loss small.

A single-observation numeric check makes the two loss terms concrete. With \(\hat p=0.681354\): if \(y=1\), the loss contribution is \(-\log(0.681354)=0.383674\); if \(y=0\), it is \(-\log(1-0.681354)=1.143674\). The asymmetry matters for teaching: a model that assigns high probability to an outcome that fails to occur is charged much more than a small miss near \(\hat p=0.5\), exactly reflecting the convexity of \(-\log(\cdot)\).

Fitting generally uses an iterative numerical optimizer, not a closed-form coefficient solution. The companion standardizes features using training rows only, then calls scikit-learn's regularized LogisticRegression. Scaling changes the relative strength of a coefficient penalty and can improve numerical conditioning. Without regularization, rescaling a feature can be offset by inversely rescaling its coefficient; a large numeric range does not inherently make it dominate the fitted score. Refitting the scaler on validation or test rows would nevertheless use their distribution to alter an otherwise training-only pipeline.

docs.title: 11.3 Regularization as a first-principles idea, not a knob
docs.text:
A maximum-likelihood fit with many candidate features and modest sample size can overfit sharply, and it can fail outright under complete separation: if some linear combination of features perfectly predicts every training outcome, the unpenalized likelihood is maximized by coefficients that grow without bound, and the optimizer either fails to converge or reports an unstable, absurdly confident model. Regularization addresses both problems by adding a penalty on the size of \(\beta\) to the objective being minimized.

Ridge (L2) regularization minimizes

\[ -\log L(\beta) + \lambda \sum_j \beta_j^2 . \]

To see where this comes from without appealing to a black box, consider the simplest possible case: ordinary least-squares fitting of \(y \approx \beta x\) from three points \((1,0.8)\), \((2,1.7)\), \((3,2.9)\), penalized the same way. Minimizing \(\sum_i(y_i-\beta x_i)^2+\lambda\beta^2\) over the scalar \(\beta\) has a closed form, \(\hat\beta=\dfrac{\sum_i x_iy_i}{\sum_i x_i^2+\lambda}\). Plugging in the three points gives \(\hat\beta=0.921429\) at \(\lambda=0\) (the unpenalized least-squares slope), \(0.860000\) at \(\lambda=1\), and \(0.678947\) at \(\lambda=5\) (values checked with a script). As \(\lambda\) grows, the fitted slope shrinks toward zero. That is the entire mechanism of ridge regularization laid bare in a case simple enough to compute by hand: it trades a small increase in fit-to-data error for a reduction in coefficient magnitude, which typically reduces the variance of the fitted coefficient across resamples at the cost of a small bias. The logistic case has the identical shrinkage intuition, without a closed form for \(\beta\).

Lasso (L1) regularization minimizes \(-\log L(\beta)+\lambda\sum_j|\beta_j|\). Because the absolute-value penalty has a kink at zero, the optimum can land exactly at \(\beta_j=0\) for some coefficients, which ridge's smooth quadratic penalty essentially never produces exactly. TIBSHIRANI1996 proposes this constrained least-squares formulation and demonstrates that it can produce exact zeros; the original abstract's primary setting is linear regression, and its extension to sparse feature selection is a genuinely useful property, not proof that a selected feature is causally relevant to the underlying event. A coefficient of exactly zero says "this feature did not help the penalized fit criterion here"; it does not certify the feature is irrelevant to the real-world process, nor does it survive automatically to a different sample or period.

Elastic net blends the two penalties, \(\lambda\big(\alpha\sum_j|\beta_j| + (1-\alpha)\sum_j\beta_j^2\big)\), and coordinate-descent methods can fit the resulting penalized path efficiently across linear, logistic, and multinomial models. FRIEDMAN2010 documents this computational machinery; it is a statement about how efficiently a penalized path can be computed, not a statement that any particular penalty improves this book's forecasting task. Choosing \(\lambda\) and \(\alpha\) is a model-selection decision like any other, and it must be made using only training and validation rows under the same point-in-time and dependence-group constraints as everything else in this book — never by peeking at test-period outcomes.

docs.title: 11.4 A Bayesian view of the same problem
docs.text:
Ridge regularization has an exact Bayesian reading: minimizing \(-\log L(\beta)+\lambda\sum_j\beta_j^2\) is equivalent to maximizing the posterior \(\propto L(\beta)\cdot p(\beta)\) under an independent Gaussian prior on each \(\beta_j\) with variance inversely related to \(\lambda\). GELMAN2008 argues for a related but more deliberately chosen default: scale predictors to a comparable range and place independent Student-t priors (heavier-tailed than Gaussian) on logistic-regression coefficients, motivated specifically by the complete-separation failure described above. A heavier-tailed prior still shrinks implausibly large coefficients toward zero, while assigning more prior mass to moderately large values than a Gaussian would, which the paper's abstract argues behaves more gracefully when separation is nearly exact. This is a proposed default, not a provably optimal choice for every dataset; treat it as a documented, reasonable starting point that still requires checking against your own data and priorities.

The Bayesian framing changes what output one can seek. A penalized optimizer with a Bayesian interpretation supplies a posterior mode, not the full posterior or a credible interval automatically. Full Bayesian inference instead represents the posterior distribution over \(\beta\) and the induced uncertainty in predictions. The bayes_update helper illustrates prior-times-likelihood normalization for a binary hypothesis; it does not fit Bayesian logistic coefficients. Posterior computation for logistic regression generally needs numerical integration or sampling/approximation machinery, none of which this companion implements.

The important caution, worth stating plainly because it is easy to elide: a posterior credible interval quantifies uncertainty conditional on the model and prior being adequate. It does not, by itself, guarantee protection against misspecification. If the true relationship between features and outcome is not close to the logistic form, if there is unmodeled dependence between "independent" observations, or if the training period does not resemble the evaluation period, a narrow credible interval can be confidently wrong. Bayesian machinery formalizes uncertainty within a stated model; it does not verify that the stated model is the right one.

docs.title: 11.5 Partial pooling: what to do with too few labels per group
docs.text:
Prediction markets often arrive in families: many structurally similar but not identical recurring questions (a weekly threshold contract, a recurring economic-release question), each with only a handful of resolved events. Two naive strategies bound the useful range. Complete pooling ignores family identity and fits one model on all events, which discards genuine differences between families.
