No pooling fits a separate model per family, which for a family with, say, six resolved events produces an estimate with enormous sampling variance; a family that happened to see 4 of 6 events resolve YES gets a raw rate of \(4/6=0.666667\), and that number is barely more informative than the coin flip that produced it.

Partial pooling is the compromise: shrink each family's raw estimate toward a shared reference (such as the overall base rate across families) by an amount that depends on how much data that family actually has. A simple, fully worked instance of the idea, before any hierarchical-model machinery, is a Beta-Binomial shrinkage estimate: if a family has \(n\) observed events with \(s\) successes, and the shared reference rate across families is \(\bar p\), then

\[ \tilde p = \frac{s + k\bar p}{n+k} \]

for a prior-strength parameter \(k\) that can be read as "worth \(k\) pseudo-observations of the reference rate." With \(n=6\), \(s=4\), \(\bar p=0.40\): at \(k=2\), \(\tilde p=(4+0.8)/8=0.600000\); at \(k=5\), \(\tilde p=(4+2.0)/11=0.545455\); at \(k=10\), \(\tilde p=(4+4.0)/16=0.500000\) (all checked with a script). As \(k\) grows, the family's own six observations are increasingly outweighed by the shared reference, pulling the estimate toward \(\bar p\). As \(n\) grows for a fixed \(k\), the family's own data dominates instead. That single formula is the entire idea behind hierarchical, partially pooled models: a family with little data borrows strength from the population; a family with abundant data is left mostly alone.

A full hierarchical logistic regression generalizes this by placing a shared prior distribution on family-level intercepts (or coefficients) whose own parameters are estimated from all families jointly, so that the amount of pooling is itself learned from the data's between-family and within-family variance rather than fixed by hand. This book does not implement that joint estimation; the Beta-Binomial case above is presented because it is small enough to verify without unfamiliar software, and it isolates the mechanism (shrink more when the group's own information is scarce) that motivates the larger machinery. GELMAN2008 is again the relevant reading pointer for weakly informative priors in this style of model; it does not certify a specific choice of \(k\) or a specific pooling structure for prediction-market families, which remain modeling decisions you must justify from your own data and its actual group sizes.

docs.title: 11.6 Sample and label constraints specific to this domain
docs.text:
Two constraints recur across every model in this part of the book, and they apply to the plainest logistic baseline exactly as much as to anything more elaborate.

First, repeated snapshots of the same event are not additional independent samples. The companion fixture deliberately generates two decision times per event; latest_per_event collapses these to one row per event before fitting or scoring specifically so that a single underlying outcome cannot be counted twice as evidence for or against a model. If you instead trained on both snapshots as if they were independent labeled examples, the fitted model would implicitly overweight events observed more often, and a model evaluated the same way could report artificially confident scores driven by duplicated labels rather than genuine sample size.

Second, features must be available at each row's decision time; training labels must be available by the later model-fitting cutoff. Requiring labels at their own earlier prediction times would defeat forecasting. grouped_chronological_split raises for feature-late rows or inconsistent identities, but excludes whole groups that straddle boundaries or lack labels at the relevant cohort cutoff. The fitting pipeline separately rejects a supplied split that violates those constraints. The default result is 89 training events, 44 validation events used for the boosted calibrator, and 45 test events, with two groups purged. The cohort counts reflect both time and group availability, not an arbitrary division into equal thirds.

docs.title: 11.7 Reading the companion's baseline output honestly
docs.text:
Running forecast_models.py reports, on 45 test events: reference_rate Brier 0.249699 and log loss 0.692562; market_probability Brier 0.207439 and log loss 0.606343; and logistic Brier 0.198372 and log loss 0.582490. Logistic beats both baselines on this synthetic run. The generator makes the label probability logistic in an unobserved latent value, while the model receives a noisy signal, not that latent value itself. This construction makes predictive signal plausible but does not guarantee logistic specification is exact or that the fitted model wins on every finite test sample. The baselines make the observed comparison interpretable rather than self-congratulatory.

Two things this comparison does not show are worth stating explicitly. It does not show that a logistic model beats a real market's own quoted probability, because market_probability here is a synthetic feature generated by the same toy process, not an executable, fee-inclusive price from an actual venue. And a single synthetic run with one random seed is not evidence of a stable advantage; the honest use of this script is to check that your pipeline behaves correctly under known ground truth, not to report its numbers as a discovered edge.

docs.title: 11.8 Failure modes
docs.text: A regularized fit does not protect against a badly specified feature set: shrinking irrelevant coefficients toward zero is not the same as having included the relevant ones. Complete separation is easy to trigger accidentally with a rare categorical feature or a near-perfect proxy, and an unpenalized fit can silently report absurd coefficients rather than an error; always inspect fitted coefficient magnitudes, not just the reported score. Fitting a scaler, an imputer, or a feature-selection step on data that includes validation or test rows is leakage even if the model itself is later fit correctly on training rows only. Partial pooling can be pushed too far: an aggressive shared prior can erase a real difference between families that would have been visible with a more modest amount of shrinkage, and there is no shrinkage amount that is correct for every dataset. Finally, a Bayesian posterior interval answers "how uncertain am I within this model," not "how likely is this model to be the right one"; treating a narrow credible interval as proof against misspecification is a category error, not a subtle numerical one.

docs.title: Exercise 1: log-odds to probability
docs.text:
A logistic model reports \(\beta_0=-0.5\), \(\beta_1=1.4\) for a single feature \(x\). Compute \(\hat p\) at \(x=0.9\), and at \(x=-0.9\). Which prediction is more confident, and why does the sign of \(x\) matter here?

Solution sketch. At \(x=0.9\): \(z=0.76\), \(\hat p=\sigma(0.76)=0.681354\). At \(x=-0.9\): \(z=-0.5-1.26=-1.76\), \(\hat p=\sigma(-1.76)\approx 0.147\). The negative-\(x\) case is more confident (further from 0.5) because the same magnitude of \(\beta_1 x\) now reinforces the negative intercept rather than partly offsetting it; the model is not symmetric around \(x=0\) because \(\beta_0\neq0\).

docs.title: Exercise 2: ridge shrinkage by hand
docs.text:
Using the three points \((1,0.8)\), \((2,1.7)\), \((3,2.9)\) and the scalar ridge formula \(\hat\beta=\frac{\sum x_iy_i}{\sum x_i^2+\lambda}\), compute \(\hat\beta\) at \(\lambda=0,1,5\) and describe the trend.

Solution sketch. \(\sum x_iy_i=1(0.8)+2(1.7)+3(2.9)=12.9\); \(\sum x_i^2=1+4+9=14\). At \(\lambda=0\): \(12.9/14=0.921429\). At \(\lambda=1\): \(12.9/15=0.860000\). At \(\lambda=5\): \(12.9/19=0.678947\). The slope shrinks monotonically toward zero as \(\lambda\) grows, trading fit for coefficient magnitude.

docs.title: Exercise 3: partial pooling toward a reference rate
docs.text:
A market family has \(n=6\) resolved events with \(s=4\) successes; the shared reference rate is \(\bar p=0.40\). Compute the shrunk estimate at prior strengths \(k=2\) and \(k=10\), and explain in one sentence why the raw rate \(4/6\) might be misleading here.

Solution sketch. At \(k=2\): \((4+0.8)/8=0.600000\). At \(k=10\): \((4+4.0)/16=0.500000\). The raw rate of \(0.666667\) is based on only six outcomes, so its sampling variance is large; shrinkage trades some of that noise for a controlled bias toward the reference rate, and the appropriate \(k\) should reflect how similar you believe this family genuinely is to the reference population, not be chosen to produce a preferred answer.

docs.title: Exercise 4: separating fitting loss from evaluation loss
docs.text:
Explain why a logistic model's log loss computed on its own training data is generally an optimistic estimate of the log loss it will achieve on a properly held-out, event-grouped test period, even before considering any leakage bug.

Solution sketch. The coefficients were chosen specifically to minimize the training log loss (Section 11.2's identity between maximum likelihood and log loss), so the training score reflects both genuine signal and fitting to that particular sample's noise. A held-out score, computed on events whose labels played no role in choosing \(\beta\), does not benefit from that fitting-to-noise effect and is the honest number to report, provided the split also respects event grouping and label availability.

docs.title: Exercise 5: reading the companion's Brier numbers
docs.text:
The companion script reports reference_rate Brier 0.249699, market_probability Brier 0.207439, and logistic Brier 0.198372 on 45 test events. Is this comparison evidence that logistic regression outperforms real market prices in general?

Solution sketch. No. market_probability here is a feature generated by the same synthetic process used to generate the labels, not an executable price from an actual venue, and the entire exercise runs on one seeded synthetic sample. The comparison is a correctness check on the pipeline (does a model with access to the true signal beat naive baselines under known ground truth), not a market-beating claim, and it says nothing about a real venue's price efficiency.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: Chapter 12 keeps the same fixture and evaluation discipline but asks how nonlinear splits are chosen, how boosting accumulates corrections, and how to assess a separate calibration step without assuming that it helps.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Read Chapter 11 before this one; the fitting/evaluation distinction, the point-in-time and event-grouping constraints, and the companion's forecast_models.py fixture are assumed rather than re-derived. You should be comfortable with basic probability (proportions, expectations) and simple algebra; no linear-algebra background beyond arithmetic on vectors is required. Keep the notation registry open for \(\hat p\), \(n\), and the Brier/log-loss definitions.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this chapter you should be able to: derive the impurity reduction motivating a tree split; explain how random forests and gradient boosting use different error-reduction mechanisms; identify the companion's capacity controls; distinguish impurity-based from permutation-based feature importance; and explain why calibration needs a separate assessment and can worsen a model's held-out score.

docs.title: 12.1 A nonlinear motivating case
docs.text: Chapter 11's logistic model assumes the log-odds of the outcome is a straight line in the features. That assumption can be wrong in an identifiable way: perhaps the outcome depends on whether signal exceeds a threshold and horizon_hours is small, an interaction a single linear term cannot represent no matter how the coefficients are chosen. Tree-based models represent exactly this kind of conditional, if-this-then-that structure directly, by asking a sequence of yes/no questions about the features. This chapter asks what that buys you, what it costs, and why the answer it gives about a probability is not automatically trustworthy on its own.

docs.title: 12.2 Decision trees from first principles
docs.text:
A decision tree partitions the feature space by repeatedly asking a threshold question ("is signal greater than 0.1?") and sending each observation to a left or right child depending on the answer. The question at each node is chosen to make the resulting groups as pure as possible with respect to the outcome label.

For a binary outcome, a standard impurity measure is the Gini index of a node containing \(n\) observations with \(p\) the fraction labeled 1:

\[ G = 1 - p^2 - (1-p)^2 = 2p(1-p). \]

\(G\) is zero when \(p\in\{0,1\}\) (the node is pure) and maximal at \(p=0.5\) (maximal disorder for a binary label). A split is scored by the weighted impurity of its two children, and the split chosen is the one that reduces impurity the most relative to the parent.

Work a small case by hand. Ten events, six YES and four NO: parent Gini is \(1-0.6^2-0.4^2=0.48\). Suppose splitting on signal > 0 sends 7 events left (5 YES, 2 NO) and 3 events right (1 YES, 2 NO). Left Gini is \(1-(5/7)^2-(2/7)^2=0.408163\); right Gini is \(1-(1/3)^2-(2/3)^2=0.444444\). The weighted impurity is \((7/10)(0.408163)+(3/10)(0.444444)=0.419048\), and the impurity reduction ("gain") from this split is \(0.48-0.419048=0.060952\) (all values checked with a script). A tree-fitting algorithm evaluates many candidate thresholds across many features at each node and greedily picks the split with the largest such gain, then recurses on each child.

Two things about this procedure matter for everything that follows. First, it is greedy: each split is chosen to be locally best, with no guarantee that the resulting tree is the globally best possible tree of a given size. Second, an unconstrained tree can keep splitting until every leaf is pure (or contains one observation), which drives training impurity to zero and is a direct route to overfitting; hence practical trees are limited by hyperparameters such as maximum depth or a minimum number of observations per leaf, exactly as the companion's boosted model does (Section 12.5).

docs.title: 12.3 Random forests: averaging decorrelated trees
docs.text:
A single deep tree fit to one training sample is a high-variance estimator: a slightly different sample can produce a noticeably different tree. Random forests address this by growing many trees and averaging their votes, using two sources of randomness to keep the individual trees from all making the same mistakes.

BREIMAN2001's author-maintained description explains the construction directly: each tree is grown on an independent bootstrap resample of the training rows (sampling with replacement, so on average roughly 63% of distinct rows appear per resample), and at each split only a random subset of candidate features is considered, rather than all of them. Averaging \(n\) independent estimates with equal variance \(\sigma^2\) reduces the variance of the average to \(\sigma^2/n\); averaging correlated estimates reduces variance by less, because correlated errors partly cancel less effectively than independent ones do. Restricting each split to a random feature subset is specifically intended to decorrelate the trees: if one feature is a strong overall predictor, an unrestricted forest would have every tree split on it near the root, making the trees resemble each other and undermining the averaging benefit.

The inspected author description aggregates class votes; its vote fraction is the proportion of trees voting positive. Implementations can instead average the class proportions in terminal leaves, as scikit-learn's random-forest probability method does. Those conventions can yield different numbers, and neither guarantees calibration. Out-of-bag predictions also do not automatically respect chronological or event-group boundaries. The companion implements boosting rather than a random forest; Section 12.7 uses it to examine calibration empirically on the toy sample.

docs.title: 12.4 Boosting: a sequence of small corrections
docs.text:
Where a forest fits many trees independently and averages them, gradient boosting fits trees sequentially, with each new tree specifically targeting the current model's mistakes. FRIEDMAN2001 is this chapter's bibliographic reading pointer for the general staged, gradient-based function-approximation idea; per the ledger, only its metadata has been inspected, so the derivation below is produced independently rather than reproduced from the unread proof.

For binary classification with log loss, the model maintains a running score \(F(x)\) (a log-odds, exactly as in Chapter 11), and each stage computes a pseudo-residual for each training observation: the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current score, which for log loss works out to \(y_i - \hat p_i\) where \(\hat p_i=\sigma(F(x_i))\). A tree is fit to predict these pseudo-residuals, and its predictions are added to \(F\) after multiplying by a small learning rate, shrinking each stage's contribution so that no single tree dominates the final model.

Work one stage by hand. Start all five observations at \(F_0=0\), so \(\hat p_0=\sigma(0)=0.5\) for everyone. With labels \(y=(1,0,1,1,0)\), the pseudo-residuals are \(y_i - 0.5 = (0.5,-0.5,0.5,0.5,-0.5)\). If the fitted stump for this step predicts the mean residual in a single leaf containing all five points, that prediction is \(0.1\). With learning rate \(0.05\), the updated score is \(F_1 = 0 + 0.05(0.1) = 0.005\), giving \(\hat p_1=\sigma(0.005)\approx 0.501250\) (values checked with a script). The single stage barely moved the prediction, which is exactly the intended effect of a small learning rate: many small, cautious corrections rather than a few large, unstable ones.

This hand calculation uses a deliberately simple raw-gradient update, not the exact first stage of the companion's GradientBoostingClassifier. That estimator starts from training class log-odds by default, fits regression trees to negative gradients, and uses loss-specific Newton updates for terminal-leaf values before applying shrinkage. The gradient direction is the shared idea; initialization and leaf-step magnitudes are implementation choices.

CHEN2016 documents XGBoost's sparsity-aware split finding and weighted quantile sketch. Its engineering and benchmark results are background, not a claim that the companion uses or reproduces XGBoost; the installed model is scikit-learn's GradientBoostingClassifier.

docs.title: 12.5 Loss functions and hyperparameters as capacity controls
docs.text:
The companion's boosted model is configured with n_estimators=35, max_depth=2, learning_rate=0.05, and min_samples_leaf=8. Each of these is a capacity control, and together they matter more at the event counts this book works with than they would with a dataset of millions of rows.

max_depth=2 limits the number of splits along a tree path; min_samples_leaf=8 prevents leaves with fewer than eight training rows. On 89 training events, that is a meaningful capacity constraint. learning_rate=0.05 shrinks each fitted stage and n_estimators=35 limits the number of stages. Their product is not a universal numerical bound on log-odds movement: fitted leaf values matter too. Choosing these settings is a training/validation decision, never a reason to watch the final test score and stop when it improves.

The tree-splitting criterion for classification is typically an impurity measure such as Gini (Section 12.2) or, for boosting specifically, the log-loss gradient framework in Section 12.4; both are proxies chosen because they are tractable to optimize greedily at each node or stage, not because they are identical to every possible business objective. If your actual decision criterion cares about a specific cost asymmetry (a missed YES matters more than a missed NO, say), that asymmetry needs to enter your evaluation and, ideally, your hyperparameter selection, not just your intuition about the fitted model afterward.

Finally, and easy to miss: any preprocessing step with parameters fit from data (a scaler, an encoder, an imputer) must be fit on the training fold only, exactly as in Chapter 11, before being applied to validation and test rows. A tree-based model's split thresholds are themselves data-dependent parameters in the same sense, which is one more reason the whole pipeline, not just the final score, needs to respect the point-in-time and dependence-group boundaries established in the data part of this book.

docs.title: 12.6 Honest feature importance
docs.text:
A fitted tree ensemble commonly reports a feature importance score, often based on the total impurity reduction attributed to each feature across all splits and all trees. This measure has a well-known bias: it tends to favor features with many possible split points (continuous or high-cardinality features) over binary or low-cardinality ones, because such features simply offer the tree more candidate thresholds to try, some of which will look useful on training data by chance alone, independent of any real relationship to the outcome.

A more defensible alternative is permutation importance: take a fitted model, shuffle one feature's values across the evaluation rows (breaking its relationship with the outcome while preserving its marginal distribution), and measure how much the model's held-out score degrades. A feature whose shuffling barely changes the score was not doing much work for this model on this evaluation set. Permutation importance is still conditional on the specific fitted model and the specific evaluation sample, and it can understate the importance of a feature that is highly correlated with another retained feature, since shuffling one of a correlated pair leaves the model able to substitute the other. Neither importance measure is a causal statement: a feature can be "important" to a fitted model's score while having no causal role in the real-world event, and a feature can be causally central while looking unimportant because it is redundant with something else already in the model.

The practical discipline is to treat feature importance as a diagnostic about this fitted model's behavior, worth investigating further (does the direction of the effect make sense? does it hold up on a fresh validation cohort?), not as a discovery about the world that a single importance ranking can certify on its own.

docs.title: 12.7 Calibration: assess the correction rather than assume it helps
docs.text:
Run the companion script from the companion project root (book\companion):

Command working directory: run this chapter's Python commands from book\companion. From the trading repository root, run Set-Location book\companion once first. The .venv belongs to that companion project; see companion setup.

.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe examples\forecast_models.py

On its default synthetic fixture (labeled SYNTHETIC / ILLUSTRATIVE in the script's own output, with live_edge_claim: false), the boosted model's raw output scores Brier 0.220607 and log loss 0.628186 on the 45 test events. After isotonic-regression calibration — fit on a separate 44-event validation cohort that played no role in fitting the trees themselves — the same underlying model's calibrated output scores Brier 0.267200 and log loss 0.751586. The calibrated score is worse than the raw score on this run. That is not a bug to paper over; it is the honest, disclosed outcome of this particular invented fixture and this particular small validation cohort, and it is exactly the kind of result this book commits to reporting unchanged. None of these numbers describes a real market, and none should be read as a measured trading edge.

Why might calibration make things worse here, rather than better? GUO2017 reports that modern neural classifiers in the studied image and document benchmarks are often poorly calibrated and that a simple rescaling (temperature scaling) improved calibration on most of the examined datasets — evidence that raw classifier outputs commonly need correction in those benchmarks, not a guarantee that any particular correction method helps on any particular small dataset. More specifically, KULL2017 warns that isotonic calibration, precisely because it is a flexible, nonparametric monotone mapping, can overfit a small calibration sample; with only 44 validation events, an isotonic fit has limited data with which to estimate that mapping reliably, and the companion's own code comment records exactly this risk: isotonic calibration can emit exact 0 or 1 endpoints, and a single such prediction that turns out wrong contributes infinite log loss under this book's stated log-loss convention (no clipping). That single design fact — a monotone step function fit on 44 points, applied to fresh test rows — is a complete, sufficient explanation for why a calibrated score can be worse than an uncalibrated one in a small sample, without needing to invoke anything more exotic.

The broader lesson is that calibration is a statistical procedure, not a free correctness upgrade. Probability distortion can depend on the ensemble, loss, regularization, and data; do not assume a universal overconfidence direction. Fit a proposed correction separately, then assess it on genuinely held-out data. Retain the raw model as a comparison rather than presuming that a respected calibration method must improve it.

docs.title: 12.8 Failure modes
docs.text: An unconstrained tree grown to purity memorizes its training sample and generalizes poorly; always check that depth, leaf-size, or estimator-count limits are actually active, not merely set in a configuration file that a different code path ignores. Random forests reduce variance through decorrelated averaging, but if the underlying signal-to-noise ratio is low, averaging many weak, noisy trees still produces a weak, if smoother, model — averaging is not a substitute for informative features. Boosting's sequential correction can overfit to training-fold idiosyncrasies if the learning rate and estimator count are too generous for the sample size; there is no universal safe setting, and the correct budget depends on how much genuine signal is present relative to noise. Feature importance rankings, of either kind, are frequently over-interpreted as causal or as robust across resamples; report them with the same "conditional on this fitted model and this sample" caveat you would apply to any other model diagnostic. And calibration applied to a small validation cohort can make a model's reported score worse, exactly as this chapter's own companion output demonstrates; always compare calibrated against uncalibrated scores on the same held-out data before adopting either one, and never fit or select a calibration method using the test period's outcomes.

docs.title: Exercise 1: computing an impurity gain
docs.text:
Ten events split into 7 left (5 YES, 2 NO) and 3 right (1 YES, 2 NO) from a parent of 6 YES and 4 NO. Compute the parent Gini, both child Gini values, the weighted child impurity, and the gain.

Solution sketch. Parent: \(1-0.36-0.16=0.48\). Left: \(1-(5/7)^2-(2/7)^2=0.408163\). Right: \(1-(1/3)^2-(2/3)^2=0.444444\). Weighted: \(0.7(0.408163)+0.3(0.444444)=0.419048\). Gain: \(0.48-0.419048=0.060952\).

docs.title: Exercise 2: one boosting stage
docs.text:
Five observations start at \(F_0=0\) with labels \((1,0,1,1,0)\). A stump predicts the mean pseudo-residual \(y_i-\hat p_0\) in a single leaf, and the learning rate is 0.05. Compute the updated score \(F_1\) and the new predicted probability.

Solution sketch. \(\hat p_0=0.5\) for all five, so residuals are \((0.5,-0.5,0.5,0.5,-0.5)\) with mean \(0.1\). \(F_1=0+0.05(0.1)=0.005\), and \(\hat p_1=\sigma(0.005)\approx0.501250\). One stage moves the prediction only slightly, which is the intended, cautious effect of a small learning rate.

docs.title: Exercise 3: why capacity controls matter more at small \(n\)
docs.text:
The companion boosted model uses max_depth=2, min_samples_leaf=8, n_estimators=35, learning_rate=0.05 on roughly 89 training events. Explain in two or three sentences why this configuration would need to be reconsidered, not simply scaled up proportionally, if the training cohort were instead 89,000 events.

Solution sketch. More data may support more leaves, deeper trees, or more stages while retaining adequate observations per leaf. It does not make a leaf of fewer than eight events more precisely estimated merely because unrelated leaves contain more data. Reconsider capacity using training/validation evidence and actual per-leaf support, not proportional scaling of every hyperparameter or an automatic reduction of min_samples_leaf.

docs.title: Exercise 4: interpreting a calibration result
docs.text:
The companion reports boosted Brier 0.220607 and boosted-and-calibrated Brier 0.267200 on the same 45 test events. Does this show that isotonic calibration is a bad technique in general?

Solution sketch. No. It shows that, on this particular run, calibrating on a 44-event validation cohort produced a worse Brier score than leaving the raw boosted output uncalibrated, plausibly because isotonic regression's flexible monotone fit is prone to overfitting a small calibration sample (as KULL2017's abstract warns for related methods). The general lesson is to compare calibrated and uncalibrated scores on genuinely held-out data before adopting either, not to assume calibration is either always helpful or always harmful.

docs.title: Exercise 5: impurity-based versus permutation importance
docs.text:
A continuous feature with many distinct values receives a high impurity-based importance score, while a binary feature with a clear real-world relationship to the outcome receives a low one. Name one plausible, non-causal explanation for this pattern.

Solution sketch. Impurity-based importance is biased toward features offering many candidate split thresholds; a continuous feature can appear informative purely because it gives the tree-fitting algorithm many chances to find a threshold that looks useful on the training sample by chance, independent of a genuine relationship to the outcome. A permutation-importance check on a separate held-out sample, or restricting candidate splits, would help distinguish a real effect from this artifact.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: Chapter 13 keeps the tree-ensemble and logistic baselines from this and the previous chapter, but asks a different question: what should change about a forecast as new information arrives before an event resolves, and how do sequential updating, state-space ideas, and survival-style hazard models fit into that picture without being confused with the settlement process itself.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Read Chapters 11 and 12 first; this chapter reuses the same fixture, the same three-feature EventRow representation, and the point-in-time discipline established there. You should be comfortable with conditional probability, Bayes' rule, and simple weighted averages. The notation registry distinguishes event time, decision time, and label-availability time; that distinction is the organizing idea of this chapter.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this chapter you should be able to: derive a sequential Bayesian update and apply it to a chain of successive evidence; derive a scalar, variance-weighted combination of a prior estimate and a new observation in the style of a linear filter, and state why bounded [0,1] probabilities should not be assumed Gaussian without justification; explain when a survival/hazard framing is actually appropriate for a prediction-market question, and why modeling when something resolves is a different exercise from modeling the probability of YES itself; and read the companion's two-snapshot example correctly, without treating repeated observations of one event as independent evaluation trials.

docs.title: 13.1 A forecast is not fixed the moment it is made
docs.text:
Every model built in Chapters 11 and 12 produces a single forecast from a single feature vector at a single decision time. But an actual event contract is typically observed repeatedly before it resolves: new information arrives, scheduled releases occur, and the horizon to resolution shrinks. A forecasting system that only knows how to answer "what is \(\hat p\) given \(x\) right now" still needs a disciplined way to handle the fact that \(x\), and therefore \(\hat p\), changes as the event approaches.

The companion fixture makes this concrete without needing a real data feed. Each synthetic event in generate_recurring is observed at two decision times, 12 hours and 3 hours before resolution, with a fresh, independently noised signal feature at each decision time. This is not a second independent draw of the outcome — it is the same underlying event, observed twice, at two different amounts of remaining uncertainty. This chapter is about the machinery for reasoning across that kind of evolving observation sequence, and about the specific labeled traps in doing so carelessly.

docs.title: 13.2 Sequential Bayesian updating from first principles
docs.text:
Chapter 11 already used single-step Bayes' rule; the sequential case simply chains it. Given a prior probability \(p_0\) and a sequence of evidence items \(e_1, e_2, \ldots\), each conditionally informative about the same underlying event, Bayes' rule after the first item is

\[ p_1 = \frac{p_0 \cdot P(e_1\mid Y=1)}{p_0\cdot P(e_1\mid Y=1) + (1-p_0)\cdot P(e_1\mid Y=0)}, \]

and the posterior \(p_1\) becomes the prior for the next update using \(e_2\), and so on. This is exactly the book's bayes_update function applied repeatedly, and it is worth checking on a small chain to see the mechanics rather than trust the formula from memory.

Start at \(p_0=0.30\). Suppose a first bulletin has likelihood ratio \(P(e_1\mid Y{=}1){=}0.70\) against \(P(e_1\mid Y{=}0){=}0.40\): the update gives \(p_1 = 0.30(0.70)/[0.30(0.70)+0.70(0.40)] = 0.428571\). A second bulletin with \(P(e_2\mid Y{=}1){=}0.65\) against \(P(e_2\mid Y{=}0){=}0.45\) updates \(p_1\) to \(p_2 = 0.428571(0.65)/[0.428571(0.65)+0.571429(0.45)] = 0.520000\) (both values checked with a script). Two pieces of moderately informative evidence moved the belief from 0.30 to 0.52 — noticeably, but not dramatically, which is the correct behavior of Bayes' rule when neither piece of evidence is overwhelming on its own.

This chain-of-updates view has an important, easy-to-miss requirement: each \(e_i\)'s likelihoods must be genuinely conditionally independent given \(Y\), or specified jointly if they are not. Two bulletins drawn from the same underlying report, restated in different words, are not two independent pieces of evidence, and feeding both into a naive sequential update as if they were double-counts whatever the shared report actually established. The companion's two-snapshot fixture sidesteps this by using latest_per_event to collapse each event to one row before scoring (Chapter 11); this chapter's sequential-update machinery is a separate tool for cases where you genuinely intend to combine successive, distinct evidence about one still-unresolved event, not a license to treat every repeated observation as new information.

docs.title: 13.3 A scalar state-space idea: combining a prior estimate with a new observation
docs.text:
A related but distinct problem: suppose you already have a running numerical estimate \(m_0\) of some quantity, with an associated uncertainty (variance) \(v_0\), and a new noisy observation \(z\) arrives with its own variance \(r\). How should you combine them? KALMAN1960 is the foundational reference for the general linear-filtering answer to this question in a state-space setting; the scalar case, which this book derives independently rather than reproducing from the unread full text, is simple enough to check by hand.

If \(m_0\) and \(z\) are unbiased estimates of the same quantity with independent errors of positive variances \(v_0\) and \(r\), the variance of \((1-K)m_0+Kz\) is \((1-K)^2v_0+K^2r\). Differentiating gives \(-2(1-K)v_0+2Kr=0\), and the second derivative is \(2(v_0+r)>0\). Thus the minimum-variance linear combination is

\[ K = \frac{v_0}{v_0+r}, \qquad m_1 = m_0 + K\,(z-m_0), \qquad v_1 = (1-K)\,v_0. \]

\(K\) (the "gain") is between 0 and 1: as \(r\to0\) (the new observation is nearly noise-free), \(K\to1\) and \(m_1\to z\); as \(r\to\infty\) (the new observation is nearly useless), \(K\to0\) and \(m_1\to m_0\). A worked instance: \(m_0=0.55\), \(v_0=0.04\), \(z=0.62\), \(r=0.01\). Then \(K=0.04/0.05=0.8\), \(m_1=0.55+0.8(0.07)=0.606\), and the updated variance \(v_1=(1-0.8)(0.04)=0.008\) (checked with a script) — smaller than either input variance, reflecting that combining two independent estimates is never worse, in expected squared error, than using either alone.

This linear-estimation derivation requires finite variances, unbiasedness, and the stated error covariance; it does not require Gaussian errors or an unbounded target. Moreover, when both input estimates lie in \([0,1]\), the convex average with \(0\leq K\leq1\) stays there. What needs extra assumptions is interpreting these formulas as an exact Bayesian posterior mean and variance, or repeatedly propagating a Gaussian state distribution. A Gaussian probability-state model can assign mass outside \([0,1]\), and a noisy observation of an underlying signal need not itself be a valid probability. One can model a transformed state such as log-odds, but then the observation model and transformation of uncertainty must also be specified. Independent unbiased probability estimates with known variances are not automatically available just because two models report numbers.

docs.title: 13.4 Scheduled releases and repeated snapshots, revisited
docs.text:
Run the companion script:

Command working directory: run this chapter's Python commands from book\companion. From the trading repository root, run Set-Location book\companion once first. The .venv belongs to that companion project; see companion setup.

.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe examples\forecast_models.py

Its output includes a block labeled same_event_updates_not_independent_trials: for one held-out event, the same fitted (frozen) logistic model is applied to that event's two decision-time snapshots, 12 hours and 3 hours before resolution. On the run recorded here, the reported probabilities are 0.258916 at the 12-hour snapshot and 0.258227 at the 3-hour snapshot — barely different, even though the actual signal feature differs between the two snapshots (it is drawn with less noise at the closer horizon in the fixture's construction). The script's own label for this limitation is exact: the model is frozen at its original training-period fit and merely re-scored at two snapshots, so its calibration at the earlier, noisier horizon is unvalidated by anything in this exercise.

Be precise about what this demonstration is and is not. It is not an application of Section 13.2's sequential Bayesian updating (nothing here chains a posterior from the 12-hour snapshot into a prior for the 3-hour snapshot), and it is not a fitted sequence model of any kind — not a recurrent network, not a state-space filter, not a model whose parameters were estimated from how an event's own history evolves over time. It is one ordinary, time-independent classifier from Chapter 11, fit once on cross-sectional training rows, applied twice to two snapshots of one event that happen to arrive at different horizons. Sections 13.2 and 13.3 describe machinery that could, in principle, treat successive observations of one event as a genuine updating chain; the companion does not currently implement either one, and this section's two-number result should not be mistaken for evidence that it does.

This is deliberately shown, not hidden, because it illustrates a genuine limitation rather than a success. A logistic model fit once on training data does not automatically know how to weight information differently as an event's horizon shrinks; if the relationship between signal and the outcome genuinely changes with horizon (which the fixture's construction, using less noise at 3 hours, suggests it should), a single frozen model applied at both horizons is not exploiting that difference, and a more horizon-aware model — for instance, one that includes horizon as an interacting feature, or that is fit and calibrated separately per horizon bucket — would need its own dedicated validation before being trusted. Nothing in this book's companion currently implements that more elaborate design; the honest lesson from this section is naming the gap, not claiming to have closed it.

The evaluation implication is the one already established in Chapter 11 and repeated here because it is easy to forget under time pressure: the two snapshots of one event are not two independent test cases. Reporting a score across "all snapshot rows" rather than "one row per event" would silently inflate the apparent sample size and could let an event whose two snapshots happen to agree with the label count twice toward an apparently strong score. latest_per_event exists specifically to prevent this, and any custom evaluation code you write for a sequential or state-updating model needs the same discipline.

docs.title: 13.5 Survival and hazard models, and where they actually apply
docs.text:
A different, and frequently confused, question is not "what is the probability the underlying proposition is YES" but "how long until this contract resolves." These are genuinely different targets, and conflating them is a specific, named failure mode this chapter asks you to avoid.

Survival analysis models the distribution of a time-to-event, \(T\), often through the hazard function

\[ h(t) = \lim_{dt\to 0}\frac{P(t\le T< t+dt \mid T\ge t)}{dt}, \]

the instantaneous rate of the event occurring at time \(t\), given it has not yet occurred. COX1972 proposes the widely used proportional-hazards form \(h(t\mid x) = h_0(t)\exp(\beta\cdot x)\), where covariates multiply an unspecified baseline hazard \(h_0(t)\) rather than requiring you to specify its exact shape. This is a genuinely useful model when the question you actually care about is a time, such as "how many days until this contract's resolution is published" or "how long until a recurring threshold is first crossed," and when a proportional-hazards assumption (that covariate effects scale the hazard multiplicatively at every time, rather than changing its shape) is independently justified for your specific contract, not merely borrowed because the model has a well-known name.

It is not automatically the right model for the ordinary binary YES/NO question this book has otherwise focused on, and applying it there without justification confuses two different things that this chapter's title deliberately keeps separate: an event's occurrence (did the underlying proposition come true) and its settlement (when and how the contractual payout is actually determined and released). A contract can be economically decided well before its formal settlement completes, or its settlement can be delayed by review or dispute processes unrelated to the underlying proposition's truth. If your genuine research question concerns settlement timing or delay risk — a legitimate and often underexplored question — a hazard model of the time to settlement, built from contract-level data about actual settlement delays, is the right tool; it says nothing by itself about the probability that the underlying proposition resolves YES, which remains a separate binary-outcome forecasting problem of the kind built in Chapters 11 and 12.

A small illustration uses discrete conditional occurrence probabilities, not the continuous-time rate defined above: let \(h_1=0.10\), \(h_2=0.15\), \(h_3=0.20\), and \(h_4=0.25\) be the probabilities of occurrence during each week conditional on survival to its start. The week-by-week occurrence probabilities are \(0.100000\), \(0.135000\), \(0.153000\), and \(0.153000\), leaving survival probability \(0.459000\). They sum to one. If a contract actually asks whether this same first-occurrence event happens by week four, its YES probability is \(1-0.459=0.541\): a time-to-occurrence model can answer a binary deadline question. A model of administrative settlement delay cannot be substituted for that occurrence model.

docs.title: 13.6 A brief note on detecting regime changes
docs.text: A related, forward-looking idea worth naming without overclaiming: ADAMS2007 derives an online algorithm for maintaining a posterior distribution over the "current run length" since the last change in an underlying data-generating process, under a changepoint model where the parameters before and after a change are assumed independent. This is conceptually attractive for a forecasting system that suspects the relationship between features and outcomes shifts over time (a market family's dynamics changing after a rule update, for instance), but the abstract's own assumption — independent before/after parameters — is a modeling choice that needs justification, and a detected changepoint is a statistical signal, not proof of a causal regime shift or evidence that a new trading opportunity has appeared. This book's companion does not implement online changepoint detection; it is mentioned here as a named, citable direction for a reader who wants to extend the sequential-updating ideas of Section 13.2 into a setting where the underlying relationship is not assumed constant, with the same caution applied to any other model in this part of the book: a fancier update rule does not, by itself, verify that it is tracking something real.

docs.title: 13.7 A real-data illustration of current-vintage versus point-in-time tension
docs.text:
The book's separate NOAA Mauna Loa monthly carbon-dioxide study, described in full in experiments/README.md, is a completed, frozen, real-data illustration of a theme this chapter has treated abstractly: a series that evolves over time is not automatically a point-in-time series, and a strong recurring pattern is not automatically a prediction-market result. The design was predeclared before acquisition or scoring, and its recorded results are hash-verified rather than adjusted after the fact.

The predeclared question is whether a calendar-month-specific ("seasonal") event rate improves on an expanding overall rate for recorded monthly increases. Both use the Beta smoothing introduced in Chapter 11, Section 11.5: add one success and one failure to the admitted counts. The overall model pools all admitted labels; the seasonal model uses only the target calendar month's admitted labels. They do not fit a hierarchical distribution or learn cross-month pooling. No regression coefficients, trees, or networks are involved.

On the predeclared primary evaluation cohort (January 2015 through December 2025, 132 monthly events, 85 realized YES outcomes), the frozen results are: overall-model Brier 0.230314 and log loss 0.653345; seasonal-model Brier 0.032459 and log loss 0.130672 — a large, one-directional improvement for the calendar-aware model on this particular real, physically seasonal quantity. A predeclared sensitivity check that conservatively excludes the December 2022-August 2023 window affected by the post-eruption Mauna Kea measurement relocation, leaving 123 events with 79 YES outcomes and models refit on the reduced admitted history, shows the same pattern: overall Brier 0.230757 and seasonal Brier 0.034709. The seasonal model's advantage is not an artifact of the excluded months.

Read this result for exactly what it licenses and no further. It shows that a real, strongly seasonal physical process (atmospheric CO2's well-known annual cycle) is, unsurprisingly, forecast better by a model that uses calendar information than by one that does not — a legitimate, disclosed, real-data finding about this series. It does not show that a real prediction-market question with different underlying dynamics would exhibit similar seasonal structure, does not compare against any executable market price, computes no fees, spread, or profit-and-loss figure, and does not establish availability at any verified historical publication time: the study's admission clock is an explicitly hypothetical retrospective convention layered onto a mutable, current-vintage NOAA extract, precisely the vintage-versus-availability distinction this chapter has emphasized throughout. A chronological, calendar-aware split of that data, however carefully constructed, still cannot recover the historical vintage — the values as they actually stood — at each past decision date, because only the current, possibly revised, extract is available for download today. See the data feasibility assessment for the full provenance and rights discussion behind the extract itself.

docs.title: 13.8 Failure modes
docs.text: Treating repeated snapshots as independent trials overstates independent outcome information; use a declared horizon or an explicitly grouped multi-horizon evaluation. A variance-weighted average is not automatically a Bayesian state update: verify unbiasedness, covariance, and any assumed distribution. A Gaussian state can misrepresent bounded probability uncertainty, although a convex average of valid probabilities remains valid. Survival models require actual time-to-event and censoring definitions; a binary label alone cannot supply them. A detected changepoint is not causal proof. Finally, date-ordering a current-vintage series does not reconstruct historical vintages or establish past input availability.

docs.title: Exercise 2: a variance-weighted combination
docs.text:
A prior estimate is \(m_0=0.55\) with variance \(v_0=0.04\); a new observation is \(z=0.62\) with variance \(r=0.01\). Compute the gain \(K\), the updated estimate \(m_1\), and the updated variance \(v_1\).

Solution sketch. \(K=0.04/(0.04+0.01)=0.8\). \(m_1=0.55+0.8(0.62-0.55)=0.606\). \(v_1=(1-0.8)(0.04)=0.008\), smaller than either input variance because combining two independent estimates reduces uncertainty.

docs.title: Exercise 3: reading the companion's two-snapshot output
docs.text:
The companion reports logistic probabilities of 0.258916 at a 12-hour horizon and 0.258227 at a 3-hour horizon for the same event. A colleague proposes scoring both as separate test observations to "get more data." Explain what is wrong with that proposal.

Solution sketch. Both snapshots belong to a single event with one eventual outcome label; scoring both as separate observations would let that one outcome be counted twice in an aggregate score, inflating apparent sample size and potentially overweighting events observed more often than others. latest_per_event (or an equivalent explicit collapse) should reduce this to one row per event before any evaluation.

docs.title: Exercise 4: occurrence versus settlement
docs.text:
A researcher wants to model "how many days until a contract's outcome is officially confirmed" using a proportional-hazards model, but instead trains it on the binary YES/NO label as if that label were a time-to-event target. Identify the specific conceptual error.

Solution sketch. The proportional-hazards model is designed for a time-to-event target, not a binary outcome; feeding it a YES/NO label conflates "did the proposition occur" with "how long until settlement." The correct approach is either an ordinary binary-outcome model (Chapters 11–12) for the YES/NO question, or a genuine time-to-event target (actual settlement timestamps and a defined start time) if settlement delay is the real object of study — not both collapsed into one model.

docs.title: Exercise 5: a discrete hazard sanity check
docs.text:
Given weekly hazard rates \(0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.25\) for four weeks, compute the probability of the event occurring in each week and the probability it has not occurred by the end of week 4. Confirm the four occurrence probabilities plus the remaining-survival probability sum to 1.

Solution sketch. Week 1: \(0.100000\). Week 2: \((1-0.10)(0.15)=0.135000\). Week 3: \((1-0.10)(1-0.15)(0.20)=0.153000\). Week 4: \((1-0.10)(1-0.15)(1-0.20)(0.25)=0.153000\). Remaining survival: \((1-0.10)(1-0.15)(1-0.20)(1-0.25)=0.459000\). Sum: \(0.100000+0.135000+0.153000+0.153000+0.459000=1.000000\), confirming the bookkeeping is consistent.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: Chapter 14 turns from numeric time-series-style features to text: the same forecasting and evaluation discipline applies, but the representation problem changes, and with it come specific new risks around training-corpus contamination and a temptation to trust a language model's own stated confidence.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Read Chapter 11 for the logistic-regression and likelihood foundations reused here, and Chapter 13 for the point-in-time discipline applied to evolving information. You should be comfortable with basic probability and simple algebra (logarithms, sums, ratios). The notation registry and the book's boundary between synthetic and real evidence, described in the research README, both apply directly to this chapter's discussion of language models trained on enormous, largely unverifiable historical corpora.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this chapter you should be able to: convert text into numeric features using bag-of-words and TF-IDF, and derive the inverse-document-frequency weighting from first principles; explain why a vocabulary or document-frequency statistic must be estimated only from training-period text to avoid leakage; describe, at a conceptual level, how dense embeddings and retrieval differ from sparse bag-of-words representations, and how a pretrained large language model's frozen weights interact with a decision cutoff; and state, precisely, why a language model's self-reported confidence is not automatically a calibrated probability and why training-corpus contamination is a distinct, serious threat to any retrospective evaluation of text-based forecasting.

docs.title: 14.1 Text as evidence, and why to start simple
docs.text:
News bulletins, official statements, and market commentary are an obviously rich source of information about many prediction-market questions, and it is tempting to reach immediately for the most capable available language model. This chapter argues for the opposite discipline: build the simplest defensible text-to-probability pipeline first, understand exactly what it does and does not use, and only then discuss richer representations, with their much larger and much harder to audit set of assumptions.

The companion script for this chapter and the next, text_and_neural.py, fits a bag-of-words TF-IDF logistic model (this chapter) and a small neural network on the same numeric features used in Chapters 11–12 (Chapter 15). Run it from the companion project root (book\companion):

Command working directory: run this chapter's Python commands from book\companion. From the trading repository root, run Set-Location book\companion once first. The .venv belongs to that companion project; see companion setup.

.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe examples\text_and_neural.py

Its text is entirely invented: a short templated sentence per synthetic event, such as "synthetic bulletin reports improving conditions with 12 hours remaining," generated from the same toy process that produces the numeric features elsewhere in this book. It is a mechanism demonstration, not a test of news understanding, and the script's own reported conclusion says so directly.

docs.title: 14.2 From words to numbers: bag-of-words and TF-IDF
docs.text:
The simplest text representation, bag-of-words, discards word order entirely and retains only which terms occur, and how often, in a document. MANNING2008 documents this representation and its refinements; the discarding of order is a real limitation ("supply concerns fall" and "concerns supply fall" become the same bag) accepted in exchange for a much simpler, much more tractable representation, especially at small sample sizes.

Raw term counts overweight common words shared across almost every document ("report", "the", "today") relative to words that actually distinguish one document from another. Term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) corrects for this. For a term \(t\) in document \(d\), term frequency is typically a normalized count, \(\mathrm{tf}(t,d) = \text{count of }t\text{ in }d / \text{length of }d\). Inverse document frequency downweights terms that occur in many documents:

\[ \mathrm{idf}(t) = \log\!\frac{N}{\mathrm{df}(t)}, \]

where \(N\) is the number of documents in the reference corpus and \(\mathrm{df}(t)\) is the number of documents containing \(t\) at all (not its total count). MANNING2008 specifies exactly this document-frequency-based construction, distinguishing it from a raw-frequency-based weighting. The TF-IDF weight of a term in a document is the product \(\mathrm{tf}(t,d)\times\mathrm{idf}(t)\).

Work a tiny, fully worked corpus. Three four-word documents: "improving demand growth report", "weak demand report today", "improving supply report today". With \(N=3\): the term "report" appears in all three documents, so \(\mathrm{df}(\text{report})=3\) and \(\mathrm{idf}(\text{report})=\log(3/3)=0\) — a term occurring in every document receives zero weight regardless of its raw frequency, exactly the intended effect. The term "growth" appears in only the first document, so \(\mathrm{df}(\text{growth})=1\) and \(\mathrm{idf}(\text{growth})=\log(3/1)=1.098612\); with term frequency \(1/4=0.25\) in that document, its TF-IDF weight is \(0.274653\). The term "demand" appears in two of the three documents, giving \(\mathrm{idf}(\text{demand})=\log(3/2)=0.405465\) and, at the same term frequency, a TF-IDF weight of \(0.101366\) (all values checked with a script). The pattern is exactly as intended: a word appearing in every document (uninformative for distinguishing them) is weighted to zero, while a word appearing in only one document is weighted most heavily.

The resulting TF-IDF vector for each document — one number per vocabulary term — is then fed into an ordinary logistic regression, exactly as in Chapter 11, except that \(x\) is now a (typically sparse) TF-IDF vector rather than a small set of hand-defined numeric features. Nothing about the fitting or evaluation machinery from Chapters 11–12 changes; only the feature construction does.

docs.title: 14.3 Reading the companion's TF-IDF pipeline honestly
docs.text:
The companion fits TfidfVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, 2), min_df=2) followed by logistic regression, using training rows only. Unigrams and bigrams retain individual words and adjacent two-word phrases, discarding terms in fewer than two training documents. Its defaults differ from Section 14.2's unsmoothed hand example: it multiplies raw term counts by \(\log((1+N)/(1+\mathrm{df}(t)))+1\), then normalizes each document vector to unit Euclidean length. A ubiquitous term therefore has IDF one, not zero, before normalization. These are explicitly different weighting conventions, not conflicting arithmetic; the chapter's hand TF-IDF numbers are not the vectorizer's literal outputs.

The vocabulary and document frequencies are themselves fitted quantities. Estimating them on test-period text would change which terms the model can use and their weights based on information outside the training boundary, just as fitting a numeric scaler on test rows would.

Running the companion script reports a training vocabulary of 21 terms — small, because the underlying bulletins are drawn from a narrow invented template, not because 21 is a target to aim for on real text. On the fixture's 45 test events, the TF-IDF logistic model scores Brier 0.206632 and log loss 0.602748, close to (and here very slightly worse than) Chapter 11's numeric-feature logistic model's Brier 0.198372. This is not evidence that TF-IDF text features are weaker than the numeric signal feature in general; the invented bulletin text was constructed as a nearly deterministic function of the same underlying signal used to build the numeric feature, so the two representations carry closely related information in this particular fixture, and neither comparison should be read as a general statement about news text versus structured numeric signals.

docs.title: 14.4 Beyond bag-of-words: dense embeddings and retrieval
docs.text:
Bag-of-words and TF-IDF represent each term independently: "growth" and "expansion" share no representation at all, even though they are related in meaning, because the vocabulary is just a list of distinct strings. Dense embeddings address this by representing each term (or, more commonly today, each token in context) as a vector of continuous numbers, learned so that semantically related terms end up with similar vectors. A document or query can then be represented by combining its token embeddings, and similarity between two pieces of text can be measured as a distance between vectors rather than an overlap of exact vocabulary terms.

Retrieval is the complementary idea of using such a representation to find the most relevant passages from a larger corpus — prior bulletins, official rule documents, historical commentary — given a query, before those passages are used as features or fed to a downstream model. This can be valuable specifically because a prediction-market question often depends on a small number of highly relevant documents buried in a much larger stream, and a well-built retrieval step can surface those documents more effectively than a fixed bag-of-words match on exact wording.

Neither dense embeddings nor a retrieval pipeline is implemented in this book's companion; text_and_neural.py's text branch is the bag-of-words/TF-IDF pipeline described in Sections 14.2–14.3, and nothing more. This section describes the concept, and names it as a plausible extension a reader might build, without claiming this book has implemented, tuned, or evaluated it.

docs.title: 14.5 Large language models as forecasters: what is actually being tested
docs.text:
A further, increasingly common idea is to prompt a large pretrained language model directly with a description of an event and ask it to state a probability, or to use it to summarize, extract, or reason over retrieved text before a separate scoring step. DEVLIN2019 documents one influential family of pretrained bidirectional text models, trained on a large text corpus and then adapted with a task-specific output layer through fine-tuning; its abstract is language-benchmark evidence, not evidence about market-forecast quality, and it does not certify any particular model's historical training cutoff.

That last point is a distinct threat from ordinary overfitting. A model pretrained on an event's reported outcome may retrieve that answer rather than forecast it. Even a training cutoff before resolution can be too late: news arriving after the stated decision time but before resolution is also future information for that forecast. Audit pretraining, fine-tuning, retrieval, and other updates against the decision's information boundary. A claim of historically deployable performance additionally needs an as-of available model and procedure, not merely a modern model with an asserted older corpus cutoff. If training provenance is undisclosed or changing, the study cannot rule out contamination; apparent ignorance in a few prompts is no substitute for that audit.

A second, related discipline concerns reproducibility. Language model providers routinely update model weights and default behavior behind a stable-looking name or API endpoint. An evaluation that reports results from "the current version of a hosted model" cannot be rerun later and trusted to reproduce the same behavior unless the specific model version and the exact prompt text are both frozen and recorded. Frozen prompts and a frozen, specifically versioned model are a minimum requirement for any language-model-based experiment reported in this space, exactly as this book insists on frozen fitting procedures and fixed random seeds elsewhere.

docs.title: 14.6 Hallucination and the trap of a self-reported probability
docs.text:
Large language models can produce fluent, plausible-sounding text that is nonetheless factually wrong — a widely observed failure commonly called hallucination: a fabricated citation, an invented statistic, or a confidently stated but incorrect claim about a rule or an event. Any feature, summary, or claim extracted from a language model's output needs independent verification against a primary source before it is trusted as evidence, in exactly the way this book's own citation ledger distinguishes an inspected primary source from an unverified secondary claim. Using an unverified model-generated summary as a modeling feature imports whatever hallucination risk exists in that summary directly into your pipeline.

A specific instance of this general risk deserves its own warning, because it is easy to be seduced by it: a language model's self-reported numeric confidence ("I estimate a 70% probability") is not automatically a calibrated forecast probability in the sense this book has defined throughout. A proper scoring rule (Chapter 10) makes stating your honest belief the optimal strategy under a specific, stated incentive structure; a language model generating text has no such incentive built in unless it was specifically elicited and evaluated that way, and its stated number is, structurally, just more generated text, subject to the same fluency-without-accuracy risk as any other output. Treating a model's self-reported number as if it had already been checked for calibration skips the entire evaluation discipline this book has built: any such number must be scored, on genuinely held-out, event-grouped, availability-respecting data, exactly like any other forecast in this book, before it earns any trust at all. A confident-sounding number is not evidence of a well-calibrated one.

docs.title: 14.7 What this book's companion actually offers, and what it does not
docs.text: To be concrete about scope: this book's default companion examples are entirely offline, deterministic, and use only small, local, CPU-friendly models on invented text; none of them requires a paid API call, a GPU, or a network connection, and none of them implements retrieval, embeddings, or a large pretrained language model. Sections 14.4–14.6 describe genuine, active areas of practice that a reader may reasonably want to build toward, with their own additional risks (contamination, reproducibility, hallucination) layered on top of everything already established in Chapters 7–13 about point-in-time discipline, dependence grouping, and honest evaluation. Building any of that is a substantial additional engineering and evaluation project, not a drop-in replacement for the TF-IDF pipeline demonstrated here, and none of its promise should be assumed without the same held-out, availability-respecting evaluation this book has insisted on throughout.

docs.title: 14.8 Failure modes
docs.text: Fitting a vectorizer's vocabulary, document frequencies, or any other text-derived statistic on validation or test documents leaks exactly as surely as fitting a numeric scaler on those rows would. Assuming a pretrained language model's training cutoff based on its release date, rather than documented evidence, risks silently including outcome-relevant information the model may already have encountered during pretraining. Treating a hosted model's current behavior as reproducible without freezing both the exact prompt and a specific, versioned model invites results that cannot be checked or repeated later. Using an unverified language-model-generated claim or summary as a modeling feature imports unverified hallucination risk directly into your pipeline. And trusting a language model's self-reported confidence as if it were already a properly scored, calibrated forecast skips the entire evaluation discipline this book exists to teach.

docs.title: Exercise 1: computing IDF and TF-IDF by hand
docs.text:
Using the three documents "improving demand growth report", "weak demand report today", "improving supply report today", compute \(\mathrm{idf}\) for "report" (in all three documents), "supply" (in one document), and "today" (in two documents). Then compute the TF-IDF weight of "today" in the second document.

Solution sketch. \(\mathrm{idf}(\text{report})=\log(3/3)=0\). \(\mathrm{idf}(\text{supply})=\log(3/1)=1.098612\). \(\mathrm{idf}(\text{today})=\log(3/2)=0.405465\). In the second document ("weak demand report today", 4 words), \(\mathrm{tf}(\text{today})=1/4=0.25\), so its TF-IDF weight is \(0.25\times0.405465=0.101366\).

docs.title: Exercise 2: why fit the vectorizer on training text only
docs.text:
A colleague proposes fitting the TF-IDF vectorizer's vocabulary on the entire dataset (train, validation, and test text combined) "to make sure no words are missed," then splitting into cohorts afterward for model fitting. Explain the leakage risk.

Solution sketch. The vocabulary and document-frequency statistics would then reflect terms and their prevalence in validation and test documents, information that would not genuinely be available at the training decision cutoff in a real deployment. A term appearing only in test-period documents, or a document-frequency count shifted by test-period prevalence, could subtly influence which terms receive nonzero weight, contaminating the evaluation exactly as fitting a numeric scaler on test rows would.

docs.title: Exercise 3: pretraining contamination
docs.text:
A researcher retrospectively evaluates a pretrained language model's stated probability for an event that resolved two years before the model's documented pretraining cutoff. What specific concern applies here that would not apply to a purely numeric logistic regression fit only on pre-event features?

Solution sketch. The language model may have encountered text discussing the event's actual outcome during pretraining, since its training corpus predates neither the event nor its resolution. This risks the model's stated "forecast" reflecting memorized post-resolution information rather than genuine ex ante reasoning, a leakage channel specific to models pretrained on broad historical text and not present in a numeric model whose features are explicitly constructed to respect a decision cutoff.

docs.title: Exercise 4: is a stated confidence a calibrated forecast?
docs.text:
A language model, prompted with a event description, replies: "I would estimate roughly an 80% chance of this occurring." Under what condition would this number be admissible as a forecast probability in this book's evaluation framework, and what condition would make it inadmissible?

Solution sketch. It is admissible for evaluation if it is a recorded probability from a frozen, versioned procedure whose information respects the stated decision cutoff, with the eventual contractual label scored afterward. It need not already have a successful evaluation to be tested. It is not yet established as calibrated or useful. A model, retrieval source, or prompt using information after the stated decision time makes a historical forecast claim inadmissible, even if that information predates final resolution. Appropriate held-out, event-grouped scores then assess the admissible forecasts; confident prose alone supplies no calibration evidence.

docs.title: Exercise 5: bag-of-words versus embeddings
docs.text:
State one concrete limitation of bag-of-words representations that dense embeddings are specifically designed to address, and one new risk that embeddings or retrieval introduce that a bag-of-words pipeline does not have.

Solution sketch. Bag-of-words treats synonymous or related terms ("growth", "expansion") as entirely unrelated dimensions, so a model trained on one wording may fail to generalize to a synonymous rewording; embeddings are designed to place related terms near each other in a continuous space. A new risk is that dense embeddings and retrieval components are typically produced by a separately trained model whose own training data, cutoff, and potential contamination must now also be verified — the leakage-verification burden does not disappear, it moves one level upstream.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: Chapter 15 returns to the small numeric-feature setting of Chapters 11–12 and asks what a neural network adds (and does not add) over a logistic baseline, deriving the forward pass and backpropagation from first principles on a network small enough to compute entirely by hand.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Read Chapter 11 for the logistic-regression and log-loss foundations this chapter directly extends, and Chapter 14 for the companion script's text branch, which shares a fixture with this chapter's neural branch. You should be comfortable with basic algebra, sums, and the chain rule of calculus in one variable; no matrix notation beyond writing out sums term by term is required. The notation registry fixes \(x\), \(\beta\), and \(\hat p\).

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this chapter you should be able to: derive the forward pass of a small feedforward network as a direct generalization of logistic regression; derive backpropagation's gradient computation using the chain rule on a network small enough to compute entirely by hand; explain how recurrent networks and attention address sequence-dependency problems that a plain feedforward network does not address, without claiming either is implemented in this book's companion; and state, with a concrete parameter count from the companion's own small network, why a deeper or wider architecture is not automatically better at the event counts typical of prediction-market research.

docs.title: 15.1 A neural network is not a different kind of model, at first
docs.text:
It is easy to introduce neural networks as something categorically different from the logistic regression of Chapter 11. A more useful framing, and the one this chapter builds from, is that logistic regression is already a neural network — one with zero hidden layers. A neural network with one hidden layer generalizes it by inserting one additional stage of nonlinear transformation between the input features and the output probability. Understanding exactly what that one extra stage adds, and what it costs in terms of the sample size needed to fit it reliably, is the entire content of this chapter.

The companion script for this chapter, shared with Chapter 14, is text_and_neural.py:

Command working directory: run this chapter's Python commands from book\companion. From the trading repository root, run Set-Location book\companion once first. The .venv belongs to that companion project; see companion setup.

.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe examples\text_and_neural.py

Its neural branch fits a small MLPClassifier with six hidden units on the same three numeric features as Chapters 11–12, not on text. The hand derivation below uses sigmoid hidden units to make a differentiable example easy to follow; the actual companion uses scikit-learn's default ReLU hidden units and a sigmoid binary output. Section 15.5 spells out that difference. The parameter-count and chain-rule principles apply to both, but their activation values and derivatives are not identical.

docs.title: 15.2 The forward pass, derived from logistic regression
docs.text:
Recall Chapter 11's logistic model: \(\hat p = \sigma(\beta_0+\sum_j\beta_j x_j)\), a single linear combination of the input features passed through the sigmoid function. A one-hidden-layer network computes several such linear-combination-plus-nonlinearity units in parallel, then combines their outputs with one more linear-combination-plus-nonlinearity step.

Concretely, for input features \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\) and \(m\) hidden units, each hidden unit \(j\) computes

\[ h_j = \sigma\Big(\sum_i W^{(1)}_{ji}x_i + b^{(1)}_j\Big), \]

exactly Chapter 11's logistic form, with its own weights \(W^{(1)}_{j\cdot}\) and bias \(b^{(1)}_j\). The output stage then applies the same construction to the hidden-layer outputs:

\[ \hat p = \sigma\Big(\sum_j W^{(2)}_j h_j + b^{(2)}\Big). \]

Every sum here is an ordinary sum of products, computable term by term with nothing beyond arithmetic; "matrix multiplication" is simply a compact notation for writing many such sums at once, not a conceptually different operation.

Work a fully explicit, tiny example: two inputs \(x=(0.6,-0.3)\), two hidden units, one output. Hidden-unit weights \(W^{(1)}_1=(0.5,-0.2)\), \(b^{(1)}_1=0.05\); \(W^{(1)}_2=(0.1,0.4)\), \(b^{(1)}_2=-0.05\). Pre-activation values: unit 1, \(0.5(0.6)+(-0.2)(-0.3)+0.05=0.41\); unit 2, \(0.1(0.6)+0.4(-0.3)-0.05=-0.11\). After the sigmoid: \(h_1=\sigma(0.41)=0.601088\), \(h_2=\sigma(-0.11)=0.472528\). Output weights \(W^{(2)}=(0.7,-0.6)\), \(b^{(2)}=0.1\): pre-activation \(0.7(0.601088)-0.6(0.472528)+0.1=0.237245\), giving \(\hat p=\sigma(0.237245)=0.559035\) (all values checked with a script). If this observation's true label is \(y=1\), the log-loss contribution is \(-\log(0.559035)=0.581544\) — the same log-loss formula used everywhere else in this book, now applied to a two-stage rather than one-stage model.

docs.title: 15.3 Backpropagation: the chain rule, one layer at a time
docs.text:
Fitting this network means choosing all the weights and biases to minimize average log loss over training data, exactly as in Chapter 11, except now there are two layers of parameters to adjust rather than one. Backpropagation is simply the systematic application of the chain rule to compute how the loss changes with respect to every parameter in the network, working backward from the output.

RUMELHART1986 was inspected by the source audit on pp. 533-535 for its feed-forward setup, chain-rule equations, and illustrative discussion. Its objective is squared error, with gradient and momentum updates, not this chapter's log loss. The shared mechanism is propagating derivatives backward through differentiable layers. The paper discusses local minima as an obstacle to a global guarantee; it does not certify that an arbitrary finite optimization run reaches an optimum. It also acknowledges independently discovered variants rather than claiming exclusive priority. These are mechanism and source-scope statements, not evidence of calibration or market skill.

For log loss with \(y=1\) and \(\hat p=\sigma(z_{\text{out}})\) where \(z_{\text{out}}\) is the output pre-activation, the gradient of the loss with respect to \(z_{\text{out}}\) has the same clean form Chapter 11 already established for logistic regression's gradient: \(\partial L/\partial z_{\text{out}} = \hat p - y\). With \(\hat p=0.559035\) and \(y=1\): \(\partial L/\partial z_{\text{out}} = -0.440965\).

The gradient with respect to each output weight \(W^{(2)}_j\) follows from the chain rule, since \(z_{\text{out}}=\sum_j W^{(2)}_j h_j + b^{(2)}\), so \(\partial z_{\text{out}}/\partial W^{(2)}_j = h_j\), giving \(\partial L/\partial W^{(2)}_j = (\hat p-y)\,h_j\): \(-0.440965(0.601088)=-0.265059\) for the first output weight, and \(-0.440965(0.472528)=-0.208368\) for the second, with \(\partial L/\partial b^{(2)}=\hat p-y=-0.440965\).

To reach the first-layer weights, continue the chain rule one layer further back.
