The gradient with respect to each hidden unit's pre-activation is \(\partial L/\partial z^{(1)}_j = (\hat p-y)\,W^{(2)}_j\,h_j(1-h_j)\) — the output-layer gradient, times that unit's contribution weight, times the sigmoid's own derivative \(h_j(1-h_j)\) evaluated at that unit's activation. Numerically: for unit 1, \(-0.440965(0.7)(0.601088)(1-0.601088)=-0.074015\); for unit 2, \(-0.440965(-0.6)(0.472528)(1-0.472528)=0.065945\) (values checked with a script). Each first-layer weight's gradient is then this quantity times the corresponding input: for unit 1's weight on \(x_1=0.6\), \(-0.074015(0.6)=-0.044409\); for unit 1's weight on \(x_2=-0.3\), \(-0.074015(-0.3)=0.022204\); and similarly for unit 2's weights, \(0.065945(0.6)=0.039567\) and \(0.065945(-0.3)=-0.019784\).

This is the entire mechanism of backpropagation, exhibited completely on a network small enough to check by hand: repeated application of the chain rule, moving backward from the loss, at each layer multiplying by that layer's local derivative (the sigmoid's derivative \(h(1-h)\), at every hidden or output unit) and by the weight connecting to the next unit forward. A network with more layers or more units repeats exactly this pattern more times; no new principle is introduced by adding depth or width, only more terms to compute, which is why this is practically always done by automatic differentiation software rather than by hand once a network grows beyond a toy size.

docs.title: 15.4 Sequence foundations: why recurrence and attention exist
docs.text:
The network uses a fixed, ordered feature vector at one decision time: swapping signal and market_probability without also changing the weights changes the prediction. What it lacks is a modeled sequence axis or persistent hidden state across observations. Recurrent networks and attention address sequence relationships, without either being implemented in the companion.

Recurrent networks process a sequence one element at a time, maintaining a hidden state that is updated at each step and carried forward to the next, so that information from early in the sequence can, in principle, influence processing much later. In practice, training such networks with a plain recurrent update tends to suffer from gradients that shrink (or occasionally explode) exponentially as they are propagated back across many time steps, making it hard to learn dependencies that span a long interval. HOCHREITER1997 introduces the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) architecture specifically to address this decaying-gradient problem, with reported experiments in the abstract on artificial sequence tasks constructed to expose exactly this long-dependency difficulty. Those artificial-task results are evidence that the architecture addresses the specific problem it was designed for; they are not evidence that an LSTM outperforms a simple probability model on the sparse, small-sample event data typical of this book's domain, where the number of independent events, not the length of any one sequence, is usually the binding constraint.

Attention, and specifically the self-attention mechanism at the center of the Transformer architecture, takes a different approach: rather than processing a sequence strictly step by step, it lets every position attend directly to every other position, with a learned weighting. ATTENTION2017's Section 4 compares, for a sequence of length \(n\), the computational complexity per layer, the number of sequential operations required, and the maximum path length between any two positions, across self-attention, recurrent, and convolutional layers; a shorter maximum dependency path is the paper's argument for why attention can make long-range dependencies easier to learn than a strictly sequential recurrent update. The paper's reported applications are machine translation and parsing — genuinely sequence-structured, large-scale language tasks — not calibrated event-probability forecasting, and attention weights are not, by themselves, causal explanations or a form of independently verified evidence about what a model actually relies on.

Neither recurrent networks nor attention is implemented here. The neural model uses one tabular row at a time; the text pipeline counts unigrams and bigrams, preserving adjacent two-word order but not a general sequence of documents or quotes. A reader extending to genuinely sequential inputs should first establish which temporal relationships the data and evaluation can support.

docs.title: 15.5 The companion's small network, read honestly
docs.text:
Run the companion script:

.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe examples\text_and_neural.py

The neural branch is MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(6,), solver="lbfgs", alpha=2, max_iter=1500) after a training-fitted StandardScaler. The omitted activation argument defaults to ReLU: hidden activations are \(h_j=\max(0,z_j)\), with derivative one for positive pre-activation and zero for negative pre-activation (the implementation uses zero at the kink). Replace the sigmoid hidden derivative \(h_j(1-h_j)\) in Section 15.3 with that derivative when tracing the actual companion. Its binary output remains sigmoid. The full-batch quasi-Newton optimizer and L2 penalty are deliberately small-CPU teaching choices, not proof of reliable estimation at this sample size.

Count the parameters this network actually has, using Section 15.2's structure with 3 input features and 6 hidden units: the first layer has \(3\times6=18\) weights plus 6 biases, and the output layer has \(6\times1=6\) weights plus 1 bias, for \(18+6+6+1=31\) parameters total. The companion's training cohort, recall from Chapter 11, is 89 events. Thirty-one parameters fit to 89 labeled observations is not an enormous model relative to its data by ordinary statistical standards, but it is a meaningfully larger and more flexible parameter space than Chapter 11's plain logistic model (4 parameters: one coefficient per feature plus an intercept, before any regularization), which is exactly why the heavier alpha=2 regularization is a deliberate, not incidental, choice here.

On the fixture's 45 test events, the reported scores are Brier 0.193973 and log loss 0.575018 for this small neural network, compared with Chapter 11's logistic model's Brier 0.198372 and log loss 0.582490, and Chapter 14's TF-IDF logistic model's Brier 0.206632. The neural network's score is marginally better than the logistic baseline's on this one run. Report that difference for exactly what it is: a small gap, on 45 test events, from one seeded synthetic run, using models that all draw on closely related underlying information in this particular fixture. It is not evidence that a neural network is generally superior to a well-regularized logistic model at this scale, and it should not be read as license to reach for deeper or wider architectures on the strength of a difference this small.

docs.title: 15.6 Small-sample warnings, and why "deeper" is not a default virtue
docs.text:
The bias-variance framing already used for regularization in Chapter 11 applies with particular force to network depth and width. A model with more parameters can, in principle, represent a wider range of functions, which lowers achievable bias if the extra flexibility is genuinely needed — but it also raises variance, because more parameters generally need more data to estimate reliably, and an under-constrained fit on a small sample can latch onto sampling noise that looks like signal only in that particular training cohort.

Prediction-market research typically works with dozens to a few hundred independent, dependence-grouped events for a given question family, not the millions of labeled examples that motivate very deep architectures in the domains where they have shown the clearest benefits. The calibration concerns already discussed for tree ensembles in Chapter 12 — GUO2017's finding that modern neural classifiers in large-scale image and document benchmarks were frequently miscalibrated — were themselves measured on datasets vastly larger than anything this book's domain typically offers; extrapolating "deep networks need calibration correction" or, worse, "a deeper network will forecast events better" from that literature to a sparse, small prediction-market sample is exactly the kind of unjustified transfer this book asks you to resist. The right question when considering a larger network is not "could it represent a richer function" (almost always yes) but "does this specific sample size support estimating that richer function's parameters reliably," and the honest default answer, at the sample sizes typical here, is that it frequently does not.

A separate caution concerns optimization. The inspected backpropagation article discusses local minima and supplies no global-optimum guarantee. RUMELHART1986 Nor does a finite optimizer run guarantee that even a local optimum was reached: stopping tolerances, saddle regions, and iteration limits matter. Greater width changes the optimization landscape but does not imply a monotonic increase in troublesome local minima. Inspect convergence and distinguish a poor optimization run from inadequate architecture or insufficient data; one seeded fit cannot settle those explanations.

docs.title: 15.7 Failure modes
docs.text: The observed Brier improvement is about 0.0044, a few thousandths, on 45 synthetic test events from one seeded run. It is a descriptive result, not established neural superiority. Three named tabular features are not themselves a temporal sequence; adding a sequence architecture without an appropriate representation and evaluation adds unsupported complexity. Under-regularization can fit noise, while heavier penalties also need validation. Benchmark findings from large image or text datasets do not automatically transfer to sparse event forecasting.

docs.title: Exercise 1: a forward pass by hand
Exercise 2: one backpropagation step
docs.text:
Continuing Exercise 1 with true label \(y=1\), compute \(\partial L/\partial z_{\text{out}}\) and the gradient with respect to \(W^{(2)}_1\).

Solution sketch. \(\partial L/\partial z_{\text{out}}=\hat p-y=0.559035-1=-0.440965\). \(\partial L/\partial W^{(2)}_1 = (\hat p-y)\,h_1 = -0.440965(0.601088)=-0.265059\).

docs.title: Exercise 3: counting parameters
docs.text:
A network has 3 input features, one hidden layer of 6 units, and 1 output unit, all fully connected with biases. Count the total number of trainable parameters.

Solution sketch. First layer: \(3\times6+6=24\). Output layer: \(6\times1+1=7\). Total: \(24+7=31\).

docs.title: Exercise 4: why 31 parameters on 89 events warrants caution
docs.text:
Explain, in terms of bias and variance, why fitting a 31-parameter network on 89 training events warrants a heavier regularization penalty than an unregularized fit, and why this concern would lessen if the training cohort instead had 89,000 events.

Solution sketch. With only 89 labeled events, 31 free parameters have comparatively little data per parameter to constrain them, so an unregularized fit risks high variance: fitting sampling noise specific to this training cohort rather than a genuinely generalizable pattern. A strong penalty (the companion's alpha=2) trades a bit of fitting flexibility for reduced variance. At 89,000 events, each parameter has far more data supporting its estimate, so the same architecture could tolerate a lighter penalty without the same overfitting risk — the concern scales with the ratio of parameters to independent, dependence-grouped observations, not with the parameter count alone.

docs.title: Exercise 5: is the neural network's small edge meaningful?
docs.text:
The companion reports neural Brier 0.193973 versus logistic Brier 0.198372 on the same 45 test events. A reader concludes "neural networks are the better choice for this problem." Evaluate that conclusion.

Solution sketch. The gap (about 0.0044 in Brier score) comes from one seeded synthetic run on 45 dependence-grouped test events, using a fixture where all models draw on closely related underlying information; this is far too small and too under-replicated a comparison to support a general claim of superiority. A defensible conclusion would require repeated evaluation across multiple independent samples or resampling schemes, explicit uncertainty quantification, and ideally a demonstration that the gap persists outside this specific synthetic construction.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: Chapter 16 asks what to do once you have several forecasters like the ones built across this part of the book — a baseline rate, a market price, a logistic model, a calibrated boosted model, and a small neural network — and shows, with a concrete constructed example, why simply averaging them is not guaranteed to preserve calibration.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Read Chapters 11–15 before this one; this chapter treats the logistic baseline, boosted-and-calibrated model, TF-IDF model, and small neural network built there as a set of forecasters to be combined, not as competitors from which you must pick exactly one winner. You should be comfortable with expectations, variance, and simple single-variable calculus (finding a minimum by setting a derivative to zero). The notation registry applies throughout, and its warning that mixing calibration with averaged predictions can change calibration is the organizing claim of this chapter, derived in full below rather than merely asserted.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this chapter you should be able to: explain why majority voting is inappropriate for combining probability forecasts and derive a proper alternative; construct and verify a concrete example showing that averaging two individually calibrated forecasters does not, in general, preserve calibration; derive the minimum-variance linear combination weight for two forecasters from first principles; explain why a combined model still needs its own held-out calibration step, using genuinely unused data; and explain how model dependence, drift, and abstention change what a responsible combination system reports, using the companion's own fixed-blend result as a concrete cautionary example.

docs.title: 16.1 Several imperfect forecasters, and the temptation to just vote
docs.text:
By Chapter 15 there are six candidate forecasts for the fixture: a base rate, invented market benchmark, logistic model, calibrated boosted model, TF-IDF model, and small neural network, with raw boosting also available as a diagnostic. No uniform winner has been established. Chapter 12's calibrator was fitted on validation and scored on test, where it worsened the raw model's score; Chapter 15's neural advantage is a few thousandths on one run. This chapter asks how to combine candidates without treating that small comparison as a definitive ranking.

A natural but wrong instinct, borrowed from classification-accuracy thinking, is to have each model vote (YES or NO) and take the majority. This discards exactly the information a proper scoring rule (Chapter 10) rewards you for reporting: a model that is 51% confident and a model that is 99% confident both cast the same single vote, even though they are making very different claims. Combining probability forecasts needs a method that operates on the probabilities themselves, not on a discarded binary summary of them.

docs.title: 16.2 Linear pooling, and forecast combination as a genuine research question
docs.text: The simplest probabilistic combination is a linear pool: a weighted average of the individual forecasts, \(\hat p_{\text{combined}} = \sum_k w_k\hat p_k\) with \(w_k\ge0\) and \(\sum_k w_k=1\). Forecast combination has its own dedicated literature. BATES1969's inspected publisher abstract reports a concrete empirical case — combining two independently produced sets of airline-passenger point forecasts — where the composite forecast achieved lower mean-square error than either original set, and it describes estimating combination weights from each forecaster's past errors rather than fixing them by hand. Read that result precisely: it is evidence that combining point forecasts of a continuous quantity can sometimes reduce mean-square error, and it explicitly describes weight estimation, consistent with this chapter's insistence (Section 16.4) that weights be fit from data, not simply asserted. It is not a theorem that combining probability forecasts of a binary event preserves calibration — a distinct question this book's own scoring conventions care about, and precisely the question Section 16.3 below answers by direct construction rather than by appeal to this or any other citation. The weight derivation in Section 16.4 is produced independently of BATES1969's specific airline-forecast setting. GNEITING2013 studies linear and nonlinear combinations of full predictive distributions through the lenses of coherence, calibration, and dispersion, with simulation and case studies in its abstract; its central, transferable warning — that combining calibrated components does not automatically yield a calibrated combination — is exactly what Section 16.3 demonstrates concretely below. YAO2018 extends stacking (a data-driven combination method, introduced generally in Section 16.4) to full Bayesian predictive distributions, comparing it with Bayesian model averaging in what its abstract calls an "M-open" setting, where no single candidate model is assumed to be the true data-generating process — a more realistic assumption for prediction-market forecasting than assuming one of your six models is exactly correct.

docs.title: 16.3 A worked demonstration: averaging can break calibration
docs.text:
Notation.md warns that mixing calibration with averaged predictions can change calibration, and asks that this not be assumed to be preserved without explanation. Here is the explanation, built from a deliberately extreme but fully explicit and verifiable construction, chosen specifically to isolate the algebra rather than to resemble a realistic forecaster.

Consider 100 events, 50 resolving YES and 50 resolving NO. Forecaster A always predicts \(\hat p_A=0.5\), regardless of the event. Among the 100 events where A predicted 0.5, the observed YES rate is exactly \(50/100=0.5\) — A is perfectly calibrated (trivially, since it only ever issues one prediction). Forecaster B is constructed, for this demonstration only, as an oracle: it predicts \(\hat p_B=1.0\) for every event that will resolve YES and \(\hat p_B=0.0\) for every event that will resolve NO. Among the 50 events where B predicted 1.0, the observed rate is \(100\%\); among the 50 events where B predicted 0.0, the observed rate is \(0\%\) — B is also, trivially, perfectly calibrated at each of its two predicted values.

Now average them, equally weighted: for a YES event, \(\hat p_{\text{avg}} = (0.5+1.0)/2 = 0.75\); for a NO event, \(\hat p_{\text{avg}} = (0.5+0.0)/2 = 0.25\). Check calibration of the average directly. Among the 50 events where the average predicted exactly 0.75, every single one resolved YES — the observed rate is \(100\%\), not \(75\%\). Among the 50 events where the average predicted exactly 0.25, every single one resolved NO — the observed rate is \(0\%\), not \(25\%\) (both counts checked with a script). The average of two perfectly calibrated forecasters is, in this construction, badly miscalibrated at both of its predicted values.

The mechanism is not exotic: A and B are looking at the same events through completely different information (A ignores the outcome-relevant information entirely; B, unrealistically, has it exactly), and averaging their outputs mixes two forecasts whose calibration was only ever established within each forecaster's own predicted-value groups, not across the specific pairing produced by averaging. Calibration is a property of a particular mapping from predicted value to observed frequency; changing the mapping (by taking an average) can and generally will change which predicted values correspond to which observed frequencies, even when every input to the average was itself calibrated. The realistic version of this same effect, with two genuinely imperfect (not oracle) forecasters whose information overlaps only partially, is milder in degree but identical in mechanism, which is exactly why this book does not let you assume a combined model is calibrated without checking it directly, exactly as you would check any other model.

docs.title: 16.4 Learned combination weights, derived from first principles
docs.text:
Rather than fixing weights by hand (as the equal 0.5/0.5 average above), a stacking or combination-weight-fitting approach chooses weights that minimize a stated loss on data the weights were not used to produce. The simplest fully worked case is two forecasters combined to minimize expected squared error (Brier score, restricted to this two-forecaster linear-pool case).

Let \(e_1\) and \(e_2\) be forecast-minus-outcome errors with variances \(v_1\), \(v_2\) and covariance \(c\). For now assume both errors have mean zero, so variance equals mean squared error. Without this assumption the following calculation minimizes error variance, not necessarily Brier score. The combined error is \(w e_1+(1-w)e_2\), with variance

\[ \operatorname{Var}(e_{\text{combined}}) = w^2 v_1 + (1-w)^2 v_2 + 2w(1-w)\,c. \]

Minimizing over \(w\): differentiate with respect to \(w\) and set to zero, \(2wv_1 - 2(1-w)v_2 + 2c(1-2w) = 0\), which rearranges to \(w(v_1+v_2-2c) = v_2-c\), giving

\[ w^\ast = \frac{v_2-c}{v_1+v_2-2c}. \]

This is the unconstrained optimum when \(v_1+v_2-2c=\operatorname{Var}(e_1-e_2)>0\). For a convex probability pool, constrain \(w\) to \([0,1]\) by taking the nearest endpoint if the formula lies outside it. If the denominator is zero, the error difference is constant and the variance is independent of weight; under the zero-mean assumption the errors coincide. For possibly biased forecasts, use second moments instead: replace \(v_j\) by \(\mathbb E[e_j^2]\) and \(c\) by \(\mathbb E[e_1e_2]\) to minimize expected Brier loss, again respecting the weight constraint.

Work a concrete instance: \(v_1=0.09\), \(v_2=0.04\), \(c=0.01\). Then \(w^\ast = (0.04-0.01)/(0.09+0.04-0.02) = 0.03/0.11 = 0.272727\) — weighting the noisier first forecaster (\(v_1=0.09\)) less than the quieter second one (\(v_2=0.04\)), exactly as intuition suggests. The resulting combined variance is \(0.031818\), compared with \(0.037500\) for a naive equal-weight (0.5/0.5) combination on the same two forecasters (both checked with a script) — the fitted weight strictly improves on the naive average here, because it accounts for both forecasters' relative noise and their correlation.

This derivation assumes \(v_1\), \(v_2\), and \(c\) are known; in practice they must be estimated from data the weight-fitting procedure did not also use to select itself, exactly the same discipline Chapter 12's isotonic calibrator required a separate validation cohort for. Fitting combination weights on the same validation fold already used to calibrate one of the base models, and then evaluating the combination on that same fold, reuses data in exactly the leakage-prone way this book has repeatedly warned against; a genuinely disciplined combination pipeline needs its own held-out fold, distinct from whatever was used to fit or calibrate each base model individually.

docs.title: 16.5 What the companion's fixed blend actually shows
docs.text:
Run the companion script:

Command working directory: run this chapter's Python commands from book\companion. From the trading repository root, run Set-Location book\companion once first. The .venv belongs to that companion project; see companion setup.

.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe examples\forecast_models.py

Its reported fixed_equal_ensemble is precisely a 0.5/0.5 linear pool of the logistic model and the calibrated boosted model — a fixed blend, not a fitted or learned combination weight, and the script's own naming is honest about this. On the 45 test events, fixed_equal_ensemble scores Brier 0.224694 and log loss 0.636406, compared with the logistic model alone at Brier 0.198372 and the calibrated boosted model alone at Brier 0.267200. The fixed 50/50 blend is worse than the logistic model by itself, and better than the calibrated boosted model by itself, on this run. Report this exactly as it is: naive equal-weight blending here does not beat the best individual component. This is a genuine, disclosed, unfavorable result for the fixed-blend approach on this fixture, not a hidden failure — and it is a direct, concrete illustration of Section 16.4's point that an unfitted weight (0.5/0.5, chosen without reference to either model's actual error variance) can be dominated by simply using the better single model, exactly as the general theory predicts when one component is considerably noisier than the other.

Moving from this fixed blend to something like the fitted weight of Section 16.4 would require a validation cohort not already spent on fitting the isotonic calibrator, and would need its own separate held-out check before being trusted — this book's companion does not currently implement that additional fold, and the honest lesson here is naming that gap rather than quietly assuming a fitted weight would have done better without checking.

docs.title: 16.6 Model dependence: why six forecasters are not six independent opinions
docs.text:
All six forecasters discussed in this part of the book are fit, directly or indirectly, from the same three underlying numeric features (or, for the TF-IDF model, from text generated as a near-deterministic function of the same underlying signal) and the same synthetic data-generating process. Their errors are therefore likely to be substantially correlated: on an event where the underlying signal feature happens to be unusually noisy relative to the true outcome, every model that relies on it, directly or through a derived representation, is liable to be misled in a similar direction at once. A combination of \(k\) such correlated forecasters does not behave like a combination of \(k\) genuinely independent opinions; its effective diversity — informally, how much distinct information the ensemble actually contains — is smaller than \(k\) suggests, exactly as Chapter 7's discussion of dependence groups warned that counting rows is not the same as counting independent information.

This matters for weight fitting. Under the zero-mean assumption, if \(v_1\geq v_2\) and \(c\) rises to \(v_2\), the optimal convex weight on model 1 reaches zero and the pool cannot improve variance on model 2. Perfect positive correlation likewise offers no convex-pooling variance benefit over the less variable component. Unrestricted negative weights can behave differently and need not yield valid probabilities, which is why the constraint matters. Estimate covariance and bias on appropriate held-out predictions instead of treating several models trained on the same information as independent opinions.

docs.title: 16.7 Drift: a combination is not fit-once-forever
docs.text:
A forecasting relationship that held during a training period can weaken, strengthen, or change direction as the underlying process evolves — a market family's rules change, a recurring event's seasonal pattern shifts, or a regime genuinely breaks. GANIN2016 documents domain-adversarial training, an approach that uses labeled data from one (source) domain together with unlabeled data from a related (target) domain to learn representations that remain useful for the task while becoming less distinguishable between domains; conceptually, this is one documented way researchers have approached the problem of a model trained under one set of conditions needing to remain useful under a related, shifted set of conditions. Its abstract's own limitation applies directly here: this is not a guarantee of successful transfer across market families or across a real regime change, and it is not implemented anywhere in this book's companion.

Practically, maintaining a forecasting or combination system over time means monitoring calibration and score on a rolling basis as new, genuinely out-of-sample events resolve (reusing Chapter 10's evaluation machinery, not inventing a new one), being willing to detect that a previously reasonable weight or model has stopped performing as it once did (Chapter 13's brief discussion of changepoint detection is one relevant, appropriately hedged tool for this), and retraining on a schedule tied to when new labels genuinely become available, not to whatever cadence is operationally convenient. None of this eliminates the risk of drift; it makes the system's response to drift auditable rather than silent.

docs.title: 16.8 Uncertainty, disagreement, and the case for abstention
docs.text: When the base forecasters substantially disagree with each other, that disagreement is itself informative, and treating it as a signal for caution rather than forcing a confident combined point estimate is a legitimate design choice. A Bayesian component's posterior distribution (Chapter 11) can in principle support such a decision by quantifying how much of the disagreement reflects genuine parameter uncertainty within its own model — but, exactly as Chapter 11 warned, a posterior's credible interval is a statement of uncertainty conditional on that model being adequate, not a guarantee against misspecification, and it should not be mistaken for a certified safety margin. A combination system that abstains when its components disagree sharply, or when a component's own uncertainty is wide, is choosing a smaller, better-supported coverage over a larger but less trustworthy one, in the same spirit as Chapter 25's abstention-under-coverage discussion; it is a design decision to be evaluated on its own coverage-versus-score tradeoff, not a way to avoid ever being evaluated.

docs.title: 16.9 Failure modes
docs.text:
Majority voting discards probability information, and averaging calibrated components need not preserve calibration. Fitting combination weights and evaluating them on the same records also creates selection optimism. Correlated models are not independent opinions.

A fixed convex blend can score worse than the better component, as the companion demonstrates, but not worse than both components on the same equally weighted cases under Brier or log loss. Each loss is convex in the reported probability, so its loss at the blend is at most the corresponding weighted average of component losses; averaging over the common cases preserves that inequality. This does not guarantee beating the best component or preserving calibration. Finally, posterior width remains conditional on a model, not a certificate against misspecification.

docs.title: Exercise 1: constructing a calibration-breaking average
docs.text:
Forecaster A always predicts 0.5 on a population with a true 50% base rate; forecaster B predicts 1.0 on every event that resolves YES and 0.0 on every event that resolves NO. Compute the average forecast for a YES event and for a NO event, and state the observed rate among each group of averaged predictions.

Solution sketch. YES event: \((0.5+1.0)/2=0.75\); among all events predicted 0.75 by the average, 100% resolve YES (not 75%). NO event: \((0.5+0.0)/2=0.25\); among all events predicted 0.25, 0% resolve YES (not 25%). Both individual forecasters are calibrated at their own predicted values; their average is not calibrated at its predicted values.

docs.title: Exercise 2: the minimum-variance two-forecaster weight
docs.text:
Two forecasters have error variances \(v_1=0.09\) and \(v_2=0.04\) and error covariance \(c=0.01\). Compute the minimum-variance weight \(w^\ast\) on the first forecaster and the resulting combined variance.

Solution sketch. \(w^\ast = (v_2-c)/(v_1+v_2-2c) = (0.04-0.01)/(0.09+0.04-0.02) = 0.03/0.11 = 0.272727\). Combined variance: \(w^{\ast2}v_1+(1-w^\ast)^2v_2+2w^\ast(1-w^\ast)c = 0.031818\), less than the equal-weight combination's variance of \(0.0375\).

docs.title: Exercise 3: reading the companion's fixed-blend result
docs.text:
The companion reports logistic Brier 0.198372, boosted-calibrated Brier 0.267200, and fixed-equal-ensemble Brier 0.224694 on the same 45 test events. What does this ordering show about naive equal-weight blending here, and what would be needed before concluding a fitted weight would do better?

Solution sketch. The blend scores worse than logistic and better than calibrated boosting on this sample. A fitted weight needs base-model predictions generated without fitting or calibrating those models on the weight-training outcomes. After weights are selected, improvement must be checked on a further untouched evaluation cohort, not on the same fold used to select the weights. A nested or chronological cross-fitting design can organize those roles, but the companion implements only the fixed blend.

docs.title: Exercise 4: correlated forecaster errors
docs.text:
Two forecasters are fit from the same three underlying features and the same data-generating process. Explain why treating their combination as gaining "two independent opinions' worth" of variance reduction would be optimistic, using the minimum-variance formula's covariance term.

Solution sketch. As the error covariance \(c\) approaches the smaller of \(v_1\) and \(v_2\) (highly correlated errors), the achievable combined variance approaches the smaller individual variance rather than dropping further, so little or no combination benefit remains; assuming independence (implicitly \(c=0\)) when the true covariance is high overstates the variance reduction the combination can actually deliver.

docs.title: Exercise 5: abstention as a design choice
docs.text:
A combined forecasting system's base models disagree sharply on a subset of events. Propose one disciplined way to handle this disagreement, and state what evaluation would be needed to check whether the approach actually helps.

Solution sketch. Abstain from issuing a forecast (or issue a wide interval rather than a point estimate) on events where base-model disagreement exceeds a predeclared threshold, and report performance separately for the covered and abstained populations. This needs to be evaluated by comparing the covered subset's score against a baseline permitted a comparable abstention budget, on held-out data, exactly as Chapter 25's coverage-versus-baseline discussion requires — abstaining is not itself evidence of improved decision quality until checked this way.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: Part Four begins with Chapter 17, on turning a forecast like the ones built across this part into an actual order-sizing and execution decision — a different set of costs, constraints, and failure modes than anything in the modeling part of this book, but one that depends entirely on the honest, calibrated, and properly combined probabilities this part has been about producing.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: You should already be comfortable with conditional probability, the difference between a modeled probability \(\hat p\) and a realized binary outcome \(Y\), executable order-book prices from the market-microstructure material, and the book's canonical accounting example from the notation registry: buying 10 YES units at USD 0.40 with an illustrative flat fee of USD 0.01 per unit. You should also know that a market midpoint \(m\) is a forecasting benchmark, not something you can actually buy or sell at. This chapter does not reintroduce probability estimation, order-book mechanics, or settlement rules from first principles; it assumes you already have a forecast and a live-looking quote and asks what a disciplined trader does next.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this chapter you should be able to: state the difference between a modeled probability and the decision threshold implied by executable prices; compute a conservative estimated edge that already accounts for the correct side of the book, fee rounding, and depth, without double-subtracting the spread; explain why abstention is a legitimate output of a decision procedure rather than a bug; compute the cash a buy order must reserve and why a sell order cannot be sized past owned inventory; distinguish a screened "candidate" decision from an actual fill; state the maximum loss of a simple hold-to-settlement position; and compare holding to settlement against selling early through an executable bid.

docs.title: 17.1 A forecast is not a trade
docs.text:
Suppose your model reports \(\hat p = 0.55\) for some event contract's YES outcome. That number, by itself, tells you nothing about whether to trade. It says nothing about whether an order can currently be filled, at what price, in what quantity, net of what costs, or with what capital already committed elsewhere. A probability estimate is an input to a decision procedure, not the decision itself.

The forecast-to-order problem is the translation step: given \(\hat p\), an executable quote, a fee schedule, a risk budget, and the trader's existing position, produce one of a small number of disciplined actions. In this book's companion library that translation is implemented as screen_buy_yes in prediction_market_lab.risk, and its output is a Decision record with a status, a reason, a quantity, an executable cost, and a modeled expected profit. The function is deliberately narrow: it screens a single proposed buy-YES order against one book snapshot. It does not place a live order, and its "candidate" status is conditional arithmetic, not evidence of a realized edge.

Two failure modes motivate this chapter. The first is treating \(\hat p\) as if it were an executable price: comparing a forecast directly to a decision rule such as "buy whenever \(\hat p > 0.5\)" ignores every cost of actually transacting. The second is computing a "cost" using a market midpoint, a last trade, or a candle's low, none of which you could actually have paid. Both failures manufacture an edge that a careful order-level calculation removes.

docs.title: 17.2 Executable prices, sides, and depth
docs.text:
An event contract's order book has two sides. The ask is what a buyer must pay; the bid is what a seller receives. A buy order sweeps asks starting from the best (lowest) price; a sell order sweeps bids starting from the best (highest) price. Because a book has finite depth at each price level, filling a requested quantity \(Q\) may require paying several different prices, not one.

The companion's OrderBook.executable(side) returns the asks for a buy and the bids for a sell, and sweep_cost(book, side, qty, fees) walks that side level by level, accumulating both the traded notional and the fee due at each level, and raises an error if the visible depth cannot fill the entire requested quantity. This models an all-or-nothing full-size sweep: a stateless candidate calculation of what the order would cost if it filled completely against the current snapshot, not a live fill.

Consider an ask side with two levels: 5 units at USD 0.40, then 10 units at USD 0.44. A buy order for 10 units consumes all 5 units at USD 0.40 and 5 of the 10 units at USD 0.44. Running this through the installed library with a flat USD 0.01-per-unit fee gives an executable cost of USD 4.30, not the USD 4.10 you would compute by pricing the entire order at the best level alone. The difference, USD 0.20 here, is exactly the cost of the depth actually consumed at the second, worse level. A decision procedure that only looks at the best bid/ask, ignoring depth, silently overstates the edge on any order large enough to walk the book.

docs.title: 17.3 Per-unit fees, total fees, and rounding
docs.text:
The canonical fee is an invented USD 0.01 per unit; ten units at USD 0.40 cost USD 4.10. Actual schedules can depend on price, side, category, size, and how fills accumulate. For the companion, define cent ceiling by \(\lceil x\rceil_{0.01}=0.01\lceil x/0.01\rceil\) when \(x\) is a USD amount. FeeSchedule.total(qty, unit_price) applies this cent ceiling to qty * (per_unit + unit_price * notional_rate), once per call. It does not round to whole dollars, as an unqualified mathematical ceiling would. That per-call distinction matters.

Take a fee schedule with zero flat component and a 0.3% notional rate, applied to a price of USD 0.40. Computing the fee for a single fill of 3 units gives USD 0.01 after rounding up. Now suppose the same 3 units instead fill as three separate 1-unit executions, perhaps because the book only offered one unit at a time. Each 1-unit fill independently rounds its own fee up to USD 0.01, for a total of USD 0.03 across the three fills, three times the fee of the single 3-unit fill. Nothing about the trader's intended size changed; only the number of separate fills did. This is not a hypothetical curiosity: Kalshi's own documentation on fee rounding explicitly distinguishes a trade fee, a separate rounding fee, a rebate, balance precision, and an accumulator applied across fills, which is a different structure from a single flat per-unit number. KALSHI_ROUNDING Polymarket's documentation similarly describes taker fees that are price- and market-dependent rather than a single constant. POLYMARKET_FEES The lesson generalizes beyond either venue: never assume a total cost equals quantity times a single per-unit number without checking whether the venue's actual schedule rounds per fill, depends on price, or depends on market category. A backtest or screening tool that assumes a flat schedule when the real schedule is fill-sensitive will misstate exactly the fills that are hardest to get in one piece: thin, illiquid books.

docs.title: 17.4 A conservative estimated edge
docs.text:
With executable prices and correctly computed fees in hand, the modeled expected profit of buying \(Q\) YES units at cost \(C(Q)\), holding to ordinary binary settlement, is

\[ \mathbb{E}_{\hat p}[\Pi] = \hat p \cdot Q - C(Q). \]

Using the canonical numbers, \(\hat p = 0.55\), \(Q = 10\), and a full ask-side sweep at USD 0.40 per unit with the flat USD 0.01 fee gives \(C(Q) = 4.10\) and \(\mathbb{E}_{\hat p}[\Pi] = 10 \times 0.55 - 4.10 = 1.40\). Running screen_buy_yes(0.55, book, 10, fees, budget, ...) against a sufficiently deep book at that price reproduces exactly this: an executable cost of USD 4.10 and a modeled expected profit of USD 1.40, with status PAPER_CANDIDATE_ONLY.

Two things about this number deserve emphasis. First, the cost already used the executable ask, so the bid/ask spread has already been paid once; a separate "slippage" deduction using the same spread would double-count it. Second, the subscript on \(\mathbb{E}_{\hat p}\) is not decorative. This is an expectation under a forecast that might be wrong. It is not a promise about the next realized outcome, and it is not, by itself, evidence of a statistically supported edge; Chapter 19 covers what would be required to make that stronger claim. Wolfers and Zitzewitz's working paper describes conditions under which a market price approximates an average belief, and biased approximations when those conditions fail; a model's own \(\hat p\) inherits the same caution in reverse, since a plausible-looking forecast is not automatically well calibrated. WZ2006

Now walk the thin two-level book from Section 17.2 through the same screen. The executable cost was USD 4.30, so the modeled expected profit becomes \(10 \times 0.55 - 4.30 = 1.20\), USD 0.20 lower purely from depth. Running the actual function on that book confirms this: Decision(status='PAPER_CANDIDATE_ONLY', ..., executable_cost=Decimal('4.30'), modeled_expected_profit=Decimal('1.20')).

docs.title: 17.5 Abstention is a valid output
docs.text:
A screening procedure needs an explicit rule for when not to trade, and that rule needs a buffer, not merely a strict-inequality comparison to zero. Consider \(\hat p = 0.41\) against the same USD 0.40 ask and USD 0.01 fee, giving a cost of USD 4.10 for 10 units. The modeled expected profit is \(10 \times 0.41 - 4.10 = 0.00\) exactly. Passing this to screen_buy_yes returns NO_TRADE with the reason "modeled edge does not exceed the stated cost buffer" and a computed expected profit of USD 0.00. Nudging the forecast down slightly, to \(\hat p = 0.409\), gives a modeled expected profit of USD \(-0.01\) and the same NO_TRADE status.

This "does not exceed" behavior is deliberate: a zero or negative modeled edge cannot justify a trade, and the function additionally accepts a minimum_modeled_profit buffer parameter so a caller can require a strictly positive margin over zero before treating an estimate as interesting at all. Requiring \(\mathbb{E}_{\hat p}[\Pi] > 0.50\) against the canonical USD 1.40 estimate still passes; requiring \(\mathbb{E}_{\hat p}[\Pi] > 2.00\) correctly abstains despite the same USD 1.40 figure, because a modeled point estimate this close to a threshold provides little protection against forecast error. Depth can also force abstention directly: attempting to buy 10 units against a book offering only 4 units total raises an "insufficient executable depth for the requested full size" condition inside the sweep, and the screen returns NO_TRADE with exactly that reason, cost and expected profit both left unset. Abstention is not a defect to be silently patched around with a partial fill assumption; it is the correct output when the stated conditions are not met.

docs.title: 17.6 Quantity, margin, and full collateral
docs.text:
A buy order reserves cash before execution. The companion allows for separate one-unit fills: FeeSchedule.buy_reserve(qty, limit) equals quantity times the sum of the cent-ceiling limit and total(1, limit). Ten units at USD 0.40 with a flat USD 0.01 fee reserve USD 4.10. Under Section 17.3's notional-rate fee, three units at USD 0.40 reserve USD 1.23, although one aggregated fill costs USD 1.21. The reserve is an intentionally conservative bound, not the actual charged notional: fill notional rounds half-up to cents, whereas the reserve rounds each potential one-unit notional upward. Checking only the optimistic sweep cost can therefore underfund fragmented execution.

A RiskBudget enforces two independent caps: max_order_cost, an upper bound on a single order's cost or reserve, and max_committed_cash, an upper bound on that cost plus whatever cash is already committed to open positions and other resting orders. Both are checked in permits(cost, available_cash, committed_cash). Setting max_order_cost to USD 2.00 against the canonical USD 4.10 order correctly returns NO_TRADE with reason "cash/reservation or loss budget fails," even though the modeled expected profit of USD 1.40 is unchanged; a favorable modeled edge does not override an explicit risk limit. The same rejection occurs if available cash is only USD 3.00, or if USD 2.00 is already committed against a USD 5.00 cap.

Selling has a mirrored but asymmetric constraint: there is no borrowing or shorting in this classroom ledger. A sell order's quantity is checked against owned inventory minus units already reserved by other resting sell orders on the same contract; attempting to sell units you do not hold, or double-reserving units already committed to an unfilled sell order, is explicitly rejected as a "naked or doubly reserved sell." Margin for a purchase is a cash question; margin for a sale is an inventory question, and conflating the two produces either an impossible short or a double-counted position.

docs.title: 17.7 Conditional fills, not guaranteed fills
docs.text:
A PAPER_CANDIDATE_ONLY decision describes conditional arithmetic: if the order is actually submitted and if it actually fills at the assumed prices, this is the resulting cost and modeled profit. Neither condition is guaranteed by the screen itself. Submitting an order creates a resting or partially resting obligation; only a subsequent fill event, driven by an actual counterparty or an explicit taker sweep against a real book snapshot, converts that candidate into cash flow and inventory.

This distinction matters most for resting limit orders placed below the current ask (to buy) or above the current bid (to sell), waiting for the market to move to them. Observing that a later quote merely touched your limit price is not evidence of a fill; queue position, size ahead of you, and the exact sequence of trades at that price are usually unobservable from public data. The companion's paper broker explicitly encodes this: calling its resting-quote observation method on an order whose limit price has been touched returns the literal message "NO_INFERRED_FILL: quotes alone do not establish queue position or a trade," and it does not credit cash or inventory. A fill-conditioned forecast, the forecast appropriate at the moment a resting order finally fills, can also differ from the forecast held when the order was placed; a counterparty willing to trade at your resting price may be reacting to exactly the information that makes the fill less favorable to you, an instance of adverse selection covered further in Chapter 21.

docs.title: 17.8 Maximum loss
docs.text: For the simple hold-to-settlement position in this chapter, the maximum loss is bounded and known in advance: it is the cost already paid, because the worst outcome for a bought YES position is an ordinary NO settlement paying zero per unit. Running an actual settlement of payout zero against the canonical position, 10 units bought at USD 0.40 with a USD 0.01-per-unit fee for a total cost of USD 4.10, realizes exactly USD \(-4.10\): cash is unchanged from its post-purchase level, and realized profit is precisely the negative of the amount paid. This is a useful sanity check for any scenario table: the NO-settlement column of a payout matrix should reproduce the negative of the initial cost, no less and no more, when there is no exit fee on settlement itself. An exceptional non-YES/NO payout, such as a half-dollar settlement, produces an intermediate outcome; the same worked position settled at a USD 0.50 payout realizes USD 0.90, not the full USD 5.90 of an ordinary YES nor the full USD \(-4.10\) of an ordinary NO. Kalshi's settlement documentation explicitly distinguishes ordinary YES/NO settlement from a scalar or sub-cent settlement path with its own fee and rounding treatment, and states that settlement timing itself can vary, which is a separate fact from the size of the payout. KALSHI_SETTLEMENT Do not assume every contract shares the ordinary binary maximum-loss shape; check the actual settlement rule before relying on "I can only lose what I paid."

docs.title: 17.9 Holding to settlement versus selling early
docs.text:
Holding to settlement realizes exactly the contractual payout net of the original cost, with no further transaction. Selling early instead realizes the executable bid at the time of exit, net of whatever exit fee applies, and locks in that value regardless of the eventual settlement. Using the notation-registry convention, selling the canonical 10-unit position at a bid of USD 0.46 with a further USD 0.01-per-unit exit fee realizes \(10 \times (0.46 - 0.40 - 0.01 - 0.01) = 0.40\). Running the broker's own sell-and-fill path against that bid, with the same fee schedule applied on the way out, reproduces this exactly: realized profit of USD 0.40 after the sale, versus a conservative liquidation mark (not yet an actual sale) of the same USD 0.40 computed from the identical bid and fee before any sell order is even submitted. The mark and the realized outcome agree here because the mark uses the same fee-inclusive bid arithmetic; they can diverge once the mark instead relies on a stale, thin, or since-moved book.

The decision between holding and selling is a genuine trade-off, not a dominance relationship. Holding retains full exposure to the contractual payout, whatever it eventually is, and locks up capital until settlement with no early exit fee in the simplest classroom case. Selling caps the outcome at a currently known, worse-than-full-payout number, releases capital sooner, and pays an exit fee that holding to ordinary settlement does not. Neither choice is uniformly better; it depends on updated beliefs about the outcome, the capital's next best use, and the marginal cost of the exit itself.

docs.title: Companion example
docs.text:
Run:

Command working directory: run this chapter's Python commands from book\companion. From the trading repository root, run Set-Location book\companion once first. The .venv belongs to that companion project; see companion setup.

.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe examples\execution_replay.py

The script (linked at ../companion/examples/execution_replay.py; see examples/README.md for the full set of 17 companion scripts, their public entry points, and their observed outputs) demonstrates finite-depth partial fills, a rejected double-spend on already-reserved cash, a rejected naked sell, and the explicit "no inferred fill" response to a quote touch, using the shared prediction_market_lab accounting module rather than a duplicated chapter snippet. Its output is real, deterministic, and synthetic; it is not evidence of a historically achievable fill, and its ledger exists only in that running process's memory, not as any durable order-management record.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 17.1. A book's ask side has 3 units at USD 0.52 and 8 units at USD 0.55. A trader wants to buy 6 units, with a flat fee of USD 0.02 per unit. Compute the executable cost, using the correct price at each level, and the modeled expected profit at \(\hat p = 0.60\).

Solution. The first 3 units cost \(3 \times 0.52 = 1.56\); the remaining 3 units come from the second level at \(3 \times 0.55 = 1.65\). Notional is \(1.56 + 1.65 = 3.21\). The fee is \(6 \times 0.02 = 0.12\), so total cost is USD 3.33. Modeled expected profit is \(6 \times 0.60 - 3.33 = 3.60 - 3.33 = 0.27\).

Exercise 17.2. Using the same book and fee as Exercise 17.1, at what integer modeled probability threshold (to the nearest whole percentage point) does the modeled expected profit first become nonpositive, holding quantity fixed at 6 units? State the exact breakeven \(\hat p\).

Solution. Breakeven requires \(6\hat p = 3.33\), so \(\hat p = 0.555\). At \(\hat p = 0.55\) the modeled expected profit is \(3.30 - 3.33 = -0.03\), negative; at \(\hat p = 0.56\) it is \(3.36 - 3.33 = 0.03\), positive. The exact breakeven is 55.5 percent; any screen using a strict "greater than zero" rule would trade at 56 percent and abstain at 55 percent, with no trade at exactly the breakeven value itself.

Exercise 17.3. A trader holds 10 YES units bought for USD 4.10 total. Write the ordinary binary profit values, then show that a half-dollar-per-unit settlement gives their arithmetic average under these fixed-cost assumptions. Explain why this does not assign 50 percent probability to any outcome.

Solution. Ordinary YES settlement realizes \(10 \times 1 - 4.10 = 5.90\); ordinary NO settlement realizes \(10 \times 0 - 4.10 = -4.10\). Their arithmetic average is USD 0.90, which happens to match a half-dollar exceptional settlement's realized profit of \(10 \times 0.5 - 4.10 = 0.90\) only because this contract's payout function is linear in the settlement value and the cost is fixed; it is not a general property, and it does not imply the exceptional payout has 50 percent probability or that it always falls exactly between the ordinary outcomes for a differently structured contract.

Exercise 17.4. Explain, without computing new numbers, why a risk budget check that only compares an order's optimistic sweep cost to max_order_cost, and ignores the conservative buy-reserve amount, could later permit an order that the budget was actually meant to block.

Solution. The sweep cost assumes the order fills exactly as one calculation against the current snapshot at the displayed level prices. The buy-reserve amount instead assumes the worst case of separate one-unit fills, each rounding its own fee up. When the fee schedule has a nonzero notional-rate component, the reserve can exceed the sweep cost, as shown for the 3-unit notional-rate example in Section 17.6. A budget check against the smaller sweep-cost figure alone could approve an order whose actual worst-case cash commitment exceeds the intended cap once fills fragment.

Exercise 17.5. A position was bought at a total cost of USD 4.10. State, in one sentence each, the difference between its "marked" profit from a conservative liquidation calculation and its "realized" profit, and explain which one changes if the reference bid used for the mark moves before an actual sell order is filled.

Solution. Marked profit is a valuation using a specified current bid and fee, without any executed sale; realized profit requires an actual (or explicitly simulated) sell fill and is fixed once that fill occurs. If the reference bid moves before a sell order actually fills, the mark changes to reflect the new bid, but realized profit remains undefined until a fill occurs and is then determined by the price actually achieved, not by any earlier mark.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: You should be comfortable with the forecast-to-order screen from Chapter 17, the point-in-time data discipline from the data-pipeline chapters, and the distinction between an event's occurrence, its public confirmation, and its contractual settlement from the rules-and-settlement material. You should know what an executable ask, an executable bid, and book depth mean, and why a midpoint is not something you can transact at.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this chapter you should be able to: list the distinct clocks a faithful simulation must keep separate; describe an order's lifecycle and why a cash reservation prevents double-spending an order not yet filled; simulate partial and no fills from finite depth without inferring a fill from a quote touch; explain why price-time queue priority usually cannot be reconstructed from public data, forcing a taker-only assumption; add latency and cancellation to the fidelity discussion; settle a position correctly, including an exceptional nonbinary payout; distinguish a marked valuation from actual cash; state what capital conservation requires of a ledger; and use a benchmark and a stress scenario to interrogate a simulated result rather than accept it at face value.

docs.title: 18.1 Correct arithmetic on historical prices is not a backtest
docs.text:
It is easy to write code that looks like a backtest: iterate over historical timestamps, compare a stored price to a model's forecast, and accumulate a running profit whenever some rule triggers. That code can be arithmetically correct and still be worthless as evidence, because arithmetic correctness says nothing about whether the assumed order could actually have been placed, at that price, in that quantity, before that information was available, and settled the way the code assumes.

A faithful event-driven backtest is a discrete-event simulation with an explicit state machine: orders move through submission, partial fills, cancellation, and settlement; cash and inventory move through a ledger that must reconcile at every step; and every price the simulation uses to fill an order must be traceable to a specific, dated, executable quote rather than to a convenient scalar such as a midpoint, a last trade, or a candle's high or low. A quote touch or a candle extreme is never proof of a hypothetical fill. A resting limit order at a price that a candle's low or high merely reached might not have filled at all, might have filled only partially, or might have filled behind other resting orders that had queue priority. Treating a touch as a certain fill is one of the most common and most silently profit-inflating errors in backtesting event contracts.

docs.title: 18.2 Seven clocks that must not be conflated
docs.text:
A faithful simulation keeps at least the following times distinct for every observation: event time (when the underlying real-world event occurred), source publication time (when information about it became public), local observation time (when the simulation's own data pipeline actually recorded it), decision time (the cutoff used by the model or strategy to act), fill time (when a simulated order actually executed), label-availability time (when the outcome became knowable for later training or evaluation), and settlement time (when the contractual payout actually became available). These are not redundant. A same-day news report can describe an event that happened hours earlier; a database snapshot can be retrieved well after a quote was actually posted; and a contract can be economically decided before its formal settlement completes.

Using a single "date" column for all of these, a common shortcut in casual historical analysis, silently permits information from later in the day, or from a later revision, to leak into an earlier decision. The point-in-time discipline introduced earlier in the book applies with full force here: a decision at time \(t\) may use only information whose local observation time is at or before \(t\), and a fill can only occur using a book snapshot whose observed time is compatible with the decision and does not itself use unavailable information.

docs.title: 18.3 Order lifecycle and reservations
docs.text:
An order moves through explicit states: submitted, partially filled, fully filled, or cancelled. Two rules protect against a subtle and easy mistake: using the same committed cash or inventory twice. A resting buy order must reserve cash the moment it is submitted, before any fill occurs, because that cash could be consumed at any later moment while the order rests. A resting sell order must similarly be checked against inventory not already claimed by another resting sell order on the same contract.

Running the companion's paper broker against a single contract with USD 3.00 of cash and a flat USD 0.01-per-unit fee illustrates this concretely. Submitting a buy order for 5 units at a USD 0.45 limit reserves USD 2.30 (the worst-case one-unit-fill reservation for that quantity and limit). Attempting to submit a second buy order for 2 more units at the same limit, before the first order has filled or been cancelled, is rejected outright with "insufficient unreserved funded cash," because the first order's reservation has already claimed the cash the second order would need. This is not a conservative inconvenience; it is what prevents a simulation from silently double-spending the same dollar across two resting orders, an error that would make simulated available capital look larger than it actually was at every subsequent step.

docs.title: 18.4 Partial and no fills from finite depth
docs.text:
Depth is finite, and a simulated taker order should only fill against the quantity actually visible at each price level, in order, stopping the instant the order's own limit price is no longer satisfied. Running the companion's execution replay against an ask side of 2 units at USD 0.40 followed by 1 unit at USD 0.44, for a resting 5-unit buy order with a USD 0.45 limit, fills exactly 3 units: 2 at USD 0.40 with a fee of USD 0.02, then 1 at USD 0.44 with a fee of USD 0.01. Two units remain unfilled on the order, confirmed by the order's own remaining-quantity field. Running the identical snapshot a second time against the same already-filled order produces zero additional fills, because the snapshot's usable depth at each level has already been recorded as consumed; a backtest that instead let the same visible depth fill the same order repeatedly across separate simulated ticks would overstate liquidity by exactly the number of times it replayed the snapshot.

This finite-depth, partial-fill behavior also interacts with the rounding effect from Chapter 17. Because each of the two consumed price levels is a separate fill, the fee for the 3 filled units is the sum of the two levels' own rounded fees, USD 0.02 plus USD 0.01, rather than a single fee computed on the combined 3-unit notional; with a fee schedule whose rounding can matter, splitting a fill across levels or across separate simulated ticks can make the realized fee total higher than a naive single-fill calculation would suggest, exactly as the earlier three-separate-one-unit-fills example showed a threefold fee increase over one combined fill.

docs.title: 18.5 Price-time queue limits and taker-only depth
docs.text:
Public order-book data usually does not reveal your own hypothetical order's position in the queue at a price level, nor the exact sequence of other participants' orders ahead of it. Without that information, a simulator has two honest choices: simulate only taker fills, where the simulated order actively sweeps visible resting depth and therefore does not depend on queue position, or explicitly model queue priority using an assumption that is clearly labeled as an assumption rather than as a verified historical fact.

The companion library takes the first, more conservative path for its accounting layer. When an order is resting and a later book snapshot shows that price merely being touched, the broker's explicit resting-order check returns the fixed message "NO_INFERRED_FILL: quotes alone do not establish queue position or a trade," rather than crediting a fill. This is a deliberately unhelpful-looking result, and that is the point: without genuine queue data, a simulator claiming a resting-order fill at a touched price is asserting information it does not have. A more ambitious historical study could attempt to model queue priority using trade-by-trade message data, but doing so honestly requires message-level detail beyond simple price levels and must be labeled as a distinct, harder modeling assumption, not folded silently into an ordinary depth sweep. Kalshi's own inspected order-book documentation, for instance, describes bid arrays with fixed-point quantities from which an ordinary binary ask is inferred, which is a schema description, not a queue-position or fill guarantee for any particular historical resting order. KALSHI_BOOK Polymarket's inspected prices/order-books documentation similarly exposes price/size levels with a timestamp and a state hash, useful for reconstructing a snapshot but not a queue position within it. POLYMARKET_BOOK

docs.title: 18.6 Latency and cancellation
docs.text:
Every fill in the companion's taker sweep is computed as an instantaneous match against the supplied snapshot: there is no simulated delay between deciding to trade and the fill being evaluated against that snapshot. This is an explicit, disclosed paper-trading assumption, not a claim about historical achievable latency. A real trader's order experiences network delay, matching-engine queueing, and the possibility that the book has already moved by the time the order actually reaches the venue; a zero-latency backtest cannot rule out that some or all of an apparent edge would have been eroded, or eliminated, by realistic delay, especially for signals that decay quickly.

Cancellation must also be represented honestly. The companion's cancel represents an effective cancellation, records a zero-cash, zero-inventory entry, and rejects later fills on that closed order. A real cancellation request is not yet an effective cancellation: an in-flight match may win the race before the venue processes the request, and its confirmation may arrive later still. The companion does not simulate that network race. A historical replay needs separate request, venue-effective, match, and receipt records rather than assuming that sending a cancel instantly prevents execution.

docs.title: 18.7 Settlement, including nonbinary payouts
docs.text:
A faithful backtest must settle a position using the contract's actual specified payout, not by forcing every outcome into a zero-or-one binary label. The companion's Settlement record carries an explicit payout value and exposes a binary_label property that returns None whenever the payout is not exactly zero or one, precisely to stop an exceptional payout from being silently coerced into an ordinary binary result.

Running three settlements against the same 10-unit position, bought for a total cost of USD 4.10, shows the range this matters over. An ordinary YES settlement, payout 1.00 per unit, realizes profit of USD 5.90. An ordinary NO settlement, payout 0.00, realizes USD \(-4.10\), the full loss of the amount paid. An exceptional half-dollar settlement, payout 0.50, realizes USD 0.90, an intermediate value that a strategy coded to only understand YES and NO would either crash on or, worse, silently mishandle. Polymarket's resolution documentation explicitly describes disputes, additional-context clarifications, and an exceptional Unknown/50-50 payout that redeems each side at 0.50; it is evidence that at least one venue implements exactly this kind of nonbinary settlement path, not a claim about how often it occurs or that every venue's exceptional-payout mechanism works identically. POLYMARKET_RESOLUTION

docs.title: 18.8 Marks versus cash
docs.text:
Cash is a ledger fact: it changes only when an order actually fills or a position actually settles. A mark is a valuation of an open position using a specified reference price, and it does not, by itself, change cash or realize any profit. The distinction is easy to blur in a running equity chart, where an unmarked, unrealized position's value is often plotted as if it were cash already in hand.

Consider the canonical 10-unit position again, bought for USD 4.10 out of an initial USD 10.00, leaving cash of USD 5.90. Marking that open position using a conservative full-liquidation calculation against a bid of USD 0.46 with the same USD 0.01-per-unit exit fee gives a liquidation value of USD 4.50 (USD 4.60 of bid proceeds minus USD 0.10 of fee), for a marked equity of USD 10.40 and a marked profit of USD 0.40, while cash itself is still only USD 5.90 and realized profit is still exactly zero, because no sale has actually happened yet. Only after an actual sell order is submitted and filled against that same bid does realized profit change from zero to USD 0.40, and cash rise from USD 5.90 to USD 10.40. A backtest's headline equity curve should make clear, at every point, whether it is reporting cash, a conservative mark, or a realized result, because a drawdown computed on a mark that assumes full liquidation at the best available bid can understate what liquidating a large or illiquid position would actually realize.

docs.title: 18.9 Capital conservation
docs.text:
A ledger that lets cash or inventory drift away from what its own recorded fills and settlements imply is not trustworthy, no matter how plausible its headline profit looks. The companion broker's reconcile() method recomputes expected cash as the initial cash plus the sum of every ledger entry's cash effect, recomputes expected inventory per contract from the same ledger, and recomputes cost basis from the lot-tracking structure used for fills, raising an assertion error if any of these disagree, or if available cash or any order's filled quantity falls outside its valid range. This is a capital-conservation invariant: every dollar and every unit of inventory in the simulation must be accounted for by an explicit, timestamped event, with no silent creation or destruction. A backtest for a real venue's data should implement, and actually run, an equivalent reconciliation at every step; a simulation that only checks its final headline number, without any running invariant, can hide an intermediate bug that happens to cancel out by the end of a lucky run.

This reconciliation is an internal consistency check on an in-memory ledger, not exchange-grade reconciliation and not a production order-management system. The companion broker holds its orders, fills, and ledger entries only for the lifetime of the running Python process; nothing here persists a book across restarts, recovers from a crash mid-fill, or reconciles against an actual venue's account statement. A backtest or paper-trading harness that needs to survive a restart, audit a real settlement report, or coordinate multiple concurrent processes needs separate, purpose-built infrastructure; treating this teaching ledger's internal invariant as a substitute for that infrastructure would be a category error, not merely an optimistic simplification.

docs.title: 18.10 Benchmarks and stress testing
docs.text:
A single equity curve, however carefully simulated, is hard to interpret in isolation. A useful faithful backtest reports at least one comparison benchmark, such as a deliberately simple baseline decision rule evaluated under the identical execution assumptions, so a reader can judge whether the additional complexity of the strategy under test actually earned its keep against realistic costs, not merely against a hypothetical zero-cost comparison.

A stress test complements the benchmark by asking what a set of already-taken positions would realize under several different settlement scenarios, independent of any probability estimate. Using the companion's scenario-stress calculation on the canonical 10-unit, USD 4.10-cost position across three scenarios, an ordinary YES settlement, an ordinary NO settlement, and an exceptional half-dollar settlement, gives realized results of USD 5.90, USD \(-4.10\), and USD 0.90 respectively: the same three numbers as the settlement examples in Section 18.7, now organized as a small scenario table rather than three separate settlement calls. This kind of table is a useful sanity check for any position report: every plausible settlement scenario the contract actually permits should appear as a labeled column, and the NO-settlement column should always reproduce the negative of the amount actually paid, not some other value.

docs.text:
Run:

Its printed result is real, deterministic output from the installed prediction_market_lab package against synthetic fixtures, not a record of any historical venue activity, and it exists only in that process's memory: rerunning the script starts a fresh, empty ledger every time.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 18.1. A resting buy order for 4 units at a USD 0.50 limit is submitted against a book showing 1 unit at USD 0.48 and 2 units at USD 0.49 on the ask side, with a flat USD 0.01-per-unit fee. Compute the fills a faithful taker sweep would produce, including any unfilled remainder, and state why the order cannot fill entirely from this single snapshot.

Solution. The sweep takes the 1 unit at USD 0.48 (fee USD 0.01), then the 2 units at USD 0.49 (fee USD 0.02), for 3 filled units and 1 unit remaining, because the visible depth at prices at or below the USD 0.50 limit only totals 3 units. The order remains open for its last unit until either more depth appears at an acceptable price or the order is cancelled.

Exercise 18.2. Explain why observing that the best ask touched exactly USD 0.50 at some later timestamp is not sufficient evidence that the remaining 1 unit from Exercise 18.1 filled at that moment.

Solution. A touch at USD 0.50 shows only that some quantity was available or traded at that price; it does not show that the specific resting order in question had queue priority ahead of other orders at the same price, nor that its full remaining size was matched rather than a smaller part of it. Without message-level queue data, the honest conclusion is "no inferred fill," not an assumed full or partial match.

Exercise 18.3. A position was bought for a total cost of USD 6.30. Using only the settlement rule that ordinary YES pays 1.00 per unit and ordinary NO pays 0.00 per unit for 15 units, write the realized profit for each ordinary outcome, and explain what changes if an exceptional payout of 0.20 per unit applies instead.

Solution. Ordinary YES realizes \(15 \times 1.00 - 6.30 = 8.70\); ordinary NO realizes \(15 \times 0.00 - 6.30 = -6.30\). An exceptional payout of 0.20 per unit instead realizes \(15 \times 0.20 - 6.30 = -3.30\), a partial loss that is neither the full gain nor the full loss and must be handled as its own labeled case, not coerced into whichever of YES or NO it is numerically closer to.

Exercise 18.4. A backtest reports a rising equity curve using a mark computed from the best available bid at each timestamp, with no distinction between marked and realized profit. Give one concrete reason this equity curve could overstate what a trader liquidating the same position at the same timestamps would actually have realized.

Solution. A mark computed from only the best bid ignores depth: liquidating a position larger than the quantity available at that single best price would require sweeping additional, worse-priced levels, or would fail to liquidate the full position at that instant at all. The mark can also use a stale snapshot, or ignore the exit fee that a real liquidation would incur, both of which make the marked value higher than an achievable realized sale.

Exercise 18.5. Explain, in general terms, why a capital-conservation check on a simulated ledger (recomputing cash and inventory from the recorded event history and comparing them to the ledger's current stated values) is a meaningful correctness test even when the backtest's final headline profit number looks plausible.

Solution. A plausible final number does not rule out intermediate errors that happen to cancel out, such as a bug that briefly double-credits cash on one fill and later double-debits it on another. A capital-conservation check verifies the invariant at every step, not only at the end, so it can catch an error whose net effect on the final number is small or coincidentally zero but whose intermediate states were never actually valid.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: You should be comfortable with the exploration and leakage material from the data-pipeline chapters, the forecast-evaluation chapter's treatment of proper scoring rules and calibration, and the execution-aware backtest from Chapter 18. You should already know why a chronological split of rows is not automatically an independence guarantee, and what a dependence group is.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this chapter you should be able to: build a walk-forward evaluation that respects both time order and event-group independence at once; explain what "untouched" outcome availability actually requires of an evaluation protocol; explain why logging every trial searched, not only the best one, is necessary context for interpreting a result; state what White's reality check, Bailey's backtest-overfitting framework, and the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate procedure each qualify and do not qualify; describe the assumptions behind block-bootstrap and cluster-robust dependence methods; explain why sequential monitoring requires different machinery than a fixed-interval peek at a test statistic; distinguish a favorable point estimate from a demonstrated positive effect once uncertainty and effect size are considered; and list concrete controls, including negative controls, for costs, slippage, and fill sensitivity.

docs.title: 19.1 A favorable backtest result is a claim, not a finding
docs.text:
Suppose a strategy search over many candidate rules, thresholds, and features produces one configuration whose simulated net profit, after the fees and depth discipline of Chapter 18, looks attractive.
