That single favorable number is a claim requiring evidence, not a finding that stands on its own. The central problem is not that the arithmetic is wrong; the arithmetic can be entirely correct and the conclusion still unsupported, because the process that produced the winning configuration searched many candidates, and search itself changes what a given point estimate means.

This is easiest to see with a simulation that contains no real signal at all. Draw 20 independent standard-normal numbers, meant to represent 20 unrelated strategy variants' scaled performance under a null hypothesis of no true edge, and report only the best of the 20. Running this simulation 200,000 times gives an average best-of-20 value of approximately 1.87, compared with an average of essentially 0.00 for any single draw considered alone, and approximately 1.16 for a best-of-5 comparison under the same null. Nothing in this simulation has any actual predictive skill; the elevated average is a pure artifact of reporting only the maximum of several noisy draws. A single favorable backtest number, without a record of how many configurations were tried, is exactly analogous: it does not reveal whether it is a best-of-1, best-of-20, or best-of-thousands draw from an unknown search.

docs.title: 19.2 Walk-forward evaluation needs both time order and event-group independence
docs.text:
A walk-forward evaluation fits a model using only information available at a chronological cutoff, then evaluates it on later data, advancing the cutoff and repeating. This controls one important failure mode, using future information to fit a model, but it does not by itself control a second, equally damaging one: two observations that share the same underlying event, or that are otherwise statistically dependent, being split across the training and evaluation cohorts.

The companion's grouped_chronological_split function enforces both constraints simultaneously. It requires strictly increasing cutoffs for a train, validation, and test cohort; it purges any dependence group whose observations straddle a cutoff boundary entirely out of the assigned cohorts, rather than assigning part of the group to one cohort and part to another; and it separately verifies that no event identifier is assigned inconsistent group identifiers or outcome labels across the data. Two record-level checks make this concrete: an event whose recorded group identifier differs across two of its own rows raises "one event cannot be split across dependence groups," and an event whose recorded binary outcome differs across two of its own rows raises "one event has inconsistent binary labels." Both are explicit failures rather than a silent average or a first-seen-wins resolution, because either condition indicates a data problem serious enough to investigate before any split is trusted.

A chronological split alone, ignoring event grouping, could place one snapshot of a not-yet-resolved event in the training cohort and a later snapshot of the same event, sharing the same eventual outcome, in the evaluation cohort. A model evaluated that way could appear to generalize well while actually only recognizing an event it has effectively already seen resolve. Event grouping and time order are joint requirements: satisfying one does not substitute for the other.

docs.title: 19.3 Untouched outcome availability
docs.text:
"Held out" only means something if the evaluation cohort's outcomes were genuinely unavailable to every decision that shaped the reported model or strategy, not merely unavailable to the final fitting step. If a researcher repeatedly inspects test-cohort scores while iterating on features, thresholds, or architectures, and then reports the best-scoring configuration, the test cohort has been used for model selection in every meaningful sense, even though no single fitting call literally trained on its rows.

A genuinely untouched evaluation requires a predeclared protocol: which cohort is the final evaluation set, what metric will be reported, and how many times it will be inspected, decided before any of those inspections happen. Bailey, Borwein, Lopez de Prado, and Zhu's framework for the probability of backtest overfitting is directly about this problem; their institutional abstract proposes a combinatorially symmetric cross-validation procedure intended to estimate how likely a reported strategy selection is to have been chosen by overfitting rather than genuine skill, and it explicitly frames repeated inspection of a holdout during investment research as the mechanism that undermines an otherwise standard train/test separation. BAILEY2017 Their specific combinatorial procedure is not reproduced or independently verified here, and its applicability to sparse, dependent event-contract labels, as opposed to the continuous return series their framework more naturally targets, would need separate scrutiny; the qualitative warning about repeated holdout inspection still applies regardless of which specific test procedure is eventually used.

docs.title: 19.4 Logging every trial, not only the winner
docs.text:
The multiplicity simulation in Section 19.1 depends entirely on knowing how many candidates were drawn; the same is true for a real strategy search. A complete research log records every configuration actually evaluated, including its features, thresholds, evaluation window, and resulting metric, whether or not it was eventually reported. Without that log, a reader cannot distinguish a genuinely rare, striking result from the expected best-of-many artifact illustrated above, and neither can the researcher, months later, when memory of exactly how many variants were quietly tried has faded.

This requirement extends beyond a final list of models formally fit. Informally adjusting a feature definition, a training window's start date, an outcome threshold, or which markets are included, each time after glancing at how the resulting score looks, is still a form of search, and each such adjustment belongs in the log. The book's glossary is explicit that this broader informal search, not just a final candidate-model list, is what "multiple testing" needs to account for.

docs.title: 19.5 White's reality check and the false discovery rate
docs.text:
Two different statistical qualifications, though sometimes discussed together, aim at different questions. White's reality check addresses whether the single best result from a search of many candidate rules could plausibly have arisen by chance, given the whole set of rules considered. Its published construction, with the relevant abstract, introduction, and Section 2a-2b now directly inspected, tests the best of several candidates' expected performance against a stated benchmark using a least-favorable-null construction, and it handles dependence in the underlying data using common random-length bootstrap blocks, the same style of block resampling covered further in Section 19.6. WHITE2000 Its stated setup assumes stationary, strong-mixing observations, point-in-time predictors, and further asymptotic regularity conditions; the Appendix's full assumptions and proofs were not independently audited here. The qualification that matters most for this book stands regardless of that audit: a reality-check-style test can tell you whether a found best result still beats a benchmark once multiplicity is accounted for, but it cannot recover an undisclosed set of tried rules, repair a leakage problem in the underlying data, or validate a simulator's fictitious fills and missing costs.

The Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate procedure instead addresses a list of candidates, each with its own test statistic, and controls the expected proportion of falsely "significant" results among those declared significant, rather than the chance of any single false result at all. Concretely: take an invented list of 10 p-values from 10 strategy-variant comparisons, sorted from smallest to largest, \(0.001, 0.004, 0.012, 0.020, 0.045, 0.060, 0.090, 0.140, 0.310, 0.620\), and a target false discovery rate of \(\alpha = 0.10\). The procedure compares each sorted p-value at rank \(k\) (out of \(n = 10\)) to the threshold \(\alpha k / n\), and finds the largest rank at which the p-value is still at or below its own threshold. Computing this directly gives thresholds of \(0.010, 0.020, 0.030, 0.040, 0.050, 0.060, 0.070, 0.080, 0.090, 0.100\) at ranks 1 through 10; the sorted p-values satisfy \(p_{(k)} \leq \alpha k / n\) through rank 6 (0.060 exactly equals its threshold) but fail at rank 7 (0.090 exceeds 0.070). The procedure therefore rejects the 6 hypotheses with the smallest p-values.

This is an independently computed arithmetic illustration using invented p-values, not a report of any actual strategy search. The published Benjamini-Hochberg abstract states the false discovery rate objective and a control guarantee specifically for independent test statistics; it does not, by itself, license an unqualified extension to strategy trials whose underlying event outcomes share dependence, which is common when several candidate strategies trade overlapping or related event contracts. BENJAMINI1995

docs.title: 19.6 Dependent data: block bootstrap and cluster-robust assumptions
docs.text:
Most resampling and inference machinery taught in an introductory statistics course assumes independent observations. Event-contract data routinely violates that assumption: repeated snapshots of the same not-yet-resolved event, several contracts tied to the same underlying process, or strategies that trade through the same market regime all induce dependence that an ordinary independent bootstrap would understate.

The inspected Politis-Romano publisher abstract describes random geometric blocks and asymptotic inference for weakly dependent stationary observations. POLITIS1994 Neither its full proofs nor a suitable block length for this book's event data was audited. Do not extend that scope to arbitrary dependence or nonstationarity.

Cluster-robust regression variance estimates allow within-group dependence while requiring independent or appropriately weakly dependent groups, suitable moment/design conditions, and enough informative clusters for the approximation used. Five election clusters do not become a reliable large-cluster sample merely because they contain hundreds of rows. Both methods require a defensible sampling and dependence unit; a convenient database key is not sufficient.

docs.title: 19.7 Sequential monitoring is not repeated fixed-threshold peeking
docs.text:
A researcher who checks a running backtest's statistical significance after every new week of simulated data, stopping and reporting as soon as a conventional fixed threshold such as a two-sided 95 percent test is crossed, is running a fundamentally different procedure from one that commits in advance to a single look at a predetermined endpoint, even if both use the identical textbook formula at each individual check.

An explicit simulation shows the mechanism. Generate a 200,000-by-20 array of independent standard-normal increments with NumPy's default_rng(20260910). At look \(k\), use \(Z_k=(X_1+\cdots+X_k)/\sqrt{k}\), and reject if \(|Z_k|>1.96\). Each individual look has the usual standard-normal null distribution, but the looks within a path are dependent. Rejecting if any of the 20 looks crosses gives 24.8105 percent false positives in this simulation; using only the twentieth look gives 5.032 percent. The difference comes entirely from the stopping rule. These are reproducible simulated proportions, not estimates from trading data.

Correctly accounting for repeated looks requires machinery designed for that purpose. Howard, Ramdas, McAuliffe, and Sekhon's time-uniform confidence sequences are built around exactly this problem, using a filtration and an exponential-supermartingale construction to produce a bound that holds simultaneously across every stopping time an analyst might choose, rather than only at one predetermined look. HOWARD2021 The important qualification is that "time-uniform" describes coverage across looks under the method's own stated model, not a general license to ignore other sources of error; it does not, by itself, repair a leakage problem in the underlying data, and it does not turn genuinely dependent, repeated observations of the same event into independent draws. A researcher who wants to monitor a live paper strategy continuously, rather than at one predeclared endpoint, should use a construction designed for repeated looks, and should still separately confirm that its independence and boundedness assumptions are plausible for the specific data being monitored.

docs.title: 19.8 Power, effect size, and the gap between a point estimate and a guaranteed edge
docs.text:
A statistically distinguishable result and a practically meaningful one are different questions, and both are different again from a guaranteed future edge. Statistical power is the probability that a testing procedure detects a real effect of a given size, given the actual sample size and its dependence structure; with the small number of independent events that many prediction-market questions realistically provide, power to detect a modest true edge can be low, meaning that even a genuine, economically relevant effect could easily fail to produce a "significant" result, and conversely that an apparently large point estimate from a small, dependent sample carries wide uncertainty.

None of the tools in this chapter converts a favorable point estimate into a promise about future performance. A confidence interval, correctly constructed for the actual dependence structure and correctly adjusted for the actual number of configurations searched, describes a range of plausible values under the stated model; it is not evidence that the true value sits at the interval's most favorable end, and it says nothing at all about a differently structured future sample. "Statistically supported edge" in this book's usage requires a specified estimand, an accounting of dependence, a defensible correction for search, and uncertainty quantification that is still favorable after all of that; a single attractive number, however it was produced, does not meet that bar on its own, and it is never established by one favorable outcome for one trade.

docs.title: 19.9 Controlling for costs, slippage, fill sensitivity, and negative controls
docs.text:
A strategy evaluation that changes its assumed costs, fill model, or slippage convention only after seeing an unfavorable result is itself a form of undisclosed search. The execution assumptions from Chapter 18, correct executable-side prices, correctly rounded fees, finite depth, and no inferred fills from mere quote touches, should be fixed in advance and applied identically whether the resulting number looks good or bad. A useful robustness check varies these assumptions deliberately and reports the resulting range: for instance, recomputing the same strategy's simulated result under a moderately worse assumed fill price, or under a higher assumed fee, to see whether a reported edge survives plausible execution friction or evaporates well within it.

A negative control applies the search and reporting procedure to data constructed to lack the signal being claimed. The normal-draw experiment is one such control. Relabeling actual data requires a justified null randomization: shuffling rows independently can destroy shared-event structure, calendar effects, and other dependence that the control must preserve. If comparable favorable results often emerge under an appropriate null, the original point estimate is less persuasive; that comparison does not prove how much of any one realized result was luck. Report the control's construction and limitations, not merely that "labels were shuffled."

docs.title: Companion example
docs.text:
Run:

Command working directory: run this chapter's Python commands from book\companion. From the trading repository root, run Set-Location book\companion once first. The .venv belongs to that companion project; see companion setup.

.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe examples\forecast_models.py

The script fits preset logistic and boosted models, a validation-fitted isotonic map, and a fixed equal blend. It records training and calibration event IDs and dependence-group IDs, and evaluate_forecaster refuses either kind of overlap. That guard complements, rather than replaces, a correct split and research-history audit. On 45 test events, logistic Brier is 0.198372 and raw boosting 0.220607, against reference 0.249699; calibrated boosting is worse at 0.2672. Small-sample calibration noise is a plausible explanation, not a cause identified by those scores alone. Reporting the deterioration is part of the evidentiary discipline, not a failure to hide. See the example and output guide.

The script also reports two rescored snapshots of one event side by side under the label "same_event_updates_not_independent_trials," illustrating Section 19.2's warning that repeated observations of one event are not separate independent trials even at different timestamps. This is a single frozen logistic model, fitted once, rescored at two invented decision times for the same event; it is explicitly not a fitted sequence model that learns how a forecast evolves through an event's life, and its near-identical scores at the two horizons (0.258916 and 0.258227) are not a validated early-horizon calibration claim. Its evidence_gate field, from the companion's synthetic_evidence check, reports REJECT_LIVE_EDGE_INFERENCE for this synthetic run, listing untouched-evaluation, dependence-and-search, and uncertainty-support failures by name; this is real, deterministic output, and it is the correct verdict for a synthetic teaching fixture, not evidence against some future well-controlled real-data study.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 19.1. A researcher reports that the best of 30 informally tried trading rules achieved a favorable simulated result and does not report the other 29. Using the multiplicity simulation logic from Section 19.1 (best-of-5 averaged about 1.16 standard deviations above zero, best-of-20 about 1.87), explain qualitatively why the reported number likely overstates the rule's true expected performance, without assuming the specific magnitude for 30 draws.

Solution. The simulation shows that the expected value of the maximum of several independent null draws increases with the number of draws even though no individual draw has any real effect. Reporting only the maximum of 30 informally tried rules, without disclosing the other 29, presents a best-of-many statistic as if it were a single a priori prediction; some of the apparent favorable performance is very likely an artifact of having chosen the best result out of many attempts rather than evidence of a genuinely superior rule.

Exercise 19.2. Two snapshots of the same not-yet-resolved event, taken 9 hours apart, are assigned to the training and test cohorts respectively by a naive chronological split that ignores event identifiers. Explain what specifically goes wrong, and what grouped_chronological_split-style logic would do differently.

Solution. Both snapshots share the same eventual outcome label; placing one in training and the other in test lets the fitted model, or the evaluator inspecting the split, benefit from information tied to an outcome the test snapshot is supposed to independently confirm. A grouped chronological split instead requires every observation belonging to one event's dependence group to fall entirely within a single cohort; if the two snapshots' decision times straddle a cutoff so that no single cohort can hold both while respecting label availability, the entire group is excluded from all cohorts rather than split across them.

Exercise 19.3. Using the sorted p-values \(0.005, 0.010, 0.021, 0.050, 0.200\) from 5 hypothesis tests and a target false discovery rate of \(\alpha = 0.10\), apply the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure and state which hypotheses are rejected.

Solution. With \(n = 5\), the thresholds at ranks 1 through 5 are \(0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08, 0.10\). Comparing: rank 1, \(0.005 \leq 0.02\), true; rank 2, \(0.010 \leq 0.04\), true; rank 3, \(0.021 \leq 0.06\), true; rank 4, \(0.050 \leq 0.08\), true; rank 5, \(0.200 \leq 0.10\), false. The largest rank satisfying the comparison is 4, so the 4 hypotheses with the 4 smallest p-values are rejected, and the hypothesis with \(p = 0.200\) is not.

Exercise 19.4. A researcher runs a stationary-bootstrap confidence interval on a series of weekly strategy returns and reports it as proof of a positive expected edge. List two specific unstated assumptions this claim would need to defend before it could be trusted, drawing on Section 19.6.

Solution. First, the bootstrap's implicit or explicit block length must be justified as appropriate for the actual dependence length in the data; an arbitrarily chosen block length is not automatically correct. Second, the underlying series must be defensibly treated as covered by whatever stationarity-like condition the procedure assumes; a series with structural breaks, regime changes, or a small number of effectively independent events dressed up as many weekly observations would violate that assumption even if the mechanical bootstrap code runs without error.

Exercise 19.5. Explain why an analyst who monitors a live paper-trading result every day using a fixed 95 percent significance threshold, stopping and declaring success the first day the threshold is crossed, is more likely to see a false positive than the simulation in Section 19.7 suggests for exactly 20 looks, if the analyst actually monitors for 200 days instead of 20.

Solution. The simulation shows that allowing the stopping rule to depend on the maximum of several interim looks against a fixed threshold inflates the false-positive rate above the nominal single-look rate, and that inflation grows with the number of looks; 200 daily looks provide far more opportunities for the running statistic to cross the fixed threshold by chance at least once than 20 looks do, so the resulting false-positive rate would be even higher than the approximately 24.8 percent observed for 20 looks in the reported simulation.

Exercise 19.6. The companion's forecast_models.py script reports an observed Brier score of 0.220607 for a raw boosted model and 0.2672 for the same model after isotonic recalibration fitted on a 44-event validation cohort, on the same 45-event held-out test cohort. Explain why this is a legitimate, reportable result rather than a failure to be hidden, and state one plausible reason calibration underperformed here.

Solution. A negative or inconclusive result is exactly as legitimate an output of an evaluation as a favorable one; suppressing it would itself be a form of undisclosed search, selectively reporting only the comparison that looks better. One plausible reason calibration underperformed is sample size: an isotonic calibrator fit on only 44 validation events has to estimate a flexible, nonparametric monotone mapping from very little data, and with so few points its estimated correction can easily add more variance to the resulting probabilities on a fresh 45-event test cohort than the systematic miscalibration it was meant to fix; this is a plausible explanation for this specific synthetic sample, not a general claim that calibration is unhelpful.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: You should be comfortable with contractual settlement rules from the event-contracts material, executable asks and bids and depth from the market-microstructure chapter, the forecast-to-order screen from Chapter 17, and the execution-aware backtest discipline from Chapter 18, particularly the rule that a quote is not a fill.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this chapter you should be able to: identify complementary, mutually exclusive, and exhaustive relationships between contracts and explain what each implies about prices; write and read a payout matrix over a complete relevant state space; state the executable-price conditions that must hold before a set of quoted contracts can even be considered arbitrage candidates; verify contract, rule, and collateral compatibility before combining any two contracts; derive simple bid/ask inequalities for a genuine complementary pair; account for cost, size, capital, and leg risk across a multi-leg basket; and explain why two contracts with similar headlines are not automatically a hedge for each other.

docs.title: 20.1 Same-looking titles, different contracts
docs.text:
Two event contracts with similar-sounding titles can differ in their resolution source, their exact observation window, their currency or collateral, their rounding convention, or an exceptional settlement path that only one of them has. None of that is visible from a title alone. Polymarket's own documentation on markets and events explicitly distinguishes individual market and outcome-token identifiers from an event container that groups several markets, and notes that only some multi-market events are actually mutually exclusive, not all of them by default. POLYMARKET_MARKETS A shared user-interface grouping is a hint worth investigating, not a proof of any particular logical relationship.

This chapter's central discipline is to treat "these two contracts look related" as a hypothesis requiring explicit verification: same underlying event, same or genuinely compatible resolution rules, same settlement currency, and a completely enumerated, mutually agreed state space, before any cross-market reasoning about prices is trusted. The companion library's scan_basket function encodes this as a hard gate: it accepts a compatibility_verified flag that the caller must explicitly set, and it separately checks that every leg shares the same event identifier, rules identifier, currency, and set of named payout states, refusing to proceed if either check fails.

Combining several related contractual questions into one priced structure is itself an established research area, not an invention of this chapter. Hanson's logarithmic market-scoring construction was designed in part to support combinatorial, cross-question information aggregation, and Abernethy, Chen, and Vaughan's convex-optimization framework for market making explicitly addresses bounded-payoff securities and convex-hull cost structures over related outcomes. HANSON2007 ABERNETHY2013 Both are mechanism-design and market-making theory: they describe how a market maker could price or structure a coherent combinatorial book, not a claim that any two arbitrarily chosen, independently quoted contracts on separate order books already form an executable, compatible basket. The verification steps in this chapter exist precisely because that gap, between a designed coherent mechanism and two independently listed real contracts, does not close itself.

docs.title: 20.2 Complements: a two-outcome partition and its price bounds
docs.text:
An ordinary binary YES/NO pair has exactly one winning side. The pricing argument actually needs the broader constant combined payout condition: the two payouts sum to USD 1 in every permitted state. A documented half-dollar payout on each side can preserve that condition even though neither ordinary binary label applies.

Assume common settlement timing, risk-free collateral, zero financing costs, no fees, sufficient depth, and feasible execution of both legs. Buying at asks \(a_{\text{YES}}\) and \(a_{\text{NO}}\) produces USD 1 at settlement, so excluding a positive deterministic purchase margin requires \(a_{\text{YES}}+a_{\text{NO}}\geq1\). The reverse inequality \(b_{\text{YES}}+b_{\text{NO}}\leq1\) requires the ability to create or sell the complete pair and fund its combined obligation; it is not an available shorting strategy in this long-only companion. Selling previously owned units also has an acquisition or opportunity cost, not free initial inventory. With nonzero financing costs, compare the combined payout's present value rather than automatically using one dollar today. These assumptions are part of each bound, not optional qualifications afterward.

Fees change the picture immediately. Consider two complementary asks of USD 0.49 and ten units per leg. With an invented flat fee of USD 0.015 per unit, each leg costs USD 4.90 plus USD 0.15, totaling USD 10.10 against a USD 10.00 payout. A flat USD 0.005 per-unit fee instead gives total cost USD 9.90, and USD 0.001 per unit gives USD 9.82. These are flat-dollar fees, not percentages of notional. Under the companion's cent rounding, notional rates of 1.5%, 0.5%, and 0.1% would instead produce USD 9.96, USD 9.86, and USD 9.82 respectively. Correct units and fee placement change the verdict; none of these schedules is claimed to be a real venue's fee.

docs.title: 20.3 Mutually exclusive and exhaustive categorical sets
docs.text:
A categorical event with outcomes that are genuinely mutually exclusive and jointly exhaustive, meaning exactly one of them occurs, generalizes the two-outcome complement case: buying one unit of every outcome in the partition guarantees a payout of exactly USD 1, whichever outcome occurs, so the same no-free-lunch logic requires the sum of the executable asks across the full partition to be at least 1, and the sum of the executable bids to be at most 1, again ignoring fees and again conditional on the partition genuinely being exhaustive and mutually exclusive under compatible rules.

A three-way partition illustrates the fee-inclusive version concretely. Take three distinct contracts, "low," "middle," and "high," each paying USD 1 if its own named state occurs and USD 0 otherwise, quoted at asks of USD 0.30, USD 0.35, and USD 0.30 respectively, summing to 0.95 pre-fee. Scanning a 10-unit basket of all three legs under a flat USD 0.01-per-unit fee gives a total executable cost of USD 9.80 (USD 9.50 of notional plus USD 0.30 of fees across the three legs) against a guaranteed payout of USD 10.00, since exactly one leg pays out in every one of the three named states, for a modeled profit of USD 0.20. This result is only valid if "low," "middle," and "high" genuinely exhaust every state the actual contracts' rules permit. If the real market instead allows a fourth possible outcome, an unresolved, voided, or otherwise exceptional state that none of the three contracts pays out on, the guaranteed-payout assumption fails exactly in that fourth state, and the calculated USD 0.20 modeled profit is not actually guaranteed; the payout matrix in the next section exists precisely to make this kind of omission visible before it becomes an expensive surprise.

docs.title: 20.4 Subsets and conditionals: payoff dominance
docs.text:
A different relationship holds when one contract's payout states form a strict subset of another's. Suppose a broad contract pays USD 1 in either a "middle" or a "high" state and USD 0 in a "low" state, while a narrow contract pays USD 1 only in the "high" state and USD 0 otherwise, both contracts sharing the identical named state space. In every one of the three states, the broad contract's payout is at least as large as the narrow contract's: USD 0 versus USD 0 in "low," USD 1 versus USD 0 in "middle," and USD 1 versus USD 1 in "high." This is payoff dominance, and the companion's payoff_dominates check, once compatibility between the two contracts' event, rules, currency, and state space has been explicitly verified, confirms exactly this relationship for the pair described here, returning True.

Under a common probability model, the broad contract's expected payout cannot be lower than the narrow contract's. The executable trade that exploits an opposite price ordering is buy broad at its ask and sell narrow at its bid, not the reverse. Its terminal difference is \(R_{\text{broad}}-R_{\text{narrow}}\geq0\) in every state, and its initial net cost is \(a_{\text{broad}}-b_{\text{narrow}}\). If \(b_{\text{narrow}}>a_{\text{broad}}\), it receives cash up front and has a nonnegative terminal payoff, under feasible shorting/creation, financing, and execution assumptions. Thus excluding this strict cash-positive opportunity requires \(a_{\text{broad}}\geq b_{\text{narrow}}\), before fees. Equality can still permit a zero-cost positive payout in some states under the usual statewise arbitrage definition. The companion verifies payoff dominance but does not implement short sales or prove those trading assumptions. Spreads alone can make the narrow ask exceed the broad bid without any executable arbitrage.

docs.title: 20.5 Building a payout matrix before trusting an optimizer
docs.text:
Check every multi-leg candidate against an explicit payout matrix: rows are permitted states, columns are legs, and each cell is payout per unit. For an equal-quantity all-buy basket, the minimum row sum, multiplied by quantity, is its payout floor; more general portfolios require signed quantity-weighted sums. The scan can evaluate only states the caller supplied. Polymarket's inspected documentation establishes disputes, clarifications, and an exceptional half-dollar payout, not their empirical frequency or a generic full-refund void policy. POLYMARKET_RESOLUTION Audit any additional tie, cancellation, or refund rule in the actual contracts rather than silently omitting it or attributing it to that one source.

The companion's scan_basket implements exactly the minimum-over-states logic once legs are supplied: minimum_payout is computed as the smallest total payout across all named states in the legs' shared payout mapping, and the reported minimum_net_profit is that minimum payout net of the actual executable total_cost. This is a deliberately pessimistic summary statistic, by design: a basket is only reported as a PAPER_CANDIDATE_ONLY when its worst named state still clears its cost, not merely when its average or most likely state does. The result also reports a separate required_cash figure, covered in Section 20.8, which is the cash every leg's order would need to have reserved with a broker before any fill, and which is not always equal to total_cost.

docs.title: 20.6 What "no apparent arbitrage" requires here
docs.text:
Because scan_basket refuses to compute anything at all unless compatibility_verified is explicitly set and the legs' event, rules, currency, and payout-state keys actually match, an unverified or genuinely mismatched pair is rejected outright, before any price comparison happens. Constructing a leg that looks like an ordinary NO contract, sharing the same payout keys as a real NO leg, but whose underlying rules identifier is deliberately set to a different resolution source, reproduces exactly this rejection when scanned alongside a genuine YES leg: the result is REJECTED with the reason "unverified or mismatched events, rules, currency or state space," and no cost, payout, or profit figure is computed at all, because computing one would imply a compatibility that was never actually established.

This gate exists because a title match is not a rules match. Two contracts that both mention the same headline event can still differ in their resolution source, their observation window, or an exceptional settlement clause that applies to only one of them, any of which can break the guaranteed-payout logic that made the earlier sections' arithmetic valid in the first place. "No apparent arbitrage after verification" is therefore a conditional statement: conditional on the verification actually having been performed correctly, on the rules genuinely being compatible, and on the collateral and currency genuinely matching. It is not a claim that no unverified-looking discrepancy could ever be a genuine opportunity; it is a claim that an unverified discrepancy should never be treated as one.

docs.title: 20.7 Bid/ask inequalities and not double-using the spread
docs.text:
Every inequality and every cost figure in this chapter has used an executable ask for a purchase and an executable bid for a sale, precisely because those are the only prices a trader could actually pay or receive. A frequent error is to compute a candidate's cost from one side, then separately subtract "the spread" again as an informal slippage penalty; this double-counts a cost that the executable price already includes. The notation registry's own canonical example makes this explicit: buying at an ask of USD 0.40 and later selling at a bid of USD 0.46 already reflects the round-trip spread in those two numbers directly, and no further spread deduction belongs in that calculation.

The same discipline applies across legs of a basket: each leg's cost must come from that leg's own executable ask (for a buy) or bid (for a sell), at the quantity actually being transacted, using sweep_cost or an equivalent full-size sweep, never from a midpoint, and never from a single best-level price if the requested quantity would actually walk further down the book, as Chapter 17 already established for a single contract.

docs.title: 20.8 Multi-leg cost, size, capital, and leg risk
docs.text:
A multi-leg basket's true cost is the sum of every individual leg's executable, fee-inclusive cost at the actually intended size, not a price-only sum. Revisiting the three-way partition from Section 20.3 with only USD 5.00 of available capital, instead of enough to cover the full USD 9.80 needed, reproduces this directly: scanning the identical three legs and quantity against that smaller capital figure returns NO_TRADE with the reason "funded capital cannot reserve all basket orders before execution," while still reporting the same USD 9.80 total cost, USD 10.00 minimum payout, and USD 0.20 minimum net profit as before, so that a trader can see exactly what capital would be required even though the trade cannot proceed at the stated size with the capital actually available.

Capital and cost differ. scan_basket sets required_cash to the larger of total modeled fill cost and summed conservative broker reservations, then compares that field with supplied capital. For three units per leg at USD 0.3333 and an invented flat USD 0.001 fee per unit, each aggregate fill costs USD 1.00 rounded notional plus USD 0.01 rounded fee: USD 2.02 across two legs. Each leg instead reserves three times (USD 0.34 cent-ceiling notional plus USD 0.01 fee), or USD 1.05; total required cash is USD 2.10. The quote remains on the four-decimal price grid; cent rounding applies to the cash bound, not a new venue tick. Capital USD 2.02 therefore returns NO_TRADE, while USD 2.10 permits the conditional candidate. Funding modeled aggregate fills alone does not necessarily fund all orders' reservations.

Even fully funded and fully compatible, a multi-leg basket carries leg risk: each leg is typically a separate order against a separate order book, and there is no guarantee that all legs fill together, at the assumed prices, in the assumed sizes, at the same moment. The companion's basket result explicitly carries a fixed leg_risk field stating that non-atomic legs can fail and that a quoted basket is not guaranteed execution, precisely because filling three of four intended legs at favorable prices while the fourth leg's book has already moved, or failed to fill at all, can turn an apparently riskless-looking combination into an ordinary, uncertain, partially hedged position. A basket scan's PAPER_CANDIDATE_ONLY status is conditional on every named leg actually filling as assumed; it is explicitly not a claim that simultaneous execution is guaranteed, and any live consideration of a multi-leg idea would need a defensible plan for what happens financially if only some legs fill.

docs.title: 20.9 Similar headlines are not a hedge
docs.text: A position is only a hedge for another position if their payoffs are verified to move in a specified, compatible, and typically opposite way across the actual relevant states, using compatible rules and collateral; "these two markets are about the same general topic" does not establish that relationship. Two contracts about superficially the same headline event can differ in observation window, resolution source, rounding convention, or an exceptional payout only one of them has, any of which is exactly the kind of basis risk that can make an apparent hedge fail precisely when it was supposed to protect a position. A researcher or trader who notices two similarly worded contracts should treat that observation as a prompt to verify compatibility using the checks in this chapter, not as a license to treat one as an automatic offset for the other. Nothing in this book's tools or examples establishes that any particular pair of real contracts is currently, or was ever, a valid hedge for each other; that determination depends on the actual rules of actual contracts, checked directly against their current documentation, not on a chapter's illustrative arithmetic. A model that produces internally incoherent probabilities across related contracts is not, by itself, an executable arbitrage opportunity; it is at most a prompt to check compatibility, verify prices are genuinely executable at the needed size, and compute fee-inclusive costs before drawing any further conclusion.

docs.title: Companion example
docs.text:
Run:

Command working directory: run this chapter's Python commands from book\companion. From the trading repository root, run Set-Location book\companion once first. The .venv belongs to that companion project; see companion setup.

.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe examples\constraints.py

The script (linked at ../companion/examples/constraints.py; see examples/README.md for the full companion-script list and observed outputs) runs a verified complementary basket, the same basket rerun against insufficient capital, a rejected mismatched-rules basket, and a payoff-dominance check between a broad and a narrow contract, all using the shared prediction_market_lab.constraints module rather than duplicated chapter arithmetic. Its printed result is real, deterministic output from the installed package against synthetic fixtures; it is not a report of any historically observed venue prices, and none of it places, or is capable of placing, a live order.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 20.1. A genuine complementary YES/NO pair is quoted with executable asks of USD 0.51 and USD 0.50. Using the pre-fee inequality from Section 20.2, does this pair already satisfy the no-free-lunch condition for a purchase of both sides? Now add a flat USD 0.02-per-unit fee on each leg for a 1-unit purchase of each side and compute the actual modeled profit or loss.

Solution. The pre-fee sum is \(0.51 + 0.50 = 1.01 \geq 1\), so the bare inequality is already satisfied; a purchase of both sides is not expected to be profitable even before fees. Including fees, the total cost for 1 unit of each leg is \(0.51 + 0.02 + 0.50 + 0.02 = 1.05\) against a guaranteed payout of USD 1.00, a modeled loss of USD 0.05. Fees make an already-unfavorable pre-fee position strictly worse, as expected.

Exercise 20.2. A three-way partition ("early," "on-time," "late") has executable asks of USD 0.20, USD 0.45, and USD 0.30, summing to 0.95 pre-fee, with a flat USD 0.01-per-unit fee and a 10-unit basket. Compute the total executable cost, the guaranteed minimum payout, and the modeled net profit, assuming the three named outcomes are genuinely exhaustive and mutually exclusive.

Solution. Notional cost is \(10 \times (0.20 + 0.45 + 0.30) = 9.50\); fees are \(10 \times 0.01 \times 3 = 0.30\); total cost is USD 9.80. Because exactly one leg pays USD 1 per unit in every one of the three named states, the guaranteed payout for 10 units of each leg is USD 10.00 in every state. The modeled net profit is \(10.00 - 9.80 = 0.20\).

Exercise 20.3. Suppose the real market underlying Exercise 20.2 actually permits a fourth state, "cancelled," in which none of the three named contracts pays out. Explain what happens to the guaranteed-payout claim from Exercise 20.2, without recomputing the fee or notional cost.

Solution. The guaranteed payout of USD 10.00 was only guaranteed across the three named states; in the newly identified "cancelled" state, all three legs pay USD 0, so the actual worst-case payout across the true, now four-state space is USD 0.00, not USD 10.00. The modeled net profit of USD 0.20 computed in Exercise 20.2 was conditional on the three-state assumption being the complete state space, and it is not valid once a fourth, unpriced state is known to exist; the position would realize a full loss of the USD 9.80 paid if that fourth state occurs.

Exercise 20.4. A trader has USD 6.00 of available capital and wants to execute the basket from Exercise 20.2, which requires USD 9.80. Using the basket-scan behavior described in Section 20.8, state what result and reason the scan should report, and what information it should still disclose despite not permitting the trade.

Solution. The scan should report NO_TRADE with the reason that funded capital cannot reserve all of the basket's orders before execution. It should still disclose the same total executable cost of USD 9.80, minimum guaranteed payout of USD 10.00, and minimum net profit of USD 0.20 that Exercise 20.2 computed, along with a required_cash figure (here also USD 9.80, since this basket's flat per-unit fee makes the worst-case reservation equal to the actual sweep cost), so the trader can see exactly how much additional capital would be required to execute the basket at its full intended size, even though the trade cannot proceed at that size right now.

Exercise 20.5. A two-leg complementary basket has a total executable cost of USD 2.02 for 3 units of each side, but its worst-case broker reservation, required_cash, is USD 2.10. A trader funds exactly USD 2.02. State whether the scan permits the trade and explain, in general terms, why the reservation can exceed the sweep cost even though both use the same quoted price.

Solution. The scan does not permit the trade: its capital check compares funded capital against the larger of total_cost and required_cash, so USD 2.02 of capital is insufficient once required_cash is USD 2.10. The reservation can exceed the sweep cost because it assumes the conservative worst case of the order filling as several separate one-unit fills, each independently rounding its own price-tick and fee contribution up, while an actual single combined fill for the full quantity rounds the combined notional and fee only once. When per-fill rounding is not negligible relative to the order's size, the fragmented worst case can require noticeably more reserved cash than the trade would actually cost if it filled all at once.

Exercise 20.6. Two contracts share an identical headline description but were confirmed to use different resolution sources. A trader proposes buying one and selling the other as a hedge. Explain, using the vocabulary of this chapter, why this proposal needs further justification before being treated as a valid hedge.

Solution. A hedge requires a verified, compatible payoff relationship between the two positions across every relevant state, not merely a shared headline description. Different resolution sources are exactly the kind of rule incompatibility that can break an assumed payoff relationship, introducing basis risk: the two contracts could settle differently even when the informally described real-world event is the same, because their formal, contractual triggers differ. The trader would need to verify compatible rules, currency, and a shared state space, following the same checks scan_basket and payoff_dominates enforce, before relying on one position to offset the other.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Read order books and automated market makers, rules, venues, and settlement risk, the forecast-to-order decision, and a backtest that respects execution before this chapter. You should already distinguish an executable ask from a bid, know why a midpoint is not a fill, and be comfortable with conditional probability and the canonical accounting example in the notation registry. The glossary entries for adverse selection, market maker, queue priority, and fill-conditioned forecast are used directly below.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this chapter you should be able to derive fill-conditioned expected profit, explain how informative order flow changes that expectation, distinguish expected loss from maximum inventory loss, and account for queueing, cancellation, fees, and rebates. You should also explain why a finite-horizon stock model with an unbounded diffusing mid-price and terminal midpoint valuation does not transfer unchanged to a contract with bounded binary payouts.

docs.title: 21.1 A market maker earns fills, not touches
docs.text:
A market maker posts a bid and an ask and hopes to buy low and sell high, or to collect a spread while eventually resolving inventory at settlement. The tempting shortcut is to compute an expected profit as if posting a quote were the same as executing a trade: multiply a model probability by an assumed always-on fill and call the result expected income. That shortcut is wrong, and it is wrong in a specific, derivable way.

Recall the book's canonical example: buying 10 YES units at an ask of USD 0.40 with an invented flat fee of USD 0.01 per unit costs USD 4.10, and at a model probability \(\hat p = 0.55\) the modeled expected net profit is USD 1.40. That calculation already assumes the trade happens at that price and that size. A market maker's resting bid to buy YES at USD 0.40 is different: it only executes when someone else chooses to sell into it. The relevant probability is not the market maker's unconditional \(\hat p\); it is \(P(Y=1 \mid \text{my bid is filled})\), a genuinely different quantity that the notation registry calls a fill-conditioned forecast.

Formally, let \(F\) denote the event that a specific resting order fills within a stated window, and let \(Y\) be the eventual binary outcome. The modeled expected profit per unit conditional on that fill is

\[ \mathbb{E}[\Pi \mid F] = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid F] - c, \]

where \(c\) is the all-in cost per unit (price plus fee). This is not the same number as \(\mathbb{E}[Y] - c\) unless \(F\) is independent of \(Y\), and there is no general reason to assume that independence. Whether a counterparty chooses to trade against your bid can itself carry information about \(Y\). That is the entire content of adverse selection: the event "someone hit my bid" is not a random, value-irrelevant coin flip.

docs.title: 21.2 Why a fill can be bad news: a worked mixture model
docs.text:
Build an explicitly invented one-opportunity discrete model, rather than equating an arrival rate with a probability. The maker's unconditional model assigns \(p_0=P(Y=1)=0.55\). One potential counterparty is sampled independently of \(Y\): with probability \(\pi\) it is informed and knows \(Y\) perfectly; otherwise it is an uninformed noise trader. A noise trader sells with probability \(\lambda\), independent of \(Y\). An informed trader sells with probability \(\mu\) if \(Y=0\) and never if \(Y=1\). Here \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\) are dimensionless response probabilities, not intensities per unit time.

Set \(\lambda=\mu=1\) for simple arithmetic. Assuming that a sale fills the specified order in full, the fill probabilities are

\[ P(F \mid Y=1) = (1-\pi)\lambda, \qquad P(F \mid Y=0) = (1-\pi)\lambda + \pi\mu. \]

Bayes' rule gives the fill-conditioned probability directly:

\[ P(Y=1 \mid F) = \frac{P(F\mid Y=1)\,p_0}{P(F\mid Y=1)\,p_0 + P(F\mid Y=0)\,(1-p_0)}. \]

With \(\pi = 0.3\): \(P(F\mid Y{=}1) = 0.7\), \(P(F\mid Y{=}0) = 0.7 + 0.3 = 1.0\). The denominator is \(0.7(0.55) + 1.0(0.45) = 0.385 + 0.45 = 0.835\), so \(P(Y{=}1\mid F) = 0.385/0.835 \approx 0.4611\). Conditional on the fill, the market maker's honest updated belief has fallen from 0.55 to about 0.461, purely because being hit is itself evidence correlated with the informed sellers' private signal.

At USD 0.41 all-in cost and ten filled units, conditional expected profit is \(10(0.4611-0.41)\approx\text{USD }0.51\), rather than the naive USD 1.40. At \(\pi=0.6\), the fill probabilities are 0.4 given YES and one given NO, so \(P(Y=1\mid F)=0.22/0.67\approx0.3284\) and conditional expected profit is about minus USD 0.82. This is a discrete selection mechanism, not a measured informed-trader proportion or a Poisson arrival model. With a time intensity \(r\), the probability of at least one arrival over duration \(\Delta\) would instead be \(1-e^{-r\Delta}\) under a Poisson assumption; one cannot silently substitute \(r\) itself for that probability.

docs.title: 21.3 Spread as compensation, not as guaranteed income
docs.text:
A market maker who also posts an ask is not simply "capturing the spread" as free income. The spread exists because some posted price has to compensate for the adverse-selection loss just derived, on top of covering fees and any inventory risk. A companion way to see this: if a market maker's bid and ask both reflect the same fill-conditioned logic, the width between them must be wide enough that the blended profit across informed and uninformed fills is non-negative, given the assumed mix. Widening the quotes reduces the fill rate (fewer noise traders willing to cross a wider spread) but improves the average bid/ask side; narrowing them raises the fill rate but concentrates exposure to the informed side of the mixture. This spread-versus-fill-rate trade-off is the same mechanism examined by a classic specialist-market model, whose inspected introduction shows that superior counterparty information can generate a positive bid-ask spread even under a risk-neutral specialist earning zero expected transaction profit, with buy/sell direction itself entering the specialist's conditional valuation; that inspected discussion also flags that binding inventory or cash constraints can force a departure from pure zero-profit pricing, foreshadowing Section 21.4's inventory-jump argument. A companion dynamic-auction model describes an equilibrium with one risk-neutral insider, random noise traders and competitive risk-neutral market makers in which, in a continuous-trading limit, prices follow a Brownian process with constant depth and the insider's information is eventually fully incorporated. Both are stock/auction-market equilibrium results under their own stated assumptions, not a numerical event-market spread estimate or empirical law about any specific prediction venue, and neither source's formal proofs were inspected beyond its introduction or abstract. GLOSTEN1985 KYLE1985

Two practical points follow directly from the derivation above rather than from either cited model. First, a market maker cannot distinguish an informed fill from a noise fill after the fact using price alone — the mixture model is unobservable in real time, so any real deployment needs an estimated, monitored proxy (fill timing relative to news, order size patterns, or realized reversal after a fill) rather than an assumed constant \(\pi\). Second, because \(P(Y=1\mid F)\) moves with the assumed informed fraction, a market maker's quotes should be risk-aware: sized and priced so that even a pessimistic, higher-\(\pi\) scenario does not produce an unaffordable loss, not sized only from the average-case unconditional forecast.

docs.title: 21.4 Inventory near a bounded expiry jump
docs.text:
A stock has no fixed binary terminal payoff. Under ordinary settlement an event contract pays exactly zero or one, so remaining inventory faces a two-point terminal payout. That does not imply its price must jump at the administrative settlement instant: information can reveal the outcome earlier or gradually. The risk is the unresolved terminal event exposure and any information jumps before settlement, not a universal price-path shape. For \(Q\) long YES units at average all-in cost \(\bar c\), terminal profit is

\[ \Pi = Q\,(R - \bar c), \qquad R \in \{0, 1\}, \]

a two-point outcome, not a smoothly distributed one. Suppose an accumulated inventory of 5 YES units carries an average cost basis of USD 0.42 per unit (a plausible blend of fills at slightly different prices and fees). If the contract settles NO, the loss is \(5 \times 0.42 = \text{USD } 2.10\) — the entire cost basis, in full, with no partial recovery, because the payout is exactly zero rather than a small negative drift. There is no way to "average out" this jump by holding longer, the way a diffusing stock price might mean-revert; expiry is a hard deadline, not a diffusing process with an indefinite horizon.

This matters because a well-known limit-order-book market-making model prices inventory risk by skewing quotes around a reservation price that adjusts for held inventory. Its inspected main text builds this on a driftless arithmetic Brownian mid-price with constant volatility, an exponential terminal-wealth utility function, and Poisson order arrivals whose intensity decays with distance from the mid-price. Crucially, this is a finite-horizon control problem: the agent trades up to a fixed terminal time and then marks remaining inventory to the prevailing midpoint. The frozen-inventory reservation price this produces is an explicitly subjective valuation adjustment for held risk, not an executable midpoint fill, and the paper's own simple, quotable bid/ask expressions (its equations 29-30) are stated as an approximation under symmetric exponential arrival-rate assumptions, not an exact solution to the underlying control problem; its reported performance comparisons come from numerical simulations under specified parameters, marked to the terminal midpoint, not from historical executable returns.

That model cannot be imported unchanged. Its arithmetic Brownian mid-price is unbounded and its terminal midpoint valuation is neither an executed liquidation nor a contractual payout. A binary contract instead has a stated payout distribution and may retain substantial outcome uncertainty close to resolution. The time at which information is revealed need not equal the time cash settles, and a price jump at the latter instant is not required. The adaptation must model bounded payouts, information arrival, liquidation feasibility, and cash-release timing explicitly. Inventory caps remain useful, but their justification is affordable full-payout risk, not a claim that every binary price follows one jump pattern. AVELLANEDA2008

docs.title: 21.5 Risk-aware quotes: a bound, not a forecast
docs.text: A concrete discipline is to cap outstanding cost basis and reservations, independently of the unconditional forecast. For long-only, nonnegative payouts and no additional liabilities, losing all currently committed cash bounds the loss on those open commitments. A conditional expected loss is not that maximum-loss bound: size against the full payoff scenarios as well as the forecast. Nor does a commitment cap alone bound cumulative session losses, because closing a losing position frees commitment capacity for another loss; a separate session-loss or drawdown stop is needed for that purpose. In the companion, the caller invokes the risk screen before submitting an order; the broker enforces cash and inventory constraints, not an independently configured session-loss policy.

docs.title: 21.6 Queueing, cancellation delay, and time-varying rebates
docs.text: Three further frictions separate a quoted price from a realized outcome. First, queue priority: even the best displayed bid does not guarantee being first in line; without genuine queue data, a market maker must not assume its own resting order is filled merely because the market touched that price, and observing a touch without confirmed matching should be reported as no inferred fill rather than as a trade. Second, cancellation delay: a market maker who decides to pull a quote because new information arrived cannot assume the cancellation lands before an in-flight counter-order matches against it; a cancel race is a real possibility whenever messages travel over a network with latency, and a market maker must be prepared to receive a fill on an order it believed was already withdrawn. Third, rebates and fees are not flat, timeless constants. Real venue documentation describes fee rounding accumulated across the fills of one order, and separately describes settlement fees and timing that can vary by contract and by clearing arrangement rather than being a single universal number. KALSHI_ROUNDING KALSHI_SETTLEMENT Public order-book documentation similarly exposes finite, quoted depth and book-state metadata rather than a promise of unlimited size or of queue position. KALSHI_BOOK POLYMARKET_BOOK POLYMARKET_FEES This book's own worked examples use an invented flat per-unit fee purely for arithmetic clarity; it is not a claim that any venue charges a constant per-unit amount, and a market-making calculation that silently assumes a rebate is fixed and always earned will misstate its own expected profit whenever the real fee or rebate schedule changes.

docs.title: 21.7 Assumptions and failure modes
docs.text: This chapter's derivations depend on assumptions that should be listed explicitly rather than left implicit. The informed/uninformed mixture in Section 21.2 is an invented illustrative construction with a chosen \(\pi\), not an estimated real proportion; a real deployment would need to monitor a proxy for adverse selection and treat its magnitude as uncertain, not fixed. The inventory-jump argument assumes hold-to-settlement accounting with no interim sale; a market maker who successfully exits early faces ordinary bid/ask liquidation costs instead, which is a different and usually smaller risk. The risk-budget bound in Section 21.5 only limits stated committed cash; it does not model correlated exposure across multiple contracts sharing one underlying uncertainty, which Chapter 22 addresses separately. No queue-position model, no realistic cancellation-latency distribution, and no time-series of an actual fee schedule is estimated anywhere in this chapter; all of Section 21.6's frictions are described qualitatively and must be measured, not assumed, before relying on them operationally. Finally, nothing here establishes that any real market maker earns a positive expected profit after adverse selection, fees, and inventory risk; the arithmetic shows how a plausible-looking naive calculation can flip sign, not that it always does.

docs.title: 21.8 Companion example
docs.text:
The companion script market_making.py builds two synthetic paths on the shared canonical fixture. In the favorable path, a resting bid at USD 0.40 receives an explicitly user-supplied synthetic fill (never an inferred one from a quote touch), and a later resting ask at USD 0.46 is also explicitly filled, producing a realized round-trip profit of USD 0.40 — consistent with the notation registry's sale-with-exit-fee example. In the adverse path, the ask is cancelled instead of filled, the position is marked against a lower quoted bid of USD 0.25 for an unrealized marked profit of minus USD 1.70, and the contract then settles NO, producing a final realized loss of USD 4.10 — the full cost basis, matching the bounded-jump argument in Section 21.4. Both paths report the same explicit note that quote touches alone never establish a fill. Run it with:

Command working directory: run this chapter's Python commands from book\companion. From the trading repository root, run Set-Location book\companion once first. The .venv belongs to that companion project; see companion setup.

.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe examples\market_making.py

Neither path estimates a real fill probability or a real adverse-selection intensity; both are deterministic, labeled illustrations of the accounting consequences once a fill (favorable or adverse) is explicitly supplied.

docs.title: Exercise 1: recomputing the conditional fill probability
docs.text:
Using the mixture model of Section 21.2 with \(p_0 = 0.55\), \(\lambda = 1\), and \(\mu = 1\), compute \(P(Y=1\mid F)\) for an informed fraction \(\pi = 0.45\), and the resulting expected profit on 10 units bought at an all-in cost of USD 0.41.

Solution sketch. \(P(F\mid Y{=}1) = 0.55\), \(P(F\mid Y{=}0) = 0.55 + 0.45 = 1.0\). Denominator: \(0.55(0.55) + 1.0(0.45) = 0.3025 + 0.45 = 0.7525\). So \(P(Y{=}1\mid F) = 0.3025/0.7525 \approx 0.4020\). Expected profit on 10 units: \(10\times(0.4020-0.41) \approx -\text{USD } 0.08\), essentially break-even and slightly negative — a useful reminder that the sign can flip well before the informed fraction looks extreme.

docs.title: Exercise 2: the bounded-jump loss
docs.text:
A market maker ends a session with 8 YES units at average cost USD 0.44 per unit. State both binary terminal profits and explain why a stock diffusion with terminal midpoint marking does not by itself represent this payout risk.

Solution sketch. YES profit is USD 4.48; NO profit is minus USD 3.52. An unbounded stock diffusion with terminal midpoint marking uses a different terminal value law from a binary payout. It can therefore misrepresent this risk, but need not always understate it for every volatility or parameter choice. Neither smooth paths nor active rebalancing guarantees escape from loss; the model must represent the contract's actual payout and execution constraints.

docs.title: Exercise 3: why a touch is not a fill
docs.text:
A market maker's bid at USD 0.40 is the best bid, and the last trade print shows a trade at USD 0.40. Is it correct to record a fill for the market maker's own resting order? Justify the answer using queue priority.

Solution sketch. No. Without confirmed matching or queue data, the print only shows that some order traded at that price; it does not establish that the market maker's specific resting order was the one matched, since other resting orders may have had priority. The correct record is "no inferred fill," not a synthetic fill.

docs.title: Exercise 4: a cancellation race
docs.text:
A market maker submits a cancel for a resting ask at time \(t\) after seeing adverse news, but a counterparty's buy order was already in flight and matches at time \(t' < t_{\text{confirmed cancel}}\). What does the ledger need to record, and why can this not be prevented purely by client-side logic?

Solution sketch. The ledger must record the fill using its actual match timestamp, not the cancellation request timestamp, and timestamps must never be treated as going backwards. This cannot be prevented purely client-side because the cancel and the counter-order both travel over a network with latency; only the venue, which sees both messages in true arrival order, can determine which one wins the race.

docs.title: Exercise 5: a rebate that is not free money
docs.text:
A market-making calculation assumes a constant USD 0.002-per-unit rebate on every filled maker order and reports a modeled profit that is positive only because of this rebate. What two features of real fee/rebate schedules described in this chapter should make the calculation's author cautious?

Solution sketch. Real schedules can round fees per fill and accumulate that rounding across an order's fills, and settlement fees/timing can vary by contract and clearing arrangement rather than being one constant. A modeled profit that depends entirely on an assumed constant rebate should be treated as fragile until the actual, currently effective schedule is checked, since either feature could reduce or eliminate the assumed rebate.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: Chapter 22 turns from a single quote's conditional profit to the separate question of how much bankroll to commit across one or several such positions, and why full collateralization removes the possibility of risk-free leverage.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Read from beliefs to decisions, the forecast-to-order decision, and Chapter 21 before this chapter. You should be comfortable with expected value under a stated model, the canonical accounting example in the notation registry, and the glossary entries for bankroll, collateral, capital lockup, drawdown, and Kelly criterion.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this chapter you should be able to derive a constant-cost binary log-wealth sizing fraction, distinguish cash spent from payout notional, explain the limits of fractional Kelly, and build joint scenario stress tests. You should also distinguish an outstanding-commitment cap from a drawdown limit and recognize when depth or fee rounding invalidates a constant-unit-cost sizing formula.

docs.title: 22.1 Why expected value alone is not a sizing rule
docs.text:
Chapters 3 and 17 computed positive modeled expected profit at \(\hat p=0.55\) and USD 0.41 all-in cost. That does not determine size. For independent repeated binary bets with constant success probability \(0<p<1\), betting the entire bankroll survives \(n\) rounds with probability \(p^n\), which tends to zero. One loss ends the sequence even when each bet has positive expected value.

Expected log wealth is one risk-sensitive sizing objective, not the only possible objective. Kelly's inspected example contrasts log growth with expected capital; his conclusion limits its comparison to fixed allocations per received symbol and requires reinvestment and stake control. His track-take treatment permits leaving capital unbet. The source's independent-symbol communication model is not an estimated event-market forecast. The derivation below is independent classroom algebra; changing Kelly's base-two log to natural log rescales growth without changing its maximizing fraction. KELLY1956

docs.title: 22.2 Deriving the sizing fraction for a fully collateralized binary bet
docs.text:
Consider a bankroll \(W\) held as available cash, with no other positions. Spend a fraction \(\phi\in[0,1]\) buying YES at constant all-in unit cost \(c\in(0,1)\), normalized to a USD 1 payout. We use \(\phi\), not the notation registry's fee symbol \(f\), for the bankroll fraction. Treating units as divisible gives quantity \(\phi W/c\). In this hold-to-settlement calculation, the entire \(\phi W\) is paid up front, there is no borrowing, and an ordinary NO pays nothing. Early resale is a different decision.

If the contract settles YES, the units bought pay USD 1 each, so terminal wealth is the untouched remainder plus the payout:

\[ W_{\text{YES}} = W(1-\phi) + \frac{\phi W}{c}\cdot 1 = W\left[1 + \phi\,\frac{1-c}{c}\right]. \]

If it settles NO, the spent fraction is lost entirely:

\[ W_{\text{NO}} = W(1-\phi). \]

Expected log growth per bet, as a function of the spent fraction \(\phi\), is

\[ G(\phi) = p\,\ln\!\left(1+\phi\,\frac{1-c}{c}\right) + (1-p)\,\ln(1-\phi), \]

where \(p\) is the trader's model probability of YES. Differentiating and setting the derivative to zero (writing \(k=(1-c)/c\) for brevity):

\[ \frac{dG}{d\phi} = \frac{pk}{1+\phi k} - \frac{1-p}{1-\phi} = 0 \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; pk(1-\phi) = (1-p)(1+\phi k). \]

Expanding and collecting terms in \(\phi\):

\[ pk - pk\phi = (1-p) + (1-p)k\phi \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; pk-(1-p) = \phi k\big[(1-p)+p\big] = \phi k. \]

So \(\phi=p-(1-p)/k=p-(1-p)c/(1-c)\), giving the interior solution:

\[ \phi^{*} = \frac{p-c}{1-c}. \]

For \(0<p<1\) and \(\phi<1\), the second derivative is \(-pk^2/(1+\phi k)^2-(1-p)/(1-\phi)^2<0\), proving strict concavity and that the feasible stationary point is a maximum. Spending all cash gives minus-infinite expected log growth when NO has positive probability. At \(p=0.55,c=0.41\), \(\phi^*=0.14/0.59\approx0.2373\): about 23.7 percent of bankroll. At \(p=0.39\), the unconstrained fraction is negative, so the long-only optimum is zero. Including the boundary beliefs gives \(\phi^*=\max(0,\min(1,(p-c)/(1-c)))\), with the endpoint limits interpreted under the stated belief. This is conditional optimization, not permission to treat an estimated probability as certain.

docs.title: 22.3 Two fractions that happen to coincide here
docs.text: The fraction of bankroll spent, \(\phi\), equals the fraction lost on an ordinary NO under these assumptions. It is not the same as face-value payout exposure: \(\phi W/c\) units can have a USD 1 payout notional larger than the amount spent when \(c<1\). Full funding removes borrowing from this classroom position, not its potentially large percentage price sensitivity. Keep cash spent, maximum loss, and payout notional separate. A statement such as "I risk 5 percent" is meaningful only after specifying that the whole spent 5 percent can be lost; calling it small does not establish affordability.

docs.title: 22.4 Fractional Kelly under parameter uncertainty
docs.text:
The single-bet derivation assumes a specified \(p\); interpreting repeated use as a long-run growth result needs additional repeated-opportunity and reinvestment assumptions. In practice \(p\) has estimation and specification error, and opportunities can be dependent and nonstationary. Locally around the interior maximum, a small reduction in \(\phi\) has a second-order effect on modeled expected growth, while reducing cash lost in a NO outcome. This motivates fractional Kelly: use \(\kappa\phi^*\) for a chosen \(\kappa\in(0,1]\). It does not derive a universally safe \(\kappa\) or guarantee a drawdown limit.

At \(\kappa = 0.25\) (quarter Kelly) with \(p=0.55\), \(c=0.41\): spend \(0.25 \times 0.2373 \approx 0.0593\), or about 5.93 percent of bankroll. This number is not arbitrary caution for its own sake; it is a deliberate trade of some expected growth for materially lower variance under the acknowledged possibility that the modeled 0.55 is wrong. A useful way to see the cost of two consecutive losing outcomes at this fraction: wealth after two independent NO settlements shrinks to \((1-0.0593)^2 \approx 0.8849\) of its starting value — an 11.5 percent drawdown from just two losing bets, even at a sizing fraction chosen specifically to be conservative. Full Kelly at the same \(p,c\) would produce a much larger two-loss drawdown of \((1-0.2373)^2 \approx 0.582\), a 41.8 percent decline. Aggressive sizing amplifies the ordinary cost of being wrong, not just the reward for being right.

docs.title: 22.5 Correlated positions and joint scenario matrices
docs.text:
A trader rarely holds an isolated position. Two contracts can share an election, release, or disputed source, making independence implausible. Correlation is one summary of dependence, not an assumption of a particular distribution shape. For a transparent loss check, enumerate plausible joint scenarios and compute portfolio payoff in each without first estimating their probabilities. If probabilities are later attached, they must form a coherent joint model rather than independent marginals chosen for convenience.

Consider two positions, each 10 units bought at an all-in cost of USD 0.41 per unit (total cost USD 4.10 apiece, USD 8.20 combined), on two contracts labeled event-a and event-b. Three joint scenarios: both settle NO (perhaps a shared adverse driver), both settle YES, or they diverge (one YES, one NO). Under the shared-bad-news scenario, receipts are zero on both, so portfolio profit is \(0 - 8.20 = -\text{USD }8.20\): the entire combined cost basis is lost at once, even though a naive independence assumption might have priced the chance of both failing as small. Under both-YES, receipts are \(10+10=20\), so profit is \(20-8.20=\text{USD }11.80\). Under divergence, receipts are 10, so profit is \(10-8.20=\text{USD }1.80\). Writing down these three numbers directly, rather than multiplying two marginal probabilities as if the positions were independent, is what actually protects a sizing decision from an unstated dependence assumption: the worst case (minus USD 8.20) is visible in the matrix regardless of how the two events are correlated, because it does not depend on estimating that correlation at all.

docs.title: 22.6 A cash risk budget as a hard ceiling on committed collateral
docs.text: The isolated sizing fraction does not prevent excessive aggregate commitments. A cash budget therefore caps both single-order cost and total open cost basis plus reservations. Start with USD 10.00 cash, no commitments, and USD 5.00 caps on each. A USD 4.10 position passes, leaving USD 5.90 cash and USD 4.10 open cost basis. A second USD 4.10 candidate fits the remaining cash but would bring commitments to USD 8.20, exceeding the cap. The companion's risk.py illustrates that second-position check. Per-order affordability and portfolio commitment are separate requirements; the existence of sufficient cash alone does not satisfy both.

docs.title: 22.7 Affordability, drawdown, and capital lockup together
docs.text: Three constraints interact and are easy to conflate. Affordability asks whether the trader can absorb the maximum possible loss on a position or portfolio without disrupting other obligations; it is a precondition, not a growth-rate optimization, and no Kelly fraction or confidence level removes the requirement to check it directly. Drawdown is the realized decline from a prior peak in bankroll; Section 22.4 already showed that even a deliberately conservative fractional-Kelly size produces a double-digit-percentage drawdown from just two losing outcomes, so a sizing rule's "on average" property is compatible with periods of substantial, real decline. Capital lockup is the duration for which spent cash is unavailable for anything else, from order submission until settlement (which official documentation shows can take a variable amount of time depending on the specific market and clearing process, not a single fixed interval). KALSHI_SETTLEMENT A trader who reports an attractive annualized return by dividing a single trade's percentage profit by a short assumed holding period, while the actual funds were locked for a much longer resolution window, has silently swapped capital lockup for an optimistic assumption; the same nominal edge looks very different once the true lockup period is used as the denominator of any per-period return calculation.

docs.title: 22.8 Constant fees versus real, price-dependent fee schedules
docs.text:
The closed form assumes that total cost is \(C(Q)=cQ\) throughout the quantities under consideration. A notional-rate fee at one fixed executable price can still satisfy this assumption if rounding is absent. Depth, fixed charges, and fill-dependent rounding can instead make cost nonlinear or discontinuous in quantity. Actual venue fee and accumulator documentation motivates checking that structure, not simply inserting a current average fee into a timeless formula. POLYMARKET_FEES KALSHI_ROUNDING

If cost depends on size, recomputing \(c=C(Q)/Q\) and plugging it into the constant-cost optimum is generally not an optimization solution. Increasing \(Q\) changes the cost of the next units, so the marginal tradeoff differs from the average cost. With no other positions, the correct quantity objective under the same binary model is

\[ G_Q(Q)=p\log\frac{W-C(Q)+Q}{W} +(1-p)\log\frac{W-C(Q)}{W}. \]

For whole-unit teaching orders, compare this objective over feasible quantities, including zero, using the actual sweep cost at each size and the conservative reservation and risk-budget limits. Keep positive wealth in every state with positive model probability. This handles stepped depth and rounding without pretending a derivative exists at every quantity.
