The companion's fractional_kelly deliberately implements only the constant-cost divisible-unit formula; this generalized optimization is a derivation, not a shipped sizing engine.

Separately, collateral itself is not always plain cash. Some venues describe a wrapped token representing an underlying stable-asset claim, with its own wrapping, unwrapping, and pause mechanics documented by the operator. POLYMARKET_COLLATERAL A sizing calculation denominated in "dollars of bankroll" implicitly assumes that collateral converts to and from cash without friction or delay; that assumption should be checked against the actual collateral instrument in use, not treated as automatically true.

docs.title: 22.9 No risk-free leverage
docs.text: This classroom ledger has no borrowing: cash and reservations bound feasible purchases. At constant unit cost, spending fraction \(\phi\) buys \(\phi W/c\) units. Those units' face payout can exceed the cash spent, but no lender finances the position and no loan is implied by that ratio. Full funding is not risk-free exposure, and it is not a claim that every real venue or trader has the same financing arrangement. Neither borrowing nor its absence makes a positive expected-value calculation a guarantee.

docs.title: 22.10 Assumptions and failure modes
docs.text: The helper assumes a specified \(p\), binary USD 1 payout, constant unit cost in \((0,1)\), divisible units, no extra exit or settlement fees, and no other holdings. Existing positions require joint terminal-wealth analysis; adding isolated Kelly fractions is not a general portfolio solution, even for independent simultaneous bets. A scenario table exposes possible losses without estimating their probabilities, but optimizing expected log wealth across scenarios additionally needs a joint probability model. Whole-unit grids and nonlinear costs require feasible-quantity checks rather than mechanically rounding \(\phi W/c\) upward. None of this chapter's arithmetic establishes that an estimated \(p\) is correct.

docs.title: 22.11 Companion example
docs.text:
The companion script risk.py implements exactly the fractional-sizing formula and the joint-scenario matrix derived above, plus the cash-budget check. Running it reports a quarter-Kelly fraction of cash spent of 0.059322 at the stated \(p=0.55\), \(c=0.41\) assumptions (matching Section 22.4), a zero fraction when the belief is below cost, joint scenario profits of minus USD 8.20 (shared bad news), USD 11.80 (both YES), and USD 1.80 (divergent) exactly as derived in Section 22.5, and a rejected second position against a USD 5.00 total commitment cap exactly as derived in Section 22.6. It also rejects an invalid binary cost outside \((0,1)\), since the closed form is undefined there. Run it with:

Command working directory: run this chapter's Python commands from book\companion. From the trading repository root, run Set-Location book\companion once first. The .venv belongs to that companion project; see companion setup.

.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe examples\risk.py

Every number above is deterministic arithmetic under explicitly stated assumptions; none of it is an empirical measurement of a real trading account's growth or drawdown.

docs.title: Exercise 1: the sizing fraction at a different edge
docs.text:
Compute \(\phi^{*}\) for \(p=0.60\) and \(c=0.45\), then the quarter-Kelly spend fraction.

Solution sketch. \(\phi^{*} = (0.60-0.45)/(1-0.45) = 0.15/0.55 \approx 0.2727\). Quarter Kelly: \(0.25 \times 0.2727 \approx 0.0682\), about 6.8 percent of bankroll.

docs.title: Exercise 2: two-loss drawdown at full Kelly versus an eighth Kelly
docs.text:
Using \(p=0.55, c=0.41\) (full Kelly \(\phi^{*}\approx0.2373\)), compute the wealth remaining after two consecutive NO outcomes at full Kelly and at an eighth-Kelly fraction (\(\kappa=0.125\)), and comment on the trade-off.

Solution sketch. Full Kelly: \((1-0.2373)^2 \approx 0.582\), a 41.8 percent drawdown. Eighth Kelly: spend fraction \(0.125\times0.2373\approx0.0297\); \((1-0.0297)^2\approx0.9414\), a 5.9 percent drawdown. The smaller fraction trades away growth rate for a much smaller realized decline from the same two adverse outcomes.

docs.title: Exercise 3: a third correlated scenario
docs.text:
Expand Section 22.5's combined "divergent" row into the specific state "event-a YES, event-b NO," and compute portfolio profit.

Solution sketch. Receipts: \(10(1) + 10(0) = 10\). Profit: \(10 - 8.20 = \text{USD }1.80\), identical to the "divergent" scenario already listed, since the payoff only depends on which single leg wins, not which specific leg it is, given identical costs and quantities on each side.

docs.title: Exercise 4: when the constant-cost formula stops applying
docs.text:
A fee is 2 percent of notional plus a flat per-unit component. Explain when the constant-\(c\) formula still applies and why depth or fill-dependent rounding can require a different quantity optimization.

Solution sketch. At a fixed executable price with no rounding or other size effects, this fee remains linear in quantity and gives a constant all-in \(c\). If larger quantities sweep worse prices or split into differently rounded fills, \(C(Q)\) is no longer \(cQ\). Evaluate Section 22.8's quantity-level log-wealth objective under actual cost and reservation limits; substituting \(C(Q)/Q\) into the constant-cost optimum ignores the changed marginal cost and need not maximize growth.

docs.title: Exercise 5: leverage intuition that does not transfer
docs.text:
A trader argues, "I'm only risking 10 percent of my account on this position, so it's low-risk even if I'm wrong." Using Section 22.3, identify the hidden assumption in this statement as applied to a fully collateralized binary contract.

Solution sketch. It assumes that calling a possible loss "10 percent" makes it affordable or unlikely. Here all of the spent 10 percent can be lost on NO; the position's payout notional can be larger than that cash amount without borrowing. Check the full loss against obligations and other commitments, rather than inferring safety from the percentage or from full funding alone.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: Chapter 23 moves from static sizing rules to policies that are learned from logged decisions and rewards, and to the specific care required before treating a simulator's reward as evidence about real trading.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Read the forecast-to-order decision, a backtest that respects execution, evidence after strategy search, and Chapters 21-22 before this chapter. You should be comfortable with conditional expectation, the notion of a decision cutoff and label availability from the notation registry, and the glossary entries for leakage, selection bias, and untouched evaluation.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this chapter, you should be able to: formalize state, action, and reward for a simple one-step wait-or-buy decision; derive the tabular greedy learning rule and explain why it needs full context-action support; derive the inverse-propensity-scoring (IPS) estimator from an importance-sampling identity and explain what it requires to be valid; compute and interpret an effective sample size as a variance diagnostic; explain why evaluating a learned policy under a shifted regime is a genuinely different test from evaluating it on more data from the same regime; state precisely why reward timing rules out any lookahead; and explain, with a concrete numeric contrast, why a simulator's reward estimate is not evidence of real trading profit.

docs.title: 23.1 State, action, and reward for a wait-or-buy decision
docs.text:
A contextual bandit observes a context, chooses an action, and receives a reward. Here \(S\in\{0,1\}\) is an invented feature bucket and \(A\in\{\text{wait},\text{buy}\}\). To match conventional bandit notation, this chapter uses \(R\) locally for net reward, not the notation registry's terminal contract payout; the settlement outcome is \(Y\), and buying earns \(R=Y-0.51\). Likewise \(b(a\mid s)\) below denotes the behavior-policy probability, not an executable bid.

Define the reward explicitly. Waiting always yields \(R=0\): no cash is committed, and (for now) no opportunity cost is charged for having declined an available trade — a simplification flagged in Section 23.6. Buying commits to an all-in invented cost of USD 0.51 per unit for this chapter's own simulator (a distinct, explicitly labeled convention, not to be confused with the book's shared canonical USD 0.41 accounting example used in Chapters 21-22); the reward is \(R = Y - 0.51\) if the underlying binary settlement is \(Y\), and \(0\) if the action was wait. This is a one-step episode: one context, one action, one reward, with no sequence of states evolving afterward. That simplicity is deliberate and is itself a limitation, addressed in Section 23.6.

Given a context-conditional probability \(p_s = P(Y=1\mid S=s)\), the expected reward of each action is immediate:

\[ \mathbb{E}[R\mid S=s, A=\text{buy}] = p_s - 0.51, \qquad \mathbb{E}[R\mid S=s, A=\text{wait}] = 0. \]

Suppose \(p_0=0.35\) and \(p_1=0.65\) (two invented, distinct context-conditional success rates). Then \(\mathbb{E}[R\mid S{=}0,\text{buy}] = 0.35-0.51 = -0.16\), so waiting (reward 0) dominates buying in context 0. In context 1, \(\mathbb{E}[R\mid S{=}1,\text{buy}] = 0.65-0.51 = 0.14 > 0\), so buying dominates waiting. The optimal deterministic policy is therefore \(\pi^{*}(0)=\text{wait}\), \(\pi^{*}(1)=\text{buy}\) — a policy this chapter's companion example actually recovers from logged data, as Section 23.8 shows.

docs.title: 23.2 Learning a tabular policy from a behavior-policy log
docs.text:
A real decision-maker does not know \(p_s\) directly; it must be estimated from a log of past decisions and their observed rewards. The log is generated by a behavior policy: whatever process (a fixed rule, a human, or a randomizer) actually chose the logged actions. A simple and instructive behavior policy logs actions uniformly at random with a known propensity — the probability the behavior policy assigned to the action it happened to take, for example \(b(a\mid s)=0.5\) for either action in either context, exactly the policy used to generate this chapter's simulated log.

Given such a log, a tabular learning rule estimates \(\mathbb{E}[R\mid S{=}s,A{=}a]\) by the empirical mean reward among logged rows sharing that exact context and action, then picks the action with the higher empirical mean in each context. This rule requires full support: every one of the four (context, action) combinations must actually appear in the log, or there is no data to estimate one of the means from, and the honest response is to refuse to produce a policy for that context rather than silently guessing. A behavior policy that never tries a particular action in a particular context makes that action's value permanently unlearnable from this log, no matter how large the log otherwise is — a first, simple instance of the off-policy support requirement developed further below.

docs.title: 23.3 Evaluating a policy without deploying it: the importance-sampling identity
docs.text:
Suppose a policy \(\pi\) has been learned (Section 23.2), and the question is how well it would have performed, without actually running it live. If the log was generated by a different policy — the behavior policy \(b\) — a naive average of logged rewards answers the wrong question, because it reflects \(b\)'s action choices, not \(\pi\)'s. Inverse propensity scoring (IPS) corrects for this with an importance-sampling reweighting. Define, for each logged row \(i\) with context \(S_i\), action \(A_i\), reward \(R_i\), and known propensity \(b(A_i\mid S_i)\), the estimator

\[ \hat V(\pi) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\mathbf 1\{A_i=\pi(S_i)\}}{b(A_i\mid S_i)}\,R_i. \]

To see why this targets \(\mathbb{E}[R\mid S,\pi(S)]\), condition on a fixed context \(s\) and take the expectation of one term over the behavior policy's own action distribution:

\[ \mathbb{E}_b\!\left[\frac{\mathbf 1\{A=\pi(s)\}}{b(A\mid s)}R \,\middle|\, S=s\right] = \sum_{a} b(a\mid s)\cdot\frac{\mathbf 1\{a=\pi(s)\}}{b(a\mid s)}\cdot \mathbb{E}[R\mid S=s, A=a] = \mathbb{E}[R\mid S=s, A=\pi(s)], \]

because only the target-action term survives. Averaging over contexts targets the policy's reward in the logging population. For the causal "what if we used this action" interpretation, the logged reward distribution must also match the reward that action would produce under the target policy: no hidden action-selection confounding after conditioning on the recorded context, and no unmodeled interference or policy-induced change in the reward mechanism. Randomized actions in this simulator satisfy that requirement by construction. A human log with a recorded propensity field does not establish it automatically.

Unbiasedness here treats \(\pi\) as fixed independently of the evaluation outcomes and requires positive behavior probability for every target action. Evaluating a policy on the same rewards used to select it reintroduces selection bias. Doubly robust methods combine reward and behavior-policy models under their own assumptions; they are related work, not implemented here and not a remedy for missing support. DUDIK2011

docs.title: 23.4 Effective sample size: a variance diagnostic, not a bias fix
docs.text:
The IPS estimator's variance depends on how uneven the importance weights \(1/b(A_i\mid S_i)\) are; if many logged rows receive weight zero (because their action differs from what the target policy would choose) and the rest carry a large uniform weight, the effective number of independent observations behind the estimate is smaller than the raw row count \(n\). A standard diagnostic is the effective sample size,

\[ \mathrm{ESS} = \frac{\left(\sum_i w_i\right)^2}{\sum_i w_i^2}, \qquad w_i = \frac{\mathbf 1\{A_i=\pi(S_i)\}}{b(A_i\mid S_i)}. \]

If nonzero weights are equal, this ESS equals their count; unequal weights reduce it. With uniform two-action logging, 409 matching rows out of 800 give ESS 409. This is a weight-concentration diagnostic, not an exact effective sample size for every reward distribution and not a correction for event dependence. Reward variance, dependence, and the relationship between reward and weight also affect the estimator's uncertainty. A healthy ESS does not prove unbiasedness, adequate support in every region, or simulator realism.

docs.title: 23.5 Same regime versus a shifted regime: two different questions
docs.text:
Holding out a fresh batch of logged rounds generated by the same simulator settings tests whether the learned policy generalizes within the regime it was trained on. Holding out a batch generated under a deliberately shifted regime — for instance, subtracting a fixed amount from every context's success probability, representing a stylized "conditions got worse" scenario — tests something categorically different: whether a policy learned under one regime remains sensible under another. Because \(\pi^{*}\) was derived in Section 23.1 from \(p_0=0.35, p_1=0.65\), and the shifted regime moves both down by 0.30 to \(0.05\) and \(0.35\), the previously profitable context-1 buy action now has expected reward \(0.35-0.51=-0.16\), no longer positive; the fixed action mapping learned under the old regime is not the optimal mapping under the new one, yet the policy still executes the old mapping because nothing in this one-step setup detects the shift. A same-simulator held-out evaluation and a shifted-regime held-out evaluation must be reported separately and neither substitutes for the other: a policy that looks robust only because it was re-tested on more of the same conditions has not been tested against a train/test market regime change at all, and a change in market regime (a shift in liquidity, information flow, or participant composition) is exactly the kind of real-world discontinuity a fixed historical evaluation window cannot promise to represent.

Reusing one learned policy, one simulator, and one train/test split repeatedly while quietly trying several regime definitions until a favorable-looking comparison appears is a form of the selection problem examined in backtest-overfitting research; recording every regime and split actually tried, not only the reported one, is necessary before treating any single comparison as informative. BAILEY2017

docs.title: 23.6 Reward-arrival timing: no lookahead, ever
docs.text:
The one-step simulator generates the settlement and reward within the same loop iteration. Real rewards may become known long after an action. A reward may enter fitting only when its availability time is no later than that fitting cutoff; it need not be known at its own earlier action time. Later evaluation of a frozen action against its eventual reward is legitimate. Using that reward to alter the earlier action, its features, or the policy that supposedly chose it is not.

A policy retrained during a log must therefore wait for each training reward's actual availability. Repeatedly improving a policy in the same simulator is a separate risk: it can optimize simulator quirks. Use a held-out evaluation log and prespecified stress regimes rather than reporting only rewards that helped choose the policy.

docs.title: 23.7 Missing support must be rejected, not extrapolated
docs.text:
Distinguish two failures. If the behavior policy gives a target action zero probability in a relevant context, population support fails and the IPS identity cannot identify that action's value. If the probability is positive but the finite sample happens to contain no matching action, the observed weights are zero, not undefined; ordinary IPS remains mathematically defined, but that sample contains no direct reward evidence for the missing pair.

The companion adopts a stricter finite-sample gate: ips_value refuses to report a value unless every target context-action pair appears at least once. This is an explicit teaching safeguard, not a theorem that IPS weights become undefined whenever a random sample misses a pair. One occurrence also does not ensure adequate precision. Fixed-batch RL literature motivates avoiding unsupported extrapolation but supplies no market-execution guarantee. FUJIMOTO2019

docs.title: 23.8 Why a simulator's IPS reward is not real profit
docs.text: Even a fully correct IPS estimate, computed on a log with adequate support and a healthy effective sample size, only answers "what would this target policy have earned under exactly this simulator's assumptions." Several of those assumptions are chosen for teaching clarity and do not describe a real market. Rewards here are independent across rounds, with no shared-event dependence, no fees beyond the flat invented USD 0.51 cost, no order depth, no partial fills, no latency, and no queue competition. Contexts are two artificial buckets rather than a genuine, high-dimensional feature vector. Propensities are known exactly by construction, because the behavior policy was built to log them; a real historical decision log rarely comes with exact, verified logging probabilities attached, and estimating them introduces its own error that plain IPS does not account for. None of the diagnostics in this chapter — support checks, effective sample size, or a shifted-regime comparison — can certify that the simulator itself resembles any actual venue's mechanics; they only certify that the estimator is behaving correctly given the simulator it was handed. A favorable IPS number is evidence about a specific labeled simulation, not about a tradable real-world edge.

docs.title: 23.9 Assumptions and failure modes
docs.text: This chapter's derivations assume a single decision round with an immediately resolved reward, a known and strictly positive logging propensity for every action a target policy would ever choose, independent rounds with no shared-outcome dependence, and a policy space restricted to deterministic, per-context action choices. Violating the positive-propensity assumption breaks the importance-sampling identity outright, not merely its accuracy. Violating round independence (for instance, if several logged rounds actually referenced the same underlying real-world event) would make the effective sample size calculation overstate genuine informational content, similar to the event-grouping cautions from earlier chapters. Extending this framework to a genuine multi-step reinforcement-learning setting, with fills, latency, and queueing folded into a state that evolves over time, requires substantially more machinery than the tabular one-step case shown here and is not attempted in this chapter.

docs.title: 23.10 Companion example
docs.text:
The companion script policy_learning.py builds an 800-round logged bandit under the Section 23.1 context-success probabilities, learns a tabular policy, and evaluates it two ways: on a fresh same-simulator held-out log, and on a log generated under the Section 23.5 adverse-selection-shifted regime. The learned policy is wait in context 0 and buy in context 1, exactly matching Section 23.1's derivation. The same-simulator held-out evaluation reports an IPS reward per round of approximately 0.091175 with an effective sample size of about 409 out of 800 logged rounds; the shifted-regime evaluation reports approximately minus 0.088825 at the same effective sample size, concretely illustrating Section 23.5's point that the same fixed policy performs oppositely once the underlying regime changes. A separate call demonstrates the missing-support rejection from Section 23.7 using a two-row log that never tries the buy action in either context. Run it with:

Command working directory: run this chapter's Python commands from book\companion. From the trading repository root, run Set-Location book\companion once first. The .venv belongs to that companion project; see companion setup.

.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe examples\policy_learning.py

The companion's own output explicitly labels its rewards synthetic and notes that IPS needs known propensities and support, not merely logged prices; nothing in this example is presented as measured trading performance.

docs.title: Exercise 1: a third context
docs.text:
Add a third context with \(p_2 = 0.20\) to Section 23.1's setup, using the same USD 0.51 all-in cost. What is the optimal action in this context, and why?

Solution sketch. \(\mathbb{E}[R\mid S{=}2,\text{buy}] = 0.20-0.51=-0.31 < 0 = \mathbb{E}[R\mid S{=}2,\text{wait}]\), so waiting is optimal, by an even larger margin than in context 0.

docs.title: Exercise 2: unbiasedness with three actions
docs.text:
Sketch, without full algebra, why the importance-sampling identity in Section 23.3 still holds if there are three possible actions per context instead of two, provided the target policy still chooses one deterministic action per context.

Solution sketch. The sum in the derivation ranges over however many actions the behavior policy can choose; the indicator still zeroes out every term except \(a=\pi(s)\), and the \(b(a\mid s)\) factors still cancel for that surviving term. The number of actions does not affect the cancellation, only how many terms exist before it.

docs.title: Exercise 3: computing an effective sample size
docs.text:
A held-out log of 4 rows has importance weights \((2, 2, 0, 0)\) for a given policy. Compute the effective sample size and compare it to the raw row count.

Solution sketch. \(\mathrm{ESS} = (2+2+0+0)^2/(2^2+2^2+0+0) = 16/8 = 2\). The effective sample size equals the count of nonzero, equal-weight rows (2), well below the raw count of 4, because the two zero-weight rows contribute nothing.

docs.title: Exercise 4: why missing support cannot be patched with an average
docs.text:
A held-out log never tries the buy action in context 1, but the target policy chooses buy there. Explain why substituting the overall average reward from other contexts is not an acceptable fix.

Solution sketch. The importance-sampling identity relies on reweighting actual observations of the action in question in that specific context; an average reward from unrelated context-action pairs answers a different conditional expectation entirely and provides no evidence, unbiased or otherwise, about \(\mathbb{E}[R\mid S{=}1,\text{buy}]\). The honest response is to report that this context-action pair is unsupported, not to substitute an unrelated number.

docs.title: Exercise 5: why a positive shifted-regime IPS number still would not license live trading
docs.text:
Suppose a modified policy is learned that shows a positive IPS reward on the shifted-regime held-out log as well as the original one. Give two specific reasons this result alone would not justify moving to real trading.

Solution sketch. The reward function still assumes one flat invented cost with no depth, latency, fees, or queueing, so it does not represent an executable price path; and the shifted regime is a single, hand-chosen perturbation, not a demonstrated model of real regime change, so success against it does not establish robustness to whatever an actual future regime shift would look like.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: Chapter 24 turns to running a paper-trading system under explicit operational discipline: read-only feeds, versioned rules, fail-closed gates, and an honest boundary between rehearsal and a live trade.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Read rules, venues, and settlement risk, a backtest that respects execution, and Chapters 21-23 before this chapter. You should be comfortable with the notation registry's time taxonomy (event time, publication time, decision time, fill time, label-availability time, settlement time) and the glossary entries for paper trading, fill, reconciliation, and abstention.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this chapter, you should be able to: describe the read-only boundary a paper-trading system must respect; explain why stable contract, rules, and snapshot identifiers matter as much as prices; walk through a fail-closed decision gate that turns staleness, missing data, ambiguous rules, or an invalid probability into an explicit no-trade outcome rather than a silent guess; trace how partial fills, cancellation races, and ledger reconciliation are handled without assuming perfect information; explain the difference between an automatic risk-budget gate and the separate manual-review boundary before any live trade; and state clearly why nothing in this chapter is, or authorizes, funded live-order code.

docs.title: 24.1 What "paper operations" means, and what it explicitly does not mean
docs.text:
A paper-trading system applies a decision process to simulated balances and fills instead of funded orders. This chapter's companion is deliberately narrow: it consumes already-fetched market data (a probability estimate and a quoted order book) and produces either a recorded paper decision or an explicit refusal to proceed. There is no daemon polling a live feed, no credential loading, no funded-order endpoint, no wallet signing, and no deposit or withdrawal logic anywhere in the book's educational companion. A read-only feed boundary means the system only ever reads already-obtained quotes and identifiers; it never issues an outbound instruction that could move real funds. Framing paper trading this way is not a stylistic choice — it is the difference between rehearsing a decision process and actually running one, and this book's final live-trade chapter treats that difference as requiring a separate, manual checklist rather than an automatic upgrade from a working paper system.

Precisely because of that narrowness, this chapter's ledger is an in-memory object living inside one running Python process, not a durable or production order-management system (OMS). It holds no write-ahead log, no crash-recovery journal, and no cross-process persistence; ending the process discards it entirely, and nothing here reconstructs state after a restart. A production paper or live system would need durable storage, restart recovery, and a real message transport in place of a single in-process object — none of which this chapter's companion attempts to provide. Treating this ledger's clean bookkeeping as a rehearsal for those durability guarantees, rather than as evidence they already exist, is essential to reading the rest of this chapter correctly.

The companion package separately offers an optional, explicitly opted-in read-only acquisition path for a handful of allowlisted public venue endpoints, requiring an affirmative terms acknowledgement rather than any stored credential. It fetches current-only metadata snapshots into new, explicitly named local files; it is not a historical archive, not a live broker, and not coupled to this chapter's ledger, decision gate, or PaperBroker in any way. No venue payload is committed with this book's educational companion as part of that path. This chapter does not document that acquisition path's exact commands or flags, since they belong to a separate part of the companion codebase and can change independently of this chapter's argument; every paper decision discussed below simply assumes its book and probability inputs have already been supplied by the caller, however they were obtained.

docs.title: 24.2 Identity and versioning discipline
docs.text:
A price by itself is not enough to trade responsibly on. A contract needs a stable contract identifier, an event identifier describing the real-world question, and a rules identifier pinning the exact resolution wording in force. Official resolution documentation for at least one venue explicitly describes clarifications that can be issued after trading has already begun, and an exceptional dispute path with its own payout convention. POLYMARKET_RESOLUTION A market's grouping under one user-facing event container does not, by itself, establish that its constituent markets are mutually exclusive or that they share one rules version; that has to be checked against the actual identifiers and rules text, not inferred from a shared title. POLYMARKET_MARKETS

A disciplined paper ledger should refuse to silently accept a change in a contract's recorded metadata once that contract has been registered: if a contract identifier reappears with different event or rules metadata than what was first recorded, that is a version conflict to raise, not to overwrite quietly. The same discipline applies to a quoted book: each snapshot carries its own identifier, and if that identifier is reused for genuinely different quote data, the ledger should treat this as an error rather than silently accepting whichever data arrived most recently. Time identifiers matter just as much as content identifiers. Official historical-data documentation for one venue describes live and historical partitions governed by moving cutoff timestamps that differ by record type, retrievable from a dedicated cutoff endpoint rather than being a single fixed boundary; treating "the current live endpoint" and "the complete historical record" as interchangeable would misrepresent what is actually available at any given moment. KALSHI_HISTORY Keeping event time, publication time, local observation time, decision time, fill time, label-availability time, and settlement time distinct, as the notation registry requires throughout this book, is not a bookkeeping nicety here — it is what lets a later audit reconstruct exactly what was knowable at the moment a paper decision was made.

docs.title: 24.3 A fail-closed decision gate
docs.text:
The central operational habit this chapter teaches is to treat missing or questionable inputs as reasons to stop, not as gaps to patch over. A paper decision gate can require every one of several boolean preconditions to hold before proceeding: that the applicable resolution rules have been verified, that the features needed for the decision were actually available, and that the fee assumptions used in any expected-value calculation are explicit rather than assumed. If any one of these is not affirmatively true, the correct output is an explicit no-trade decision with a stated reason, such as "ambiguous rules, unavailable features, or unspecified fees" — not a decision computed anyway on the hope that the gap does not matter.

Beyond those preconditions, a decision needs an actual quoted book and a probability estimate; if either is absent, the gate returns "missing quote or probability" rather than falling back to some default price or a stale cached number. If a supplied book's contract identifier does not match the decision's own contract identifier, that mismatch is itself a reason to refuse, since acting on the wrong contract's quote is a bookkeeping error the caller must have made upstream. A book's own freshness check compares its observed timestamp against the current decision time and a maximum permitted quote age; a book older than that permitted age is rejected as "stale or future quote," converting an easy-to-miss timing bug into an explicit, loud failure. And a probability value that is not a finite number in \([0,1]\) — including the not-a-number value NaN, which naive numeric comparisons can pass through silently because most ordinary comparisons against NaN evaluate to false rather than raising an error — is rejected outright rather than silently coerced into some default. Five concrete input states illustrate the gate's behavior: an explicit, fresh, fully specified input becomes a genuine paper candidate; a stale book, a missing book, an unverified-rules flag, and an invalid (NaN) probability each produce their own distinct no-trade reason. None of these five paths silently substitutes a plausible-looking default; each failure is a labeled, inspectable outcome.

docs.title: 24.4 Partial fills, cancellation races, and reconciliation
docs.text:
A paper take consumes remaining displayed depth, level by level, within the order's limit. It remembers consumed quantities so the same snapshot cannot be spent twice. An order can fill completely across several levels; a partial fill means that some requested quantity remains unfilled. PaperBroker.take records feasible fills and leaves that remainder open when depth runs out. By contrast, the stateless full-size sweep_cost raises on insufficient depth, and the decision screen converts that into NO_TRADE. These are different interfaces: candidate screening asks whether the whole requested trade is supportable, while execution accounts for what actually filled in the supplied paper scenario.

A cancel race pits a cancellation request against an incoming match. Sending the request does not establish that the venue processed it first. The companion assumes caller-supplied events arrive in a valid replay order and interprets cancel as already effective; it rejects later fills and backward operation timestamps. It does not implement real asynchronous race reconciliation. A real system must preserve separate match, effective-cancel, and local-receipt times and venue sequence/identity records. A delayed report of a match that preceded effective cancellation remains a real fill even if its match time is earlier than the latest locally received message. Do not rewrite that timestamp or discard the report merely to fit this teaching ledger's ordered-call interface.

Reconciliation here means an internal arithmetic consistency check on the paper ledger itself, not a claim of exchange-side reconciliation with a real venue. A sound reconciliation should verify at least three separate identities: that cash equals the initial cash plus the sum of every recorded ledger cash movement; that recorded inventory equals both the sum of ledger inventory movements and the sum of open cost-basis lot quantities; and that cash plus remaining open cost basis, minus the initial cash, equals the recorded realized profit. These are closed-form bookkeeping identities that must hold by construction; a violation signals a bug in the ledger implementation itself; it does not signal, and cannot detect, whether the ledger's own inputs (a stale quote fed in as if fresh, or a fabricated fill) were themselves realistic. Ledger reconciliation is an internal consistency check, not exchange reconciliation, and the ledger itself is not persisted across Python processes — it audits arithmetic within one run, not truth, and not any durable history across runs.

A concrete walkthrough ties these pieces together. Starting from USD 10.00 cash, a paper buy order for 10 units at a limit of USD 0.40 fills entirely at the book's best ask (USD 0.40, with ample displayed size), incurring the book's flat USD 0.01-per-unit fee, so the ledger records a cash movement of minus USD 4.10 and an inventory increase of 10 units — the exact canonical cost from the notation registry. Remaining cash is USD 5.90. Marking the resulting 10-unit inventory against a quoted bid of USD 0.38 (again with the flat USD 0.01-per-unit fee applied to a hypothetical full liquidation) gives a liquidation value of \(10\times0.38 - 10\times0.01 = \text{USD }3.70\); total marked equity is \(5.90+3.70=\text{USD }9.60\), and marked profit relative to the original USD 10.00 is minus USD 0.40, while realized profit remains exactly zero because no sale has actually occurred. This mark is a hypothetical, conservative full-liquidation valuation, not a realized trade; it depends entirely on the bid depth actually available at the time it is computed, and it should never be reported as if it were cash in hand.

docs.title: 24.5 Kill switches, no-trade gates, and the manual-review boundary
docs.text: A cash risk budget, as built in Chapter 22, functions as an automatic circuit breaker: it caps a single order's cost and the total cash committed across open positions and pending reservations, and a paper decision that would breach either cap must be refused before any fill is attempted, regardless of how attractive its modeled expected value looks. This is a necessary automatic gate, and it is not by itself sufficient to authorize anything beyond continued paper rehearsal. A manual-review boundary is a separate, deliberately non-automatic checkpoint: no combination of a clean paper reconciliation, a passed risk-budget check, and an attractive backtested or simulated metric should, by itself, flip a system from paper to funded operation. That transition belongs to an explicit, human-performed checklist — covering account eligibility, current rules verification, evidence quality, true cost structure, and affordable risk — addressed as its own final chapter in this book, not to any automatic promotion inside the paper system itself. A paper session that behaves impeccably is evidence that the bookkeeping works; it is not evidence that a live deployment decision has been made responsibly.

docs.title: 24.6 Metrics, drift, and audit under continuous monitoring
docs.text:
Operating a paper system over time invites a specific statistical trap: watching a running metric (a hit rate, a Brier score, a cumulative modeled profit) and stopping to declare success the moment it looks good. An ordinary fixed-sample confidence interval is built to be valid at one predetermined sample size; treating it as valid after repeatedly peeking and stopping whenever the number looks favorable inflates the true error rate well beyond its nominal level. Time-uniform confidence sequences are constructed specifically to remain valid under continuous monitoring, offering simultaneous coverage across an entire sequence of looks rather than only at one fixed endpoint, under a stated filtration and an exponential-supermartingale condition on the underlying process. HOWARD2021 This is a genuinely useful tool for an audit process that wants to monitor a running paper metric honestly rather than banning monitoring outright — but it is not a universal fix: it does not repair a dataset that has already leaked a shared event's outcome across supposedly separate observations, and it does not turn dependent, event-grouped repeated observations of one underlying uncertainty into independent trials merely because the monitoring procedure is sequential. An audit trail built on top of this discipline should retain immutable, append-only, timestamped ledger entries as its source of truth, since any metric computed after the fact is only as trustworthy as the record it was computed from.

Drift in this operational sense means the paper system's own embedded assumptions — an assumed instantaneous full fill against displayed depth, a flat invented fee, a fixed maximum quote age — starting to diverge from whatever the real environment the system is rehearsing for would actually do. A demo or mock-funds environment offered by a real venue is explicitly described by its own operator as potentially not reflecting real-market prices or behavior; treating clean, extended performance in such an environment as proof of real-market fidelity confuses a mechanics rehearsal with a live-market fidelity claim the operator itself declines to make. KALSHI_DEMO Recording, rather than discarding, every operational failure a paper system produces (a stale-quote rejection, a missing-book rejection, a risk-budget refusal) is itself part of a useful audit trail: a system that never refuses anything over a long run is more likely to have a gap in its checks than to have encountered uniformly perfect conditions.

docs.title: 24.7 No automated funded mode, anywhere in this system
docs.text: To close the loop explicitly: nothing described in this chapter submits a real order, moves real collateral, signs a wallet transaction, loads an API secret, or attempts to bypass a venue's geographic or eligibility restrictions. A retrieved terms page for at least one venue displayed a geographic/product restriction notice without exposing its complete operative terms in the response actually inspected; this is a reminder that eligibility and permission questions remain open and venue-specific, not a detail this book's paper system resolves or works around. POLYMARKET_TERMS There is no configuration flag in the educational companion that converts a paper session into a funded one; that capability does not exist in this teaching project, by design. This is not a statement about separate trading-system components outside book\companion.

docs.title: 24.8 Assumptions and failure modes
docs.text: This chapter's paper ledger assumes deterministic, in-process execution with no genuine network latency, no true queue-position information, and an explicit, caller-supplied notion of "now" for every operation; a real deployment must additionally handle out-of-order message delivery, venue-side partial acknowledgments, and reconnection after an outage, none of which this in-memory design attempts to simulate. Reconciliation checks internal bookkeeping identities only; they cannot detect an unrealistic upstream input, such as a quote that was stale when captured but presented to the ledger as fresh. Time-uniform confidence sequences require their own stated process assumptions and do not, by themselves, fix event dependence or a leaked label. Nothing in this chapter's fail-closed gates, reconciliation checks, or monitoring tools establishes that a paper strategy would be profitable if funded; they establish only that its bookkeeping is internally consistent and that its stopping conditions fire correctly when data is missing, stale, or invalid.

docs.title: 24.9 Companion example
docs.text:
The companion script paper_session.py builds a fail-closed monitor over five input states: a fresh, fully specified input; a stale book; a missing book; an unverified-rules flag; and an invalid (NaN) probability. Only the first becomes a genuine paper candidate; the other four each return an explicit no-trade decision with a distinct stated reason, exactly as derived in Section 24.3. It then executes a 10-unit paper buy against the book's displayed ask, leaving cash at USD 5.90, and reports a reconciliation record confirming the internal identities from Section 24.4, plus a hypothetical mark against a lower quoted bid showing marked equity of USD 9.60 and marked profit of minus USD 0.40 against zero realized profit, matching the worked walkthrough above exactly. Its own reported operating boundary states plainly: "in-memory deterministic replay; no daemon, credential loading or external order endpoint." Run it with:

Command working directory: run this chapter's Python commands from book\companion. From the trading repository root, run Set-Location book\companion once first. The .venv belongs to that companion project; see companion setup.

.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe examples\paper_session.py

docs.title: Exercise 1: tracing a stale-book decision
docs.text:
A paper decision is attempted with a book observed 30 seconds ago against a maximum permitted quote age of 5 seconds. What decision status and reason should result, and why should the system not simply use the stale quote anyway if it is the only one available?

Solution sketch. The decision should return NO_TRADE with a reason indicating a stale or future quote. Using a stale quote anyway risks acting on a price that no longer reflects current conditions; the entire point of the freshness check is that "the only quote available" is not the same as "a usable quote," and a missing fresh quote is itself informative.

docs.title: Exercise 2: reconciliation by hand
docs.text:
A paper ledger starts with USD 20.00 cash, records one fill with a cash movement of minus USD 8.20 and an inventory increase of 20 units, and no other activity. Verify the cash identity and state what a violation would indicate.

Solution sketch. Expected cash equals \(20.00 - 8.20 = \text{USD }11.80\); if the ledger's reported cash differs from this sum, the discrepancy indicates a bug in how the ledger applies or records cash movements, not evidence about whether the fill's underlying quote was realistic.

docs.title: Exercise 3: why a cancel race needs timestamp discipline, not prevention
docs.text:
Explain why a paper ledger cannot simply refuse to record any fill on an order the caller has already tried to cancel, and what it should do instead.

Solution sketch. A cancellation request may lose the race to a venue match. Retain request, match, effective-cancel, and receipt information and reconcile the authoritative execution, including delayed reports. The companion can replay a known fill-before-cancel sequence in order, but cannot directly ingest arbitrary out-of-order venue messages or recover a fill after its cancel call. That requires a separate reconciliation design, not changing the fill's true timestamp to satisfy the toy ledger.

docs.title: Exercise 4: why NaN needs an explicit check
docs.text:
A probability field is populated with NaN due to an upstream division-by-zero bug. Explain why an ordinary check such as "if probability < 0, reject" would fail to catch this, and what kind of check is needed instead.

Solution sketch. Ordinary numeric comparisons involving NaN evaluate to false, so a check like probability < 0 silently passes a NaN value through without raising an error. The needed check is an explicit finiteness test (confirming the value is a genuine finite number) combined with the ordinary range check, rejecting non-finite values outright rather than relying on comparisons that quietly ignore them.

docs.title: Exercise 5: what continuous monitoring does and does not fix
docs.text:
A team monitors a paper system's running Brier score using a time-uniform confidence sequence so they can check it whenever they like without invalidating coverage. Their evaluation set still contains two snapshots of the same real-world event treated as independent rows. Does the confidence sequence fix this problem?

Solution sketch. No. Time-uniform confidence sequences address the validity of repeated looks at accumulating data under their own stated process assumptions; they do not address whether the underlying observations are actually independent. Two snapshots sharing one real-world event remain a dependence problem that must be fixed at the data-construction stage, not compensated for by the choice of monitoring procedure.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: Part 5 turns to open research questions this book's own methods raise but do not settle; Chapter 25 proposes falsifiable research protocols rather than finished conclusions, continuing the same discipline of stating assumptions and failure conditions explicitly.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Read the foundations, data, modeling, and strategy parts before this chapter. In particular, be comfortable with the distinction between an economic event and a contractual payout, event-grouped evaluation, executable prices, adverse selection, and the limits of a paper simulator. The notation registry supplies the common symbols.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this chapter, you should be able to turn an interesting prediction-market idea into a falsifiable research protocol, identify its nearest established literature, separate a forecasting target from an execution target, and explain what evidence would make you abandon the idea. You should also recognize why combining several familiar techniques can create a useful project without establishing an original scientific discovery.

docs.title: 25.1 A research agenda is not an inventory of hidden profits
docs.text:
Suppose a researcher notices that event contracts have explicit rules, bounded payouts, related questions, uncertain settlement delays, and many repeated quote observations but relatively few independent outcomes. Those features suggest research problems. They do not establish that the market has failed to price them.

The important distinction is between a mechanism and an opportunity. A mechanism explains how a relationship could arise. An opportunity additionally requires that the relationship is measurable with available information, sufficiently stable, not already reflected in executable prices, and large enough to survive costs and risk. An elegant mechanism can fail at any of those steps.

Prediction markets also have a substantial history. Information aggregation, market scoring rules, and combinatorial market design are established research areas, not inventions of the most recent trading interface. Hanson's market-scoring work and the convex-market-design framework of Abernethy, Chen, and Vaughan are relevant foundations, but they do not certify that the proposals below are new or profitable. HANSON2007 ABERNETHY2013

The five proposals in this chapter are therefore untested research hypotheses. Their proposed contribution is a particular question and experimental arrangement, not a claim of priority. Each combines known ideas with a prediction-market-specific measurement problem. A serious research project would extend the related-work search, inspect the relevant full texts, and revise its novelty statement before publication.

The book's research directory contains machine-readable protocols for these proposals. They are design artifacts, not completed experiments. No return estimate, statistically significant effect, or successful deployment is being reported here.

docs.title: 25.2 Proposal H1: forecast the payout process, not only the headline
The question
docs.text:
Can a model that represents contractual resolution uncertainty make better-calibrated payout forecasts or more defensible abstention decisions than a model that predicts only the ordinary YES/NO event?

The motivation is concrete. A market's title is a compressed description, while its rules determine its payoff. The inspected Polymarket documentation describes disputes, additional context, and an exceptional 50/50 payout. That is evidence about a documented mechanism, not a measurement of how frequently it occurs or an assertion that every venue uses the same rule. POLYMARKET_RESOLUTION

Let \(Z\) denote an informal real-world proposition and \(R\) the actual payout per unit. A model of \(P(Z=1)\) is not automatically a model of the distribution of \(R\). The relationship depends on the contract's wording, resolution source, observation window, and permitted exceptional states.

For a contract whose allowed payout values are explicitly known, a payout model could estimate

\[ \mathbb{E}[R\mid\mathcal I] =\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}r\,P(R=r\mid\mathcal I), \]

where \(\mathcal I\) is the decision's permitted information and \(\mathcal R\) is the contractual payout set. This is simply the definition of an expectation for a discrete payout. It neither identifies the probabilities nor demonstrates that a useful model can estimate them.

docs.title: A worked thought experiment
docs.text:
Consider an invented contract with payouts of zero, one-half, or one dollar. A headline classifier assigns an ordinary YES probability of 0.60. A separate hypothetical payout assessment assigns probability 0.56 to a one-dollar payout, 0.04 to a half-dollar payout, and 0.40 to zero. These probabilities sum to one; the expected payout is USD 0.58.

At an executable ask of USD 0.57 and a hypothetical fee of USD 0.01 per unit, the headline-only calculation suggests USD 0.02 expected profit. The payout calculation suggests zero. A positive-looking opportunity has disappeared before any discussion of estimation uncertainty or capital lockup.

This arithmetic is illustrative. It is not evidence that headline models systematically overprice a real market. The alternative payout probabilities were invented to expose the target mismatch, not estimated from observations.

docs.title: What the experiment would require
docs.text:
Collect prospective rule snapshots and retain their observation timestamps. Record later clarifications without retroactively inserting them into earlier feature vectors. Preserve final payout values and their availability times. Keep unresolved cases visible, because excluding difficult unresolved markets can erase the very phenomenon being studied.

Start with a simple baseline: the ordinary event forecast plus a rule-completeness checklist. Compare it with a structured payout model and with an abstention rule based on observable ambiguity flags. Evaluate payout-distribution scores where meaningful, calibration of exceptional-state probabilities, coverage of issued forecasts, and decisions under identical executable-cost assumptions.

A model that refuses almost every difficult market may appear accurate merely by changing the population. Report performance as a function of coverage and compare to a baseline with a comparable abstention budget. Do not choose the set of excluded markets after learning their outcomes.

docs.title: Why it might fail
docs.text:
Exceptional outcomes may be too rare for reliable estimation. Labels can depend on changing institutional procedures. Ambiguity scores derived from text can simply proxy for domain or maturity. Prices may already discount uncertainty. A forecast of the payout process might improve scoring without identifying any tradable difference.

The useful null result is that the structured model does not improve a predeclared evaluation measure at comparable coverage, or that any benefit disappears after current fees and conservative execution assumptions. An even earlier stopping condition is the inability to reconstruct rule versions without future information.

The nearest literature includes price interpretation and contract-mechanism design, while the immediate evidence motivating the target is venue resolution documentation. None of these sources establishes the empirical success of this proposal. WZ2006 ABERNETHY2013

docs.title: 25.3 Proposal H2: a contract graph with uncertainty-aware consistency
The question
docs.text:
Can a graph of verified contractual relationships improve forecasts or reject false trading candidates more effectively than treating every market as an unrelated binary classifier?

A graph's nodes could represent contractual outcomes. Edges could encode verified subset, complement, exclusivity, or partition relationships. The word verified is doing important work. Text similarity can suggest an edge for review; it cannot prove the relationship. A shared event container does not by itself make all included markets mutually exclusive. POLYMARKET_MARKETS

For compatible events with \(A\subseteq B\), probability coherence requires \(P(A)\leq P(B)\). If two independently fitted models produce 0.65 and 0.55, respectively, their estimates violate that relationship. An elementary correction is to project them onto the feasible set.

For equal squared-error weights, the closest pair satisfying the constraint is 0.60 and 0.60. To see why, a solution retaining the violation cannot be feasible; at the closest boundary the estimates coincide, and their common value minimizes the sum of squared distances at their average. Different uncertainty weights change that correction.

For this exact equal-weight squared-error projection, there is a useful guarantee: if the true outcome vector satisfies the constraint, projecting onto the closed convex feasible set cannot increase the sum of squared errors to that vector. In the two-contract example, admissible binary vectors are \((0,0)\), \((0,1)\), and \((1,1)\); projecting \((0.65,0.55)\) to \((0.60,0.60)\) lowers summed squared error in each case. More generally, if \(z\) is the Euclidean projection of forecast vector \(x\) and \(y\) is feasible, the projection inequality \((x-z)\cdot(y-z)\leq0\), together with expanding squared distances, gives \(\|z-y\|^2\leq\|x-y\|^2\). Here \(\|v\|^2\) means the sum of squared components of \(v\).

The guarantee is narrow. Incorrect graph edges can make the realized vector infeasible; uncertainty-weighted projection protects the corresponding weighted squared loss, not necessarily the unweighted reported score; and other metrics or individual-contract scores need not improve. It also does not guarantee calibration, strict improvement over an already coherent baseline, or profit. Forecast-distribution aggregation has an established literature on coherence, calibration, and dispersion; this elementary projection argument is independently derived, not attributed to an unread theorem. GNEITING2013

docs.title: Forecast consistency and executable consistency are different experiments
docs.text:
One study could test projection of model forecasts. A separate study could test whether compatible market quotes admit a cost-covered basket. Do not use success in the first study as proof of the second.

In the simplest invented complementary pair, both sides can be bought for USD 0.49 each. The gross purchase cost is USD 0.98 for a combined terminal payout of USD 1, under the stated compatibility assumption. If each leg costs an additional USD 0.015, total cost is USD 1.01. The apparent USD 0.02 discrepancy is not a positive net opportunity.

For a larger basket, write down a payout matrix over the complete relevant outcome space. Each column is a contract; each row is a possible settlement scenario. The strategy must survive every included scenario, and the scenario set itself must be justified. An optimizer cannot protect against a legitimate outcome that the researcher omitted from the matrix.

Convex market design supplies important conceptual tools for bounded-payoff securities, but designing a mechanism is not the same as executing a basket across independent order books. Capital requirements, partial fills, settlement differences, and leg risk remain. ABERNETHY2013

docs.title: A falsifiable protocol
docs.text:
Freeze a manually audited relationship set before evaluation. Keep a record of rejected or ambiguous edges. Compare unprojected forecasts, a simple equal-weight projection, and a prespecified uncertainty-weighted projection using identical event-grouped chronological splits.

For an executable-candidate study, compare a headline-similarity scanner with a rule-audited scanner. Measure false candidates and audit cost as well as any modeled basket margin. Keep the candidate's book timestamp, depth, fee assumptions, and compatible payout proof.

An attractive contribution may be fewer false opportunities, not higher profit. If the graph mostly discovers relationships that already hold within spreads, that can still be a useful negative finding about how efficient the observed prices are at that resolution.

Abandon a trading interpretation when the required edge cannot be verified, simultaneous quantities cannot be supported, or the complete payout space is uncertain. Abandon the forecasting improvement claim if the effect depends on selecting graph weights after inspecting the evaluation period.

docs.title: 25.4 Proposal H3: calibrate on fills, not on all posted quotes
The question
docs.text:
Can a quote-conditional probability model improve the assessment of adverse selection compared with applying an unconditional event forecast to every potential maker fill?

The first-principles issue is selection. A quote is not filled by drawing a random event observation from the forecaster's dataset. Someone chooses to trade against it, and that choice can convey information.

For a single-unit bid, let \(F\) be the event that it fills, \(d\) the quote decision, and \(\mathcal I\) the information available when it is posted. Under a simplified hold-to-settlement model with a fee charged only on a fill,

\[ \mathbb E[\Pi\mid d,\mathcal I] =P(F\mid d,\mathcal I) \left(\mathbb E[R\mid F,d,\mathcal I]-b-f\right). \]

The identity follows by splitting expected profit into the filled and unfilled cases, assigning zero transaction profit to the unfilled case. It omits the opportunity cost of reserved capital and any other costs of maintaining the quote. Those must be added separately when relevant.

For varying fill quantities, this simple factorization is insufficient unless the dependence between filled quantity and payout is handled. Replacing both with their unconditional averages can introduce another optimistic approximation.

docs.title: A worked thought experiment
docs.text:
Suppose an event model assigns YES probability 0.58. A maker posts a bid at USD 0.50 with no transaction fee in this invented example. It is tempting to assign USD 0.08 expected profit to every unit that fills.

Now suppose the actual subset of fills has a YES frequency of 0.43 in the relevant population. Conditional expected profit per filled unit is minus USD 0.07. The forecaster's unconditional estimate could have been reasonable across all posted opportunities while being unsuitable for the fill-selected population.

The values are invented, but the selection calculation is exact under the hypothetical population. The challenge is estimating the conditional population without using information that arrives after the quote decision or treating a simulator's assumptions as observations.

docs.title: The hardest part is the dataset
docs.text:
A useful dataset needs decisions, quote states, actual or defensibly reconstructed fills, subsequent outcomes, and the behavior policy that generated the decisions. A passive sequence of public prices is not automatically a log of the fills that alternative quotes would have received.

Policy-evaluation research explicitly studies the difference between logged actions and target actions. Doubly robust methods combine models of rewards and historical action selection, but their existence does not give unsupported actions observable outcomes. DUDIK2011

If the only fills come from an invented replay mechanism, the study can examine that mechanism but cannot estimate a live venue's adverse selection. If genuine authorized logs exist, they may still cover only one narrow quoting policy. A substantially different quote distance or cancellation rule can lie outside the data's useful action support.

The default book companion does not collect funded-order experience. This proposal therefore remains a design for future authorized data or a clearly labeled simulator investigation. It is not a reason to weaken the paper-only boundary.

docs.title: Baselines, falsification, and restraint
docs.text:
Compare an unconditional forecast, a simple stratification by quote distance and event horizon, and a prespecified conditional model. Evaluate fill prediction and payout prediction separately, then inspect their combined decision implication. Use future event groups, not randomly split fills from the same event.

Do not tune a maker's price and then report performance on the same fills used to choose it. Report whether calibration improvements survive changes in behavior policy and whether intervals widen appropriately in poorly supported regions.

The hypothesis fails as a useful improvement when a simple stratified model is just as good, the conditional model merely memorizes event identities, or any apparent advantage vanishes under plausible fill uncertainty. A finding that the available logs cannot identify the proposed policy's value is a substantive result.

Offline reinforcement-learning research provides another warning: extrapolating beyond a fixed dataset's action distribution can produce unreliable estimates. That literature motivates caution, not a guarantee that a particular restriction makes a trading policy safe. FUJIMOTO2019

docs.title: 25.5 Proposal H4: value information under changing prices and locked capital
The question
docs.text:
When should a researcher spend time or money on an additional information source rather than place a paper order now or abstain?

The naive answer is "whenever it improves the forecast." The decision-theoretic answer depends on whether the improvement can change a feasible action before the market and the opportunity change.

For a one-unit binary purchase at a fixed ask and cost, the modeled value of the best available action is the larger of zero and the expected net value of buying. Suppose a signal changes the forecast, and suppose, only for this first classroom calculation, that the quote remains executable after observing it. The value of the signal before its acquisition cost is the expected best post-signal action value minus the best pre-signal action value.

docs.title: A transparent calculation
docs.text:
The initial forecast is 0.55. The ask is USD 0.56 and the hypothetical fee is USD 0.01, so buying has modeled value minus USD 0.02 and abstaining has value zero.

An invented signal has two equally likely results, leading to posterior probabilities 0.70 and 0.40. Their average is 0.55, consistent with the prior in this simplified construction. The favorable signal permits modeled value USD 0.13; the unfavorable signal still leads to abstention. The expected post-signal decision value is therefore USD 0.065.

If observing the signal costs USD 0.02 for this single-unit decision, the net hypothetical information value is USD 0.045. This is not the difference in classification accuracy. It is the value of a changed action under a fixed executable quote and the stated signal distribution.

Now remove the fixed-quote assumption. If the favorable signal moves the executable ask to USD 0.69 before the researcher can act, the favorable branch's value after the USD 0.01 fee is zero. The apparent information advantage disappears. Better information and a profitable trading opportunity have separated.

docs.title: What makes the prediction-market version interesting
docs.text:
Markets differ in announcement schedules, liquidity, time until outcome observation, and delay until collateral release. A useful research model could estimate the joint distribution of information arrival, quote response, and capital availability, rather than optimizing forecast score in isolation.

Capital lockup introduces a resource-allocation problem. Two trades with the same modeled total expected profit can have different opportunity costs when one ties up scarce cash for much longer. But dividing profit by an optimistic duration is not a complete solution: outcome risk, uncertain release times, and correlated opportunities remain.

An experiment should start with observable operational quantities. Measure when the source actually publishes, when the collector receives it, and which quotes remain available under a stated latency policy. Keep source acquisition costs in the same units as the decision value. A fixed subscription cost cannot be subtracted as though it were a per-unit fee without defining how it is allocated.

docs.title: What would count as evidence
docs.text:
Predeclare the information source and compare a no-additional-source baseline with a delayed-information policy under identical cost and capacity rules. Separate forecast-score gain, decision changes, and feasibility after the observed quote response. Report how conclusions change when the execution delay is longer than hoped.

The hypothesis fails economically if the signal's incremental decision value is absorbed by acquisition expense, quote movement, or capital cost. It fails scientifically if the researcher uses a retrospective source timestamp that did not correspond to actual availability.

This proposal is an original experimental combination, not a claim to have invented the value of information. The illustrative decision-value calculation is derived directly from the specified action payoffs. Existing price-interpretation research also cautions against assuming that a useful signal is absent from prices merely because one particular forecaster has not used it. WZ2006

docs.title: 25.6 Proposal H5: hierarchical transfer with permission to abstain
The question
docs.text:
Can related event families improve a sparse target family's probability estimates without producing unjustified confidence when the target changes?

Prediction-market datasets often contain an awkward combination: many price snapshots and few genuinely new outcome labels. A model can appear data-rich while learning from a small number of events. Pooling across related families could reduce variance, but it also risks transferring the wrong base rate or mechanism.

A minimal classroom model illustrates the tradeoff. With a beta prior having parameters \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), and \(k\) successes in \(n\) conditionally Bernoulli observations from one homogeneous family, the posterior predictive probability is

\[ \frac{k+\alpha}{n+\alpha+\beta}. \]

This follows by multiplying the prior density by the Bernoulli likelihood and recognizing the updated beta density. It does not establish that real event families are homogeneous, exchangeable, or independent. Those are the assumptions the example exposes.

If a family has two successes in three events, the unsmoothed estimate is about 0.667. A beta prior with both parameters equal to two gives a posterior predictive probability of about 0.571. The estimate is less extreme because the prior contributes information. Whether that is an improvement depends on the relevance of the prior, not on shrinkage being inherently virtuous.

docs.title: From pooling to selective transfer
docs.text:
A practical research proposal could fit a hierarchical model across prespecified related families, compare it with fully pooled and unpooled baselines, and abstain when observable target conditions fall outside a declared support region. The abstention mechanism must be defined using information available before the outcome.

Forecast-combination research supplies related ideas about combining predictive distributions. Domain-adversarial learning supplies another transfer-learning direction, but its studied image and sentiment tasks do not prove that features can safely transfer across changing event contracts. YAO2018 GANIN2016

Do not treat shared vocabulary as proof of a shared data-generating process. A "monthly increase" question about a government release can differ fundamentally from one about a financial price. Even within one release series, a rule change or measurement revision can change the target.

docs.title: A study that could reject the idea
docs.text:
Choose families before inspecting comparative results. Use chronological evaluation and a separate held-out-family analysis if the intended claim includes transfer to new families. Keep every shared-event outcome out of conflicting splits. Report both probability scores and the coverage at which the model is willing to forecast or trade.

Compare selective transfer to a simpler baseline allowed the same coverage budget. Otherwise the complicated model might win only because it declines more cases. Examine whether apparent improvements come from easy families dominating the average.

The proposal fails if gains vanish on new families, if uncertainty remains narrow during known rule changes, or if a simple reference-rate model performs comparably. It also fails as a live-decision claim when improved scores do not survive executable costs.

docs.title: 25.7 A common protocol and a publication standard
docs.text:
Across all five proposals, use the same sequence: state the mechanism, identify the estimand, define the admissible information, identify a baseline, freeze the sample and decision rules, specify uncertainty under a defensible dependence model, and name the result that would reject the hypothesis.

Maintain a trial log that includes discarded graph definitions, ambiguity scores, quote distances, transfer families, and evaluation windows. Strategy selection is broader than the last model fit. Backtest-overfitting research is relevant to this discipline, but it does not make a particular split or test universally valid for sparse dependent events. BAILEY2017

Three separate conclusions may emerge from the same project. First, a measurement system may work: it correctly records rule versions or quote timing. Second, a forecast model may improve an out-of-sample score. Third, a trading decision may have credible positive expected value after costs. Each conclusion needs its own evidence. Do not jump from the first to the third because the engineering was difficult.

A responsible report includes limitations that could change the interpretation, not just implementation inconveniences. Missing historic rules, unsupported actions, uncertain fees, and revised source data are not cosmetic gaps. They can remove the very quantity the study was supposed to estimate.

If the result is inconclusive, publish the protocol and the limitation honestly where data permissions allow. The practical contribution may be demonstrating why a popular apparent edge cannot currently be measured. That is more useful than a confident strategy whose evidence depends on an invented fill or a hidden future label.

docs.title: Exercise 1: a payout rather than a headline
docs.text:
A model assigns probabilities 0.50, 0.10, and 0.40 to payouts of USD 1, USD 0.50, and zero. The ask is USD 0.53 and the fee is USD 0.02 per unit. Compute expected payout and modeled net value. State what remains unknown before making a trading claim.

Solution sketch. Expected payout is USD 0.55, so modeled net value is zero. The probability estimates, actual size and freshness of the ask, fee applicability, exceptional payout rules, and capital constraints remain relevant. The calculation supplies no positive modeled margin even before uncertainty.

docs.title: Exercise 2: consistency without profit
docs.text:
Compatible complementary contracts have asks of USD 0.48 and USD 0.50, with USD 0.015 cost per leg. Does buying one of each produce a positive guaranteed net payout under the simplified settlement assumption?

Solution sketch. Total cost is USD 1.01 and total payout is USD 1, so the net outcome is minus USD 0.01. The gross price sum below one was insufficient. In a real setting, compatibility and executable quantity would still require verification.

docs.title: Exercise 3: conditioning on a fill
docs.text:
A one-unit bid at USD 0.45 fills with probability 0.20. Conditional on a fill, expected payout is USD 0.42. A USD 0.01 fee applies only when filled. Compute modeled transaction profit per submitted order, ignoring reservation cost.

Solution sketch. Profit conditional on a fill is minus USD 0.04. Multiplying by 0.20 gives minus USD 0.008 per submitted order. An unconditional event forecast is not part of this calculation unless it correctly determines the conditional payout distribution.

docs.title: Exercise 4: a transfer model's impressive score
docs.text:
A hierarchical model has a better average Brier score than a baseline but declines to forecast 80 percent of events. The baseline predicts all events. What comparison is needed before concluding that selective transfer improved the decision system?

Solution sketch. Compare scores on the same event population and compare coverage-performance curves with a baseline permitted a comparable abstention policy. Check chronological and family holdouts, availability cutoffs, and whether exclusions were chosen before observing outcomes. A lower score on a different, easier population is not by itself evidence of superior transfer.

docs.title: Exercise 5: naming the contribution
docs.text:
A project combines a language model to propose contract relationships with a deterministic rule audit and a convex projection. No related-work search beyond this chapter has been performed. What novelty statement is justified?

Solution sketch. Describe the implementation and proposed experimental combination. Do not claim a new algorithm, the first contract graph, or a discovered market inefficiency. Conduct and record a broader primary-literature search, distinguish known components, and evaluate the actual contribution against simple baselines.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: The first practical guide begins with a deliberately simple pattern investigation. It is a useful antidote to research excitement: before building a complex system, establish what a small, reproducible experiment can and cannot tell you.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: You should already be comfortable with the exploration discipline of Chapter 9, the proper-scoring-rule and calibration material of Chapter 10, and the evidence-after-search reasoning of Chapter 19. Chapter 25's falsifiable-hypothesis discipline is the direct predecessor to this one. You should know what a dependence group is, why a chronological split is not automatically an independence guarantee, and why the single-YES Brier convention in the notation registry is the one this book always reports.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this chapter you should be able to run the pattern quickstart from a clean checkout, read its JSON output correctly, and explain in your own words why two fixed probability bins inspected once are a different kind of evidence than the same two numbers found after trying many bins. You should be able to distinguish a post-hoc diagnostic from a predeclared confirmatory comparison, explain why this script's evidence_gate always rejects a live-edge inference regardless of how attractive its numbers look, and optionally run the book's one real-data forecasting exercise well enough to state exactly what it does and does not show.

docs.title: 26.1 A concrete goal and a clean setup
docs.text:
The goal of this chapter is narrow and deliberately unglamorous: run one already-written script, read its output line by line, and understand exactly what kind of evidence it does and does not supply.
