That habit, applied consistently, is worth more than any individual technique in the preceding chapters. From the companion project root (book\companion), with a fresh shell:

Command working directory: run this chapter's Python commands from book\companion. From the trading repository root, run Set-Location book\companion once first. The .venv belongs to that companion project; see companion setup.

python -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -r requirements.lock
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -e . --no-deps

The first command creates a virtual environment. The second installs version-pinned runtime dependencies, not hash-locked wheels; requirements.lock is a version lock, and platform wheels, numerical-library builds, and the build backend are not frozen by it. The third installs prediction_market_lab in editable mode without resolving its runtime dependencies again. Installation may download packages, but requires no trading account, API key, GPU, or paid model. After installation all default examples run offline. The documented environment supports numerical reproduction; bit-for-bit portability across every platform is not promised.

Now run the script this chapter is about:

.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe examples\quickstart_pattern.py

docs.title: 26.2 Reading the actual output
docs.text:
The script prints one JSON object. This excerpt selects central fields from the observed Python 3.12.6 run; additional labels, reasons, and boundary fields remain in the full output:

{
  "data": "SYNTHETIC / ILLUSTRATIVE",
  "result": {
    "groups": {
      "market_below_half": {
        "events": 30,
        "observed_yes_rate": 0.333333,
        "market_brier": 0.223735,
        "training_reference_brier": 0.274418
      },
      "market_at_least_half": {
        "events": 15,
        "observed_yes_rate": 0.933333,
        "market_brier": 0.174846,
        "training_reference_brier": 0.200261
      }
    },
    "no_trade_baseline_profit": "0.00",
    "evidence_gate": {"status": "REJECT_LIVE_EDGE_INFERENCE", "eligible_for_research_review": false}
  }
}

Read the numbers in order rather than jumping straight to the Brier scores. There are 45 held-out test events in total, split by whether the synthetic market's own quoted probability was below one-half (30 events) or at least one-half (15 events). Within each bin, observed_yes_rate is simply the fraction of those events whose eventual binary label was YES: 0.333333 in the low bin, 0.933333 in the high bin. market_brier scores the synthetic market's own quoted probability against that realized label using the single-YES convention from the notation registry; training_reference_brier scores a single constant reference rate, estimated only from the training cohort, against the same realized labels. In this toy run, the market's own quoted number scores better than the flat training-derived reference in both bins, which is unsurprising: the invented market probability in this fixture was constructed, by the generator in prediction_market_lab.data.generate_recurring, to correlate with the same latent signal that drives the outcome. That correlation is a property of the synthetic fixture, not a discovery about any real venue.

no_trade_baseline_profit is the constant string "0.00". This script places no order of any kind; the field exists only to make explicit, at every stage, that reading these numbers is not the same activity as trading on them. evidence_gate reports REJECT_LIVE_EDGE_INFERENCE with eligible_for_research_review set to false. This is not a bug to route around. It is the correct answer for any all-synthetic input, and Section 26.4 explains exactly why the gate is built that way.

docs.title: 26.3 What the reader does next: reading the code, not just the output
docs.text:
Open examples/quickstart_pattern.py alongside the printed output. The script calls teaching_split(recurring()) from _support.py, which loads the fixed fixture at data/fixtures/recurring_events.csv through prediction_market_lab.data.load_recurring and then applies grouped_chronological_split with three predetermined cutoffs baked into teaching_split. It then takes latest_per_event of the resulting test cohort, which keeps exactly one decision-time snapshot per event, chosen by its latest decision_at timestamp, so that the two snapshots a single recurring event contributes are never both counted as if they were independent test rows.

The script fixes two bins, market_probability >= 0.5 or not, and performs no threshold search during execution. That makes the run reproducible, but fixed source code alone does not prove a choice preceded all author inspection. Trying many cutoffs and reporting only the most striking one would add selection bias. Treat this repeatedly inspected synthetic fixture as a demonstration of how to specify a comparison, not as untouched confirmatory evidence.

The script deliberately reports no p-value or confidence interval. Its 45 rows are one latest snapshot from each of 45 separately generated events; sharing a generator family does not itself make distinct events dependent. The two original snapshots within each event do share a latent value and label. One could analyze simulation uncertainty under that stated generator, but it would still be uncertainty about an invented process, not evidence of market performance. This quickstart reports descriptive scores rather than claiming either a real-market interval or more independent outcomes than were generated.

docs.title: 26.4 Distinguishing post-hoc diagnostics from predeclared confirmatory discovery
docs.text:
A post-hoc diagnostic inspects data after the fact to generate candidate explanations: "the market's quoted probability seems informative when it is extreme," or "recorded rates in this bin look higher than I expected." This is a legitimate and useful step in exploratory work; Chapter 9 dedicates an entire chapter to doing it honestly. But a diagnostic observation earns no claim of confirmed discovery by itself. It has not been checked against data that could not have influenced its own formulation, and it has not accounted for how many other candidate patterns were silently considered and discarded before this one was noticed.

A predeclared confirmatory comparison fixes its cohort, bins, metric, and procedure before relevant inspection can shape those choices, then reports the result whether favorable or not. This quickstart demonstrates that procedural shape, but its authors constructed and repeatedly inspected the fixture. It is not a confirmatory discovery, even if the current code has only one threshold. Confirmatory status depends on the actual research history, not merely on a constant appearing in a script.

The practical failure mode to watch for in your own later work is silent bin curation: running the analysis once, not liking the result, adjusting a cutoff, a fixture parameter, or an inclusion rule, and running it again, without recording that the first attempt happened. Each such adjustment, even an apparently reasonable one like excluding an inconvenient outlier month, is a trial. A trial log, as Chapter 19 describes, is the only defense against later mistaking a best-of-several result for a first and only look.

Three qualified statistical tools bear directly on how this discipline scales past a single fixed comparison, and it is worth naming what each one does and does not repair, rather than treating "predeclare it" as a slogan that makes every subsequent statistic automatically trustworthy. White's reality check addresses whether the single best rule out of an entire searched family could plausibly have arisen by chance given the whole family considered, under a specific bootstrap construction whose stationary-data assumptions require checking against your own data before relying on it. WHITE2000 The Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate procedure addresses a related but distinct question, controlling the expected proportion of false rejections across many simultaneously tested hypotheses, and it still requires a well-defined test family and valid input significance values to mean what it claims. BENJAMINI1995 Bailey, Borwein, Lopez de Prado, and Zhu's backtest-overfitting framework targets a third question again, the probability that a reported strategy selection reflects overfitting from repeated holdout inspection during the research process itself, rather than genuine out-of-sample skill. BAILEY2017 None of these three tools, individually or together, cures an event-group leak, an unavailable label used as if it were available, or a cost assumption that turns out to be wrong; they qualify a search process's own statistics, not the underlying data discipline this book spends its first eight chapters establishing.

docs.title: 26.5 An optional real-data exercise: the frozen NOAA study
docs.text:
Everything in Sections 26.1 through 26.4 uses an invented fixture. This section describes an optional exercise using genuinely real observational data, so you can see the difference in evidentiary weight directly, not just read about it. The research feasibility assessment and the experiments README explain the full protocol; this section summarizes what running it teaches.

.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe experiments\noaa_study.py

Do not pass --refresh-data or --replace-results. The plain command makes no network request and writes no files; it recomputes the study from the committed extract and verifies the frozen input and output bytes. The protocol was locally predeclared before acquisition or scoring; the results were frozen after that evaluation, not before their values existed. The following primary-result excerpt omits the subsequent paired-difference and sensitivity lines:

VERIFIED OFFLINE (no files changed)
FINAL-VINTAGE retrospective teaching study; NOT a trading backtest.
primary: n=132, YES=85
  overall: Brier=0.230313524, log loss=0.653345440
  seasonal: Brier=0.032459388, log loss=0.130672065

The 132 events are calendar target months from January 2015 through December 2025, each scoring whether that month's recorded Mauna Loa CO2 mean exceeded the immediately preceding month's mean, under the predeclared clock and Beta(1,1) models fixed in protocol.json. The overall model's Brier score of 0.230313524 reflects an expanding constant-rate forecast; the target-month seasonal model's 0.032459388 reflects a strong, well-known annual cycle in atmospheric CO2 concentration. This gap did not require any strategy search: the protocol, the training scheme, and the two candidate models were all fixed, in writing, before either score was computed, and the experiments README records the exact predeclaration and freeze timestamps. The same README also reports a predeclared 123-event sensitivity cohort, conservatively excluding the alternate-location Maunakea measurement period, which shows the same pattern (overall Brier 0.230757404, seasonal 0.034708546), together with a reproducible, no-plotting-dependency calibration figure; neither addition changes what this study can or cannot establish.

Read this result for exactly what it is and nothing more. NOAA_CO2, NOAA_DATA, and NOAA_POLICY establish that these are real, attributed, public-domain government observations, not synthetic fixtures. NOAA_CO2 NOAA_DATA NOAA_POLICY They are also current-vintage data: the source file can be revised, and this study's clock is a hypothetical retrospective admission rule, not a verified historical publication timestamp. There are no prediction-market contracts, prices, fees, order books, or fills anywhere in this study. A forecast-scoring improvement on a recorded rise in atmospheric carbon dioxide is not evidence about pricing efficiency in any prediction market, and this book does not claim otherwise.

docs.title: 26.6 Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If creating .venv fails, check the supported Python 3.12 interpreter and directory permissions; do not delete an environment containing unrelated work. The runtime lock pins versions but contains no artifact hashes, so it is not itself a wheel-integrity check. Installation failures should be diagnosed from their actual messages, not bypassed by silently changing dependency versions. For ModuleNotFoundError, confirm the editable install and invoke .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe rather than an unrelated interpreter on PATH. If numerical output differs, record Python/package versions and platform details; do not change fixtures, seeds, or rounding merely to obtain the quoted result.

If experiments\noaa_study.py reports a hash-verification failure instead of VERIFIED OFFLINE, do not "fix" it yourself by rewriting the flagged file's line endings, re-saving it in an editor, or passing --refresh-data/--replace-data/--freeze-results/--replace-results to make the check pass; the frozen hashes are bound to the exact original bytes of the data, protocol, source, and results files, and any of those actions can silently produce a different, unreviewed frozen artifact rather than reproducing the one this chapter quotes. A hash mismatch on an otherwise unmodified checkout is a checkout-integrity or repository-configuration question, not a data or environment problem for a reader to work around; report it and keep the checkout as received rather than normalizing, replacing, or re-encoding anything to make the numbers agree.

docs.title: Exercise 1: recomputing a bin's Brier score by hand
docs.text:
Suppose a fixed bin contains three held-out events with market-quoted probabilities 0.60, 0.70, and 0.55, and realized labels YES, YES, NO. Compute the single-YES Brier score by hand.

Solution sketch. Squared errors are \((0.60-1)^2=0.16\), \((0.70-1)^2=0.09\), and \((0.55-0)^2=0.3025\). The mean is \((0.16+0.09+0.3025)/3 = 0.184166\overline{6}\). Note that this toy bin has only three events; a bin this small would ordinarily be too sparse to support any confident interpretation on its own, which is one reason this chapter's fixture uses bins of 30 and 15 events instead.

docs.title: Exercise 2: why a third bin is not free to add later
docs.text:
Suppose after seeing the two-bin result above, you notice the fixture also records a horizon_hours field and consider adding a third split by horizon to see if it produces an even larger score gap. Explain what is wrong with adding this comparison now, and what would make it acceptable.

Solution sketch. It is acceptable as a clearly labeled additional exploratory comparison, recorded in the trial log. It is not an untouched confirmation of a new horizon hypothesis on the same inspected data. Freeze the new hypothesis before examining a fresh evaluation cohort and report that comparison regardless of outcome. The current latest-per-event cohort also contains only the three-hour snapshot, so a genuine horizon comparison requires an explicitly redesigned, grouped multi-horizon evaluation rather than merely relabeling these rows.

docs.title: Exercise 3: distinguishing the market's Brier from the training reference
docs.text:
Explain, in one or two sentences, why market_brier and training_reference_brier answer different questions, and why a favorable gap between them is still not permission to trade on the difference.

Solution sketch. market_brier asks how well a specific quoted number tracked the eventual realized label; training_reference_brier asks how well a single constant rate, learned only from earlier training data, would have done instead. A gap between them says the market's quote carried information beyond the base rate in this particular fixture, but it says nothing about executable prices, costs, fill probability, or whether that information is already reflected in what a real trader could actually pay to acquire the same position, so it cannot license a trading decision.

docs.title: Exercise 4: interpreting the NOAA result correctly
docs.text:
A colleague reads the NOAA study's frozen Brier scores and concludes "seasonal patterns beat the market in prediction markets about climate contracts." Identify every part of that sentence that is not supported by the study, and restate a version that is.

Solution sketch. The study contains no prediction-market contracts, prices, or trades of any kind, so "beat the market" is unsupported; it compares two forecasting models against each other, not against any executable quote. It is also not specific to "climate contracts," a category the study never constructs. A supported restatement: "a target-calendar-month seasonal rate produced a substantially lower Brier score than an expanding overall rate when forecasting month-over-month recorded CO2 increases across 132 evaluation months, using real but current-vintage NOAA observations and a hypothetical two-month reporting lag."

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: Chapter 27 moves from a batch-level pattern comparison to a single timestamped event, carrying an already-fitted forecaster through the same paper-decision machinery used in Chapter 24, and shows what an honest no-trade outcome looks like when a model's own forecast does not clear the cost of acting on it.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: You should have already run the pattern quickstart in Chapter 26 and understand its evidence gate. You need the forecast-evaluation material from Chapter 10, the sequential-forecast discussion in Chapter 13, the combination methods in Chapter 16, and the paper-decision machinery from Chapters 17 and 24, particularly PaperInputs, RiskBudget, and paper_decision. Keep the notation registry's distinction between event time, publication time, observation time, and decision time close at hand; this chapter depends on all four staying separate.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this chapter you should be able to run a single recurring event through an already-fitted forecaster, correctly distinguish the event's own historical timestamps from a newly invented quote time attached only for this chapter's arithmetic, explain why both example order books in this quickstart produce NO_TRADE, and state exactly why that is the correct, honest outcome rather than a demonstration failure. You should also be able to explain how this quickstart's synthetic books differ from the real, current-vintage NOAA study introduced in Chapter 26, and why neither one supplies price, fee, or queue evidence for any real venue.

docs.title: 27.1 A concrete goal: one event, one forecast, two quotes
docs.text:
This chapter's script picks a single held-out event, generates a forecast for it using an already-fitted model, and then checks that forecast against two different hypothetical order books to see whether either would clear a simple cost-and-budget screen. From the companion project root (book\companion), after the setup described in Chapter 26:

Command working directory: run this chapter's Python commands from book\companion. From the trading repository root, run Set-Location book\companion once first. The .venv belongs to that companion project; see companion setup.

.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe examples\quickstart_event.py

Open examples/quickstart_event.py while you read this chapter. It calls fit_forecaster(split) on the same teaching_split used in Chapter 26, then selects latest_per_event(split.test)[0], the chronologically first held-out event by decision time. On this checkout that event is toy-0135.

docs.title: 27.2 Reading the actual output
docs.text:
The observed run includes the following excerpt (some wrapper and explanatory fields are omitted):

{
  "result": {
    "source_event": "toy-0135",
    "feature_publication": "2025-05-16T14:50:00+00:00",
    "feature_observation": "2025-05-16T14:58:00+00:00",
    "historical_decision": "2025-05-16T15:00:00+00:00",
    "forecast": 0.200542,
    "new_synthetic_quote_time": "2025-07-01T12:00:00+00:00",
    "illustrative_screen": {
      "status": "NO_TRADE", "quantity": 0,
      "executable_cost": "4.10", "modeled_expected_profit": "-2.094580",
      "reason": "modeled edge does not exceed the stated cost buffer"
    },
    "costly_no_trade": {
      "status": "NO_TRADE", "quantity": 0,
      "executable_cost": "9.60", "modeled_expected_profit": "-7.594580",
      "reason": "modeled edge does not exceed the stated cost buffer"
    },
    "evidence_gate": {"status": "REJECT_LIVE_EDGE_INFERENCE"}
  }
}

Four timestamps appear, and they mean different things. feature_publication at 14:50 UTC is when the invented upstream bulletin for this event was notionally released. feature_observation at 14:58 UTC is when the model's inputs became available to a decision process. historical_decision at 15:00 UTC is the timestamp the fixture generator originally attached to this event's decision point, back when toy-0135 was constructed. new_synthetic_quote_time, 2025-07-01T12:00:00Z, is a wholly different and much later timestamp: it is NOW from _support.py, attached only so this chapter's illustrative PaperBroker and order books have a valid, internally consistent clock to validate against. Do not read new_synthetic_quote_time as if it were a later observation of the same real historical order flow; it is a new invented moment purely for the arithmetic demonstration, more than a month after the event's own historical decision time.

forecast is 0.200542, the fixed_equal_ensemble prediction from FittedForecaster.predict, an equal blend of a logistic model and a validation-calibrated boosted model, rounded to six decimal places only for this printed display. The rounding note in the output is important: "six decimals for this printed arithmetic; scoring uses unrounded model probabilities". Any evaluation elsewhere in the companion uses the full-precision value; the six-decimal figure shown here exists only so the arithmetic below is checkable by hand.

docs.title: 27.3 Walking through the arithmetic behind both no-trade decisions
docs.text:
The script builds two invented order books using _support.book(): a "cheap" book with ask 0.40, and a "costly" book, labeled expensive, with bid 0.90 and ask 0.95. Both are passed through PaperInputs and screened by paper_decision, which in turn calls screen_buy_yes from prediction_market_lab.risk. Before doing so, paper_decision first asks the broker for its own remaining_book view of whichever quote it was handed, not the raw snapshot as supplied: any depth this same broker has already consumed against that identical snapshot in an earlier fill is subtracted out first, so a level a prior order already swept cannot silently reappear and be sized against a second time. Both books in this script are freshly constructed and have never had any depth consumed against them by this broker, so the remaining view here is identical to the quote as constructed, and the arithmetic below is unaffected; this consumed-liquidity accounting matters more once a broker has already taken from the very same book snapshot it is being screened against.

For the cheap book, buying 10 YES units at an ask of 0.40 with the fixture's flat USD 0.01 per-unit fee costs \(10 \times (0.40 + 0.01) = 4.10\), exactly the canonical executable_cost shown. The model-conditional expected profit is \(10 \times 0.200542 - 4.10 = 2.00542 - 4.10 = -2.09458\), rounded to -2.094580 in the printed decimal string. Because the model assigns this event only a 20 percent chance of resolving YES, the expected value of paying 41 cents per unit including fees is sharply negative; the screen correctly reports NO_TRADE with the reason "modeled edge does not exceed the stated cost buffer".

For the costly book, the ask is 0.95, so the same ten units cost \(10 \times (0.95 + 0.01) = 9.60\), and the modeled expected profit is \(10 \times 0.200542 - 9.60 = -7.59458\). This is an even worse trade, for the obvious reason that the price is higher while the forecast has not changed. Both screens reject the trade for the identical stated reason, which is exactly what a coherent risk screen should do: a forecast well below the executable price produces NO_TRADE whether the price is moderately or severely unfavorable, and the size of the negative modeled edge, not just its sign, is preserved in the output so a reader can see how far the quote was from being attractive.

Do not treat the no-trade result as a defect. Replacing these quotes after seeing the result and presenting the replacement as the original experiment would hide selection. A separately labeled hypothetical sensitivity exercise is legitimate, as Section 27.5 shows. The original two books both cost more than the roughly 0.20 forecast supports, and that unfavorable result must remain visible.

docs.title: 27.4 Why the forecast is a blend, not a single model's raw output
docs.text:
The 0.200542 figure is fixed_equal_ensemble, not one model's raw output. Chapter 16 explains why combining probabilities is a modeling choice rather than an automatic improvement. Gneiting and Raftery's inspected scoring treatment supplies the propriety framework; its categorical quadratic convention must be reversed from reward to loss and divided by two for this book's single-YES score. GNEITING2007 Bates and Granger's inspected abstract gives an empirical point-forecast combination example, while Gneiting and Ranjan study predictive-distribution combinations. Neither establishes that this fixed equal blend is optimal, calibrated, or profitable. BATES1969 GNEITING2013

None of these three sources certifies that this particular equal-weight blend is optimal for this particular fixture, and the companion's own forecast_models.py observed results, quoted in the examples README, show a validation-calibrated boosted model alone scoring worse than an uncalibrated logistic model on this same held-out cohort, a reminder that a more elaborate combination or calibration step is not automatically an improvement. The equal-weight blend used in this script is a defensible, simple default precisely because it does not require estimating additional combination weights from the same data being evaluated; it is not a claim that this is the best possible combination for toy-0135 or for any other event.

docs.title: 27.5 What the reader does next
docs.text:
For a clearly labeled local sensitivity exercise, change the cheap book construction from book(ask="0.40") to book(bid="0.14", ask="0.15"), leaving the costly book unchanged. Changing only the ask would leave the default USD 0.38 bid above it and correctly raise ValueError("crossed book is ambiguous"). The valid hypothetical book costs \(10(0.15+0.01)=1.60\) and gives modeled expected profit \(10(0.200542)-1.60=0.40542\). With the unchanged fresh inputs, cash, and USD 5.00 budget, the screen returns PAPER_CANDIDATE_ONLY. Restore the example afterward and report the modified run as a sensitivity exercise, never as newly discovered evidence or a replacement for the original no-trade result.

The script states that its hypothetical books are not joined to the historical event and cannot form a P&L backtest. The fixture supplies two dated feature snapshots for toy-0135, including a synthetic market forecast benchmark in each; prediction consumes the selected row's features even though model parameters are frozen. Neither row supplies the later executable books constructed here. Those books exist only to exercise the decision code at an invented clock. A historical execution claim would require actual as-of quotes and depth, not a newly manufactured book attached to an old forecast.

docs.title: 27.6 Real current-vintage data versus this quickstart's synthetic books
docs.text:
It is worth being precise about a distinction that is easy to blur: this chapter's event, forecast, and order books are entirely synthetic and illustrative, generated by prediction_market_lab.data.generate_recurring and _support.py, and none of the ensuing arithmetic represents anything that happened in the real world. The NOAA study introduced in Chapter 26 and detailed in experiments/README.md and experiments/protocol.json is different in kind, though not in trading relevance: it uses genuinely real, attributed atmospheric CO2 observations, under a predeclared and frozen protocol, with a hypothetical two-month admission lag standing in for an unverified historical publication clock.

Both examples share an important limitation, and it is worth stating clearly rather than glossing over: neither supplies price, fee, or queue evidence for any real prediction-market venue. This chapter's order books are invented numbers chosen to exercise code paths; the NOAA study has no prediction-market contract, price, or fee of any kind attached to it at all, because its subject is monthly greenhouse-gas measurements, not an event-contract market. A reader who wants a current real venue quote can run the companion's optional, explicitly gated market_data snapshot collector, documented in data/README.md; it is not called by this or any other default script. Even its output is only a current public GET snapshot, not a historical order book, a fee/execution adapter, or a verified conversion into this book's classroom OrderBook. Building that fuller, validated venue pipeline remains the permission-gated, unimplemented future study described in the book's data-feasibility assessment, and neither quickstart script performs it.

docs.title: 27.7 Troubleshooting
docs.text: If the forecast differs, check fixture, model seed, Python, and dependency versions; a fixed seed is not a guarantee across every numerical-library build. paper_decision returns NO_TRADE when any supplied verification field is not the literal True; omitting a required PaperInputs constructor argument instead raises a construction error. Stale or mismatched books passed through the gate return stated no-trade reasons. Invalid book construction, such as a crossed bid/ask, can raise before the gate is called. Distinguish these stages when diagnosing a local modification.

docs.title: Exercise 1: recomputing the costly-book arithmetic
docs.text:
Using the values printed in Section 27.2, verify by hand that the costly book's modeled expected profit is -7.594580, and state what price would make this specific ten-unit trade break even given the same 0.200542 forecast and USD 0.01 fee.

Solution sketch. Cost is \(10\times(0.95+0.01)=9.60\); expected value is \(10\times0.200542-9.60=2.00542-9.60=-7.59458\), matching the printed figure. For break-even, solve \(10p - 10(a+0.01) = 0\) for the ask \(a\) given \(p=0.200542\): \(a = p - 0.01 = 0.190542\). Only an ask at or below about 0.19 would make this particular quantity's modeled expected value nonnegative before any risk-budget check.

docs.title: Exercise 2: why quantity is zero rather than a smaller positive number
docs.text:
Both screens report quantity: 0. Explain why the screen does not instead try a smaller quantity, such as one or two units, to see if a smaller trade clears the cost buffer.

Solution sketch. The sign of the modeled expected profit per unit does not depend on quantity in this flat-fee, constant-price construction: each additional unit contributes the same \(p - (a+f)\) margin, so if that per-unit margin is negative, no quantity, large or small, produces a nonnegative expected value. screen_buy_yes correctly reports the requested quantity as rejected outright rather than searching for some other quantity that might happen to look better.

docs.title: Exercise 3: separating the fitted forecast from the quote time
docs.text:
A colleague argues that because new_synthetic_quote_time is more than a month after historical_decision, the forecast must be "stale" and should be refit before use. Evaluate this argument.

Solution sketch. The forecast is a fixed function of the event's own features, computed once by an already-fitted model at prediction time; it does not depend on which later clock timestamp is used to validate an unrelated order book. The real concern is different: attaching a much later quote time to an old forecast is only valid as an illustrative accounting exercise, precisely because the quote itself has no relationship to the historical event. It would be a modeling error to imply the forecast was made using information available at the later quote time, which is why the script's limitation field flags this boundary explicitly rather than leaving it implicit.

docs.title: Exercise 4: constructing a scenario that would pass the risk budget too
docs.text:
Suppose an ask of 0.15 produces a positive modeled expected profit, as in Section 27.5's edit. Explain what additional check, beyond a positive expected value, screen_buy_yes still applies before returning PAPER_CANDIDATE_ONLY, and why that check exists separately from the cost comparison.

Solution sketch. screen_buy_yes also calls budget.permits(...), comparing the order's cost and reserve against RiskBudget.max_order_cost and max_committed_cash, together with the broker's currently available and already-committed cash. A positive modeled expected value describes an attractive bet in isolation; it says nothing about whether the trader has enough uncommitted capital, or whether taking this position would push total committed cash past an explicit risk limit. Chapter 29 shows a case where a positive modeled expected profit is still rejected for exactly this second reason.

docs.title: Exercise 5: why an equal blend is not the same claim as an optimal blend
docs.text:
A reader proposes replacing the fixed equal-weight blend with weights chosen to minimize Brier score on the same 45-event test cohort used to report results throughout this part of the book. Explain what would go wrong with reporting that reweighted blend's score as this chapter's result.

Solution sketch. Choosing combination weights by minimizing error on the very cohort being used for the headline evaluation is a form of fitting on the test set: the resulting score would no longer describe an untouched evaluation in the sense Chapter 19 requires, even though no traditional model-training step touched that data. Weight selection is itself a decision that needs its own held-out data or a predeclared fixed rule, such as the equal weighting actually used here, precisely to avoid quietly inflating the reported score through cohort-specific tuning.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: Chapter 28 moves from a single-contract forecast decision to a basket of contracts spanning a complete outcome partition, and shows both a conditional multi-leg candidate and the concrete loss that results when only one leg of that basket actually fills.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: You should be comfortable with the cross-market and no-arbitrage-constraint reasoning of Chapter 20, the rules-and-settlement discussion of Chapter 6, and the paper-broker accounting from Chapter 24. You need to know what sweep_cost, FeeSchedule, and executable depth mean from Chapter 5's market-microstructure material, and you should already understand why a paper fill is not a live fill.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this chapter you should be able to run the consistency-scanning quickstart, explain exactly what manual verification step makes a basket a candidate rather than an automatic trade, distinguish a depth failure from a compatibility failure, and compute by hand the loss that results when only one leg of a multi-leg basket fills before the position is settled against you. You should also be able to state precisely why this scan cannot be, and is not, driven by matching contract titles or natural-language similarity.

docs.title: 28.1 A concrete goal: scanning one exhaustive, mutually exclusive partition
docs.text:
The idea behind this quickstart is old and simple: if a set of contracts covers every possible outcome of one event, exactly once each, then buying one YES unit in every contract in the set guarantees exactly one of them pays out, so the position's minimum possible payout is fixed and known in advance. If the total cost of buying all legs is less than that guaranteed minimum payout, the position has a positive payoff floor before any model or forecast is involved at all. This is a classical no-arbitrage-style construction, not a forecasting technique, and its entire value depends on the partition genuinely being complete, mutually exclusive, and governed by one resolution process.

Run the script from the companion project root (book\companion):

Command working directory: run this chapter's Python commands from book\companion. From the trading repository root, run Set-Location book\companion once first. The .venv belongs to that companion project; see companion setup.

.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe examples\quickstart_consistency.py

Open examples/quickstart_consistency.py while reading. It defines three invented contracts over the states "low", "middle", and "high", each paying USD 1 exactly when its own state is realized and zero otherwise, an explicit, hand-constructed complete partition. Each leg's order book quotes bid 0.25 and ask 0.30, with only four units of executable ask depth per leg (ask_size=4).

docs.title: 28.2 Reading the actual output
docs.text:
The observed run includes the following excerpt (some wrapper and explanatory fields are omitted):

{
  "result": {
    "verified_partition_candidate": {
      "status": "PAPER_CANDIDATE_ONLY",
      "quantity_each": 4, "total_cost": "3.72", "required_cash": "3.72",
      "minimum_payout": "4.00", "minimum_net_profit": "0.28",
      "reason": "conditional on complete verified payout states and all legs filling"
    },
    "depth_failure": {
      "status": "NO_TRADE", "quantity_each": 0,
      "total_cost": null, "required_cash": null, "minimum_payout": null, "minimum_net_profit": null,
      "reason": "insufficient executable depth for the requested full size"
    },
    "only_first_leg_fills_then_loses_profit": "-1.24",
    "required_manual_checks": [
      "same event and resolution source", "complete exceptional payout state space",
      "fresh executable depth", "fees", "funded capital", "non-atomic leg failure"
    ]
  }
}

At quantity 4, each of the three legs costs \(4 \times (0.30 + 0.01) = 1.24\) to buy at the ask with the fixture's flat USD 0.01 fee, for a total cost across all three legs of \(3 \times 1.24 = 3.72\), matching total_cost. Because exactly one state resolves YES, the guaranteed minimum payout is \(4 \times \text{USD }1.00 = 4.00\) regardless of which of the three states occurs, since whichever leg wins pays exactly \(4 \times 1\) and the other two pay zero. The minimum net profit is \(4.00 - 3.72 = 0.28\), conditional on every leg actually filling at the quoted price and the partition genuinely being complete. scan_basket reports this as PAPER_CANDIDATE_ONLY, not as an executed trade or a certain profit; the leg_risk field attached to every BasketResult, "non-atomic legs can fail; quoted basket is not guaranteed execution", is repeated for exactly this reason.

required_cash is separate from total_cost. They equal USD 3.72 here because each leg has one cent-aligned price and a cent-aligned flat fee, so fragmented reservation rounding adds nothing. The field is the larger of modeled full-fill cost and summed reservations under the teaching broker's conservative rules, not an implementation of real venue collateral requirements. Differences can arise from deeper executable limits and per-fill rounding even when a snapshot has only one price level. Check both cost and required cash before treating the requested size as funded.

At quantity 5, the same three legs each have only 4 units of executable ask depth, so scan_basket correctly reports NO_TRADE with reason "insufficient executable depth for the requested full size", and every numeric field, including required_cash, is null rather than a fabricated partial-fill estimate. The script does not attempt to silently fill 4 of the requested 5 units and report a scaled-down profit; an unmet request is reported as a clean rejection with an explicit reason, which is the same fail-closed discipline used throughout the companion's risk and operations modules.

docs.title: 28.3 The loss when only one leg fills: only_first_leg_fills_then_loses_profit
docs.text:
The most important number in this script is -1.24, and it is worth tracing through completely, because it is the concrete answer to the question "what happens if I attempt this basket and only some of it actually executes." The script submits and fills only the "low" leg: 4 units bought at the 0.30 ask with the same USD 0.01 fee, for a cost of \(4 \times (0.30+0.01) = 1.24\), exactly matching the single-leg cost computed above. It then settles that one contract at a payout of zero, with the settlement comment "invented middle state; other legs never filled". Because only the "low" leg was ever submitted, and its state did not occur, the broker's realized profit is \(0 - 1.24 = -1.24\).

This is not a contrived worst case invented to scare the reader. It is the literal, arithmetic consequence of a basket strategy's central operational risk: the legs are separate contracts on separate order books, executed as separate orders, and nothing in the system guarantees they fill together, at the same moment, at the quoted prices, or at all. If a trader submits all three legs of this basket and only one fills, perhaps because the other two books moved, emptied, or were cancelled before the trader's orders reached them, the trader is left holding a single directional bet with none of the completing legs that made the original arithmetic attractive. The 0.28 minimum profit computed in Section 28.2 was conditional on every leg filling; a partial fill removes that conditioning entirely and can leave a straightforward loss, exactly the -1.24 shown here.

docs.title: 28.4 What makes a partition candidate, and why that check cannot be automatic
docs.text:
scan_basket accepts a compatibility_verified flag, and in this script it is passed as the literal True, supplied by the person writing the script, not computed by any code in the package. Read _compatible in prediction_market_lab.constraints: it checks that compatibility_verified is exactly True, and that all legs share the same event_id, rules_id, currency, and set of declared payout states. None of this is derived from comparing contract titles, descriptions, or any natural-language similarity between the three contracts' names. Two contracts whose short titles look related, for example two headlines both mentioning the same underlying quantity, are not thereby verified to share one resolution process, one exceptional-settlement rule, or one complete state space; that verification is a human responsibility, informed by actually reading both contracts' rules, not a property any string-matching or embedding-similarity check could establish.

The required_manual_checks list printed by the script names exactly what that human responsibility covers, and each item deserves its own explanation rather than a bare repetition of the label:

  • Same event and resolution source. Two contracts can describe superficially similar questions while resolving from different official sources, different observation windows, or different underlying definitions. A partition is only exhaustive and mutually exclusive with respect to one shared resolution process; if the three legs here actually resolved from different sources, "exactly one of them pays" is no longer guaranteed.
  • Complete exceptional payout state space. This script's legs pay one dollar or zero. The inspected Polymarket resolution page documents an exceptional 50/50 payout; it does not establish a generic void or refund convention. POLYMARKET_RESOLUTION Check any tie, cancellation, refund, or other exceptional rule in the specific contracts. A genuinely possible omitted state invalidates a claimed complete payout floor, while a 0.50/0.50 pair can still retain a constant combined payout.
  • Fresh executable depth. The quoted ask and its size must reflect a currently valid, unexpired snapshot, not a stale quote from moments or minutes earlier; validate_at enforces a maximum quote age precisely because a basket built from mismatched-in-time snapshots is not describing one coherent market moment.
  • Fees. This script's flat USD 0.01 per unit is an invented teaching cost. Real fee schedules can be price- and size-dependent, as the inspected Kalshi and Polymarket documentation both describe; KALSHI_ROUNDING POLYMARKET_FEES a basket margin computed with the wrong fee model can turn an apparent profit floor into a loss floor.
  • Funded capital. scan_basket compares required_cash, the larger of the total fill cost and the summed worst-case per-leg reservation at each leg's executable limit price, against a stated capital argument, and rejects the basket outright, with reason "funded capital cannot reserve all basket orders before execution", if that larger figure would exceed it. Because reservation and fill cost can round differently per leg and per fill, required_cash is not always identical to total_cost, so a reader sizing a basket must check the reported required_cash, not just the fill-cost total, and the capital figure itself, and whether it is genuinely available and not already committed elsewhere, remains the caller's responsibility to state honestly.
  • Non-atomic leg failure. Section 28.3's -1.24 result is the concrete consequence of ignoring this check. Nothing in a typical venue guarantees that submitting three separate orders results in three simultaneous fills; a plan that only works if all legs fill together needs an explicit answer for what happens if they do not.

docs.title: 28.5 A concrete illustration of why titles are not rules
docs.text:
Suppose one rule pays YES when an index closes strictly above 100, while another pays YES at or above 100. With the same index, time, and precision, these are nested events, not complements, and they differ exactly at 100. Buying YES on the strict-above contract and NO on the at-least contract pays zero on both at that boundary. The reverse pair pays on both there. Neither basket has the ordinary exactly-one-winner property. Check the rules' inequalities and measurement precision, not just their similar titles.

The same caution applies even more strongly across two different underlying instruments that merely sound related, two different index providers measuring a similar quantity, or two contracts on the same nominal event hosted by different venues with different resolution sources and different dispute processes. scan_basket's _compatible check only inspects event_id, rules_id, currency, and the declared set of payout-state names on BasketLeg objects that a human has already constructed; it has no access to, and makes no attempt to interpret, either contract's actual title text. This is a deliberate boundary, not a missing convenience feature. A short title is a marketing-quality summary; a rules document, read in full by a person who understands where its boundary conventions and exceptional-payout provisions live, is the only thing that can establish whether "same event, complete partition" is actually true, which is exactly why compatibility_verified must be supplied by that person and cannot be inferred by matching strings or embeddings, however similar two descriptions might look at a glance.

docs.title: 28.6 Troubleshooting
docs.text: Setting compatibility_verified=False makes scan_basket return REJECTED with unset cost fields. Nonempty but different state-key sets across legs produce the same compatibility rejection in the scan; an individual BasketLeg cannot compare itself with legs it has not seen. Its constructor instead raises "an explicitly complete state space is required" for an empty mapping or empty state name. That structural check cannot establish real-world completeness. Stale or future books are caught by scan_basket and returned as NO_TRADE, not propagated as quote-age exceptions; malformed quantities or invalid leg construction can fail earlier.

docs.title: Exercise 1: recomputing the basket at a different quantity
docs.text:
Using the same three-leg fixture, compute the total cost, minimum payout, and minimum net profit at quantity 3 instead of 4, still within the 4-unit depth limit.

Solution sketch. Per-leg cost is \(3\times(0.30+0.01)=0.93\); across three legs, total cost is \(3\times0.93=2.79\). Minimum payout is \(3\times1.00=3.00\). Minimum net profit is \(3.00-2.79=0.21\), still conditional on all three legs filling and the partition remaining verified and complete.

docs.title: Exercise 2: why a two-state partition is not automatically the same as a two-outcome market
docs.text:
A market interface might display "low" and "not low" as if they were two contracts covering a full binary partition. Explain what would need to be true for this displayed pair to satisfy the same compatibility requirements as this chapter's three-state example.

Solution sketch. "Not low" would need to be an actual tradable contract, sharing the same event, resolution source, currency, and payout convention as "low," and its payout would need to be exactly the complement of "low" in every possible resolved state, including any exceptional or void outcome. A user-interface grouping of two labels is not itself evidence of this; the same manual checks from Section 28.4, particularly complete exceptional-state coverage, apply identically to a two-leg partition as to a three-leg one.

docs.title: Exercise 3: pricing the effect of a fee change
docs.text:
Suppose the flat fee in this fixture were raised from USD 0.01 to USD 0.03 per unit, with the ask still at 0.30 and quantity still 4. Recompute the total cost and minimum net profit, and state whether the basket would still be reported as a candidate.

Solution sketch. Per-leg cost becomes \(4\times(0.30+0.03)=1.32\); total cost across three legs is \(3.96\). Minimum payout remains \(4.00\), so minimum net profit falls to \(0.04\). The basket would still clear scan_basket's strictly-positive-profit check and be reported as PAPER_CANDIDATE_ONLY, but with a much thinner margin, illustrating how sensitive a small guaranteed floor can be to an unverified or outdated fee assumption.

docs.title: Exercise 4: a different single filled leg
docs.text:
Suppose instead the "middle" leg is the one that fills, at the same 4-unit quantity and price, and the eventual state is "high". Compute the realized loss using the same method as Section 28.3.

Solution sketch. Cost is identical, \(4\times(0.30+0.01)=1.24\); the payout for holding only the "middle" leg when "high" occurs is zero, since "middle" did not resolve. Realized profit is \(0-1.24=-1.24\), the same magnitude as the chapter's worked example, because the arithmetic depends only on which single leg filled and whether it happened to be the one that ultimately resolved YES, not on which specific label was involved.

docs.title: Exercise 5: a boundary-convention mismatch
docs.text:
Two contracts are titled "closes above 100" and "closes at or below 100," and a reader assumes without reading either rules document that they form a complete two-state partition. State one concrete boundary scenario under which buying one of each could leave the trader with neither leg paying out, and explain what document would have revealed this risk in advance.

Solution sketch. If the first contract's rules define "above" as strictly greater than 100, and the second contract's rules were independently written by a different desk to mean "at or below 99," a closing value of exactly 100 would fail both contracts' stated conditions, leaving no leg paying out despite the titles suggesting full coverage. Only each contract's own rules document, read directly rather than inferred from its title, would reveal this specific boundary gap; this is precisely why compatibility_verified in scan_basket must be a human's affirmative, informed judgment rather than a string comparison between two headlines.

docs.title: Exercise 6: why required_cash can exceed total_cost
docs.text:
The companion's own regression tests verify a two-leg basket at quantity 3, with a per-unit fee of USD 0.001 and both legs' ask quoted at 0.3333: total_cost is 2.02 but required_cash is the larger 2.10, so a capital of 2.02 is rejected while 2.10 is accepted. Reconstruct both figures by hand and explain why they differ.

Solution sketch. Use Chapter 17's cent-ceiling notation \(\lceil x\rceil_{0.01}=0.01\lceil x/0.01\rceil\), not a whole-dollar ceiling. Each leg's aggregate notional \(3(0.3333)=0.9999\) rounds half-up to USD 1.00; its fee is \(\lceil0.003\rceil_{0.01}=0.01\), giving USD 1.01 per leg and USD 2.02 total. Each reserved unit instead allows \(\lceil0.3333\rceil_{0.01}=0.34\) plus \(\lceil0.001\rceil_{0.01}=0.01\): USD 0.35 per unit, USD 1.05 per leg, USD 2.10 total. This is a conservative cash bound, not a change to the four-decimal quoted price grid. required_cash is the larger of summed reservations and modeled fill cost.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: Chapter 29 turns from a static multi-leg scan to a simple two-sided quoting exercise, and shows how an inventory and total-risk budget, not just a favorable-looking spread, determines whether a paper market maker keeps quoting.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: You should be comfortable with the market-making and adverse-selection material of Chapter 21, the bankroll and portfolio-survival discussion of Chapter 22, and the paper-operations machinery from Chapter 24, particularly PaperBroker.synthetic_fill, PaperBroker.mark, and RiskBudget. You should already know why a resting order's touch by the market is not evidence of a fill, and why an unrealized mark is not the same thing as a realized profit.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this chapter you should be able to run the market-making quickstart, reproduce its marked-loss arithmetic by hand, explain precisely why the script's second, more attractive-looking bid is still rejected, and state what real data, beyond anything this script or its companion package can supply, would be required before treating any of this as evidence about a live maker strategy. You should also be able to explain the difference between an inferred fill and a supplied synthetic fill, and why this distinction matters more in market making than anywhere else in the book.

docs.title: 29.1 A concrete goal: quoting, filling, and marking a position, then stopping
docs.text:
Market making means posting resting orders on both sides of a market and hoping to earn the spread between them repeatedly. It also means holding inventory whenever one side fills before the other, and inventory carries the same directional risk as any other open position. This quickstart deliberately shows a market maker's least glamorous moment: a one-sided fill, an unfavorable mark, and a stopped second order, rather than a completed favorable round trip.

Run the script from the companion project root (book\companion):

Command working directory: run this chapter's Python commands from book\companion. From the trading repository root, run Set-Location book\companion once first. The .venv belongs to that companion project; see companion setup.

.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe examples\quickstart_market_making.py

Open examples/quickstart_market_making.py alongside this chapter. It creates a PaperBroker with USD 10.00 cash and the fixture's flat USD 0.01 per-unit fee, submits a resting buy order for 10 YES units at a 0.40 limit, and then explicitly supplies a synthetic fill for all 10 units at that price, with the evidence string "invented one-sided flow".

docs.title: 29.2 Reading the actual output
docs.text:
The observed run includes the following excerpt (some wrapper and explanatory fields are omitted):

{
  "result": {
    "filled_buy_units": 10, "filled_sell_units": 0,
    "inventory_liquidation_mark": {
      "cash": "5.90", "inventory_liquidation_value": "2.40",
      "equity": "8.30", "realized_profit": "0",
      "marked_profit": "-1.70", "unrealized_profit": "-1.70"
    },
    "additional_bid_budget_check": {
      "status": "NO_TRADE", "quantity": 0,
      "executable_cost": "4.10", "modeled_expected_profit": "1.90",
      "reason": "cash/reservation or loss budget fails"
    },
    "stop_reason": "inventory concentration and one-sided fills outweigh a displayed spread",
    "evidence_gate": {"status": "REJECT_LIVE_EDGE_INFERENCE"}
  }
}

Trace the cash and inventory arithmetic from the start. Buying 10 units at 0.40 with a USD 0.01 fee costs \(10\times(0.40+0.01)=4.10\); starting cash of 10.00 minus that cost leaves cash of 5.90, exactly matching the printed cash field inside the mark. The broker now holds 10 units of inventory at a cost basis of 4.10 and has not sold anything, so filled_sell_units is 0 and realized_profit is exactly "0", not an approximation: no sale, and therefore no realized gain or loss, has actually occurred yet.

The script then marks the position against a deliberately unfavorable new book, snapshot="inventory-stress", quoting bid 0.25 and ask 0.28. PaperBroker.mark computes a conservative full-liquidation value using only the bid side, net of the same exit fee: \(10\times(0.25-0.01)=2.40\), matching inventory_liquidation_value. Equity is cash plus this liquidation value, \(5.90+2.40=8.30\). Marked profit is equity minus the broker's initial cash, \(8.30-10.00=-1.70\), and because realized profit is still zero, unrealized profit equals the same \(-1.70\). This is a mark, not a sale: the ten units are still held, no exit order has actually been submitted, and the -1.70 figure describes what liquidating right now, at this specific hypothetical bid, would produce, not a number that has actually hit the broker's cash balance.

docs.title: 29.3 Why the additional bid is rejected despite a positive modeled edge
docs.text:
The script's second decision is the one worth studying most closely, because it is not rejected for the same reason as Chapter 27's no-trade outcomes. additional_bid_budget_check screens a fresh PaperInputs with model probability 0.60 against the fixture's default book, ask 0.40. The cost of buying 10 more units is again \(10\times(0.40+0.01)=4.10\), and the modeled expected profit is \(10\times0.60-4.10=6.00-4.10=1.90\), a clearly positive number. If this were the only consideration, the trade would look attractive.

screen_buy_yes does not stop at that comparison. It also checks budget.permits(cost, available_cash, committed_cash) against the RiskBudget("5.00", "5.00") supplied by the script. After the first fill, the broker's open cost basis is already 4.10 and its reserved cash for any still-open orders is zero, so committed cash going into this second check is 4.10. Adding the new order's cost of 4.10 gives a combined committed total of \(4.10+4.10=8.20\), which exceeds the budget's max_committed_cash of 5.00. The screen therefore returns NO_TRADE with reason "cash/reservation or loss budget fails", even though the same screen's own expected-value comparison was favorable. This is the central lesson of the chapter: a positive modeled edge is a necessary condition for a candidate trade, never a sufficient one, and a risk budget exists precisely to stop a trader from concentrating too much capital in one direction even when each individual step looks attractive in isolation.

stop_reason names this directly: "inventory concentration and one-sided fills outweigh a displayed spread". The broker already holds a full ten-unit position acquired through a one-sided fill; adding another ten-unit buy would not diversify that exposure, it would double it, in the same direction, against a market that has just shown a materially worse marked value than the entry price.

docs.title: 29.4 How this connects to bankroll discipline, not just this one screen
docs.text: RiskBudget.max_committed_cash caps outstanding cost basis and reservations, regardless of an individual candidate's expected value. Multiple positions can have an unaffordable combined worst case even when independent; correlation changes the probability of joint outcomes, not whether the cash limit matters. Fractional Kelly is one optional sizing framework under stronger assumptions, not a necessary tool for every responsible system. This script uses the hard commitment cap, not a Kelly optimizer, and it does not infer an optimal stake from the market's unfavorable move.

docs.title: 29.5 No proof of a touch fill, and what a supplied synthetic fill actually means
docs.text:
Read PaperBroker.observe_resting in accounting.py: calling it on a resting order against a book that merely touches the order's limit price returns the fixed string "NO_INFERRED_FILL: quotes alone do not establish queue position or a trade", and changes nothing about the order's state. This script does not call observe_resting at all; instead it calls synthetic_fill, which requires an explicit, non-empty evidence string, in this case "invented one-sided flow", and raises ValueError if that string is blank. The distinction matters. A real resting limit order's fill depends on queue priority ahead of it at the same price, the exact sequence of incoming market orders, cancellations by other participants, and latency between an event and the trader's own order reaching the venue, none of which this fixture observes or models. synthetic_fill is a deliberately manual escape hatch for constructing a teaching scenario; it is not a claim that any real resting order would have filled under comparable conditions, and the required evidence string exists specifically so a reader cannot silently invoke it without stating, in writing, what assumption is being made.

This quickstart shows one supplied fill, an unfavorable mark, and a budget-blocked follow-up. It does not show a completed two-sided round trip; the separate market_making.py demonstration does supply a synthetic favorable round trip realizing USD 0.40. Neither script estimates an empirical fill-conditioned forecast or queue-position model. Supplied scenario fills demonstrate accounting, not the frequency or profitability of those paths in a real market.

docs.title: 29.6 What real data would be required before treating any of this as live evidence
docs.text:
A defensible empirical maker study needs fill and queue evidence, fill-conditioned outcome forecasts, cancellation latency, and current fees that this script does not supply. Glosten-Milgrom and Kyle offer qualified stock-market mechanisms for informative order flow, not measured fill probabilities for these contracts. GLOSTEN1985 KYLE1985

Avellaneda-Stoikov's inspected equations 29-30 are approximate quote formulas under arithmetic Brownian stock prices, exponential utility, and Poisson arrivals. Its comparisons include simulated fills and terminal midpoint valuation, not historical executable returns. AVELLANEDA2008 The source therefore motivates inventory-risk questions but does not validate this quickstart's stopping rule or supply a binary-payout execution model. The actual venue/product fee schedule also needs independent checking; the classroom USD 0.01 charge is not that schedule. KALSHI_ROUNDING POLYMARKET_FEES

None of that data is supplied by the book's educational companion. The market_data module, whose exact commands, four allowlisted public-GET endpoints, and native-field schemas are documented in data/README.md and the examples README, is a complete but strictly optional, explicitly gated, read-only public-snapshot collector: every call requires --acknowledge-terms, it is not connected to PaperBroker, and it acquires only current market metadata and current order-book snapshots, never historical fill-rate, queue, or latency records. It is not a live broker, not a historical archive, and the companion ships no acquired venue payload; running it is a separate action a reader must take, and its output is a new, gitignored .snapshot.json file, never a committed dataset. Building the genuine market-making study this section describes remains a real, unimplemented, permission-gated future project, honestly labeled as such in the book's data-feasibility assessment, not something this quickstart, the collector, or any other script in the book already delivers.

docs.title: 29.7 Troubleshooting
docs.text: If you call synthetic_fill with an empty or whitespace-only evidence string while experimenting, it raises ValueError("an explicitly supplied synthetic fill needs an explanation"); this is intentional friction, not a bug, so that every invented fill in your own experiments carries a written justification. If PaperBroker.mark raises ValueError("insufficient bid depth for full liquidation mark"), your stress-test book does not quote enough bid-side depth to liquidate the full held position; either supply more depth or treat the resulting error as informative about a real liquidity constraint rather than something to silently suppress. If your local risk-budget experiment unexpectedly permits a trade you expected to be blocked, double-check that you are passing the broker's actual reconcile()-derived open_cost_basis plus reserved_cash as the committed-cash argument, not zero; a budget check performed against the wrong committed-cash baseline will pass trades it should not.

docs.title: Exercise 1: recomputing the mark at a different stress bid
docs.text:
Using the same ten-unit position and USD 0.01 exit fee, recompute the liquidation value, equity, and marked profit if the stress book's bid were 0.35 instead of 0.25.

Solution sketch. Liquidation value is \(10\times(0.35-0.01)=3.40\). Equity is \(5.90+3.40=9.30\). Marked profit is \(9.30-10.00=-0.70\), still negative because the entry price of 0.40 plus its own 0.01 entry fee exceeds this hypothetical exit bid net of its own exit fee, but noticeably smaller in magnitude than the chapter's -1.70 example.

docs.title: Exercise 2: finding the break-even stress bid
docs.text:
At what stress bid would the ten-unit position's marked profit be exactly zero, holding the same USD 0.01 exit fee and the same 4.10 entry cost?

Solution sketch. Solve \(10\times(b-0.01)-4.10=0\) for the bid \(b\): \(10b-0.10=4.10\), so \(b=0.42\). A bid of 0.42 or higher would produce a nonnegative marked profit under this fee convention; the actual stress book's bid of 0.25 is well below that break-even level, which is exactly why the mark is negative.

docs.title: Exercise 3: recomputing the rejected second order at a smaller size
docs.text:
Suppose the additional bid in Section 29.3 were sized at 2 units instead of 10, with the same 0.40 ask, 0.01 fee, and model probability 0.60. Would the risk budget now permit it?

Solution sketch. Cost is \(2\times(0.40+0.01)=0.82\). Combined committed cash would be \(4.10+0.82=4.92\), which is at or under the budget's max_committed_cash of 5.00, and the order's own cost of 0.82 is under max_order_cost of 5.00 and under available cash. The modeled expected profit, \(2\times0.60-0.82=0.38\), remains positive. At this smaller size, the budget check would likely permit the trade, illustrating that the earlier rejection was specifically a sizing and concentration problem, not a rejection of the underlying model-conditional edge itself.

docs.title: Exercise 4: distinguishing a touch from a fill in your own words
docs.text:
A resting bid at 0.38 is posted, and a later book snapshot shows the best available ask at exactly 0.38. Explain why observe_resting still returns NO_INFERRED_FILL in this situation, and name one concrete piece of missing information that would be needed to justify treating this as an actual fill.

Solution sketch. A matching price alone does not establish that any counterparty actually traded at that price against this specific resting order, nor where this order stood in the queue relative to any other resting orders at the same price. A genuine fill claim would need an actual trade record, or an authoritative venue confirmation, identifying the executed quantity, price, and timestamp against this order specifically, not merely a coincidence between a resting limit price and a later quoted level.

docs.title: Exercise 5: a bankroll-level view of the same decision
docs.text:
Using the reasoning from Section 29.4, explain why a trader who tracks only per-trade expected value, and never a running total of committed cash across all currently open positions, could eventually violate their own affordable-loss limit even if every individual trade they accepted looked favorable in isolation.

Solution sketch. Per-trade expected value is computed one decision at a time and says nothing about how much capital is simultaneously at risk across every position still open at once. A trader who accepts a sequence of individually positive-expected-value trades without tracking cumulative committed cash can end up with a combined exposure, especially under correlated outcomes, that exceeds what they could actually afford to lose, even though no single decision along the way was individually unreasonable. This is exactly the failure mode RiskBudget.max_committed_cash is designed to prevent by checking the running total, not just the newest trade's own arithmetic.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: Chapter 30 is the book's final chapter. It does not introduce new theory; it walks through the manual checklist a reader would need to work through, entirely outside the educational companion, before even considering a first real, funded trade, and explains why every one of the preceding four quickstarts, however carefully honest, still leaves that decision firmly with a human being.

docs.title: 30. From paper evidence to a first live trade
Prerequisites
docs.text: This is the book's final chapter, and it assumes you have worked through, or at least read, everything before it: the contract and probability foundations of Part I, the data and evaluation discipline of Part II, the modeling chapters of Part III, the execution, evidence, risk, and paper-operations chapters of Part IV, the research-hypothesis discipline of Chapter 25, and all four preceding quickstarts. You need the canonical accounting example from the notation registry, the evidence-gate concept introduced in Chapter 26, and a clear memory of every NO_TRADE and every honestly reported loss in Chapters 27 through 29.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this chapter you should be able to run the first-trade checklist script and correctly interpret its DO_NOT_PROCEED_FROM_SYNTHETIC_EVIDENCE status, reproduce the book's canonical cost, profit, and expected-value accounting from memory, work a first-dollar illustrative sizing exercise while keeping expected profit and realized profit conceptually separate, explain in detail what each item on the manual checklist actually requires a reader to do, and state precisely why no configuration of the educational companion's evidence flags can automatically authorize a live trade. This chapter does not introduce new theory. It concludes the book by turning everything already developed into one guarded, still-manual decision.

docs.title: 30.1 What this chapter is, and deliberately is not
docs.text:
Every preceding quickstart ended in an honest NO_TRADE, a marked loss, or a conditional candidate that depended on assumptions the script could not itself verify. That pattern was not an accident of which examples happened to get written. It reflects the evidence supplied by the educational companion: every default script is synthetic, illustrative, or, in the NOAA case, a real but current-vintage forecasting exercise with no attached market, price, or fee. None of it, individually or combined, constitutes verified evidence that a specific real trade, on a specific real venue, at a specific real price, would have a positive expected value net of actual costs.

This chapter therefore does not attempt to supply the missing piece with a cleverer model, a bigger dataset, or a new theoretical result. It instead does the only honest thing left to do: lay out, in concrete and checkable detail, what a reader would need to independently verify before placing a first real, funded, cash-settled trade, using the book's own canonical accounting to make the arithmetic of that decision precise. The book ends here, with a checklist and a decision left to a human, not with an appendix promising a shortcut around it.

docs.title: 30.2 Running the checklist and reading its output
docs.text:
From the companion project root (book\companion), after the setup described in Chapter 26:

Command working directory: run this chapter's Python commands from book\companion. From the trading repository root, run Set-Location book\companion once first. The .venv belongs to that companion project; see companion setup.

.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe examples\first_trade_checklist.py

Open examples/first_trade_checklist.py while reading; its module docstring states that it cannot place a funded order. The following is an excerpt of the observed output, with some wrapper and explanatory fields omitted:

{
  "result": {
    "status": "DO_NOT_PROCEED_FROM_SYNTHETIC_EVIDENCE",
    "evidence_gate": {"status": "REJECT_LIVE_EDGE_INFERENCE", "eligible_for_research_review": false},
    "invented_accounting_only": {
      "cash": "5.90", "reserved_cash": "0", "available_cash": "5.90",
      "inventory_units": 10, "open_cost_basis": "4.10", "realized_profit": "0"
    },
    "maximum_loss_if_this_binary_position_settles_NO": "4.10",
    "manual_checks_not_automatically_verified": [
      "eligibility, jurisdiction and current venue terms independently checked",
      "exact contract rules, exceptional payouts and collateral understood",
      "real point-in-time evidence independently reviewed after strategy search",
      "current fees, rounding, executable depth and maximum affordable loss checked",
      "open inventory, reserved cash and correlated loss reviewed",
      "a written manual decision, rejection conditions and outcome journal prepared"
    ],
    "boundary": "no API keys, network requests, order submission, wallet signing or automatic promotion"
  }
}

status is the literal string DO_NOT_PROCEED_FROM_SYNTHETIC_EVIDENCE. This is not a placeholder waiting for a future software update; it is the correct and permanent answer for any run of this script against its own bundled fixtures, because those fixtures are, by construction, synthetic. invented_accounting_only reflects the same canonical_position() helper used throughout the companion: ten YES units bought at a 0.40 ask with the fixture's flat USD 0.01 fee, for an open cost basis of 4.10, leaving cash of 5.90 from an initial 10.00. maximum_loss_if_this_binary_position_settles_NO is exactly that cost basis, 4.10: if this position resolves NO, the entire 4.10 already paid is lost, and nothing further is owed beyond it, because this is a fully collateralized, long-only binary position with no borrowing.

docs.title: 30.3 The canonical accounting this whole book has used
docs.text:
It is worth restating the book's one canonical worked example here, at the end, exactly as the notation registry fixes it, because every risk and sizing decision in this final chapter reduces to the same four numbers. Buying 10 YES units at an ask of USD 0.40, with the book's invented flat USD 0.01 per-unit fee, costs

\[ 10 \times (0.40 + 0.01) = 4.10. \]

Under ordinary binary settlement this position pays USD 10 if YES and USD 0 if NO, for a net profit of USD 5.90 or a net loss of USD 4.10. If a model assigns this contract a probability of 0.55, the modeled expected net profit is

\[ 10 \times (0.55 - 0.40 - 0.01) = 1.40. \]

This 1.40 figure is a model-conditional expectation, computed under a forecast that might simply be wrong; it is not evidence that the position has a real edge, and it says nothing about what the very next resolution of this contract will actually produce. If the position is instead closed early by selling all ten units at a bid of USD 0.46, with a further USD 0.01-per-unit exit fee, the realized round-trip profit is

\[ 10 \times (0.46 - 0.40 - 0.01 - 0.01) = 0.40. \]

Keep these four numbers, 4.10 cost, 5.90 or minus-4.10 at settlement, 1.40 modeled expected value at \(\hat p = 0.55\), and 0.40 realized on an early resale, distinct in your own head before reading further, because Section 30.5's checklist depends on a reader being able to keep exactly this kind of distinction straight under the pressure of an actual decision.

docs.title: 30.4 A first-dollar illustrative sizing exercise
docs.text:
Here is a deliberately narrow, purely deterministic accounting exercise, separate from the modeled expected-value calculation above, and it is worth being precise about which question each one answers. Suppose a reader wants to know: at the same 0.40 ask and USD 0.01 per-unit fee, what is the smallest whole number of units that would produce at least USD 1.00 of net profit if the position resolves YES? This is a conditional, deterministic accounting question. It is not an expected-value calculation, and it requires no probability estimate at all.

Per-unit cost is \(0.40+0.01=0.41\); per-unit profit if YES is \(1.00-0.41=0.59\). Solving \(Q \times 0.59 \geq 1.00\) gives \(Q \geq 1.6949\ldots\), so the smallest whole unit quantity is \(Q=2\). At \(Q=2\), cost is \(2\times0.41=0.82\), well within the 5.90 of available cash left in the canonical position's broker after its first ten-unit fill, and the planned profit if YES is \(2\times0.59=1.18\). The maximum loss on this same two-unit lot, if it instead resolves NO, is the full 0.82 cost basis.

State plainly what this exercise does and does not establish. It answers "how many units, at this price and fee, would be needed to reach a round number of profit conditional on winning." It does not answer "should I expect to win," which requires an actual probability estimate and produces the different, expected-value quantity computed in Section 30.3. It also does not promise that USD 1.18 will ever be realized: this is a target computed under a hypothetical favorable outcome, not a guarantee, and a binary contract that resolves NO instead loses the full 0.82, regardless of how carefully the quantity was chosen to hit a round profit target on the other branch. Confusing this deterministic "if YES" accounting with either a promised or an expected outcome is exactly the kind of error this book has repeatedly warned against, and it is worth naming explicitly here, in the chapter where a reader is most likely to be tempted to skip past the distinction under real time pressure.

docs.title: 30.5 Working through each guarded manual check
docs.text:
The checklist script's six items are deliberately terse in its own JSON output. Here is what each one actually requires a reader to do, in detail, not merely to acknowledge.

Eligibility, jurisdiction, and current venue terms independently checked. Visit the venue's own current terms and eligibility pages yourself, at the time you are actually trading, rather than relying on this book's research notes, which are dated to one audit day and explicitly could not establish a complete eligibility or reuse-permission picture. The inspected Polymarket terms response, for example, displayed a geographic/product restriction notice without exposing its complete operative terms. POLYMARKET_TERMS Never attempt a VPN, IP masking, or any other bypass of a displayed restriction; an unclear terms page is a reason to stop, not a problem to route around.
